5h ago 04.21 EDT Manchester City: The club’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, said yesterday that “nothing has changed” after the news that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the Premier League, which the club have always strenuously denied. Al-Mubarak wrote on social media yesterday afternoon: double quotation mark While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity. We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family. Thank you, as always, for your constant support. The City manager, Enzo Maresca, had earlier posted a cryptic message on social media to say: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Manchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict Read more Share

5h ago 04.13 EDT Manchester City: Tony Pulis said he feels cheated over his Stoke team’s 1-0 defeat to Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final. Yaya Touré’s winner delivered the first trophy since Man City’s 2008 takeover by Abu Dhabi royalty. In a column on the BBC Sport website, Pulis responded to the news on Friday that Man City have been found guilty on virtually all of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League, which the club have always denied. The alleged financial rule breaches span the 2009-10 to 2022-23 seasons. The 2011 final was Stoke’s only FA Cup final in their history. Pulis wrote that Stoke fans had been asking him: “When do we get our FA Cup?” double quotation mark I thought exactly the same. While the process is far from over because Manchester City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth. I don’t expect Manchester City to phone me or the club up and offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners’ medals their players received. I don’t seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely. But I still feel cheated. View image in fullscreen Tony Pulis’s Stoke lost the 2011 FA Cup final. Photograph: Dave Thompson/PA Share

5h ago 03.55 EDT Republic of Ireland: Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson yesterday admitted he regretted his choice of words in comments made earlier this week about Ireland “playing against genocide” in reference to their fixtures against Israel. After the Israel football federation accused Hallgrimsson of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy”, the Irish prime minister, Micheál Martin, responded from the UN general assembly in New York: “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.” Yesterday Hallgrimsson said he had used a “strong” word and now regretted it. “It was a wrong word for me to use,” he said, arguing that he had meant to say that “by playing we are not accepting what is happening”. If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrimsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.” Israel’s head coach, Ran Ben-Shimon, said he will shake hands with Hallgrimsson before kick-off in Debrecen. Ireland’s players will not partake in “elements of the pre-match ceremony”, namely the handshake and exchange of pennants, said the FAI chief David Courell. Ireland’s players will also wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” in Gaza. Share

6h ago 03.44 EDT Republic of Ireland: Today’s Nations League fixture against Israel will go ahead after a “significant majority” of Ireland’s players voted to play. The game – an away fixture for Ireland – is taking place in Debrecen, Hungary without the attendance of Irish fans. The Ireland team have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott both tonight’s game and the reverse fixture, to be played next weekend behind closed doors in Dublin, due to Israel’s military action in Gaza. Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu will not play this evening in protest against “the killing of innocent people”. He wrote on Instagram yesterday: double quotation mark Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people. However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel. My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region. There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them. Centre-back Jimmy Dunne has been named as a reserve goalkeeper in Bazunu’s place. Caoimhin Kelleher is expected to start in goal as usual. Sports.title: Meet the new minute 55 England collapse, not the same as the old minute 55 England collapse | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
You could feel it inside the stadium, one of those moments where the air starts to shift, the birds fly backwards through the sky, and outside on Wembley Way an old man clutches his copy of the England Pathway Blueprint to his chest and cowers up at the moon. Welcome to the witching hour, 55 minutes in, when things just seem to happen to Thomas Tuchel’s England.

Before this Nations League opener there was general agreement on the desirability of systems, pattern, repeatability. And you can’t say England aren’t consistent. Their last two significant matches, here and in Atlanta in July, have both involved going a goal ahead against the World Cup finalists, playing well and dominating parts of the game, right up until the 55-minute mark.

At which point a kind of voodoo descends. On both occasions the final 35 minutes have been lost 2-0. On both occasions there will, inevitably, be an attempt not just to blame the manager for decisions made in the game, but for some kind of wider vibes-based DNA-related betrayal. “Cowardice” is a word most often used, because football is of course war, bravery and pluck. But it is, as ever with England, technical and tactical. As it was once again here.

There were 55 minutes gone against Argentina in Atlanta when Anthony Gordon put England 1-0 up. At which point the team fell apart like an over-dunked digestive biscuit, reduced suddenly to a collection of hollow men, stuffed shirts, 12% possession merchants, the manager spooked into fielding a back five.

Here the game also changed on 55 minutes. England were 2-1 up from 1-0 down at that point. For a while at the start of the second half it looked like they might be turning this game into an ordeal for their opponents, playing in surges, winning physical duels, making Spain into a team that has to run.

Jarell Quansah smashed a shot into Marc Cucurella’s face, drawing huge cheers. The crowd had begun to sing the Tuchel song, to the tune of War’s Low Rider, the official notation for which is “Foot-ball’s coming home uh-gain – with Thom-as Tuch-el”. On 54 minutes a lengthy VAR check ended with a penalty awarded for a trip on Jude Bellingham that was combined also with a dive, but trip plus dive does not cancel trip. Was this an exorcism? Are we good now? Is everything going to be OK?

View image in fullscreen Spain were left trailing in England’s wake by the speed of the counterattack for Anthony Gordon’s equalising goal. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Well, no, as it turned out. Harry Kane had already scored England’s second goal. He waited a little longer than usual, slipped on his standing leg as he planted it and pumped the kick on to the bar. 54 ticked over into 55 minutes.

And at that point Spain just seemed to sense it, the pressure shifted and we were back in Georgia under the lights. Tuchel was up again on his touchline, arms wheeling, shiny blue gilet gleaming. The ball began to tick about between the red shirts. And suddenly Spain had regained that basking quality, easing about with that familiar sense of control, always with more angles, more space, a superior geometry, like trying to keep up with a team of 11-year-old chess prodigies.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Within five minutes the game was level. Fourteen minutes later Spain were 3-2 up, a lead they would hold on to. The most unfavourable interpretation of this is a pattern being established. England lost another game where they just seem to get close, to lose control, to fail to hold the midfield. Both of Spain’s decisive goals were either made or scored by Luis de la Fuente’s two attacking substitutes, neither of whom looked much like Dan Burn.

But it wasn’t quite like that. For a start, England were much better here than in Atlanta, and against a better team. Wembley was its usual chilly self at kick-off, a place where even on a Saturday night the general vibe is echoey, corporate space, like a visit to the Ideal Home exhibition or a peculiarly low-throttle ABBA tribute event.

And Spain scored almost immediately, the goal made by a horrible moment for Marc Guéhi and a smart finish from Yamine Lamal. For a while this was the sum of all fears, one of those games where facing this team is like trying to play football against water. Ferran Torres wasted some outrageously inviting chances. Rodri shuttled about like a man operating inside his own portable demilitarised zone. Spain will make you crawl in those moments. But England didn’t let them.

There were periods of hard high pressing. Elliot Anderson was aggressive in midfield. On 36 minutes England scored a brilliant goal, one that Spain will hate, caught on the counterattack by a wonderful three-man surge from box to box, made by Anderson’s tackle, Bellingham’s surge and pass, and a lovely Gordon finish into the corner.

View image in fullscreen The simultaneous bringing-on of Pedri for Spain and James Garner for England highlighted the gap in midfield between the two teams. Photograph: Michael Regan/The FA/Getty Images

They kept running from there. And even after the 55-minute fade England were better. There was no long-ball stuff, no panic and some decent late chances. But really the key moment here came on 70 minutes, when both teams brought on a midfielder: Pedri for Spain, James Garner for England.

Pedri immediately began to do his thing, romping about like a playful little horse, a footballer who just loves the ball, and whom the ball loves right back. At that point Spain had Pedri, Rodri and Dani Olmo, the entire Barcelona midfield, on the pitch. And for all England’s efforts, the late surge, the front-foot style, it always felt that they were being held at bay in those final moments, one hand on the forehead, arms windmilling in the space in between.

But then Spain are the ultimate system team, an expression of a deep, functioning coaching culture, not to mention the footballing nation that tortures England the most. We are all you could have had, the thing you are not. Lose again, lose better. But this was at least some kind of progress.

Sports.title: Ever feel you’ve been cheated? Consequences could be profound after Manchester City guilty verdict | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
So it turns out none of that was real. Nothing that happened in English football between 2009‑10 and 2017-18 that involved Manchester City actually happened. City beating Manchester United 6-1 at Old Trafford? Fake. Sergio Agüero’s 94th‑minute winner to clinch the title in 2012? A figment of the imagination. That season City reached 100 points? Bobby Ewing dreamed it in the shower.

Without those successes, City wouldn’t have been in the position they were for the past eight seasons (and 35 of the charges relate to a failure to cooperate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023). The 14 successive wins that took them to the league title in 2018-19 would not have happened without what went before. Neither would the Treble of 2023 or the record four league titles in a row.

So while it may turn out that those successes did indeed happen, they are tainted by what went before. “We’re not really here”? Turns out none of us have been for quite some time.

There will be an appeal. This is not yet the final truth, which could still be a long way off. But it may turn out that Jürgen Klopp was a lot more successful than anybody thought, that Brendan Rodgers and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are title‑winning managers.

Probably not, because the authorities seem reluctant, even if titles are stripped from a club, to reallocate those titles – and understandably: if one side is streaking clear, priorities for others change. None of this feels right, but it would feel off if a team won a league because a rival had chosen to prioritise a cup or European campaign at the expense of an apparently unwinnable title. Ersatz glory satisfies nobody.

If the guilty verdicts are upheld, the consequences will be profound. There will be appeals for mitigation. There are wheels within wheels. Bloomberg reported last month that the government had been warned of potential negative consequences for UK-United Arab Emirates relations should the verdict go against City.

Andy Burnham was mayor during a period when the UAE made significant investments in Manchester and spoke to the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed, within a week of becoming prime minister in July. But it is hard to see how a systematic campaign of cheating over a period of nine years could bring anything except severe punishment.

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola and the Manchester City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, in May 2018 after winning the league. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

Everton’s one breach in 2022, overspending the profitability and sustainability threshold by £19.5m, earned them a six-point deduction and they had to pay Burnley, who were relegated, £26m in damages plus £9m in interest. City’s offences are almost incalculably worse and they failed to cooperate with the investigation.

It is not just that they could be forcibly relegated; it is that potential for financial claims against City and not just from those sides who missed out on titles during the ghost years. Other sides were denied European places. Prize money was lost. Even relegated sides may argue that City were a factor in them dropping out of the Premier League.

There are knock-on effects to the years after the period in question. Leicester, for instance, narrowly missed out on Champions League qualification in 2020 and 2021. Would they have qualified had City, who finished above them, not been artificially juiced? Had they played in the Champions League then, would they be in the mess they are in now? Then there are the less direct consequences: what might it have meant for a club’s – or a manager’s or a player’s – global reputation and thus their capacity to generate commercial income, had they won the league or remained in the Premier League for a further season?

Somehow, somebody will have to calculate which, if any of those claims, are worth pursuing and what they might be worth. The financial cost to City, irrespective of the official sanction, could be crippling. When City were found guilty of illegal payments to players in 1906 and forced to sell off the bulk of their squad, it took them 30 years to recover; when Sunderland were similarly convicted in 1957, they were relegated for the first time the following season and have never retained their previous status.

But the biggest cost, perhaps, is the one that is hardest to calculate: emotional energy. The Agüero goal was arguably the most famous moment in Premier League history. What does it mean to say it didn’t happen? Even if City are not stripped of the 2012 title, it is tainted. Marseille’s 1993 Champions League success remains on the record, but is inevitably undermined by being stripped of the Ligue 1 title that season for match-fixing.

That emotion, the euphoria of City fans, the despair of United fans, the amazement of everybody else, cannot be dismissed. For many connected to City, it must be the greatest surge of emotion they have experienced. Little wonder several City fans online have been desperately trying to find a way to cope, pretending this is conspiracy or irrelevance, rather than the consequence of the actions of their club’s owners.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Sergio Agüero scored the goal that sealed their first Premier League title in 2012 but, given the guilty verdicts, it may have counted for nothing. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters

Those actions are a consequence of the Premier League’s laissez‑faire attitude to club ownership, which itself sits in the context of a world where anything can be sold off to foreign states or private equity. The fans’ anger is understandable enough, even if it is often misdirected.

For everybody else? There’s a sense of being cheated, and not just by City. This great human drama wasn’t real? What about now? Why should I care about this season when an independent panel might decide in 17 years that it wasn’t real, either? Will interest wane, revenues drop?

For the Premier League, that is a big issue – a potential problem whenever a competition becomes concerned with profit; revenue generation and sporting justice do not necessarily go hand in hand. But what is the alternative? Not to act is to legitimise rule-breaking, to say the game is not about technical excellence or tactical coherence, but about who can afford the best lawyers.

It is a painful route the Premier League has chosen. There could be lean years ahead, consequences as yet unimagined. But it is also the right path, because if a sport cannot govern itself, if its regulations can simply be ignored if you’re wealthy enough, it is no longer a sport.

Sports.title: Gateshead’s fruitless trip south offers hint of Manchester City’s doomsday future
Sports.content:
Among many doomsday scenarios facing Manchester City is plunging down the football pyramid. Would that be so bad? Instead of yawning at the prospect of yet another meeting with Real Madrid or repeated Aviva train-hampered journeys to Wembley, how about the exoticism of away travel to Wealdstone? In the National League, City’s ownership may wish to know, there are no formal financial fair play or strict salary cap regulations.

Wrexham, Notts County and Chesterfield have taken advantage of such lax constraints to regenerate. For City fans, Ruislip’s buzzy high street, full of nail bars, estate agents and a couple of homely pubs, would represent a welcome world away from Milan’s Via Monte Napoleone, as would the suburbia of Grosvenor Vale, Wealdstone’s home in the middle of a housing estate, which may jog memories of late-90s visits to Macclesfield and Lincoln. Simpler, happier times, perhaps.

On the fringes of west London, with rich, non-league history, last season’s FA Trophy finalists, managed by the 1980s QPR hero Gary Waddock, Wealdstone is the club from where Stuart Pearce, Vinny Jones and Jermaine Beckford began their journey.

In the digital age, the club became famous for the meme pioneer Gordon Parmar Hill, AKA the Wealdstone Raider, whose “you’ve got no fans” war cry went viral on a pandemic scale in 2014, the same year his assault on the UK Christmas No 1 with, naturally, “Got No Fans”, reached No 5. The Raider even made himself available for hire on stag weekends, though despite a recent social media comeback that revenue stream has been shuttered, a quieter life now observed.

Kicking off fifth from bottom in the National League, if this season’s outlook could be brighter for the Stones, then Saturday confirmed there is always someone worse off. Gateshead hosted a Football League club on the southern bank of the Tyne from 1930 to 1960, the last team the legendary Hughie Gallacher turned out for, though extinction came in 1973. The re-founded Gateshead that has been knocking around the non-league pyramid since 1977 has little hope of reaching the Football League anytime soon.

Before kick-off, the Vale club bar outside the stadium was doing brisk business. At a fifth-tier club, drinking in view of the pitch is verboten. A revocation of the 1985 alcohol statute the prime minister this week floated would prove a significant revenue driver for clubs of Wealdstone’s size; clubs in the divisions below make considerable cash from in-game hospitality.

In the Gateshead dugout, the familiar face of Lee Cattermole. For the time being, at least – his first senior management role is not going at all well. The former hard-tackling Middlesbrough, Wigan and Sunderland midfielder, collector of 88 yellow cards and seven reds in 271 Premier League games, has approached management in a characteristically uncompromising fashion. His team bottom of the National League, one win from 10 matches, Cattermole has employed the “bomb squad” approach favoured by Enzo Maresca at Chelsea and Ruben Amorim at Manchester United.

Eight players are reported to be training at alternative times to the first team, having also been removed from WhatsApp group chats. Neither Maresca nor Amorim’s shunning of players was particularly successful at an elite level, and being six goals down by half-time at home to Southend the previous week hardly heralded the success of Cattermole’s tough-love strategy either.

Alfie McCalmont, a Northern Ireland international lately of Central Coast Mariners in Australia, joined the Heed in midweek. Anchoring midfield, after what were bright beginnings for the team that had travelled 278 miles, about 100 away fans willing them on, the new arrival soon found himself dragged into the torpor of his new teammates.

Gateshead’s manager visibly sagged once Olufela Olomola scored the first of two unanswered goals before half-time. Not half as bad as Southend, but bad enough. “Make them work,” bellowed Cattermole while his team were still level, among other, more colourful, language.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Once Wealdstone’s second goal came, Luke Norris converting a softly conceded penalty, Cattermole sat himself down, distractedly fiddling with notebook and pen before a half-time team talk delayed by his slow return to the away dressing room.

Whatever was said, a third Wealdstone goal came within two minutes of the resumption, and a fourth just before the end. Waddock, who as a player was not dissimilar to Cattermole – combative, lover of a tackle – could keep quiet counsel, relaxedly leaning on a handy gatepost. Such serenity in a difficult season for Wealdstone came by contrast to the portentous chants of “sacked in the morning” from the away end, followed by “time to go”.

It was Ben Clark, Cattermole’s assistant, sent out to deliver a post-match verdict. “We conceded a soft goal, and struggled from there on in,” he said. “The lads are struggling a bit with their confidence.”

The possibility of Cattermole being bombed out had heightened, such news likely to be accompanied by a corner-flag image on the club website. Should City drop down the divisions to alight on suburban outposts such as Wealdstone, it is already unlikely Cattermole would get the chance to face them, let alone manage them.

Sports.title: Footgolf and the Jabulani: a second life for ‘the worst ball I’ve seen in my life’
Sports.content:
About once a month, Ben Clarke, the world’s leading footgolfer, carefully pumps up his collection of coveted Adidas Jabulani footballs.

Like most elite players, Clarke possesses an extensive array of balls, all of which require regular inflation to prevent degradation, even those sitting pristine in their original boxes, unsullied by a single boot. Footballs are prime currency in a niche sport that tasks players with kicking one around a course, and into 18 oversized holes, in as few strokes as possible. Precision is everything.

It seems absurd, then, that pride of place among Clarke’s hoard is the infamous Jabulani, once described by Fabio Capello as “the worst ball that I have seen in my life”. The former England manager was far from alone in his scathing assessment. England goalkeeper David James called it “dreadful”, his Brazilian counterpart Júlio César said it was “like one of those you buy in the supermarket”, while Brazil forward Robinho suggested “the guy who designed this ball never played football”.

Few balls have been so widely derided as the one created for the 2010 World Cup, where its unpredictable flight saw it denounced as uncontrollable. Yet 16 years later, the demands of the world’s best footgolfers mean anyone in possession of a Jabulani is now sitting on a goldmine, with boxed models going for upwards of £500 and the value only increasing.

“It’s a bit mad,” admits Hertfordshire-based Clarke, who has topped the footgolf world rankings five times. “No one could control the ball in the [2010] World Cup, but here we are using it for a precision sport. We all trust it and rely on it. It’s very strange.”

View image in fullscreen The Adidas Jabulani ball proved unpopular at the 2010 World Cup but is coveted by footgolfers. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

The reason lies in the Jabulani’s precise engineering defect that so frustrated footballers on the biggest stage. Constructed from eight thermally bonded panels – a decrease from the 14 in its 2006 World Cup Adidas Teamgeist predecessor – the Jabulani reduced seams to a bare minimum, creating the smoothest, roundest ball ever made.

When struck with minimal spin at the high speeds that top-level footballers tend to shoot or cross, it caused a chaotic knuckle-ball effect, generating sudden swerves or dips. Conversely, for footgolfers, who hit a ball with the inside of their foot to generate consistent spin, the Jabulani’s reduced seams help it travel further than any other ball. Only Adidas’ offshoots from the same era – including the Teamgeist, Terrapass, Speedcell and original Torfabrik – come close.

With none of these models in production for close to 15 years, elite footgolf’s demand has coupled with a scarcity in supply to send prices soaring.

View image in fullscreen Ben Clarke has not bought a Jabulani for years due to cost. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

“They are getting rarer and more expensive,” says Clarke, who has three boxed Jabulanis, alongside a host of other Adidas balls from that era. “I haven’t bought one for a few years, just because of how expensive they are. You tend to get them off other footgolfers or collectors who sell them because they see the footgolf market.

“The last one I got was around £250 about three years ago, but they are now £500 or more. It can be an expensive mistake if you kick it into a tree and it bursts.”

There is a consensus within the sport that the situation is unsustainable. Sean Rontree, a director of footgolf’s governing body in England, has three Jabulanis and three Speedcells in his own personal collection. He foresees an imminent end point.

“There will come a time when there won’t be any more on the market,” says Rontree. “Adidas won’t entertain making any more. We’ve had conversations with them, but the numbers they would have to ask for to make it profitable – around 10,000 balls – were out of our reach.”

The shortage has sparked an arms race. Targeting the 1,200 players who competed in this summer’s Footgolf World Cup in Mexico, a host of entrepreneurs are attempting to create a bespoke ball that can achieve the holy grail of challenging the Jabulani. Brands including the FGB (Malaysia), Squb (the Netherlands), Triero (Britain) and Birdie (Brazil) have all released footgolf-specific balls that retail for about £100.

View image in fullscreen Ben Clarke: ‘The world of footgolf and balls is ridiculous.’ Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

“I think, overall, our ball is superior in terms of quality and not needing repairs,” says FGB founder Jeffrey Cottam, whose company are now on their third-generation ball. “But in terms of trying to beat the Jabu, I don’t think anyone is there yet.

“The hardest bit is distance. Our ball is maybe five, six, seven metres behind the Jabu. We want to replicate the bounce of the Jabu, because that thing continuously bounces down the fairway. I’m trying to bring out a ball next year that beats the Jabu in all departments. There has to be a ball that comes out which is just as competitive as it. It’s the natural course of things.”

Clarke remains pragmatic. He knows the sport cannot survive for ever on a finite, decaying stock. But until a true heir emerges, he will continue his monthly ritual of tending to his dwindling Jabulani flock.

“It’s bizarre what we have to do to extend the life of a ball, just so it’s there when we need it,” he says. “One of them gave up on me last week and started chucking air out of one of the panels, so maybe I didn’t pump it up enough. The world of footgolf and balls is ridiculous.”

Sports.title: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
It isn’t quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.

Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.

Then Messi retired, distraught after a missing a penalty in the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.

Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.

This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry will Argentina be able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.

The best example came almost at the end, when Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.

Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.

But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.

The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi cries at the end of the World Cup final after Argentina’s loss to Spain. Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Other than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.

The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

With Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.

In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.

And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.

That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.

No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.

Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.

Sports.title: USA thrash Peru as teenage newcomers shine in first step toward 2030
Sports.content:
Playing in their first match of the 2030 World Cup cycle, the US men’s national team crushed Peru 4-1 in at Orlando’s Inter&Co Stadium on Saturday, riding goals from newcomers Justin Ellis, Zavier Gozo and Justin Hall to victory. The win marked the US debut of 16-year-old Philadelphia Union midfielder Cavan Sullivan, whose appearance in the US starting XI makes him the youngest player to feature for the national team in over two decades.

Sullivan received the lion’s share of the attention in the lead-up to Saturday’s match but it was Orlando City’s Ellis who stole the show early, nodding home a Gio Reyna free kick in the fourth minute to give the US an early lead. Playing in his home stadium, Ellis himself was involved in the build-up that led to the free kick, part of a nifty interchange with midfielder Malik Tillman that ended with Ellis drawing a foul at the near side of the pitch some 25 yards from goal. Reyna’s service was excellent; Ellis’ headed finish was awkward but perfectly-placed at the far post.

USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino’s roster for this international window features a blend of regulars alongside a host of uncapped young players, many of whom featured in Saturday’s match. All told, 11 players received their first cap for the US, with three of them – Sullivan, Ellis and New England Revolution defender Peyton Miller – in Pochettino’s starting XI. Bournemouth and 2022 World Cup captain Tyler Adams was given the captain’s armband for the first time during Pochettino’s two-year term as US head coach.

Peru answered the US opener quickly, equalizing in the 14th minute. Midfielder Yoshimar Yotun found Universitario forward Gianluca Lapadula with a cross just outside the six-yard box. Lapadula eluded Miller and easily nodded the ball home from close range. Peru were well-represented in Orlando, unsurprising given the fact that 20% of all Peruvian immigrants in the US claim central and south Florida as their adopted home.

Led by former Brazil head coach Mano Menezes, La Blanquirroja are in the midst of a generational turnover after failing to qualify for two consecutive World Cups. Missing a few notable pieces, the 60th-ranked Peruvians were badly out-possessed by the US and found their best chances via an occasional counterattack. Just as Pochettino did, Menezes rotated his squad heavily yet never found any real chemistry.

View image in fullscreen Cavan Sullivan and Frankie Westfield celebrate after the United States’ victory over Peru at Inter&Co Stadium in Orlando. Photograph: Alex Menendez/USSF/Getty Images

The US winner came from the penalty spot and involved another newcomer, Crystal Palace attacker Zavier Gozo. A foul on Gozo’s run into the far side of the box in the 65th minute led to the spot kick, which Tillman converted coolly. Yet another debutant – Red Bull New York attacker Hall, who has found himself courted by the US and Poland alike – iced things for the US with a flying finish from six yards only moments later. Middlesbrough midfielder Sebastian Berhalter added another to the pile-on in the 90th minute.

For his part, Sullivan was effective during his 60-minute shift. The 16-year-old has been a revelation for the Union since the World Cup break, with six goals and eight assists, and he displayed some of that energy on Saturday for the US, combining well in attack with Ellis and others and proving a difficult match for Peru’s defenders. That enthusiasm overflowed a bit in the 23rd minute, when a goal-crashing Sullivan collided with Peru goalkeeper Pedro Gallese, earning Sullivan his first US yellow card.

The 11 first-timers for the US on Saturday are the most since 2024, when the same number debuted in a 1-0 friendly loss to Slovenia. The US record for first-time caps is a dozen, having happened twice: against Poland in 1973 and 15 years later in a friendly against Guatemala.

The US will head to St Louis on Saturday evening ahead of Tuesday’s match against Chile at Energizer Park before heading to Phoenix and Minneapolis for matches against Mexico and Canada, respectively.

Sports.title: Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in Slovenia
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli grimaced on Friday when recalling his debut as an international player for Belgium. Alessandro del Piero and Italy discovered favourable opposition when preparing for the 2006 World Cup. Pocognoli will also look back, in time, at his first game as the manager of Scotland.

Blue skies, a dainty stadium in Ljubljana and a second-half display that provided glimpses of optimism in respect of Scotland’s world, post-Steve Clarke. The best-forgotten first 45 minutes can be explained away by a squad operating under a new regime. By full time, Slovenia were grateful for their point. Scotland’s players took deserved applause.

Scotland’s failing here was a familiar one. A lack of goals haunted Clarke. Nonetheless, this version of Scotland did at least create a series of openings. Scott McTominay, a key attacking threat, was missing. Instilling ruthlessness in a team is no easy task; it is one, however, Pocognoli has the coaching credentials to meet. Slovenia, on this evidence, have the more significant challenges.

“The feeling in the dressing room is positive because of the second half,” said Pocognoli. “We should have scored but I am very happy with the general performance of the strikers. It was only the last details we missed.” His demeanour was upbeat.

Ninety-four days had passed since Scotland’s loss to Brazil all but confirmed World Cup elimination. When that meek exit was certain, Clarke announced his resignation. Players and supporters alike seem caught between being highly grateful to Clarke for materially altering Scotland’s fortunes and heralding regime change.

In Slovenia, Pocognoli sampled international management for the first time at the age of 39. Slovenia failed to reach the World Cup, with the rows of empty seats telling the story of a country that is not at all convinced by its footballing outlook. The absence of Benjamin Sesko did nothing to help a shot-shy side.

Scotland could hardly bemoan poor preparation. Pocognoli had whipped his squad and mini-army of backroom staff to La Manga in the buildup to this Nations League game. With a sense of revolution in the air, the head coach unleashed a hitherto unseen front two: Robbie Ure was making his international debut while Oli McBurnie returned after years in the wilderness. The opening half only proved there is little point deploying multiple strikers if there is no adequate means of supplying them.

Scotland were awful in that first period. The football was passive and directionless. Players looked well-enough drilled off the ball, but descended into a state of panic when in possession. Slovenia, who were little better than ordinary, should have seized upon these shortcomings. To his credit, whatever message Pocognoli forcefully pressed home during the break had an effect.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli barks instructions during his first game in charge of Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Andraz Sporar had the ball in the net for the hosts in the eighth minute only for an offside flag to go up. Sporar subsequently missed a golden opportunity from six yards after fine work from Danijel Sturm. As Aljosa Matko shanked wide of Angus Gunn’s goal, the Tartan Army’s groans were audible.

Save a Ure shot from 20 yards that clipped the outside of a post, Scotland were nonexistent as an attacking force. An overhit Billy Gilmour pass that flew out of play when intended for the marauding Andy Robertson rather summed things up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McBurnie should have marked his Scotland return with a goal within five minutes of the restart. He opted to try to jink around Jan Oblak rather than slam a shot past the goalkeeper. Oblak morphed into Inspector Gadget, stretching out his arms while grounded to pinch the ball from McBurnie’s feet.

This triggered Scottish improvement; Gilmour forced a save after a one-two with McBurnie. Aaron Hickey could not quite divert a John McGinn corner on target. Oblak had to be sharp to deny the Scotland substitute Kieron Bowie before doing likewise to McBurnie from the resultant corner.

Second-half Scotland involved a huge upturn. McBurnie said he would not be able to sleep due to his profligacy. Seventeen Scotland caps are yet to yield a goal.

Bowie’s miss, 12 minutes from time, was in the category of howler. Gilmour, increasingly influential as Scotland dominated, had fed his teammate. Pocognoli was emboldened, sending on Ben Gannon-Doak to replace Hickey. In old money, that represented a winger for a full-back.

Scotland huffed, puffed, pushed and wheezed. Slovenia stood firm. Pocognoli nodded with approval as the whistle blew. Next up, a Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday.

Sports.title: How Courtney Lawes' audition for England recall did NOT go to plan: There were great expectations over his return to domestic rugby but he'll have to do more to convince Steve Borthwick, writes NIK SIMON
Sports.content:
How Courtney Lawes' audition for England recall did NOT go to plan: There were great expectations over his return to domestic rugby but he'll have to do more to convince Steve Borthwick, writes NIK SIMON

This was not what Courtney Lawes had in mind when he traded his life in France.

There were great expectations for the forward's return to English rugby but Sale's opening day at the CorpAcq Stadium did not go to plan.

Alex Sanderson went on a heavy recruitment drive over the summer – Lawes being the headline signing – but it was Bristol's more settled squad that came out on top.

Harry Randall and Louis Rees-Zammit scored two tries apiece for the visitors, who left delighted with their bonus-point victory. 'Very happy', was the summation last night from Bristol coach Pat Lam.

Sale are under pressure to deliver a return on their investment and there are only so many results like this that will be tolerated. Home victories will be key if they are going to make the top four this season.

Ill-discipline gifted Bristol easy entries into the red zone. Lawes spent much of the game trying to put out fires caused by penalties but Bristol's ruck intensity was a notch higher than what he had faced during his two years in France's second division.

There were great expectations for Courtney Lawes' return to English rugby but Sale's opening day did not go to plan

England suddenly have a wealth of locks who can operate at No 6, and Lawes would come in as fifth choice

Sanderson, however, remains supremely confident that his squad will hit the right notes quickly. He said: 'We know there's more in us. We need to improve. We need to be honest and we will be. There are a lot of good players who are going to have better games moving forward.'

There is great debate around whether Lawes will be recalled to the England squad – three years after his last Test – and it will take more than this to convince the national selectors.

Thanks to the rapid development of Alex Coles and the return to fitness of George Martin, England suddenly have a wealth of locks who can operate at No 6. Ollie Chessum is the pick of the bunch and skipper Maro Itoje, who was rested over the summer, must prove that he is still worthy of a place in the starting XV.

Lawes would come in as fifth choice. But head coach Steve Borthwick's move towards a lineout-jumping flanker means Coles, Martin, Chessum and Itoje should all make the matchday 23, meaning Lawes could only be one injury away from a return during the autumn Tests.

When England were selecting their squad for their latest alignment camp, Lawes was listed in the 'maybe' category and Sale must show an all-round improvement if his status is going to change. You suspect he will get there eventually.

Bristol centre Benhard Janse van Rensburg delivered the standout display of the England contenders. He charged down George Ford's channel in the early exchanges, ensuring the No 10 did not have a gentle return to the new season.

It was an underwhelming day for Ford, who dropped the ball inside Bristol's 22 and missed a routine penalty kick to touch. Sale's scrum impressed but their lineout faltered.

There were flashes of energy from Xavier Roe, Joe Marchant and Alex Lozowski but Bristol showed more life in the opposition 22. The visitors took the lead after half an hour and the hosts failed to wrestle their way back in front.

Bristol were frustratingly inconsistent last season but Lam believes the workrate on display in Manchester will patch together some of their flaws.

'You want some evidence from the hard work you do in pre-season,' said Lam.

'Ellis Genge spoke on Thursday and said, "I'm ready, I'm confident, let's go". The biggest thing was our work-rate. When we started here 10 years ago, we built our game on being world class at the things that don't require talent. If you get consistency in work-rate, you will get consistency in your attack shape and consistency in your defence shape.

'Too many times last year, we had guys on the ground and guys not in the right places. Our defence and attack wasn't as good last year as it has been and a lot of that comes down to working off the ball.'

The forlorn look on Sanderson's face at the final whistle told a different story to Lam's delight. Ford missed a late penalty that would have scraped a losing bonus point and Sale were left to do some early season soul-searching.

Sports.title: Man City could still lift the Premier League title THIS season despite being found guilty of 'vast majority' of rule breaches - with hefty legal delays expected over appeal process
Sports.content:
Man City could still lift the Premier League title THIS season despite being found guilty of 'vast majority' of rule breaches - with hefty legal delays expected over appeal process

Legal experts expect Manchester City to be free to lift this season’s Premier League trophy, despite having been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges brought against them.

City’s anticipated appeal, hinted at by chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in a statement at the weekend, could ultimately see them take the case to the High Court.

The Financial Times reported at the weekend that the single charge against City which has not been proven was one of the most serious. That may strengthen the club’s resolve.

Experts say that the grounds for a successful appeal, which would have to be heard by a separate and newly convened independent commission, are narrow. But if an appeal failed, City could seek a judicial review of the commission's findings at the High Court.

To do so, they would need to demonstrate that the Premier League acted outside its powers or reached a conclusion which no reasonable authority could have reached. If either could be proved by City's legal team, the outcome could be quashed. But City would need the High Court’s permission to make a judicial review application and the bar is high.

Legal experts expect Manchester City to be free to lift this season’s Premier League trophy

Man City were found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges brought against them on Friday

It is unclear how much of the independent commission's findings will be made public. Most arbitration processes have strict confidentiality rules in place. Though City and the Premier League are likely to have waived some of the right to confidentiality, it is possible that only a summary or redacted version of the judgement will be published.

The likely legal delays mean it is entirely possible that Premier League executives may be left to watch City lift the title at the Etihad Stadium next spring, should they maintain their strong start to the season. The side are currently three points clear at the top of the table. ‘The final outcome of this case, particularly in relation to sanctions, may still take considerable time to be resolved,’ said Chris Partington, a lawyer at Brandsmiths.

The independent commission’s findings are likely to be straining relations between the UK and the United Arab Emirates, whose sovereign wealth funds have been embedded in Manchester's urban development during Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s time as the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

Asked if City should be stripped of previous titles, Burnham said on Friday: ‘People shouldn’t jump to those kind of conclusions. I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some detail.’

Sports.title: Liverpool suffer worrying injury blow as Alexander Isak is forced to withdraw from Sweden duty - after 'heavy stamp' left striker limping with bloody toe following win over Romania
Sports.content:
Liverpool suffer worrying injury blow as Alexander Isak is forced to withdraw from Sweden duty - after 'heavy stamp' left striker limping with bloody toe following win over Romania

Liverpool star Alexander Isak has suffered another injury blow with Sweden, forcing him to withdraw from international duty.

The forward, who has enjoyed his best-ever start to a Premier League season, will be assessed by Liverpool's medical staff at the AXA Training Centre.

He scored in Sweden's 2-1 win over Romania on Friday but was spotted after with a blood-soaked sock after a heavy challenge.

'You can see it... It was a heavy stamp,' he told reporters in the mixed zone.

'Those of you who have played might know that it takes a few minutes for the pain to subside, but it was okay.’

While it appears minor on the surface, Liverpool fans will have their fingers crossed that Isak does not suffer the same fate as last season, when he missed 30 matches for club and country due to various injuries.

Alexander Isak has withdrawn from Sweden duty with a 'minor injury' after a 'heavy stamp'

He has enjoyed a fine start to the Premier League campaign, scoring four goals in five games

The £125million record signing suffered a broken leg and was sidelined for months after a robust challenge by Tottenham's Micky van de Ven in December.

It left him unavailable until April and unable to gain any momentum in a debut season where he scored just four times in all competitions after signing from Newcastle.

He has started this season much more like himself, banging in four goals in five Premier League games, a personal best start to the campaign.

The 27-year-old scored in the 2-2 draw against Nottingham Forest, struck both goals in the 2-0 win over Ipswich, and netted the 1-0 winner against Bournemouth.

Sweden's statement on his exit described the injury as 'minor', but it means he will play no part in their upcoming Nations League games against Poland, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Romania.

Alongside scoring goals, Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola wants Isak to step up by leading Liverpool's press with more ferocity.

Daily Mail Sport has reported how Iraola has even been showing Isak clips of academy graduate Lewis Koumas as a model of off-the-ball work.

Isak seems to be getting the message, telling BBC Sport recently that defending is an 'attacking weapon'.

Sports.title: Jason Cundy reveals how he became football's most notorious wind-up merchant, the truth behind THAT Ange Postecoglou mask - and insists he will never let up on Spurs foe Jamie O'Hara
Sports.content:
Jason Cundy reveals how he became football's most notorious wind-up merchant, the truth behind THAT Ange Postecoglou mask - and insists he will never let up on Spurs foe Jamie O'Hara

Jason Cundy's public life seems to have one main purpose: to make Jamie O'Hara as miserable and mortified as possible.

Cundy is, by now, football's biggest wind-up merchant. It is a role he revels in, and one which has brought talkSPORT's Sports Bar show immense popularity on social media.

He is in his element with that ridiculous Ange Postecoglou mask stretched comically over his head, firing wisecracks and shameful stats about Tottenham over at O'Hara, who can only sit with his head in his hands and take the mockery.

So, how much pleasure does Cundy take in tearing his radio co-pilot to shreds?

'A huge amount,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I don't feel for Jamie.

'Every single game, they lose or manage not to score. Never has the expression 'the gift that keeps giving' been more appropriate to Spurs at any other time.'

Jason Cundy has become football's biggest wind-up merchant due to Tottenham's decline

His Ange Postecoglou mask and jibes have been a menace to talkSPORT co-host Jamie O'Hara's

Cundy even turned up to O'Hara's wedding wearing the mask and takes 'huge' pleasure in annoying him

There is something relentlessly funny about the Postecoglou mask. Something about the sheer smugness of it, the expressionlessness, as O'Hara sits a metre away having meltdown after meltdown as this warped face just... watches him, unblinking.

O'Hara couldn't even escape the crinkly visage at his wedding to Keziah Grubb this year – Cundy turned up to that

In the week after our interview, Cundy posts no fewer than eight clips of him ripping into O'Hara's former club Tottenham, who are bottom of the Premier League and winless. In one, he labels the club with 'Spursitis'.

TalkSPORT has often fallen foul of accusations of ragebaiting its listeners too much, but the mask is almost universally loved by its viewers on social media – unless they're Tottenham fans.

'I came up with the idea to get masked because talkSPORT is so visual,' Cundy says. 'I didn't realise it would take on a whole life of its own.

'We bought them from South America and we order a new mask every year.

'We bought the Ange mask when he was the manager at Nottingham Forest, and by the time the mask turned up he'd got sacked, so I had to find a role for it.

'We've got a Gary Neville one, an Arne Slot one, and now we've got a Jamie Carragher one, that'll come out soon.

Cundy was speaking to Daily Mail Sport on behalf of TENA Men, who were sponsoring the 2026 Prostate United launch event

'It's the same mask each time. It absolutely stinks! It's got a weird smell about it. I tell Jamie it's the smell of failure. That's what it stinks of.

'I did clean it but think it's best to just leave it now, just to do what it does, somehow just let it lie in its own stink, and the worse the mask gets the worse Spurs get.'

Cundy was speaking to Daily Mail Sport on behalf of TENA Men, who were sponsoring the 2026 Prostate United launch event. The 56-year-old is a survivor of testicular cancer, so the issue of men's health is close to his heart.

'I have a voice to speak and spread a message - go and get yourself checked for testicular cancer, or get a PSA check. You have a duty to yourself and your family.'

He has brought his cancer experience onto the airwaves before, recording a long-form interview with talkSPORT on the subject in 2022, showing a deeper, more sensitive side to his personality than the joker we typically get to hear.

There is a pitfall in the show's reliance on Spurs being bad: namely, what if the north Londoners start being good?

Maybe O'Hara would then have the chance to turn the tables on his mate and have a dig at his alma mater Chelsea.

In any case, Cundy isn't too worried about Tottenham becoming sensations overnight.

Tottenham are bottom of the table and winless this season under manager Roberto De Zerbi

'You can't finish 17th, 17th, and go into a new season expecting there to be a huge dramatic change,' he says.

'Spurs aren't in the big six. Spurs would be in the big six in the Championship if they're not too careful.

'If they carry on being c***, Roberto De Zerbi will get the sack. That's football. That goes for every manager, not just him. But because it's Spurs, history is repeating itself.

'They've signed players that don't score goals: Omar Marmoush scored eight last season, Savio four. Mathys Tel, meh, four. Richarlison's not in the Premier League squad.

'If you put Erling Haaland up top, he still wouldn't score. They don't create chances.'

Jason Cundy was speaking on behalf of TENA Men, who sponsored the 2026 Prostate United launch event. To find out more about Prostate Cancer UK’s football fundraising challenge visit – prostateunited.prostatecanceruk.org/

Sports.title: Why Thomas Tuchel is still ignoring Trent Alexander-Arnold as his England exile closes in on 500 days - and how he could have made all the difference against Spain, writes KIERAN GILL
Sports.content:
Trent Alexander-Arnold will probably not make it to 500 days since he last played for England. He is on 477 as of today, and would need to be overlooked by Thomas Tuchel in the next three games of this international break for that criminality to come to pass.

Yet his exile not ending here at Wembley against Spain – the country where he now resides as a right back for Real Madrid – prompted questions. Some of which were put to England's manager.

Tuchel was squirming in his seat a little at his press conference, it never being nice to be quizzed on why your side lost, even if it was to a team as terrific as Luis de la Fuente’s Spain.

It was the topic of Alexander-Arnold and his preference for Jarell Quansah – of Bayer Leverkusen, ordinarily a centre back – in the position of right back which drew the tetchiest exchange.

Told he could have used the technical qualities of Alexander-Arnold, especially towards the end while chasing an equaliser at 3-2 down, Tuchel said: ‘There was a lot of defending to do as well. One-on-one defending. Marc Guehi followed in midfield so we ended up in a back three. We needed Jarell’s speed and Jarell’s quality to think also as a central defender. Jarell did excellent.’

What sort of game would you use Alexander-Arnold in, then? Tuchel: ‘We have three more games. I have a choice to make for 11 players and for five subs. Nothing else.’

Trent Alexander-Arnold should be trusted by Thomas Tuchel during this international break

Tuchel snubbed him for Jarell Quansah's defensive qualities - but England still conceded three goals against Spain

You seem to be suggesting it came down to his defensive qualities versus his technical qualities? Tuchel: ‘I made a decision for Jarell Quansah to stay on the pitch.’

And that is fair enough. He is the England manager. He decides what’s what. He wanted to stop Spain, a side now unbeaten in their last 39 matches, from winning again.

Yet we can still wonder – and indeed Alexander-Arnold must have been wondering – why he went unused. The last time he won a cap for England was June 7, 2025 – 477 days ago as a substitute in a 1-0 win against Andorra. The last time he started was October 13, 2024 – 714 days ago in a 3-1 win over Finland in which he scored from a 25-yard free-kick.

England were trailing 3-2 here after 74 minutes. Alexander-Arnold watched as Morgan Gibbs-White, Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Jarrad Branthwaite were introduced thereafter. Good header of the ball, Calvert-Lewin. Might have been nice to have a crosser in there, too. A quarterback capable of a Hail Mary.

Alexander-Arnold, still only 27, is a positive player. Some criticise him for his primary focus being to progress play. Whether that be via a pass punched into an attacking area, a switch across the pitch, a cross into those two yards of space beyond a striker – whatever.

Yet we can spin this the other way. He assisted six goals for Liverpool in the Champions League quarter and semi-finals in his career. He creates. He sees. He tries.

Tuchel appears concerned by what he has seen, the times he did not track this runner or that.

Without him, England still conceded three goals. Two came directly from Guehi and Nico O’Reilly giving up the ball – a Manchester City duo adding to the train of thought that the news of this week has been a distraction, their players’ WhatsApp group presumably a stream of speculation. The third involved a few at fault as Quansah, Guehi and Ezri Konsa all watched the passing move happen in front of them while the ball went from Aymeric Laporte to Alex Baena to Mikel Oyarzabal to the goal. Konsa exchanged words with Quansah after Spain’s winner.

The Real Madrid star's ball-playing ability would have been useful to break down Spain late on

Tuchel is still searching for ways to improve England and help them show their DNA

It was a game which did not carry the tension of that seen at a World Cup. It felt like a Nations League fixture. Certainly in its concentration levels from England’s defenders.

Reece James is England’s right back, we know that, but his injury history is what it is and Chelsea think of him as more of a midfielder nowadays, presumably partially because of his body. Ben White has his historical issues when it comes to his country. Tino Livramento withdrew from this camp. Without them, Quansah was picked over Alexander-Arnold, and he played to the end.

But for a slip from Harry Kane as he took his penalty, England might have made it 3-1 and won. Then we might never have been discussing this problem. Yet they did, and we are, picking over the carcass of another match which Tuchel could have been celebrating rather than lamenting.

Alexander-Arnold might be a little low on confidence, understandably so. He has only started three of Real Madrid’s eight games in all competitions this season, twice a substitute, a trio of times unused. Going ignored against Spain will hardly have helped him in that regard. Now to see if he gets a crack against Czechia on Tuesday. He should in some form.

Sports.title: Former Man United star Juan Mata sticks the boot in on Man City - and jokes he may finally be a Premier League winner after their guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United star Juan Mata joked he may finally be a Premier League winner after Manchester City were found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges against them. The Premier League accused City of widespread financial doping over an era of sustained success and Daily Mail Sport understands they have succeeded in proving all of the substantive claims. Sanctions have not yet been announced but stripping the club of titles and expulsion are among the options on the table following the seismic ruling, which leaked on Friday. Mata, 38, finished second with United under Jose Mourinho in the 2017-18 season - the last campaign covered by the charges against their arch rivals - and would be in line to benefit in the unlikely event City are stripped of their titles. Asked about the City decision, the Spaniard told ITV: 'It directly affects me. 'I've been lucky enough to play many games and win some trophies but never won the Premier League — or have I? Former Manchester United star Juan Mata has joked that he may finally be a Premier League winner after Man City were found guilty of most of the 115 charges against them He was part of the side that finished second to Manchester City in the 2017-18 campaign 'I don't know what's going to happen.' Mata is the latest former United star to publicly respond to the guilty verdict, with Roy Keane telling 'cheating' City they need to 'take their medicine' and 'deserve to be punished. David De Gea on Saturday echoed Rio Ferdinand's calls for City to be stripped of the title in 2011-12. 'So…… Let’s talk,' he posted on X. 'How many Premier League titles have I won then?' City deny wrongdoing and are set to appeal the decision. On Saturday, chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said the club is confident it will clear its name. In a letter to fans, Al Mubarak writes that, despite reporting, the Premier League's process 'still has a long way to run' and adds 'our confidence in proving the club's innocence remains as strong as it was when this began'. 'We have faced challenges before and prevailed,' he added. Daily Mail Sport also reported the Premier League's victory over Manchester City will trigger a series of legal claims for as much as £800m – although the case itself may rumble on for another two years. Arsenal, Tottenham, Liverpool and Manchester United served formal notices reserving their right to take action in the event that City – who could now face expulsion from the top flight - be found guilty. Representatives have already begun putting together a case on how much they feel they have a claim for, pointing out that they have lost potential income on the back of City's cheating. It is thought that those who feel most badly done to, with Tottenham having missed out on a Champions League spot on a number of occasions, will ask for the biggest sums. According to those with knowledge of the situation, £200m would not be an outrageous estimate. City have won 26 trophies since the Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008, including eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups and the Champions League as part of their 2023 Treble-winning season.

Sports.title: Man City star Rayan Ait-Nouri sent home from Algeria duty after furious altercation with coaches on substitutes' bench
Sports.content:
Manchester City star Rayan Ait-Nouri has been dismissed from international duty after an altercation with Algeria's staff.

The defender, 25, appeared enraged at the decision to leave him on the bench in the 3-1 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying victory over Zambia.

Footage circulated on social media shows the full-back gesticulating in frustration after being denied a chance to get on the pitch.

Algerian outlet Ennahar reports that Ait-Nouri had been asked to warm-up by manager Brahim Hemdani, only to be sat back down when Zambia scored.

He then 'rejected all attempts to calm him down' from general manager Moussa Saib and his team-mates, causing a 'great stir'.

Algeria have now announced his departure, saying: 'The national coach, Mr Brahim Hemdani decided this Saturday to release the player Rayan Ait-Nouri from the current training camp of the national team.

Manchester City star Rayan Ait-Nouri has been sent home from international duty by Algeria

'The Algerian international will return to his club, Manchester City.'

Ait-Nouri has racked up 34 caps for Algeria and starred in the World Cup over the summer, but the Paris-born man also holds French nationality.

It has been a frustrating time for the former Wolves star, who is yet to feature in the Premier League this campaign.

When he has played, he has been highly effective. He provided two assists in the 5-0 demolition of Norwich in the Carabao Cup third round, while he also assisted Erling Haaland off the bench against Porto in the Champions League.

He signed for City in July last year for £33.7million and was a bit-part player in his first campaign too.

Enzo Maresca has generally preferred the marauding Josko Gvardiol on the left side of his defence.

Manchester United made a shock deadline day swoop for him, enquiring about a loan, but would not commit to an obligation to buy, an arrangement which would have been acceptable to City.

Sports.title: 'He's got far too many bad habits': Roy Keane savages Cole Palmer after his England withdrawal and claims Chelsea star WON'T win Thomas Tuchel's side trophies
Sports.content:
Roy Keane believes England fans should 'forget' about the idea of Cole Palmer elevating the national team to another level.

The Manchester United legend has accused Palmer of 'bad habits' after he withdrew from England duty with fitness issues for a second time since Thomas Tuchel was named as head coach.

England did not lack a spark but did lack control against Spain at Wembley on Saturday night as they allowed the visitors to win 3-2 from a goal down.

And Keane told ITV Sport before the game: 'Well, I think, whatever his injuries, and if he is injured… I watched his last game against Brentford and if you think he’s going to get England to another level and win trophies, forget about it.

'I like Palmer, he’s a talented boy, but he’s got far too many bad habits, for me.'

Palmer has enjoyed a fairly successful start to the season, registering two goals and as many assists in the first five Premier League games.

Roy Keane tore into Cole Palmer before England's Nations League defeat by Spain at Wembley

He does not believe Palmer - who withdrew from England duty for a fourth time - would elevate the national team

Tuchel named him in his squad for this international break but the Chelsea star withdrew alongside Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, and Tino Livramento.

The 24-year-old, who had the summer off to recover after being excluded from the World Cup squad and played every minute of Chelsea's recent 3-0 drubbing by Brentford, also withdrew from Lee Carsley's final interim squad in November 2024 after Tuchel had been named as Gareth Southgate's successor.

It is the fourth time he has withdrawn from England duty in total and Tuchel has questioned his commitment.

Tuchel said ahead of Saturday's Nations League game against world champions Spain at Wembley ‘everybody is desperate to come’ and represent England.

But when it was suggested that Palmer’s decision to withdraw from the squad despite playing 90 minutes for Chelsea last Friday appeared to suggest otherwise, Tuchel said: ‘It’s hard to argue against what you are saying.’

Asked where it leaves Palmer and what advice he would give him were he his friend, Tuchel added: ‘It leaves us with Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze in that position.

‘All in camp. All desperate to be here. All available. And all ready to go, ready to stop a holiday [like Gibbs-White] after one day in Dubai.

‘I am not his friend. I am his national team coach and I can only judge him on what he is delivering for the national team and he is just missing too many opportunities.’

Thomas Tuchel has questioned Palmer's commitmetnt to the Three Lions cause

England failed to control the game as they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley on Saturday night

Tuchel also stressed that the door is not closed on any player, saying he was ‘not worried’ about the issue.

Equally, he pulled no punches when it comes to the Chelsea player’s future opportunities.

‘My understanding is that Cole plays with discomfort and pain and he cannot compete on the highest level with discomfort and pain, so he withdrew and informed us and Chelsea informed us,’ Tuchel explained.

‘He misses too many opportunities, and I don't blame him for it. It's just the fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries and I only want to rely on what I personally witness and what I see within my team, and for that you have to be in camp.

‘If you're not in camp, there's a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you only can do it when you're actually with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch so, yeah, it is a missed opportunity.

‘What sticks with me is the week that I have with the others.

‘They [the absentees] lose that. That sticks. It sticks because we create something.

‘We actually work off the field, on the field, about our principles, on how to be in.

‘This brotherhood is so important and you miss out if you’re not there.’

Whether Palmer would have been of much help to England against Spain is a matter to be debated.

Marc Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal inside two minutes to give Spain the lead, but England went into half-time 2-1 up thanks to goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane.

Kane actually had a chance to extend the Three Lions' lead from the penalty spot, but he slipped and hit the bar.

The World Cup champions proved their quality and their mettle in the second half as Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal scored to give them a strong start to the Nations League campaign.
