World.title: Floods and landslides kill at least 56 people in India, 12 in Nepal
World.content:
Authorities report increasing death toll over three days as rivers rise above danger levels across parts of neighbouring countries.

Share Floods and landslides kill at least 56 people in India, 12 in Nepal on social media

Heavy rainfall has triggered floods and landslides that have killed at least 56 people in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh in recent days while 12 people have been reported dead in neighbouring Nepal.

Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod, Uttar Pradesh’s relief commissioner, said on Sunday that India’s most populous state had registered 66.5mm (2.6 inches) of rain from Friday to Sunday morning, compared with a normal 7.6mm (a quarter of an inch) for the period.

The deaths, in addition to 46 injuries, were reported during a spell of “exceptionally heavy rain that has affected much of Uttar Pradesh”, according to the commissioner’s office.

More than 1,000 houses were damaged after “a depression over the Bay of Bengal moved inland and intensified rainfall across the region,” it added.

Home to more than 240 million people, Uttar Pradesh is frequently hit by rain and thunderstorms during the annual monsoon season from June to September.

In India’s eastern state of Odisha, more than 70,000 people living in low-lying areas were evacuated after rivers rose due to heavy downpours, the NDTV news network reported. The rains have damaged bridges and culverts, forcing officials to shut down Devkund, a popular tourist spot in the state.

Separately, India’s Central Water Commission said 30 river-monitoring stations across seven states were in a “severe situation”. Major rivers that flow through India, including the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi, Bagmati and Narmada, had risen above danger levels.

In Nepal, where a devastating flood in late August killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing, a new wave of flooding and landslides has killed at least 12 people since Thursday, according to officials, with several others missing.



Authorities warned of possible flash floods in 49 of the country’s 77 districts, with more than half facing high flooding or flash-flooding risks as water levels in major rivers and tributaries continued to rise.

Power supplies have been disrupted in the Manang, Mustang, Myagdi and Baglung districts, with authorities working to ⁠restore electricity, officials at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation said.

Flooding of the Rahuganga River damaged the structure and transmission-line towers of a 40-megawatt hydropower project, Water Resources and Energy ⁠Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said.

Shanti Mahat, a spokesperson for the National ⁠Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, said Rasuwa and Nuwakot, areas hit by ⁠last month’s deadly floods, should remain “alert” but were not currently considered high-risk areas.

World.title: ‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines?
World.content:
Board of Peace excludes UNRWA from Gaza, aligning with repeated Israeli calls to sideline the refugee aid agency.

Share ‘No role for UNRWA in Gaza’: Does the Board of Peace toe Israeli lines? on social media

The United States-led Board of Peace (BoP) has said the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) will have no role in Gaza – echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation considered a lifeline for millions of Palestinians.

The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the “ceasefire” and Gaza’s reconstruction, said on Friday it would work only with partners it deems reliable and who it believes can meet the needs of Gaza’s population – a standard it says UNRWA does not meet.

The move comes as the BoP unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan on Wednesday aimed at beginning Gaza’s reconstruction, nearly a year after a so-called “ceasefire” came into effect in the devastated Palestinian territory.

The plan, presented on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly (UNGA), comes as key elements of the “ceasefire” remain stalled, including the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hamas.

UNRWA was established in 1949 to cater to tens of thousands of Palestinians displaced from their homes by Jewish militias from areas that currently form part of Israel.

BoP’s stance on UNRWA comes as Israel’s genocide in the coastal enclave continues, with Palestinians facing nonstop attacks, severe restrictions on humanitarian aid and stalled reconstruction plans.

“Excluding UNRWA is not a neutral administrative decision; it is a deeply political one,” Palestinian political analyst and playwright Ahmed Najar told Al Jazeera.

“It aligns the Board of Peace with Israel’s longstanding campaign to marginalise and ultimately dismantle the agency, removing it not only from Gaza’s present but from its future.”

So what has BoP said about UNRWA, and does it keep toeing the Israeli line on the future of Gaza?

What did the Board of Peace say?

The BoP unveiled a 66-project reconstruction blueprint on the sidelines of the UNGA, with $2.4bn proposed for projects aimed at beginning Gaza’s recovery.



UNRWA was left off the list of UN agencies the board identified as partners.

“The Board of Peace’s policy as it relates to UNRWA’s involvement in Gaza is unchanged,” the BoP said in a post on X on Friday.

“We will only work with trusted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalised Strip. UNRWA fails on those litmus tests.”

However, a BoP official, speaking to The Associated Press news agency on condition of anonymity, confirmed that board members had met UNRWA officials several times.

The official said the agency’s programmes could continue if they served Gaza’s residents well, but maintained that “UNRWA’s days are over”.

The BoP, which US President Donald Trump launched earlier this year, was conceived to oversee the rebuilding of Gaza after nearly three years of Israel’s genocidal war on the Strip.

What has UNRWA said?

In an indirect response, UNRWA acting Commissioner-General Christian Saunders said on Friday in Gaza, “UNRWA remains an institution of considerable humanitarian and strategic value, with capabilities and expertise that are difficult to replicate today.”

“To disregard these capabilities at a moment of such profound need is neither logical nor responsible,” Saunders said in a statement.

Former UNRWA chief Philippe Lazzarini on Thursday warned that removing the agency would have a “devastating” effect on Palestinians.

“They want to get rid of the agency, but on the other hand they know that if you get completely rid of the agency today, it might have a further … devastating impact on the population,” Lazzarini told AP on Friday.

In a separate statement on X, Lazzarini said, “grandiose plans are what the Board of Peace does best”, noting widespread suffering across Gaza amid Israel’s ongoing genocide.

The agency has about 11,000 Palestinian employees in Gaza and remains heavily involved in healthcare, education, water and sanitation services. Its exclusion is particularly significant given the scale of displacement and the continuing restrictions on aid entering Gaza.

UNRWA has for decades provided aid and education services to Palestinians in Gaza, occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank as well as Jordan, Syria and Lebanon – the neighbouring countries where the Palestinian refugees have been living.

Palestinians see the agency as safeguarding their right of return to their homeland, while Israel wants it dismantled.

What has been Hamas’s response?

Hamas accused the BoP of adopting Israel’s position.



Spokesperson Hazem Qassem on Saturday called the decision to exclude UNRWA “a complete alignment with the Zionist [Israeli] position”, saying it was aimed at ending the agency’s operations, preventing it from delivering aid and undermining Palestinian refugees’ right of return.

Qassem said it was “strange for the peace council to adopt this hostile stance towards UNRWA while simultaneously failing to provide aid to Gaza or compel the occupation to abide by the ceasefire agreement and halt the daily killings of Palestinians in the Strip”.

Does the Board of Peace toe the Israeli line?

Experts say the workings and demands of the BoP align closely with Israel’s vision of the Gaza Strip and the Palestinians.

“The composition of the board reinforces this concern,” analyst Najar told Al Jazeera,” he said.

“Israel is a founding member, while Palestine is not. Not a single Palestinian sits on either the central executive board or the Gaza executive board. Yet these bodies include senior Trump officials, strongly pro-Israel figures, private-equity executives and Israeli businesspeople who will exercise influence over Gaza’s governance and reconstruction.”

Nevertheless, Najar said, while other members such as Turkiye may “provide some counterweight”, so the board does not present itself to be “entirely uniform”, the structure of power is “clear”.

“Palestinians are excluded from the bodies taking the strategic, financial and security decisions about their own land,” he added.

On UNRWA

Israel has for years sought to remove UNRWA from Gaza, accusing the agency of being infiltrated by Hamas.

The International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion in October, said allegations that “a significant part of UNRWA’s employees are ‘members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions'” had not been substantiated.

The BoP’s position strengthens the Israeli efforts to dismantle the UN agency.

Najar said Israel’s “hostility” towards the UN agency is also connected to what the agency represents: “the continuing existence of Palestinian refugees, their rights – including their right of return – and the international community’s unresolved responsibility towards them”.

“Removing UNRWA, therefore, serves a political purpose extending far beyond the delivery of aid,” he added.

Najar said Gaza could not be “credibly reconstructed” by excluding the UN agency. “Nor should reconstruction be used to erase Palestinian refugee rights or replace an internationally mandated institution with mechanisms that are more politically compliant. If the board is serious about rebuilding Gaza for its people, UNRWA must be part of that process, and Palestinians must be at its centre, not placed at the bottom of a foreign-controlled hierarchy,” he noted.

On Hamas disarmament

Hamas and other Palestinian factions agreed in July to a roadmap under which weapons would be surrendered in stages as Israeli forces gradually withdrew. The two processes were explicitly linked.

But following an August meeting between Nickolay Mladenov, the BoP’s director-general, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the board said Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the “Yellow Line” until Hamas’s decommissioning was complete, including “light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike”.



Hamas maintains that it will not implement its obligations unless Israel fulfils its own.

Israel currently occupies more than 60 percent of Gaza while most of the territory’s 2.3 million people remain displaced.

On reconstruction

Article 17 of the BoP plan calls for “temporary reconstruction” beginning in areas designated free of Hamas control, including humanitarian compounds for unarmed civilians.

The proposed system would direct reconstruction, aid and shelter towards areas outside Hamas’s control while Israeli forces remain behind the so-called “Yellow Line”.

However, Israel has refused to allow the Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza, open crossings or begin reconstruction until Hamas is completely disarmed.

After unveiling the reconstruction plan on the sidelines of the UNGA, BoP high representative Mladenov said once again the proposed plan depends on Hamas’s disarmament.

What is the situation in Gaza?

Almost a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin on any meaningful scale and Israeli forces continue to occupy large parts of the Strip.

At least 1,451 Palestinians have been killed and 4,953 wounded in Israeli attacks since the “ceasefire” began in October 2025, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

The healthcare system is on the verge of “total collapse”, the ministry said last week, while shortages of fuel, medical supplies and spare parts have disrupted hospitals, water and sanitation services.

The scale of destruction is also immense. More than half of Gaza’s hospitals and clinics remain nonfunctional, less than 1.5 percent of cropland is accessible and undamaged, and reconstruction needs have reached an estimated $71.5bn.

Nearly 84 percent of Gaza’s population – more than 1.76 million people – are living in displacement sites or damaged and inadequate shelters, the UN has said.

World.title: ‘My hands are empty’: Displaced Palestinians struggle to survive
World.content:
In the West Bank, displaced Palestinians are getting deeper into debt and living in poverty.

Tulkarem, occupied West Bank – Hakim Mar’i spends his days lying on a single bed, his disfigured leg raised. The windows of Mar’i’s dilapidated apartment, his latest temporary shelter, are covered with old blankets. Unable to work, Mar’i has no money for electricity, so the blankets have to do. At night, his family lives in near darkness.

The apartment is just around the corner from mounds of rubble and gnarled iron structures that mark one entrance to the now-emptied Tulkarem refugee camp. For Mar’i and other Palestinians, the camp was a home once considered temporary. But generations lived there, and now, the physical structure – their home – that tied his family together over the years is gone.

Impoverished, Hakim’s family is in disarray. With its debts mounting and its members facing another eviction, he said he has considered taking his life several times over the past year and a half.

Mar’i cannot afford treatment for his debilitating leg injury, which has developed severe infections. He said he sustained it while working as a labourer inside Israel in 2019. The wound worsened after Israeli soldiers severely beat him when they forced his family from the Tulkarem camp. Diabetes and other untreated conditions have piled on, but he is unable to pay for the needed medical care.

“This joint here is completely gone,” he said, gesturing at the swollen, blackened lower leg that prevents him from working.

“The medicine – by God, the medicine, I haven’t been able to get. My wife and kids tell me: get out travel. Go to America, Turkey – so I can the medical treatment I need… I’m a sick man.”



His mother, Salwa, sat beside him, less than a kilometre (0.6 miles) from their former four-storey home. She wept when asked about the family home that was built floor by floor after they were first displaced in 1948 from al-Khudayra, the Arabic name for Hadera, a city in Israel. “We really put a lot into that house,” she said.

After their removal, the Israeli military razed the Mar’i home so a road traversing the now-emptied camp could be built. “Seeing it destroyed was really painful for us – all of us,” she said.

It has been more than 20 months since Israeli forces emptied the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps in a sweeping military operation in the northern West Bank, displacing tens of thousands of Palestinians whose families had already been refugees for three generations. Constantly renewed orders for a closed military zone now prevent their return.

Since January 2025, Hakim’s family has been forced to move four times. First, they fled to a converted youth centre before landing in a cramped apartment with their four children, all under 15.

Unable to pay rent, the family could see the landlord’s generosity run its course as this once-temporary housing arrangement now has no end in sight. Hakim owes money at the local shops for food he bought on credit. Some nights, the children eat at neighbours’ houses.

“I have children. I have food. I have drink,” he said. “My hands are empty. Nobody is with me. Nobody is standing beside me.”

‘We’re already at the brink’

The Mar’i family is among more than 33,000 Palestinians forcibly removed from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem camps by Israeli forces in early 2025. This is the largest single episode of forced displacement in the West Bank since Israel’s occupation began in 1967, according to the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA).

UN satellite imagery shows that 20 percent of all buildings across the three camps have been destroyed and another 28 percent are damaged.

“The level of destruction we are seeing is severe and unprecedented,” said Roland Friedrich, director of West Bank affairs for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

According to Friedrich, 85 percent of those displaced have no regular income after many lost jobs when the camps were emptied. More than 80 percent of residents are renting, an unfamiliar expense for families who never paid for housing or utilities inside the camps.



The closed military zone covering the camps is renewed every two months, Friedrich said, with no indication of when – or whether – residents will be allowed to return. “What we saw there is forced displacement,” Friedrich said. “The UN’s position is very clear: People have to be allowed to return. The camps must be rebuilt.”

Unlike after the 2000-2005 second Intifada when the Jenin camp was rebuilt, displaced families and UNRWA staff fear there is no return plan this time.

The Israeli military stated the camps were emptied for “operational security” in its effort to root out fighters from the camps. Friedrich worried the aim of the military operations is to “change the geographical expression of the Palestinian refugee issue”.

Now more than 20 months into what was meant to be an emergency response, funding shortages have left UNRWA unable to cover the vast needs of the displaced population. It has moved some operations to keep schools and basic health clinics functioning. With funds dwindling, the agency has shifted to a “targeted approach”, leaving thousands without support.

Friedrich pointed to a rise in gender-based violence linked to the economic strain on families and to growing depression and anxiety among displaced children observed by UNRWA’s psychosocial teams. “We’re already at the brink now,” he declared.

‘Everyone went their own way’

While Hakim’s displacement plays out in the shadow of the camp, the family of Khadija Zbeidat face their own imminent eviction on the outskirts of Tulkarem. They live in the neighbourhood of Dhinnaba, where sparse houses are interspersed with greenhouses. They are unable to afford a residence closer to the city centre.

As Khadija sat on a couch in the middle of the yard, her many children and grandchildren ran past a small patch of plants she has planted – one of her few remaining joys. “I love plants,” she said. “We had many flowers in our home in the camp. Having the plants here is all I have to feel like myself,” she told Al Jazeera.

Khadija, a widow, shares a tiny spartan room with nine family members, nearly all children, along with a small bathroom and a kitchen barely big enough for one person to cook in. A worn couch takes up one corner. The ceiling is peeling above it.

The room was given to them rent free by a relative of Khadija’s brother-in-law after they spent four months crammed into her daughter’s house with nine other people. “It got really cramped, the pressure on each other,” Zbeidat said. “And we became a burden too.”

Khadija’s family was displaced in January 2025 from the Tulkarem camp’s Haret al-Nadi section, a significant part of which has been destroyed, she said.

“The camp was excellent,” she said of their life before. “I swear, I wish they’d take us back. Everything was close to us, dear – … the closeness, that sense of belonging and the warmth, the company and the neighbours.”

The memories that she cherishes most dearly and that bring her to tears are of food: the stuffed grape leaves and the maamoul cookies made as a neighbourhood together for Eid. This year, there was none of it.



“Nothing. No cookies,” she said. “Nobody even had it in them to do anything any more. Everyone went their own way – scattered.”

Like the Mar’i family and others, they were not allowed to bring their belongings during their abrupt displacement. Some residents have since been allowed to retrieve belongings once or twice from their homes in the camps, but much of what they own remains left behind. Khadija’s daughter-in-law at one point returned to the ruins of the camp – at the risk of being shot – to retrieve a doll left behind that Khadija’s granddaughter Sandy would not stop crying about.

In Tulkarem, displaced families live either in the poorest areas closest to the camp, like the Mar’is, or on the cheaper outskirts, like the Zbeidats, remaining close enough to the health and schooling services that UNRWA still provides. But even a simple trip to buy groceries requires Khadija, who has no car, to travel 2km (1.2 miles).

At night, the family sits outside rather than in the stifling heat of the poorly ventilated room, watching Israeli military drones pass low overhead. “What to do? We’re used to seeing them, to having them around, to them raiding houses,” Khadija said. “It doesn’t matter any more.”

The military raids that always haunted life in the refugee camps have now come to wherever the displaced refugees have fled to. “We don’t feel safe,” Khadija said. “Nor the kids. It’s dangerous. When they want to go out somewhere, my heart stays busy until they come back.”

Waiting to be kicked out again

For months after the displacement, landlords, relatives and shopkeepers absorbed much of the shock, allowing families to stay for free or buy food on credit. But as the emergency stretches to almost two years now, that informal safety net is fraying. The pressure is felt particularly in economically moribund Tulkarem, where many families had relied on jobs inside Israel before Palestinian work permits were revoked after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023.

The owner of the property where Khadija’s family is staying recently sent his sister to tell Khadija’s family to leave. “They think it’s been too long,” Khadija explained. “They want the land, to benefit from the land and the room. … But where can we get money, where to pay from? The rent is very high, and we can’t afford it. We don’t know what to do if she comes again and kicks us out.”

Hakim’s family is on the brink of eviction too. Like others, he received from UNRWA a one-time rental subsidy of 3,000 shekels ($985) and a separate 1,700-shekel ($560) multipurpose cash payment for short-term assistance. “Every minute, I am waiting for the landlord to kick us out,” he said.

Khadija’s family survives on credit from shopkeepers who know their situation and, for now, still extend it – but patience is wearing thin.

Hakim said this goodwill is collapsing: “You tell them: ‘Give me a day, two days. Be patient with me.’ They won’t bear it.”

As distant as a return to her family’s lands in 1948 feels now, Khadija still hopes to return to the camp one day. But she worries that her children may inherit an even more precarious existence than the one that preceded this latest dispossession – refugees for generations displaced yet again. “Only God knows what tomorrow will bring us,” Khadija said.

World.title: Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich calls for war in occupied West Bank
World.content:
Smotrich comments come as Israeli authorities announce a week-long comprehensive military closure across the occupied West Bank, citing the Jewish holiday Sukkot.

Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says the Israeli military should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and repeat what it “did in Gaza”.

Using a biblical term for the occupied West Bank, the minister told Ynet News in an interview published on Sunday that Israel needs to “go to war in Judea and Samaria, to do there what we did in Gaza, to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, which is a terror authority”.

Smotrich was responding to a question on how Israel should combat the increasing “security tensions” in the occupied West Bank, where Israeli violence against Palestinians has been steadily growing since the eruption of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, but the attacks have intensified significantly this year.

“We need to tell” Israeli forces, he said, “Just as you dismantled Hamas in Gaza, there won’t be terror infrastructure in Judea and Samaria”. “No terrorists, no weapons, no tunnels.”

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day, the highest rate in about 20 years.

Various settler groups, often supported or protected by Israeli soldiers, have attacked Palestinians in several ways, including shootings, besieging homes and engaging in other forms of communal violence that experts have described as “pogroms“.

Rights groups warn that settlers are increasingly armed with military-issued weaponry and wear military uniforms during attacks, blurring the line between settler and soldier.



In a statement later on Sunday, the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said Smotrich’s comments come within the context of Israeli government policies that involve the killing and displacement of Palestinians, as well the expansion of illegal settlements, land confiscation and attempts to impose annexation by force.

It also warned that continued international silence over inflammatory Israeli statements and policies encourages the Israeli government to pursue its plans and risks further regionall tension and instability.

Military closure

The comments come as Israeli authorities announced a comprehensive military closure across the occupied West Bank, citing the Jewish holiday of Sukkot. The heightened restrictions on the movement of Palestinians are set to remain in place until October 3.

Meanwhile, in occupied East Jerusalem, hundreds of Israelis stormed the courtyards of Al-Aqsa Mosque under heavy protection from Israeli police on Sunday.

Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that the Israelis entered the compound through the Moroccan Gate and performed Talmudic rituals, as Israeli forces increased restrictions around the mosque and across Jerusalem’s Old City.

World.title: Yemen government forces widen attacks against Houthis: What we know
World.content:
Yemeni government forces claim to have carried out multiple air and ground operations across the southwestern governorate of Taiz in 24 hours.

Share Yemen government forces widen attacks against Houthis: What we know on social media

Yemen’s government forces have conducted multiple air and ground operations in the southwestern governorate of Taiz in 24 hours as they intensify attacks against the Iran-backed Houthi group.

The government’s military media centre on Sunday claimed several operations against the rebels, including air raids on Houthi positions in five locations across the governorate.

More than 146,000 people have been displaced since the fighting erupted in July, following a period of relative calm after a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have made dramatic territorial gains against the government forces, seizing the strategic Red Sea coastal city of Mocha and expanding their control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a global maritime chokepoint connecting Europe to Asia.

⁠Rashad ⁠al-Alimi, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, has called on citizens to mobilise and join the fight against the Houthis as the government has stepped up its attacks against the Iran-backed group in an effort to stop their advance and regain lost territory.

Ibrahim al-Huri, from the University of Saba in Marib governorate, said the Yemeni government’s call for a general “mobilisation” of the population will likely receive more support in the government-controlled areas, especially in Taiz and Marib, where people have been suffering more.

“Even in the Houthi-controlled areas, there would be many people who would like to answer the call for mobilisation, but there will be some obstacles and challenges like the fear of retaliation and facing the brutality [of the militia].”



Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, which has faced Houthi attacks on its soil since fighting escalated this month, has been turning to its allies, including Pakistan and Turkiye, for support.

Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Here’s what we know about the latest fighting and the humanitarian conditions the impoverished country faces:

What to know about the latest fighting

The military media centre said on Sunday dozens of Houthi fighters, including field commanders, were killed or wounded in the last 24 hours of fighting near Taiz’s capital, which is also named Taiz.

Government forces have carried out operations in several areas of the governorate, including the al-Waziiya district in the west, weapons sites and ammunition depots at Mafraq Mawiya and al-Dhukrah in the east, a Houthi gathering in the Hayfan district in the south and against military vehicles in the Gurab area in the northwest.

Government forces also thwarted infiltration attempts on the al-Ahtoub front and in Hadran as they carried out shelling of Houthi gatherings on the al-Kadha and al-Aqroud fronts, the media centre said.

It added that several Houthi military vehicles were damaged in the attacks.

Al Jazeera could not verify the battlefield claims.

“Government forces say they have made advances in the southern Taiz governorate, taking control of several areas and higher ground. Among them is Jabal Bazel, a mountaintop that places Houthi supply lines within target range,” Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali said on Saturday, reporting from Taiz.

“These developments point to significant and potentially decisive ground operations in recent hours.”

Ali said al-Alimi expressed confidence that government forces were capable of restoring control over the whole country. Houthis currently control vast swaths of northern and western Yemen while the government controls the south and east.

Since the current fighting erupted, the Houthis have accused the Saudis of carrying out attacks in Yemen and promised to prevent Saudi tankers from passing through Bab al-Mandeb, which Riyadh has been using as an alternative shipping route to the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Tehran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel began the war in February. Before the conflict, a fifth of the world’s oil supplies had passed through Hormuz.

Government forces, meanwhile, accused the Houthis of using Iranian air defence weapons and said they pose a danger to aircraft.



“These Houthi weapons pose a serious threat to international flight paths over the Red Sea and operate using a heat-tracking system,” Brigadier-General Majed al-Nazili, the Yemeni government forces’ spokesperson, said on social media.

“The weapons employed are capable of attacking military or civilian targets without the ability to distinguish between them, thereby endangering the safety of civil aviation and the lives of passengers.”

Early on Saturday, a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said its air defence systems intercepted two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh and Khamis Mushait in Saudi Arabia.

What has been the regional response to the conflict?

On Saturday, Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud addressed the UN General Assembly (UNGA) and called on the international community to condemn Houthi actions against the kingdom and in Yemen.

At the same forum, Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al-Alimi-Bawzer warned that the Houthis were using shipping security “as a tool for blackmail”.

“It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he said.

The secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), Jassim Mohammed al-Budaiwi, on Saturday strongly condemned the recent Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia.

“This dangerous escalation constitutes a flagrant violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and poses a direct threat to the security and safety of civilians and the stability of the region,” al-Budaiwi said in a statement.

Iran has denied it has any role in the Yemen conflict. President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that the actions of the Houthis were not connected to Iran and that it stands in solidarity with “everyone subjected to injustice”.

He urged the Houthis and Saudi Arabia to resolve their differences through dialogue, saying “a brother should not fight his brother” and offered Iran’s help in ending the dispute. “We will not be warmongers,” he said.

On Friday, Iran delivered a ceasefire offer, which US President Donald Trump has rejected. It included Yemen and Lebanon. Tehran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz if the US fulfils its conditions, which include the lifting of Washington’s naval blockade on Iranian ports, a sanctions waiver and the release of Iran’s frozen assets.

Could Saudi allies join the conflict?

Saudi Arabia’s allies have rallied behind it amid intense fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis.

Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman Al Saud said on Saturday joint efforts with Pakistan would continue to confront attacks against the kingdom in accordance with the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed last month.

He held talks with Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir on Thursday. A day earlier, the military chiefs of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye jointly reviewed Houthi threats at a meeting in Riyadh.

Multiple Saudi cities, including Riyadh, have been hit by drones and missiles attributed to the Houthis.

Meanwhile, France confirmed on Friday that it was sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu, a Saudi port city on the Red Sea, but added that it was not joining the conflict. Yanbu has major oil storage and refining facilities and is connected by the East-West Pipeline, which can carry up to seven million barrels a day. The pipeline was damaged in a drone attack carried out by a group based in Iraq.



The US has so far not pledged military involvement, but the Saudi foreign minister said the kingdom was “continuing to work with our partners in the US”. On September 14, the commander of the US military’s Central Command, Brad Cooper, met the de facto Saudi ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in Jeddah in the wake of the Houthis’ seizure of Mocha.

What’s the state of humanitarian conditions?

At least 146,000 people have been displaced in the Arab region’s most impoverished country over the past three weeks, most of whom were uprooted from or within Taiz governorate, according to Yemen’s UNICEF country representative, Akhil Iyer.

More than 3,000 people fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti over several days earlier this month, Djibouti state media have reported, with the UN warning that the number could rise.

The number of casualties is still not confirmed as the rival sides have made conflicting claims. As per media reports, the death toll runs into the hundreds.

UNICEF has verified that at least 15 children have been killed and 14 injured in the conflict since early September, while three have been reported missing.

According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 22 million people in Yemen require humanitarian assistance and protection services; 18.3 million people face acute food shortages; and 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished.

Al-Huri, from the University of Saba, said millions of Yemenis have been suffering from war and “it’s high time for it to come to an end”.

“According to reports by UN organisations, more than five million Yemenis have left their homes for different places across Yemen, and those people are eager to return home. Their families want to live safely and with dignity,” he told Al Jazeera.

World.title: Plane carrying DR Congo military delegation crashes
World.content:
NewsFeed Plane carrying DR Congo military delegation crashes

A plane carrying a Congolese military delegation crashed in DR Congo, killing 17 people, including four civilians. Two senior members of the armed forces were among the victims, with the cause of the crash under investigation.

World.title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
World.content:
Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping within seven days because "they're losing so badly".

In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.

He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.

Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.

Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.

The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.

"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.

Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".

He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."

Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful.

He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".

Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"

He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.

Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.

Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.

Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.

World.title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope, during Lourdes visit
World.content:
Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors.

The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.

A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.

The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later.

Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.

"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."

The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.

The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.

Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.

On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.

World.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
World.content:
Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country.

Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured.

In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.

In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing.

Police said thirteen men and four women were killed.

Deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to AFP news agency.

Speaking at the scene, he said police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects.

In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital.

No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning.

The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township.

World.title: Killer Christa Pike is to be executed within days but her defence say she's a victim too
World.content:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.

Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.

"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.

Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

World.title: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
World.content:
At least 10 Nepali climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp in the Himalayas on Sunday.

The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning.

Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126 metre (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.

Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site.

Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told AFP news agency: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing."

The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.

Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.

Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.

The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja.

Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.

It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.

More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.

World.title: Four killed in helicopter crash near Montreal
World.content:
Four people have died after a helicopter crashed in a small town 50km (31 miles) from Montreal, Quebec's provincial police have told the BBC.

Emergency services were called to Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville shortly after 14:30 local time (19:30 BST) on Saturday afternoon, where they found the aircraft on fire and declared its occupants dead at the scene.

The victims have not yet been identified but the aircraft appeared to be a private helicopter, Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said.

An investigation into the crash is being led by the Major Crime Unit of the SÃ»retÃ© du QuÃ©bec, working alongside crime scene technicians as well as investigators from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.

The crash site is located near the Rang des Ãcossais road off Highway 10, according to Bilodeau.

In an emergency call, police were notified of a helicopter in distress that may have crashed and caught fire.

An hour after the call, the fire at the site had been brought under control though officials were still working at the crash site just before 22:00 local time (03:00 GMT).

The victims have not yet been identified and Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said this process may "take a few days."

World.title: Nor'easter brings flooding as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
World.content:
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.

The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.

States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.

In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree.

World.title: British national among six dead in building explosion close to Acropolis in Athens
World.content:
Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.

The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.

Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.

Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.

All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.

The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

World.title: 66th Independence: Kaduna prays for Nigeria as contractors praise Uba Sani’s debt payment plan
World.content:
Kaduna State Government has undertaken activities ahead of Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary with special prayers for peace, stability and economic prosperity, as contractors commended Governor Uba Sani for introducing a monthly payment plan to settle verified liabilities inherited from the previous administration.

The special prayers were held at the Sultan Bello Mosque in Kaduna after the Friday congregational prayer, with the Secretary to the State Government, AbdulKadir Mu’azu Meyere, other senior government officials and Muslim faithful in attendance.

The prayers, led by the mosque’s Deputy Chief Imam, Malam Abdullahi Aliyu, focused on the peace and stability of Nigeria and Kaduna State.

The cleric prayed for divine wisdom and guidance for President Bola Tinubu and Governor Uba Sani in steering the affairs of the country and the state respectively.

Imam urges leaders to uphold integrity

Mr Aliyu also urged political leaders and citizens to uphold trust, truthfulness and integrity, saying these values were essential to national development.

He reminded leaders that political offices and worldly power were temporary and that those entrusted with positions of authority would be accountable for how they discharged their responsibilities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“God tests us with trust, our wealth, our families, and the positions He has given us, whether big or small, to see how we will manage them—whether or not we will act with honesty, truthfulness and fairness,” he said.

The Deputy Chief Imam said the obligation to uphold trust and honesty applied to both governance and commercial activities.

He added that while those who uphold trust could be elevated in this world, betrayal of trust carried serious consequences.

“No matter how long a person lives, he will leave everything behind, and only his good deeds will accompany him to the grave,” he said.

Contractors hail Uba Sani’s payment plan

Meanwhile, the Chairman of the Contractors Association of Kaduna State, Ahmed Baba, has commended Governor Uba Sani for introducing a monthly payment arrangement to settle verified debts inherited from the previous administration.

Mr Baba spoke after a meeting between senior state government officials and the leadership of the association in Kaduna.

He said Mr Sani inherited substantial liabilities but had demonstrated that government was a continuum by taking steps to settle outstanding payments owed to contractors who executed projects for the state under the previous administration.

According to him, the monthly payment arrangement would enable the government to systematically clear verified inherited liabilities while reducing the financial burden on affected contractors.

“Despite inheriting a huge burden of outstanding liabilities, His Excellency has demonstrated true leadership. He has made it clear that government is a continuum and that contractors must not suffer for their service to the state.

“The monthly payment structure that the Governor has approved is a lifeline to many of our members,” he said.

Mr Baba also said contractors handling projects awarded by the present administration had not been owed since the inception of Mr Sani’s government.

He described the development as encouraging for the construction sector and pledged the association’s support for the administration’s infrastructure development programme.

He urged contractors to maintain quality and ensure timely delivery of projects across the state.

Independence activities

The Commissioner for Information and Culture, Ahmed Maiyaki, said the special prayers were part of activities lined up to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary.

He said an inter-denominational church service would be held at Living Faith Church, Barnawa, on Sunday, with the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, James Kanyip, representing the governor.

According to him, the activities will culminate in an official Independence Day parade at Murtala Mohammed Square, Kaduna, on Thursday, October 1, to be presided over by Governor Uba Sani.

World.title: ‘I’m like three women’: Olori Atuwatse says Olu of Warri won’t embrace polygamy
World.content:
Olori Atuwatse III, wife of the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, has said her husband will not change his position on polygamy.

The Queen commented during an exclusive interview with BBC News Pidgin published on 23 September.

She was asked whether she would accept her husband taking another wife if he changed his mind about polygamy.

Olori Atuwatse said she did not expect the monarch to change his position.

“First of all, His Majesty will not change his mind about polygamy, so let us settle that first,” she said.

She added jokingly, “I alone, one person, I am like three women, so I am fine with that.”

The Queen also acknowledged that sharing her husband’s time can sometimes be difficult because of his many responsibilities as the Olu of Warri.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She said the couple is learning how to manage the demands of his role, but added, “I just want him for myself.”

What the Olu said

Olori Atuwatse’s comments come months after her husband explained why he had chosen not to marry more than one wife.

In January, PREMIUM TIMES reported Olu’s position, including his explanation for choosing to remain married to one woman.

He said his role as king already placed heavy demands on his time and that he did not want to complicate his family life.

“As for marrying many wives, I do not know; God did not give me that grace,” he said.

The monarch also said he valued the peace and stability of his home and wanted to spend time with his family when he was away from his public duties.

Ogiame Atuwatse III and Olori Atuwatse married in 2014 and have three children.

The Queen’s latest comments come as she speaks publicly about the same issue her husband addressed earlier this year, making clear that she supports his decision to remain in a monogamous marriage.

World.title: Nigeria, UK advance negotiations on trade cooperation deal
World.content:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC) of the United Kingdom have deepened discussions on a trade cooperation deal.

The development followed a high-level bilateral meeting with the HMRC delegation, led by its Policy Adviser, Syed Moinuddin, at the NCS headquarters in Abuja.

A statement on the meeting was issued to journalists in Abuja by NCS’s Spokesperson, Abdullahi Maiwada, on Sunday.

Mr Maiwada said the meeting was to finalise a Customs Mutual Administrative Assistance Agreement (CMAA) to strengthen information sharing, compliance and trade facilitation between the two countries.

The NCS Comptroller-General (C-G), Bashir Adeniyi, said the engagement was part of efforts to conclude negotiations on the agreement ahead of its proposed signing in December.

The C-G was represented by Nafi’u Isyaku, the assistant comptroller-general (ACG) of customs in charge of the Strategic, Research and Policy Department.

Mr Adeniyi said negotiations had been conducted virtually for about six months before the two sides decided to meet physically at the NCS headquarters to finalise outstanding issues.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We decided to come here in person so that we can finalise the negotiations before the final signing, which hopefully is coming up in the first week of December during the World Customs Organisation Policy Commission meeting,” he said.

On his part, HMRC official Syed Moinuddin described the meeting as an opportunity for both customs administrations to work through areas of cooperation and establish a framework that reflected the interests of the two authorities.

Mr Moinuddin said the engagement had provided an opportunity to strengthen the relationship between the NCS and HMRC within the wider customs family.

Also speaking, Louisa Bentley, head of bilateral relations and agreements at HMRC, said negotiations held over the two days had been successful, and both sides were close to finalising the agreement.

Ms Bentley said the agreement would boost trade by improving compliance and information sharing between HMRC and the NCS, while also enhancing compliance and trade facilitation for both partners in global trade opportunities.

She commended the reforms and operational improvements observed during a tour of key NCS facilities, including the Trade Modernisation Project Limited office, the Pre-Arrival Assessment Report office, and the Nigeria Customs Broadcasting Network station.

ALSO READ: BRICS countries to trade in local currencies

“We have seen significant developments in technology and personnel training, adding that the reforms would support more modern and efficient trade processes,” she said.

The two-day meeting ended with a tour of key Customs departments to showcase the NCS reforms and operational developments to the HMRC delegation.(NAN)

World.title: CARSPO 2026: Philips praises Uzodimma, Disu for police retreat
World.content:
Shina Philips, one of the organisers of the Conference and Retreat for Senior Police Officers (CARSPO), has praised Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma and Inspector-General of Police Olatunji Disu for their roles in the just-concluded 2026 edition of the conference.

Mr Philips, in an interview with PREMIUM TIMES on Sunday, said their contributions supported the broader objective of CARSPO, which is to help the Nigeria Police Force review and adapt its strategies in response to the changing nature of crime and security threats.

He said criminals were constantly evolving their methods, making it necessary for the police to regularly reassess their strategies, technology, and approach to policing.

“Crime is evolving. Criminals are evolving. So, the police are rethinking their strategic and tactical approaches. They are looking at themselves to rejig the system and reposition themselves,” he said.

Mr Philips illustrated the need for constant adaptation with an expression: “Any man watching a masquerade cannot stand in one place.”

His comments offer an insight into the thinking behind CARSPO, which began in 2019 and has evolved in its themes and format as new security challenges have emerged.

The sixth edition was held in Owerri, Imo State, from 21 to 23 September, with the theme, “Developing a Nigerian Police Roadmap for Effective Management of Security During Elections.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

While the 2026 edition focused largely on election security ahead of the 2027 general elections, participants also examined broader policing issues, including artificial intelligence, intelligence-led policing, leadership, communication, inter-agency cooperation and public trust.

CARSPO’s changing approach

Mr Philips said the conference itself had changed over the years in response to developments in policing and the wider security environment.

Previous editions featured syndicate meetings where participants broke into groups to discuss specific issues.

This year, organisers introduced panel discussions involving retired senior police officers who shared their experiences and answered questions from serving officers.

Mr Philips said the format allowed serving officers to draw from the experience of retired officers while examining whether previous approaches remained relevant to present-day policing.

Another feature introduced at the 2026 edition was the participation of the host state’s governor in discussions on policing.

Why Imo featured prominently

Imo State has hosted three of the six editions of CARSPO since its inception, making Owerri the venue for half of the conferences.

Governor Uzodimma welcomed participants to the 2026 edition and delivered a lecture from the state government’s perspective.

He discussed the state’s approach to security, including its engagement with security agencies and communities, as well as the establishment of the Imo State Vigilante Service.

Mr Philips said bringing the governor into the programme provided police officers with a perspective different from the operational and administrative discussions within the Force.

He said the arrangement allowed officers to understand government expectations and consider how state authorities and the police could work together on security.

Mr Philips also expressed appreciation to the governor for supporting the conference and making Imo available to host CARSPO for the third time.

Mr Uzodinma later hosted the police leadership, participants and other guests to a dinner in Owerri.

Election security takes centre stage

While CARSPO has addressed broader policing issues since its inception, the 2026 edition placed election security at the centre because of the 2027 elections.

Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, warned officers against political bias and stressed the need for the Force to remain neutral.

“We protect citizens and enforce the law. We do not decide political outcomes,” Mr Disu said.

He warned that officers who take sides, collude with political actors, harass voters or abuse police powers would be investigated and punished.

“Our duty does not begin on election day. It covers the whole electoral cycle,” he said.

The conference subsequently recommended a comprehensive election-security roadmap covering the period before, during and after elections.

It also called for stronger intelligence gathering, inter-agency coordination, adequate logistics, specialised training, effective communication, and accountability.

The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Joash Amupitan, said the police had made efforts to improve their professionalism during recent elections.

“The question is whether the Nigerian police is playing its role properly as far as the election is concerned. And in answer as far as I’m concerned, the police have tried so much. They are trying to be professional in recent elections,” Mr Amupitan said.

He also raised the issue of funding, saying effective election security required adequate resources.

“If we want the election to be perfect, there must be a cost for it,” he said.

Technology changes policing

The question of adapting to new threats also featured in discussions on technology.

Ross Alabo-George, principal consultant at Proxy Logic, a tech-based company, said the police needed to improve their processes before attempting digital transformation.

“You cannot digitise or transform digitally without a solid process,” he said.

He advocated greater integration of police data, artificial intelligence and analytics, performance management and public trust.

Mr Disu said the Force was already deploying technologies including CCTV, facial recognition and analytics.

“Talking about AI in the police is not a new thing,” he said.

“I’ve seen instances where I’ve been able to solve matters through CCTV and facial recognition.”

He, however, cautioned that artificial intelligence must be used carefully.

“What you get out of AI is as good as the prompt you impute in it. Prompts make the difference in the use of AI,” he said.

Beyond the 2027 elections

For Mr Philips, the election-security focus of the 2026 conference should not be interpreted as the entire purpose of CARSPO.

“That’s our prayer. That’s the target,” he said when asked about the 2027 elections.

“But there is a life beyond 2027, and there’s a life beyond the next year’s election.”

The President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Oyinkansola Badejo-Okusanya, also stressed the need for cooperation between the police and lawyers in protecting the rule of law, lives and property.

“As partners in progress, aiming for the same goal, [protection] of the rule of law, [protection] of lives and property, we all have a role to play. And we are working together,” she said.

The conference ended with recommendations covering election security, intelligence-led policing, technology, training, communication and institutional accountability.

Mr Disu told senior officers that the real test would be how the resolutions were implemented upon their return to their commands.

He asked that the lessons be shared with deputy commissioners of police, area commanders, divisional police officers, and tactical commanders.

For Mr Philips, that process of reviewing and adapting is central to the continuing purpose of CARSPO: ensuring that the police do not confront new security challenges with strategies designed for an earlier era.

World.title: Army raids terrorists’ enclave, neutralises suspect, recovers arms – Official
World.content:
Troops of Sector 2 Operation FANSAN YAMMA have raided a suspected terrorists’ hideout where they neutralised a suspected terrorist and recovered weapon and motorcycle in Gudu Local Government Area.

This was contained in a statement issued by the spokesperson of the 8 Division, Nigerian Army, Olaniyi Osoba, on Sunday in Sokoto.

Mr Osoba, a Lt. Col., said the troops acted on credible intelligence and advanced toward a suspected terrorists’ camp in the vicinity of Karani village.

According to him, upon making contact with the hostile elements, the troops responded with decisive firepower, neutralising one terrorist while others fled to the nearby bushes.

He said an exploratory search of the camp led to the recovery of one AK-47 rifle with ammunition.

“The troops recovered items which include one AK-47 rifle loaded with live ammunition, one operational motorcycle, military camouflage uniforms and various maintenance tools and logistical supplies.

“Troops executed clearance operations in the surrounding forest axis to dominate the general area and deny fleeing elements freedom of action,” Mr Osoba said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

(NAN)

World.title: Sowore returns to Nigeria, set for 2027 presidential campaign
World.content:
Omoyele Sowore, the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), has returned to Nigeria from the United States on Sunday to resume his 2027 presidential campaign.

Mr Sowore disclosed this in a statement issued to journalists on Sunday.

He expressed excitement about his return to his family and country after his trip to the US.

According to him, he left for the US over what he described as arrests, detention, travel restrictions and the seizure of his international passport by Nigerian security agencies.

Mr Sowore said that while in the United States, he engaged Nigerians in the diaspora, supporters, activists and other stakeholders on the state of the country and his political agenda.

He also said he participated in a solidarity march for Palestine in New York and continued his advocacy for voting rights for Nigerians living abroad.

The AAC presidential candidate said he remained committed to the participation of Nigerians in the diaspora in the country’s democratic process.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said an AAC administration would pursue the implementation of diaspora voting if elected president in 2027.

Mr Sowore said he was expected to arrive at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos before proceeding to Abuja.

He said he would also continue to attend court proceedings in connection with the cybercrime case instituted against him by the State Security Services (SSS) in 2025.

The candidate said his return would mark another phase of his nationwide campaign ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

“I plan to engage workers, students, youths, women, farmers, traders, professionals and communities across the country, ” he said.

He said the engagements would focus on the political, social and economic issues contained in the AAC’s 2027 agenda.

He said the campaign would seek to mobilise Nigerians around issues including equal rights, justice, peace, security and economic development.

Mr Sowore said the 2027 election would provide Nigerians with an opportunity to decide on the direction of the country’s political leadership.

“My campaign will continue to advocate fundamental political, social and economic transformation, ” he said.

The AAC candidate said he remained committed to taking his message directly to Nigerians across the country.

“I will continue the campaign and engagements with Nigerians as the 2027 election approaches, “he said.

(NAN)

World.title: NDLEA intercepts N3bn opioids at Lagos airport, arrests man with 72 cocaine wraps
World.content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) says it has intercepted 2.55 million tablets of opioids worth more than N3 billion at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport (MMIA), Lagos.

According to a statement on Sunday by the NDLEA spokesperson Femi Babafemi, the drugs, weighing 1,640.55kg, were seized on Tuesday, 22 September, during a joint examination of three consignments at the airport’s import shed.

The consignments contained Tramaking 225mg, Tramaking 250mg and Royal Tapentadol 250mg. They were imported from India and Bangladesh through Qatar Airways, RwandAir and Ethiopian Airlines.

The seizure adds to a series of major opioid interceptions reported at the Lagos airport this year.

In August, the NDLEA said it seized 3.9 million tablets of Tramaking and Tapentadol, weighing 2,787.40 kg and valued at more than N4.6 billion.

In May, it reported another seizure of 1,825,710 tablets of Tapentadol 250mg, which it valued at N2.19 billion.

Newlywed arrested with 72 cocaine wraps

At the Akanu Ibiam International Airport (AIIA), Enugu, NDLEA operatives arrested a 25-year-old businessman, Lovely Chukwulobelu, who allegedly ingested 72 wraps of cocaine before attempting to travel to Portugal.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Chukwulobelu was arrested at the departure hall on Thursday, 25 September, while preparing to board an Ethiopian Airlines flight to Portugal through Addis Ababa.

The agency said it placed him under observation, and he later excreted all 72 wraps.

NDLEA noted that the suspect was wearing a wedding ring when he was arrested. He told investigators that he previously operated a car decoration business at the Trade Fair Complex in Ojo, Lagos.

He relocated to Portugal in May 2023 but returned to Nigeria for his wedding on 13 September.

The NDLEA stated that he told investigators that he became involved in drug trafficking to raise money to offset expenses from the wedding.

Two Togolese arrested with cannabis in Oyo

In Oyo State, operatives arrested two Togolese nationals, Yinusa Abdulsamad, 35, and Fatai Baba, 33, along the Iganna-Ilero Road in Iganna in the Kajola Local Government Area of Oyo State, on Saturday.

The agency noted that the men were using two pickup vans to transport 305.6kg of cannabis allegedly sourced from Ghana.

At the Seme border in Badagry, Lagos, five other men were arrested with 420 cartons of nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas.

The consignment weighed 1,688.4kg and was allegedly being transported from the border into Lagos in two vehicles.

The suspects were identified as Kingsley John, 40; John Chibuike Okeke, 44; Lamidi Ismaila, 40; Babatunde Samuel, 42; and Afeesu Idowu, 47.

Cannabis seized in Bauchi, farms destroyed in Edo

In Bauchi State, NDLEA operatives arrested Umar Hamidu, 35, and Abdulkarim Salihu, 45, along the Maiduguri bypass.

They were allegedly carrying 300 compressed blocks of cannabis weighing 262.5kg, concealed in a false compartment of a truck marked MUB757 YH.

In Edo State, operatives, assisted by soldiers, destroyed two cannabis farms at Eko Camp, Ilushi, on Wednesday, 23 September.

The farms had an estimated combined yield of 1,360.23kg of cannabis, the agency said.

In Lagos, two women, Odumabo Kehinde, 36, and Obiekwe Chioma, 40, were arrested during a raid on Anifowoshe Street, Mushin, on Saturday.

The NDLEA said 3.4kg of cannabis was recovered from them.

In a separate operation the same day, operatives arrested 58-year-old Ugwu Johnson at Ebute-Ero motor park.

The agency said officers recovered 5.920kg of cannabis, 2,400 ampoules of pentazocine injection, 8,400 tablets of nitrazepam and 40,000 pills of tramadol from him.

The NDLEA also said its commands across the country continued their War Against Drug Abuse (WADA) sensitisation activities during the week.

Its chairman, Buba Marwa, commended officers involved in the operations.

Mr Marwa, a retired brigadier general, urged them to sustain efforts to curb drug trafficking and abuse.

World.title: Air Peace blames fuel shortage, weather for Abuja-Maiduguri flight cancellation
World.content:
Air Peace has attributed the cancellation of its Abuja-Maiduguri flight on Saturday to aviation fuel shortage in Abuja and a subsequent restriction on operations at the Maiduguri airport.

The airline said the initial delays to its Abuja operations were caused by the unavailability of Jet A1 aviation fuel, which also affected other airlines operating from the airport.

It added that the situation improved after fuel became available and affected flights resumed, but its Abuja-Maiduguri service could not operate after the Maiduguri control tower withdrew an earlier extension for the flight to arrive beyond sunset.

Air Peace disclosed this in a statement following videos and reports of passengers expressing frustration over the disruption at Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja.

Why the flight was cancelled

According to the airline, the Maiduguri flight was initially expected to operate after the delay in Abuja operations had been resolved.

It said the control tower at the Maiduguri airport had initially granted an extension for the flight to arrive, but later, around the time passengers were being called for boarding, informed the airline that the airport had become subject to visual flight rules and would no longer operate beyond sunset.

Visual flight rules, or VFR, generally require pilots to operate with specified visual conditions rather than relying on instrument flight procedures.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Air Peace said the change meant it could no longer operate the Abuja-Maiduguri service as planned.

The airline noted that it subsequently cancelled the flight and made arrangements to accommodate the affected passengers in a hotel.

It added that arrangements had been made to operate the flight the following day.

Passengers’ rights

The disruption comes amid increased scrutiny of flight delays and cancellations in Nigeria, as well as of how airlines handle passengers when services are disrupted.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) recorded 7,961 domestic flights in August, of which 4,765 were delayed, and 36 were cancelled.

Air Peace accounted for 1,330 of the delayed flights in the NCAA’s dataset, representing 71.4 per cent of the 1,864 flights recorded for the airline.

The airline, however, disputed the figures, saying it operated 2,564 flights during the month and that more than 700 flights were not captured in the NCAA data. It also said only 391 of its delayed flights were caused by factors within its operations.

The latest disruption also comes days after the NCAA directed Air Peace to prepare a compensation package for passengers affected by a delayed Lagos-Enugu flight.

The regulator said its preliminary investigation found that the airline had sent passengers the wrong notification about the rescheduled flight.

Under the NCAA’s Part 19 regulations, airlines have obligations to passengers during delays and cancellations, including providing information and assistance within specified circumstances. For domestic flights, passengers are entitled to refreshments after a two-hour delay, while longer disruptions can trigger reimbursement, rerouting, accommodation, and, in qualifying circumstances, compensation.

The NCAA has also repeatedly stressed the importance of timely information and passenger care during disruptions.

Air Peace’s response

Air Peace said passengers affected by Saturday’s disruption were informed about the delays and provided with refreshments.

Following the cancellation, the airline said the affected passengers were provided with hotel accommodation and that arrangements were being made for the flight to operate the next day.

“We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused to our esteemed passengers and appreciate their patience and understanding,” the airline said.

It added that the safety and well-being of passengers remained its priority.

World.title: LAWMA arrests 14 over illegal waste dumping
World.content:
By Olasunkanmi Akoni

LAGOS — The Lagos Waste Management Authority, LAWMA, has intensified its enforcement operations across the state, arresting 14 persons for alleged waste-related offences and seizing scores of carts from suspected illegal waste collectors.

The enforcement operations were carried out on Lagos Island and along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway as part of efforts to strengthen compliance with waste management regulations and curb activities undermining orderly waste collection and disposal.

The Managing Director of LAWMA, Dr Muyiwa Gbadegesin, said the 14 suspects were arrested at the weekend during an operation covering Idumota, Oke-Popo, Tom Jones and Tinubu areas of Lagos Island.

According to him, the suspects were arrested for various alleged waste-related offences, including the illegal disposal of waste into the lagoon.

The suspects were identified as Buhari Danbaba, 35; Ayo Akindele, 25; Shamsudeen Lawal, 25; Ibrahim Isiaka, 20; Azeez Alatilehin, 20; Quadri Adisa, 23; Ogunbado Sobur, 20; Salimonu Oluwadamilare, 29; Odunayo Arinola, 35; Azeez Roqeeb, 24; Sherifdeen Mudashiru, 31; Nurudeen Saliu, 19; Zazilo Bello, 21; and Augustine Eje, 35.

Gbadegesin said the authority also intensified enforcement against illegal waste collection along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway, where its operatives conducted an operation from Mile 2 to Okokomaiko and seized scores of carts allegedly used for unauthorised waste collection.
