World.title: LAA Seeks Aviation Partnerships, Investment at Major African Airports Conference in Nigeria
World.content:
Hughes-led delegation explores technical cooperation, infrastructure support and funding opportunities to modernize Liberia’s airport system

HARBel, Margibi County — The Liberia Airport Authority (LAA) says it is seeking technical partnerships, investment and logistical support to strengthen Liberia’s aviation infrastructure as it participates in a major regional airport conference in Abuja, Nigeria.

The LAA delegation, led by Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Ernest R. Hughes, with Chief Financial Officer Victor Debah, is attending the Airports Council International (ACI) Africa 35th Annual General Assembly, 75th Board and Committee Meetings, Regional Conference and Exhibition, running from September 19 to 25, 2026.



According to a press release issued by the Authority, the weeklong gathering is bringing together airport executives, policymakers, regulators, development partners and aviation industry stakeholders to discuss the future of African aviation under the theme, “Next-Gen Airports: Driving Performance and Resilience.”

The LAA said its participation is intended to strengthen Liberia’s engagement with regional and international aviation institutions while exploring opportunities to improve airport operations, infrastructure and service delivery.

During the conference, the delegation is expected to hold bilateral and multilateral discussions with airport authorities, aviation agencies, development partners, financial institutions and industry stakeholders.

The proposed engagements will focus on technical assistance, operational support, logistics cooperation, capacity development, infrastructure advancement and institutional strengthening.

The Authority said it also plans to explore opportunities for investment, innovation, knowledge transfer and resource mobilization to support the development of Liberia’s airports.

Hughes Pursues Regional Aviation Cooperation

Beyond the ACI Africa conference, Hughes is undertaking separate engagements with key Nigerian aviation institutions, including the Nigeria Airspace Management Agency (NAMA), the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) and the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN).

The discussions are intended to strengthen technical cooperation and secure logistical and capital support that could improve the safety, efficiency and sustainability of Liberia’s aviation infrastructure.

The LAA said the engagements align with its broader objectives of strengthening aviation safety, advancing airport infrastructure development and building technical partnerships to support the long-term growth of the sector.

The Authority also views the conference as an opportunity to deepen regional integration, exchange best practices with other airport operators and explore emerging technologies that could support Liberia’s aviation modernization efforts.

LAA Links Participation to National Development

The Authority said its participation reflects its commitment to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s national development agenda, particularly in improving infrastructure, strengthening regional cooperation and expanding transportation connectivity.

ACI Africa, the regional arm of Airports Council International, represents African airports and promotes advocacy, capacity-building, innovation, connectivity and sustainable growth across the continent’s aviation industry.

The LAA said it remains committed to developing a modern, safe, secure, efficient and resilient airport system capable of supporting economic growth, trade, tourism and regional connectivity while improving services for the traveling public.

The press release did not specify the amount of funding or capital support being sought, identify any agreements finalized during the engagements, or provide a timeline for the anticipated infrastructure improvements.

World.title: Speaking Out Is Citizenship, Not Rebellion, Matambo Tells Zambians
World.content:
Opposition Tonse Alliance figure Brian “Coach” Matambo has said Zambia’s post-election crisis is the result of five years of public silence. In a video address released on Sunday, he said citizens repeatedly allowed the boundaries of political freedom to shift because those under attack were opposition politicians.

The 31-minute address, titled “The Cost of Silence: How Zambia Reached the Crisis of 2026”, accompanies the documentary “Silence Brought Us Here”. In it, Mr Matambo traces what he describes as a steady erosion of democratic space from 2021 to the treason arrests that followed the August polls. “We did not just land here. We did not just wake up after the 2026 election and suddenly discover that something had gone terribly wrong with our democracy,” he said. “This has been coming.”

Watch the full video and read the complete column here.

Mr Matambo began with the 2021 transfer of power, when former President Edgar Lungu conceded defeat and handed over peacefully. That moment strengthened Zambia, he said, but what followed began to weaken it. He cited the loss of parliamentary seats by Bowman Lusambo and Joseph Malanji, and what he called concocted criminal cases against Ronald Chitotela. Many Zambians, he said, dismissed these as the PF paying the price for losing power.

“Democracy is not tested by how government treats its friends. Democracy is tested by how government treats its opponents,” Mr Matambo said. “The rights of your political opponent are also your own rights.”

He listed a series of developments he said the public had accepted in turn: police blocking opposition rallies, cyber laws passed despite warnings from lawyers, civil society and journalists, and Bill 7. He noted that the Constitutional Court had itself found the Bill 7 process inconsistent with the spirit of the Constitution and requiring wider consultation. Parliament passed it anyway, and “again, Zambia moved on,” he said.

Mr Matambo reserved some of his sharpest criticism for the appointment of Mwangala Zaloumis as chairperson of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). He said she had previously acted as President Hakainde Hichilema‘s lawyer, and that opposition MPs had raised concerns at the time. He compared it to a World Cup qualifier refereed by someone who once worked for the opposing coach. “You cannot have a referee who supports one of the teams,” he said.

Turning to the former head of State, Mr Matambo said Zambians had watched Edgar Lungu humiliated after leaving office, from police involvement in his jogging to disputes over his travel and medical care abroad. He also cited the arrest of former First Lady Esther Lungu, and the Government’s legal battle with the family in South Africa over Mr Lungu’s remains, which he said lasted more than a year. “You don’t defend somebody’s rights because you like them. You defend their rights because they are rights. Otherwise, they are not rights. They are favours,” he said.

Mr Matambo named opposition figures who he said had spoken out and ended up behind bars. They include Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu, Munir Zulu, Celestine Mukandila, Jay Jay Banda and Raphael Nakacinda. He said they were among hundreds held “for merely speaking out”.

On the August election, he said he personally witnessed blocked roads, police surveillance and disrupted rallies. He described a suspension of counting for more than two hours, the military taking over polling stations, raids on Mr Mundubile’s home and on Tonse offices in Ibex Hill, and the arrest of Bishop Trevor Mwamba among others.

He called 14 August “the night democracy died”. Mr Matambo said former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead by soldiers who found him unarmed in a wardrobe during a security operation at Mr Mundubile’s home. He said a militia story was then used to charge Mr Mundubile and his running mate, Mr Zulu, with treason. He described the events as “a coup against the democratic process itself”, adding: “I choose my words very, very carefully.”

“August 2026 was not the beginning. August 2026 was the consequence,” he said. “We walked here.”

The address closes with an appeal for peaceful civic speech. Mr Matambo said speaking out did not mean insulting, lying or threatening anyone. “It means telling those in power: I disagree. That is not rebellion. That is citizenship,” he said.

He urged fellow opposition leaders to set aside party interests until democratic institutions are secured. “I want a Zambia where my candidate can lose and I can believe that he genuinely lost,” he said. “I want a Zambia where UPND can lose and peacefully hand over power.”

Mr Matambo ended by calling on Zambians to act now rather than wait. “Zambia must speak before the boundaries move again,” he said.

Watch the full video and read Brian Matambo’s complete column here.

World.title: The cost of silence: how Zambia walked into the crisis of 2026
World.content:
The cost of silence: how Zambia walked into the crisis of 2026

Democratic decline rarely arrives in a single dramatic moment. It comes gradually, when actions that once seemed exceptional become normal, and when citizens begin treating the rights of political opponents as somebody else’s problem. Democracy is not protected only when our own side is under attack. Its real test comes when we are prepared to defend the rights of people with whom we disagree.

Zambians, we need to talk. There is something very important we are missing about the crisis our country finds itself in today. We did not just land here. We did not wake up after the 2026 election and suddenly discover that something had gone terribly wrong with our democracy.

No. This has been coming. It has been building slowly, one incident after another, one institution after another, one boundary after another. And every time the boundary moved, Zambia adjusted.

We complained for a few days. We fought it out on Facebook and discussed it on the radio. Then we moved on, and the Government learned something from our silence: that Zambia would always move on. That is how we got here.

Go back to 2021. Edgar Lungu lost an election, conceded and handed over power peacefully. Whatever you thought of him, that moment strengthened Zambia. Power changed hands with no soldiers, no refusal to leave State House and no constitutional crisis. One president handed over to another, and that was the Zambia we inherited in 2021.

But look at what happened afterwards. Bowman Lusambo and Joseph Malanji had their parliamentary seats taken from them through the institutions of Parliament and the judiciary. Remember Ronald Chitotela? Concocted criminal cases, one after another. Because these were PF politicians, many Zambians convinced themselves that this was simply the PF suffering the consequences of losing power.

So we stayed quiet. Some even celebrated. But we missed the bigger questions. What was happening to our institutions? What precedents were being set?

Democracy is not tested by how a government treats its friends. It is tested by how a government treats its opponents. The rights of your political opponent are also your own rights. The institution you allow to be abused today against somebody you dislike may be the very institution you will need tomorrow, when the Government comes for somebody you love.

We did not see it that way. We said: that is Bowman, that is Malanji, that is Chitotela, that is PF. And we moved on.

Then opposition rallies became almost impossible to hold. Police stopped meetings, roads were blocked and political gatherings were cancelled. In a multi-party democracy, an opposition party increasingly had to negotiate with the police simply to speak to the people it wished to govern. Again, Zambia adjusted. We normalised it.

Then came the cyber laws, and we were warned. Lawyers warned us. Civil society warned us. Journalists warned us. They said these laws were dangerous, that the powers they created could and would be abused, and that they could become an instrument for controlling speech.

Many Zambians simply replied: if you have done nothing wrong, what are you afraid of? Again, we missed the point. The question was never whether President Hakainde Hichilema would personally sit somewhere reading your WhatsApp messages and decide that you were guilty.

The question was how much power we were comfortable giving the State over the speech of its citizens. How much power? Governments change and presidents change, but the powers handed to the State remain.

Then came Bill 7, and it was the Constitutional Court itself that raised the alarm. Not the PF, not Mundubile, not Makebi, not some opposition blogger: the Constitutional Court. It found that the process undertaken was inconsistent with the spirit of the Constitution and required wider consultation.

That should have been a major constitutional moment for this country. When the Constitutional Court speaks about the Constitution, the Government is supposed to listen. But we all know what happened. Somehow the political process found its way around the obstacle. Bill 7 was retained, the vote happened in Parliament, Bill 7 became law, and again Zambia moved on.

Somewhere along this road, something else happened that I believe Zambia will one day look back on and ask: why did we allow this? Mwangala Zaloumis was appointed chairperson of the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ).

Concerns were raised immediately. This was somebody who had previously acted as Hakainde Hichilema‘s lawyer, so there was a relationship there. Opposition MPs raised concerns about links to the UPND. People questioned the political associations surrounding appointments to the very institution that would eventually referee an election involving Hakainde Hichilema. And again, Zambia moved on.

But think about this. Forget the UPND. Forget the opposition. Forget Hakainde Hichilema. Forget Mwangala Zaloumis. Let us just use common sense: you cannot have a referee who supports one of the teams.

It does not matter how qualified the referee is. It does not matter how professional he promises to be. The moment a referee walks onto the field carrying the history and associations of one of the competitors, confidence in the match is already damaged.

Imagine Zambia playing a World Cup qualifier where the referee previously worked for the opposing coach. Would we wait until the 89th minute, when he awards a penalty, before raising the question? Of course not. We would say: we know this man, he worked for that coach, he cannot referee this game. We would demand a change of referee before kick-off.

We would not do it because we had proved he was going to cheat. We would do it because the integrity of the competition requires a referee whose independence cannot reasonably be questioned. That is how serious institutions protect themselves, and the ECZ should have been protected from even the appearance of political allegiance.

We failed to do that with the ECZ and Mwangala Zaloumis. Four years later, that same institution was refereeing the most consequential election in our country’s history. We were warned. Again, we moved on.

Then there was Edgar Lungu, and this is another place where our politics blinded us. He had lost an election and handed over power. He was no longer president, but he was still a former Head of State. And we watched the State humiliate him again and again.

There was a time when a former president of this country could not even go jogging without the police becoming involved. Imagine that. A man who had commanded the armed forces of this Republic, who had occupied State House and who had handed over power peacefully, could not go for a jog. He could not step out of his house.

We found ourselves watching a dispute over whether Edgar Lungu could go jogging, and some Zambians laughed because they did not like him. Then came the disputes over his movements and his travel. Even his attempt to get medical care outside the country became another point of confrontation. How petty. How petty.

And again, people said: that is Lungu, that is the PF, that is their problem.

Then his wife was arrested. Former First Lady Esther Lungu, a woman who had occupied State House as First Lady of this country, found herself locked up. It arose from what was presented as a family property dispute, one in which she maintains she was herself the aggrieved party. Somehow the State, the UPND, whoever was in charge, found it necessary to make her the victim.

Again, many Zambians stayed quiet because it was Esther Lungu, because it was the Lungu family, because it was PF. That is where we fail to understand something fundamental.

You do not defend somebody’s rights because you like them. You defend their rights because they are rights. Otherwise they are not rights; they are favours, and favours disappear when the wrong person comes to power. The Bill of Rights is not a list of favours. It is a list of rights.

When Edgar Lungu died, you would think death would finally end this political war. It did not. The man died in South Africa, leaving a widow, children and a grieving family.

Instead of allowing that family to bury their husband, father, brother and relative, the full might of the Zambian State sued the widow in the courts of a foreign country. Imagine that for a moment. The Government fought the family over the remains of Edgar Lungu for more than a year. And even when it lost the case, it refused to pay the costs.

Forget the politics for a moment. A woman loses her husband and then spends more than a year fighting the government of her own country, in a foreign court, over his body. If you think that is normal, if you can find a way to justify it, you need to be checked. Where was our humanity? Where was Zambia? Where were our voices?

Some people celebrated because the dead man was Edgar Lungu. Others simply looked away. And again, the boundaries moved.

This is the pattern I want you to see: every time the boundary moves, the people warning us are dismissed. Brian Mundubile spoke. Makebi Zulu spoke. Munir Zulu spoke. Celestine Mukandila spoke. Jay Jay Banda spoke. Raphael Nakacinda spoke. Others spoke.

And what happened? One after another, they became enemies of the State: troublemakers, threats to the UPND, people who needed to be arrested and silenced. Today they sit in prison alongside hundreds of others, merely for speaking out and exercising their rights. So perhaps Zambia needs to ask herself whether these people were really the problem, or whether some of them were warning us about the problem.

Then came the 2026 election, and suddenly all the things we had treated as separate incidents began to come together. I hope that one day we go to our colleagues in prison and say: you warned us.

The referee we had questioned was now refereeing the match. The opposition had been restricted by the police and the system for years, struggling even to hold rallies, and now it had to campaign for national power. The cyber security machinery we had warned against was now in place, and the constitutional boundaries we had watched being pushed had already moved.

The political opponents arrested over the years had already taught Zambia what would happen to dissenters. They were made an example: you speak, we lock you up.

When the August 2026 election came, we saw opposition campaigns blocked. We experienced it ourselves; I was there. Roads were blocked, police followed us, rallies were stopped, meetings were disrupted and people were arrested. Ruling party violence reached even the police, with an officer hacked on the head by a ruling party cadre. And Zambia kept moving.

Then came election day. Counting was suspended for more than two hours, and then the military took over polling stations. Next came the raids on Brian Mundubile‘s home and on our offices; some of you may have seen that they raided our offices in Ibex Hill. Then innocent people were arrested, among them Bishop Trevor Mwamba and Dr Emmanuel Nkoma.

Then came Honourable Mutotwe Kafwaya. For me, 14 August 2026 is the night democracy died, because when Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed, something fundamental changed.

This was no longer Bowman Lusambo‘s parliamentary seat. It was no longer Edgar Lungu‘s jogging, an opposition rally being cancelled, or somebody being arrested for something they had said. This was much deeper. A man was dead. A former government minister was killed in cold blood, murdered during what was called a security operation at the home of Brian Mundubile, the principal opposition presidential candidate, in the middle of an election dispute.

Armed soldiers descended on Mr Mundubile‘s home and faced no armed resistance at all. They subdued everyone in the yard and went up the stairs to the master bedroom. There they found Mutotwe Kafwaya taking cover in the wardrobe, unarmed. They shot him in the chest, and he was pronounced dead.

Then came the cover story: militias, an insurrection, threats to national security, all the flamboyant security language they could find. On the strength of that militia story, which UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero has described as concocted, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu were arrested and charged with treason.

For me, what happened that night was a coup d’état against our democracy, and I choose my words very carefully. I am not talking about the old-fashioned African coup, where soldiers appear on television and announce that they have taken over the government. These ones were clever. I am talking about a coup against the democratic process itself.

What is democracy? It is elections, institutions and courts. It is the right to change, the right to organise, the right to disagree and the right to seek legal remedy when you believe something has gone wrong.

So what happens when the electoral process fails, and the judicial process meant to correct it also becomes inaccessible? What happens when the courts are surrounded at the very moment citizens need them? What happens when the opposition candidate who should be challenging the result ends up in prison, accused of treason?

And what happens when his running mate ends up in prison with him, even though he was not at the scene of the alleged militia and nothing connects him to it? What do Zambians do?

We stop examining each incident separately and finally look at the complete picture. Let us try that. Let us stop looking at these events one by one. That is my case: August 2026 was not the beginning. August 2026 was the consequence. It did not suddenly arrive. We walked here.

The funeral. Celestine Mukandila. The campaign restrictions. The military. Treason. One incident after another, all painting a single picture that is painful to reflect on. And every time something happened, Zambians found a reason to remain silent.

That is the opposition. That is Lungu. That is politics. Maybe he said something wrong. Let the courts decide. The Government knows what it is doing. Until eventually we arrived here. That is how we got here.

So the question today is no longer simply how we got here. I think we know. We got here through silence, by being quiet, by not speaking when we should have spoken. The question now is what more will be done on the back of our silence.

That is what frightens me. If this much became possible while Zambia was quiet, what becomes possible if Zambia stays quiet? What is the next boundary? The next institution? Who is the next person? What will we normalise next? That is the big question.

This is where I want to speak directly to Zambians. Speaking does not mean insulting anybody. It does not mean lying, threatening anybody or turning to violence. Speaking simply means airing genuinely held views. It means telling those in power: I disagree. I am concerned. Explain this. Show us the evidence.

Speaking means telling them to respect the Constitution, the courts and our rights. It means telling them to release the people they are holding unlawfully and to give people due process. Let political parties organise. Let journalists work. Let citizens question power. That is not rebellion. That is not resistance. That is citizenship.

I think we have reached the point where Zambians must stop defending democracy according to political colours. If somebody’s rights are violated, do not first ask which party they belong to or what tribe they are. If an opposition rally is stopped, do not first ask whether you support that party. If somebody is arrested for expressing an opinion, do not first ask whether you agree with it.

That is the lesson in democracy this country needs. What we must ask is whether what is happening is right. Today it may be Brian Mundubile; tomorrow it may be somebody you support. Today it may be Makebi Zulu; tomorrow it may be you.

That is why I am saying something even to my own colleagues in the opposition. For now, put the parties aside. There will be time for party politics, but first we have a country to defend and a democracy to defend. What is the point of fighting over who gets to live in a house whose foundation is broken? The foundation comes first.

There is a verse I like in the Bible that asks: when the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do? Zambia’s foundations are cracked right now, and that foundation is our democracy.

We must first defend the electoral process, the judiciary, freedom of expression, political competition and the right to disagree. We must defend the principle that no president, no government and no political party is bigger than Zambia. When that foundation is secure, then let us fight politically. That is democracy.

I do not want a Zambia where my candidate can never lose. I want a Zambia where my candidate can lose and I can believe he genuinely lost. I want a Zambia where the UPND can lose and peacefully hand over power, and where the opposition can lose and remain free to organise. That is the Zambia we must strive for.

I want a Zambia where an opposition leader can criticise the President today and still sleep in his own bed tonight. I want a Zambia where a journalist can ask a difficult question without wondering whether somebody will knock on the door. I want a Zambia where a citizen can say, “Mr President, I think you are wrong,” and wake up free the next morning, and where a civil servant can support whoever they want without anyone coming after them.

That is not asking for too much. That is the Zambia we are supposed to be: tolerant and united. And we will not recover that Zambia through silence.

So I challenge you: speak. Peacefully, responsibly and truthfully, but speak. Speak because you understand what is at stake. Speak because democracy cannot defend itself, and institutions cannot defend themselves when the citizens who own them have surrendered their voices.

Do not wait until it reaches your house. That is the mistake we have been making: because it was not your son who died, you felt comfortable. When it was Bowman, we waited. When it was Edgar Lungu, we waited. When it was Munir Zulu, we waited. When rallies were being stopped, we waited in silence.

When people warned about the ECZ, we waited. When people warned about the cyber laws, we waited in submissive silence. When people warned about Bill 7, we rested on our laurels and waited like little men and women.

And now Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu are in prison facing treason charges, and Mutotwe Kafwaya is dead and buried, six feet under. So tell me, what exactly are we waiting for now? That, my fellow Zambians, is the question.

No foreign country is coming to build our democracy for us. No international organisation can substitute for the voice of the Zambian people, and no politician can carry this responsibility alone. Zambia belongs to Zambians. If we believe something has gone terribly wrong in our democracy, then Zambians must say so: not violently, not recklessly, but clearly and together.

This is bigger than any of us. Presidents will come and go. Political parties will rise and fall. Those of us holding political positions today will one day be gone. But Zambia will remain, and what kind of Zambia remains will depend partly on what this generation is prepared to defend today.

Our parents gave us a multi-party democracy. We cannot be the generation that hands our children something less. This is the moment to find our voices again. We can refuse to be silent.

The question is no longer whether Zambia should have spoken yesterday. Yesterday is gone, and there is no use crying over spilt milk. The question is whether Zambia will speak today. My answer is that Zambia must speak, before the boundaries move again.

By Brian “Coach” Matambo, Tonse Alliance

Source: “The Cost of Silence: How Zambia Reached the Crisis of 2026”, video address accompanying the documentary “Silence Brought Us Here”

World.title: Maamba Solar Injects 100MW Into National Grid As El Niño Threatens Hydropower
World.content:
Maamba Solar Energy Limited (MSEL) has injected 100 megawatts of electricity into the national grid, bringing one of Zambia’s largest solar plants online just as the country braces for an El Niño season expected to squeeze hydropower generation. First power from the Maamba Solar PV Project entered the grid on 24 September, marking the start of the plant’s commissioning phase.

The project is a joint venture in which ZCCM Investments Holdings (ZCCM-IH) holds a 35 per cent stake, with the remaining 65 per cent held by Nava Global PTE Limited, the international arm of India-listed Nava Limited. Total investment in the project stands at about US$90 million.

ZCCM-IH Chief Executive Officer Kakenenwa Muyangwa said the timing could not have been better. In a statement issued on Friday evening through corporate affairs manager Loisa Mbatha, he said that with Zambia bracing for El Niño and the pressure it would place on hydropower, 100 megawatts of solar capacity was a direct and timely response to the country’s energy security needs.

Mr Muyangwa said the project strengthened the diversification of Zambia’s energy mix, reducing reliance on a single source and building resilience into the national grid. “As a sovereign-anchored investor, ZCCM-IH is proud to play its part in Zambia’s energy transformation,” he said.

He said the investment reflected ZCCM-IH’s commitment to deploying capital into strategic energy projects that would underpin economic growth, support the Grow Zambia agenda and contribute to the national ambition of 10,000 megawatts of generation capacity. The company, he said, would keep working with its partners to bring more reliable and clean power to the grid, create lasting value for shareholders and support industry.

The plant sits in Maamba, Sinazongwe District, in Southern Province, alongside the existing Maamba thermal power operations. It is a 100 MWac utility-scale photovoltaic facility using bifacial panels mounted on single-axis trackers, which follow the sun through the day to maximise output.

A dedicated 330 kV substation connects the plant to the grid. Its output is contracted to ZESCO Limited under a 20-year Power Purchase Agreement, giving the project long-term, predictable revenue.

Commissioning will now move through testing and verification of the generation system, trackers, inverters, medium-voltage collection network, substation, protection and control, metering, SCADA and communication systems. The plant will then go through synchronisation, reliability and performance checks, including confirmation of its response to grid requirements, before full commercial operation, and ZCCM-IH said it would update shareholders and the market on further milestones.

The new capacity arrives while the country’s main hydropower reservoir is declining but holding. The Zambezi River Authority (ZRA) put Lake Kariba at 481.15 metres on 21 September, with 26.21 billion cubic metres of usable storage, or 40.44 per cent of the water available for power generation. That is above the 477.87 metres recorded in 2025 but below the 485.67 metres of 2018.

Energy expert Engineer Bornface Zulu said electricity supply remained stable despite the falling lake, but warned that the situation showed why Zambia must keep diversifying away from hydropower. National demand stands at about 2,400MW, peaking at around 2,800MW, against current generation of about 3,500MW, with Kafue Gorge Upper producing about 990MW and Kafue Gorge Lower about 750MW.

Solar is already carrying more of that load. More than 841MW of solar power has been added to national generation capacity, and a further 159MW is expected from Chipata West and Senga by December 2026.

Maamba now moves through synchronisation and performance testing towards full commercial operation, adding its 100 megawatts to the grid before the rains.

World.title: Chief Choongo Condemns Katele Kalumba Over Attack On President Hichilema
World.content:
Chief Choongo Condemns Katele Kalumba Over Attack On President Hichilema

Chief Choongo of Monze District has condemned remarks attributed to former Cabinet minister Dr Katele Kalumba against President Hakainde Hichilema, describing them as disappointing and un-Zambian. In a video widely circulated online, Dr Kalumba is heard making disparaging remarks about the President and issuing threats against him.

The traditional leader, a former chairperson of the House of Chiefs, said leadership should be rooted in fostering unity and promoting dialogue rather than sowing discord. He said Dr Kalumba’s standing made the remarks harder to accept. “First and foremost, it is a disappointment to have a person of the stature of Dr Kalumba because his stature is highly respected. He served as a Cabinet minister for many years in the MMD regime, he is an accomplished academician, he is a doctor and, above all, he is a traditionalist,” Chief Choongo said.

A man of that calibre, the chief said, should never have turned on the Head of State. “So it is disappointing, really, to get a person of his calibre to insult the Head of State,” he said.

Chief Choongo said Dr Kalumba, as a senior figure in both politics and academia, understood what the presidency represents. He questioned the example the former minister was setting for those coming up behind him. “For him to attack a sitting President in that manner, I feel it is disappointing. What message is he sending to the younger generation? What message is he sending to young politicians and upcoming politicians?” he said.

The traditional leader said Dr Kalumba had other and better ways to advise the Government and the President than attacking the presidency on social media. “That is very disappointing and unfortunate. His language was not good. It must be condemned by all well-meaning Zambians,” he said.

He said there was a time and season for everything, including political campaigns, during which some people deliberately resorted to lies and hate speech. That season, Chief Choongo said, had ended, and the people had spoken at every level. “The people of Zambia have decided who their MP should be, who their council chairperson should be, who their mayor should be and, above all, the people of Zambia overwhelmingly decided who they wanted to be the President of this country. And they have decided that President Hichilema should continue,” he said.

Respect for the office, the chief said, should rise above party loyalty. He said anyone who understood how a president must be treated, whether a supporter of the ruling party or not, should recognise that the presidential seat belonged to all Zambians.

Chief Choongo said whoever served as President deserved respect because the people had chosen that person to lead. He also answered those who question why traditional leaders work closely with the State. “People ask why ‘we’, traditional leaders, work with the government of the day. The answer is always because that is the leadership which is there at that particular time,” he said.

The video remains in circulation, and Chief Choongo has called on all well-meaning Zambians to condemn its language.

World.title: Harrington Warns UPND Against Removing Presidential Term Limits
World.content:
Zambians Have Always Rejected Removing Presidential Term Limits, Says William Harrington

Former transport and communications minister William Harrington has said Zambians have consistently rejected proposals to remove presidential term limits, pointing to submissions made to the Chona, Mvunga, Mwanakatwe and Mung’omba constitutional review commissions. He spoke while the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) pushes for a constitutional amendment to remove the limit, which would allow President Hakainde Hichilema to continue ruling beyond 2031.

William Harrington’s insights on governance resonate strongly with the public’s sentiments regarding term limits.

The push has come from within the party’s own ranks in Parliament. UPND proportional representation MP Florence Chileshe Chama, one of 17 women the party nominated to the 20 seats reserved for women, said in a video shared on 20 September that women in Zambia “don’t want democracy but development”. She suggested this could be achieved by supporting Mr Hichilema beyond his final term, and other UPND members have made similar calls in recent days.

Civil society has pushed back hard. Civil rights activist Brebner Changala warned that “if there’s something Zambians will not tolerate even in their collective docility, it is a third term,” and said the UPND should not take the public’s silence after the disputed August elections for granted. Governance campaigner Mulenga Kapwepwe asked: “What is wrong with the Constitution for people to start pushing a narrative that the Constitution should be changed?”

Mr Harrington took the argument back to the historical record. In an interview, he said citizens who took part in successive constitutional reviews overwhelmingly supported limiting a president to two five-year terms, because they feared unlimited tenure would concentrate power and undermine democratic succession.

He said the Constitution guaranteed freedom of speech and conscience, but that citizens on either side of the amendment question had a duty to reach their positions through education and research rather than political expediency. Such research, Mr Harrington said, would point in only one direction.

“If citizens cared to take time to study the submissions made to various constitution review commissions such as the Chona, Mvunga, Mwanakatwe and Mung’omba commissions, they will discover that the overwhelming number of citizens consistently and persistently rejected unlimited or ‘freehold’ presidential terms, insisting that the presidential term of office must be limited to only two five-year terms,” he said.

The main case for term limits, he said, had always been the need to prevent dictatorship and the prolonged concentration of power in one individual. Mr Harrington recalled that the Council of Churches in Zambia (CCZ) and various political commentators had warned that removing the limit risked breeding a dictatorial leader or creating a life president, undermining the country’s democratic process.

Term limits also protect orderly change at the top, he said, allowing a country to experience regular and peaceful transfers of leadership. “Presidential term limits serve as a critical mechanism to ensure periodic, peaceful political succession,” Mr Harrington said.

He spoke directly to leaders who believe a decade in office is too short. Where a president felt that 10 years were not enough to achieve their objectives, Mr Harrington said, the answer lay in strengthening institutions and developing future leaders, not in changing the Constitution to extend tenure.

Zambians, he said, had rejected constitutional changes before when they saw them as driven by self-serving political interests. The country’s own history offered the clearest lesson, and he cited the failed third-term bid by former president Frederick Chiluba in 2001.

The amendment question is now open inside the ruling party. Mr Harrington says the answer has already been given four times, by citizens before four commissions: two terms of five years, and no more.

World.title: Mandevu, Lumezi North And Mbala Return To The Polls On 5 November
World.content:
Voters in Mandevu and Lumezi North will elect Members of Parliament on 5 November because the August general election produced no result in either constituency. Mbala will choose a new mayor after the mayor-elect died days after winning. The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) announced the polls on Friday, together with by-elections in 11 wards, including the crucial Mandevu by-election.

Mandevu’s contest was lost in the days after polling. On 18 August, unknown individuals stormed the Mandevu totalling centre, attacked staff, destroyed result transmission kits and fled with election documents. Ballot papers were later found dumped in drainages and burnt, which left the returning officer unable to declare the National Assembly result for one of Lusaka Province’s key constituencies, leading to the upcoming Mandevu by-election.

Acting on a report from the Lusaka District Electoral Officer dated the same day, ECZ Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro announced at the end of August that the seat would be contested afresh. “In view of this, the Commission has resolved to hold a by-election for Mandevu Constituency, referred to as the Mandevu by-election, on a date to be communicated in due course,” he said.

The Foundation for Democratic Process (FODEP) and the Anti-Voter Apathy Project backed the decision as consistent with electoral standards where materials have been compromised. The Zambia Civil Liberties Union (ZCLU) challenged the commission’s authority, saying “there is no law that mandates the Electoral Commission of Zambia to cancel and conduct fresh parliamentary elections”. Politician Peter Sinkamba urged the ECZ to extend the fresh poll to Mandevu’s mayoral and councillor elections as well.

Lumezi North’s vacancy goes back to before polling day. Clement Mwale, the parliamentary candidate for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) within the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, died in the early hours of 16 July, after nominations had closed. He had been running against Anderson Banda of the UPND and Nebby Manda of the Leadership Movement.

Under Constitutional Amendment No. 13 of 2025, the death of a candidate after nominations obliges the commission to cancel the election in that constituency, and the sponsoring party then has 30 days to field a replacement. ECZ Commissioner McDonald Chipenzi said at the time that “once a sponsored candidate has died, the Commission is empowered to cancel that election and call for fresh nominations for that party.”

Mbala lost its new mayor within days of the vote. Steward Simutenda, elected on 13 August on the NRPUP ticket, died around midnight on 18 August following an illness, his brother Gabriel Simutenda said. A former Patriotic Front (PF) district chairperson for Mbala, he had been admitted to hospital about a week before polling.

The 11 ward vacancies arose from the deaths of nominated and elected candidates, from wards left uncontested at the general election, and from nominations nullified by the Local Government Elections Tribunal. The wards are Lungwishi in Mansa, Makaba and Nkonge in Chipili, Nachikufu in Mpika, Lubaleshi in Kanchibiya, Maako in Kasempa, Siluwe and Upangoma in Kalabo, Mbeta in Sioma, Mulimambango in Sesheke and Simanvwa in Choma.

Nominations open on Thursday 8 October, and campaigns run from 10 October until 18:00 hours on 4 November. Parliamentary and mayoral candidates will pay non-refundable fees of K17,000 for men, K14,000 for women, K10,500 for youths and K10,000 for persons with disabilities.

For the ruling party, the contests are a chance to renew its claim on voters. UPND deputy spokesperson Elvis Nkandu said the party would use the by-elections to make the case for the New Dawn Government. “This is another opportunity for us to appeal to the citizens and ask them to give us the mandate to continue delivering development,” he said.

Mr Nkandu said the party remained focused on service delivery and on the interests of ordinary Zambians. “We remain the voice of the voiceless, particularly when it comes to service delivery. Our focus is on ensuring that development reaches the people,” he said, adding that the UPND expected to take a strong share of the seats.

“We are going into these by-elections prepared, and we believe the people will have confidence in the UPND and its ability to deliver development,” Mr Nkandu said. He appealed to voters in the affected areas to back the party’s candidates.

Nominations open on 8 October. Mandevu, Lumezi North, Mbala and the 11 wards vote on 5 November.

World.title: Lusaka Catholics Called To Cathedral As Archbishop Banda Answers Fresh DEC Summons
World.content:
The Catholic Archdiocese of Lusaka has called its clergy and faithful to a solidarity Mass at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus on Monday morning. Archbishop Alick Banda reports to the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) a few hours later on a renewed summons. The Church said it feared for his safety and well-being and urged Catholics to stand with him in prayer.

The Mass begins at 08:00 hours. From the cathedral, the Archbishop is expected to go on to the commission, where he is due at 10:00 hours.

“Mass will be celebrated at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus on Monday 28th September, 2026 at 08:00 hours in solidarity with the Archbishop, before he proceeds to the Drug Enforcement Commission at 10:00 hours,” the Archdiocese said.

The announcement came in a statement dated 25 September and signed by the Archdiocese’s Communications Office, which also published it on the Church’s official Facebook page. The statement calls the DEC call-out a “renewed” summons, which means the commission has called the Archbishop before.

The Church did not say what the commission wants to take up with him, or what happened with the earlier summons. The statement dealt only with the Archbishop himself and with the Church’s resolve to stand around him.

“The Archdiocese of Lusaka expresses its deep concern and unwavering solidarity with our Local Shepherd, His Grace Most Rev. Dr. Alick Banda, following renewed summons by the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC),” the Church said.

Church leaders built their appeal around one line of Scripture, placed at the head of the statement. They chose Matthew 26:38, the words Christ spoke in the Garden of Gethsemane when he asked his disciples to keep vigil with him: “Stay here and keep watch with me.”

Concern for the Archbishop’s safety runs through the statement. The Church said more than once that it was deeply concerned for his safety and well-being, but it did not say what specific fear lay behind those words.

Even so, the Archdiocese made clear that the Archbishop would honour the summons. It asked the faithful to meet the moment with composure rather than alarm, and tied its call for calm directly to respect for the law.

“We therefore call upon the clergy, religious and lay faithful to remain united in prayer, calm in spirit and steadfast in faith as our Archbishop responds to the summons in accordance with the law,” the statement read.

With that emphasis on the law established, the Church turned to the Archbishop’s standing among his people. It presented him not as a lone figure going before a State agency, but as a pastor whose congregation would walk with him.

“Our Archbishop is not alone. He remains a shepherd surrounded by his flock, and the Church stands firmly with him in prayer, communion and solidarity,” the Archdiocese said.

The Church then cast the moment as a test for the faithful themselves. It told Catholics that fear had no place in their response.

“At this moment, we are called not to fear, but to remain vigilant in prayer and steadfast in our commitment to truth, justice and peace,” the statement said.

The Archdiocese invited Catholics across Lusaka to pray earnestly for the Archbishop’s safety, strength, wisdom and well-being. It also asked them to pray that justice, truth and peace would prevail “throughout this process”.

Everyone able to attend the cathedral service was encouraged to come. The Church asked the faithful to “stand together as one family” on Monday morning and closed its appeal with a four-part charge.

“Let us be united in prayer, steadfast in faith, peaceful in spirit and unwavering in our pursuit of truth,” the Archdiocese said.

The statement’s closing lines placed the matter in God’s hands. Church leaders said they trusted the Lord to carry the Archbishop through the days ahead.

“We place our trust in God, who is our refuge and strength. We entrust our Local Shepherd to God’s providence, confident that the Lord will sustain him and guide him through this moment,” the Church said.

The Archdiocese also entrusted itself, and what it called “the Archbishop’s cause”, to the intercession of Our Lady of Lusaka, the Mother of the Child Jesus.

Catholics will gather at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus from 08:00 hours on Monday. The Archbishop is due at the Drug Enforcement Commission two hours later.

World.title: TECH Global University, regarded as the ‘online Harvard’ thanks to its Ivy League faculty
World.content:
TECH Global University, regarded as the ‘online Harvard’ thanks to its Ivy League faculty

With over 6,000 top-tier international professors across all areas of knowledge, TECH Global University continues its global development journey

“Teaching is more than imparting knowledge: it is inspiring change,” said the famous American writer William Arthur Ward. Today, with digital learning, this statement makes more sense than ever, as educators play a key role. This is the foundation of TECH Global University‘s educational mission, recognized by Forbes as the best online university in the world, where excellence in teaching is its hallmark.

Various studies highlight that the quality of educators is one of the most influential factors in academic success. According to UNESCO reports, “the experience and commitment of teachers are essential for improving educational outcomes.” Moreover, an article published by The Chronicle of Higher Education states that educators with international experience not only bring advanced technical knowledge but also enrich students’ cultural perspectives, preparing them for a globalized world.

TECH Global University boasts a faculty of over 6,000 specialists holding prominent positions at leading companies, organizations, and hospitals worldwide. Among them are professionals holding senior roles in tech giants like Google and Amazon, as well as executives from the banking sector, such as Mastercard directors. Also, there are leaders from global corporations like Coca-Cola or Shell, and top hospitals like MD Anderson Cancer Center and Mayo Clinic. In this context, the university has earned the title “Harvard online.”

This transformative vision aims to “bring and diversify university education to make it accessible to all corners of the world,” according to Manuel Sánchez-Cascado de Fuentes, CEO of TECH Education. This ensures multifaceted teaching and “fosters a learning environment that transcends borders, allowing students to gain a global and up-to-date perspective of their respective disciplines.”

Its high academic quality is also reflected in its employment rate. 99% of its graduates secure qualified employment after completing their degrees. For this reason, it is the highest-rated university in the world by its students, with an overall rating of 4.9 out of 5 on the leading digital opinion platforms.

TECH Global University offers 20 faculties covering the most relevant areas of knowledge and their practical application. In all of them, the faculty becomes the backbone of educational excellence, enabling students to connect scientific research with the most current and demanding professional realities.

TECH Global University, leader in healthcare education

Since its foundation, TECH Global University has positioned itself as a leader in the healthcare field. This has allowed it to establish close ties with four centers that rank among the top 5 hospitals in the world, with guest directors in various fields of Medicine and Nursing.

Notable professors include Dr. Michael Hinni, who leads the Department of Head and Neck Surgery at Mayo Clinic, Dr. Susan Linder, Director of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation at Cleveland Clinic, Dr. David Lin, Director of the NeuroRecovery Clinic at Massachusetts General Hospital, and Dr. Konstantinos Aronis, Director of the Complex Ablation Program for Congenital Heart Disease at The Johns Hopkins Hospital.

Also noteworthy is Dr. Stefan G. Hofmann, who contributes to the Master’s in Cognitive Behavioral Psychology at TECH Global University. This distinguished expert has dedicated much of his career to treating anxiety disorders through the most disruptive Cognitive Behavioral Therapy techniques. He has won numerous awards and has been included in the list of Highly Cited Researchers worldwide.

The world’s largest Business School

TECH Global University features a Business School faculty that has become a global reference in executive education. A distinctive trait of this institution is its ability to connect students with active business leaders who bring their knowledge and experience directly to virtual classrooms. This approach allows future executives to immerse themselves in the daily practice of global business, receiving first-hand advice and strategies from those leading their respective industries.

Some of the most recognized faculty members include international figures such as Romi Arman, Chief Digital Transformation Officer (CDO) at Shell; Scott Stevenson, Digital Marketing Director at Warner Bros Discovery; Andrea La Sala, Global Director of Brand and Merchandising at Armani Exchange (Giorgio Armani); and Rick Gauthier, Regional IT Director at Amazon.

The presence of these leaders gives students a privileged view of current trends, real challenges, and the strategic solutions implemented by the world’s most influential companies. Interaction with these active executives provides students with a competitive advantage by helping them understand how key decisions are made and how adaptation and innovation are essential in a globalized market.

Technological innovation and video games at the academic core

Rebeca Hwang, Director of Thunderbird School of Global Management at the University of Arizona, is another key figure in the TECH Global University faculty. She is considered a leading expert in business management with high technological capital, an area in which she innovates using resources like Artificial Intelligence. All her knowledge is shared with students in the Master’s in Digital Business Creation and Entrepreneurship.

Thanks to her teaching, graduates “will be better positioned to apply modern tools in entrepreneurship and business creation processes ahead of their competitors.” Her knowledge will delve into “the technological implications of the AI revolution and the key aspects of leadership, culture, and other soft skills needed in the business world,” according to Hwang herself.

Another standout in the TECH Global University faculty is Joshua Singh. With more than 20 years of experience in the video game industry, he has worked with prestigious companies like Marvel Entertainment, Wildlife Studios, Wavedash Games, Blizzard Entertainment, and Riot Games. His successes in projects like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, League of Legends, and Overwatch have led him to his current position as Art Director at Epic Games.

TECH Global University, at the forefront of professional sports

TECH Global University has direct ties to the world’s leading sports specialists. Its faculty includes figures such as the renowned Isaiah Covington, high-performance coach for the Boston Celtics.

This expert has worked in the world’s most competitive and demanding basketball league. He has been a key figure in the recovery and performance improvement of players on iconic teams like the Golden State Warriors, bringing his experience in designing personalized rehabilitation and conditioning programs.

Other experts in Sports Sciences at TECH Global University include Tyler Friedrich, Director of Sports Performance and Applied Sports Science at Stanford. His work in data analysis and the integration of sports technology into conditioning programs has made him a leader in optimizing results in disciplines like football, swimming, volleyball, and hockey.

Social Sciences and their impact on current research

Alexander Carter, Director of Philosophy and Interdisciplinary Studies at the University of Cambridge, has led projects studying philosophical dilemmas, encouraging critical and creative thinking among researchers. This expert also joins TECH Global University as International Guest Director of the Master’s in Teaching Philosophy and Ethical Values.

In the realm of Social Sciences, Fayyaz Vellani stands out as the International Guest Director of the Master’s in Philosophy and Theory of Society at TECH Global University. Vellani, who also directs the Research Program at College House, University of Pennsylvania, has conducted several studies on Disability, Geopolitics, and Sustainable Development and their impact on the contemporary world. His career has earned him the Excellence Award from the International Journal of Diversity.

TECH Global University, the largest digital university in the world

TECH is the world’s largest online university. With an impressive catalog of more than 14,000 educational programs available in 11 languages, it is positioned as a leader in employability, with a 99% job placement rate.

It is officially recognized in America, such as TECH Universidad (Mexico). It also has a strong presence in Africa, with TECH RUCU University (Tanzania) and TECH Euromed University (Morocco), and in Europe through TECH Global University (Andorra) and TECH Universidad (Spain).

Thanks to its international scope, TECH has a presence in more than 150 countries and has twice been recognized by the Financial Times as one of the 250 fastest-growing companies in Europe in recent years.

On the other hand, the prestigious Forbes magazine has distinguished it as the “world’s best online university,” highlighting its innovative learning methodology, Relearning, as well as the implementation of the Harvard Case Method.

In addition, it boasts an Ivy League faculty, at the level of Harvard or Stanford. Its more than 6,000 professors work in the best companies, organizations and institutions in the world. The largest multinationals (Amazon, Apple, Google, Nike…), the best hospitals (Mayo Clinic, MD Anderson Cancer Center…) and the best sports institutions (Boston Celtics, Dallas Cowboys…) collaborate with their best professionals to lead TECH’s academic programs.

The quality of its digital infrastructure and its high educational standards have been recognized by Google with Google Premier Partner status, a distinction reserved only for the top 3% of online institutions.

TECH is also considered the top-rated university by its students, with an average rating of 4.9 out of 5 in more than 25,000 public ratings on leading international portals.

World.title: Nigeria: 'Dangote Refinery IPO Opens Ownership to Nigerian Investors'
World.content:
Nigerians can invest in Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals with a minimum subscription of N5,250 under an initial public offering launched recently. The company is offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 each. The offer, valued at about N2.15 trillion if fully subscribed, opened September 14 and is scheduled to close October 13.

FCMB Group Chief Executive, Ladi Balogun, said the offer gives Nigerians access to a world-scale business while demonstrating the growing reach of the country's capital market.

"It presents an opportunity for every Nigerian to experience the benefits of investing in world-class and world-scale businesses that would otherwise be inaccessible,"Balogun said at the opening gong ceremony and Facts Behind the Offer presentation at the Nigerian Exchange in Lagos.

Balogun said Nigeria's capital market was deepening as it attracted retail, high-net-worth, institutional and international investors through a widening range of channels.
