World.title: Anger grows across Spain after elderly woman evicted from her home of 70 years
World.content:
An 87-year-old Spanish woman was forcibly evicted Wednesday from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for more than 70 years, in a case that highlights a growing housing crisis in the country.

Video showed Maricarmen Abascal, who is a wheelchair user, being taken out of the building in the Spanish capital’s Retiro neighborhood on a stretcher and driven away in an ambulance.

Supporters had gathered outside her building overnight on Friday, with dozens of police officers holding them back as some tried to stop the eviction from going ahead. In a social media video posted Friday by the Madrid tenants union, Abascal gave thanks for the support she had received.

Maricarmen Abascal is carried out her apartment building on a stretcher on Wednesday. The building was acquired by an investment fund in 2018. Luciano Lima / Getty Images

Abascal’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, described the force used in the eviction as “completely disproportionate and unnecessary” and decried the intransigence of the building’s owners.

The case has brought new attention to an ongoing housing crisis in major cities across Spain, as gentrification has caused rents to skyrocket and the stock of affordable housing to shrink, leading to fierce public anger.

On Saturday, tens of thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction, some setting off flares. They carried placards reading “Not one more eviction, not one less neighbor, we are all Maricarmen” and “right to housing at a fair price.”

Demonstrators shouting during a protest against evictions at Puerta del Sol, Madrid on Sept. 26. Marcos del Mazo / LightRocket via Getty Images

At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza, some pitching tents. They remained in place early Sunday as dozens of activists staged a sit-in. A model of a vulture, decrying so-called “vulture funds,” hung above the camp.

Earlier in the week, tenants unions and other housing groups held protests and rallies in 16 cities, including Granada, Logroño and Zaragoza.

An investment fund acquired Abascal’s building in 2018 and sought a steep increase in her rent, and she had been fighting eviction for more than five years, according to the Madrid tenants union.

Duro said court officials and representatives of the fund, Urbagestión, had refused to suspend the eviction despite a pending court filing, humanitarian appeals and evidence that public authorities were working to secure alternative accommodation.

“They’re all inhumane,” Abascal said in a Spanish television interview the day before her eviction. “It’s as if I’m living with a machete at the back of my neck, ready to be chopped off at any moment.”

Demonstrators gather in Madrid on Wednesday to protest Abascal's eviction. Marcos del Mazo / LightRocket via Getty Images

Duro also said an anonymous individual had offered to cover the rent payments, but the landlord declined to sign a new lease.

“We’ve been trying to negotiate with the landlords right up until the last moment, and they’ve flatly refused everything,” she said, decrying “a lack of humanity” in her treatment and “all these public resources” channeled into enabling the eviction.

Urbagestión did not respond to a request for comment.

The fresh wave of anger comes after protests in recent years against overtourism in Barcelona, where activists say a surge in apartments being used for short-term vacation rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing.

The European Union announced new rules earlier this month aimed at tackling the housing crunch caused by short-term rentals in tourism hot spots.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described the eviction as “a social tragedy that we cannot accept either as a country or, of course, from the perspective of public institutions.”

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sánchez accused Madrid’s conservative regional government of pursuing luxury penthouses while ignoring demand for social housing.

Abascal weeps during a rally on Tuesday. Fernando Sanchez / Europa Press via Getty Images

Irene Hernández López, a 31-year-old test engineer living and renting in Chamberí, about 2 miles from Retiro, said what had happened to Abascal was “outrageous,” and she is worried similar evictions were already happening to other tenants around the city.

“Housing has become a product that people do business with,” she told NBC News. “It no longer matters that it’s your personal world, where you live and where you do your life.”

Hernández López, who pays 500 euros ($570) for a room in an apartment she shares with two others, said she was currently looking to move because the property was old and needs repairs, but that the rental market in Madrid was “terrible,” with prices “rising extremely quickly” and very little available.

“Some rooms are 500 euros or 600 euros and you think, ‘How am I supposed to live here? How can I pay 500 euros for this?’” she said. “I do think prices should be regulated, because wages aren’t going up while housing prices keep increasing. I don’t know how we’re supposed to keep going.”

Dan Nicander, secretary-general for the International Union of Tenants, said the situation in Spain was something his organization had seen in many countries in Europe.

“It’s a part of the financialization problem, seeing housing as an asset more than a home to people,” he told NBC News.

It’s “really tough” for the people living in the houses to do anything about it, he added, saying the responsibility lay with politicians “to regulate the market in a way that it shouldn’t be that easy to buy and invest and then not [be] using the houses as homes.”

“Housing is a right,” he said. “It’s a fundamental right, first and foremost. It shouldn’t be a commodity.”

World.title: New York Knicks’ Jalen Brunson kicks off the new season of ‘SNL’
World.content:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”

During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during the Knicks’ Finals games.

“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”

The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.

00:56 Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL' 00:00 00:00

“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”

Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.

“Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked.

In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson played a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”

It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with an over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.

The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than Culhane’s character’s. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.

Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.

He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.

Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players, Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.

Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.

The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.

Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed Season 2 of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”

“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

World.title: It’s cute. It’s cuddly. And it wants your data.
World.content:
Meta hopes its new AI agent will win people over by being cute.

Muse, the tech giant’s cuddly, doll-like AI agent, shot to the top of the Apple App Store charts after it was featured this week at the company’s Meta Connect conference.

The company is touting the tool, designed to help people with their everyday tasks, as an AI agent “built for everyone,” including those who lack experience with technology.

AI agents, which are systems that automatically execute tasks on a user’s behalf, are rapidly becoming ubiquitous in online workspaces, social apps and personal devices.

02:43 Meet Mark Zuckerberg's personal Muse AI agent 00:00 00:00

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the default Muse avatar, which is cream-colored and has beady black eyes and an upward smile, is named “Jolly,” for its “jolly and completely customizable character and personality.”

Muse is being launched as tech companies seek to make their AI-powered products more palatable to humans, often by giving them cute, almost petlike appearances, voices and personalities. Experts have said design choices that humanize technology may become more common as robot-human interaction grows more prevalent in everyday spaces, as cuteness evokes “deep-seated biological responses” in people.

“It was only about six months ago that having a personal agent running on your own computer was the sign of someone who is completely AI-pilled and thinking nonstop about agents,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, said Wednesday. “But for that small group of nerds ... it looked like the beginning of personal superintelligence. And today with Muse, we’ve brought that magic to everyone.”

Mark Zuckerberg's Muse AI Agent, Agrippa. Meta

Muse agents can take on a variety of appearances, with users able to customize everything from their names to their attire. Zuckerberg’s agent, which wears a toga and a wreath around its head, is named Agrippa, after the Roman general and statesman.

During the event, Zuckerberg also teased what he calls the “Muse charm,” a small handheld device that can activate the agent on the go. He raised the keychain charm onstage at Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, showing off what looks like a blend of a Labubu and a Tamagotchi.

“Talking to your Muse is often the fastest way to get things done, and it is also just really fun and cute,” he said, saying he used Agrippa to come up with a baking recipe and order ingredients for him and his daughter.

Muse is also being integrated directly into Meta’s expanding lineup of AI-powered glasses, which have been criticized over fears of casual surveillance. Zuckerberg has told NBC News that Meta will continue to bolster privacy safeguards for its smart glasses.

Zuckerberg said every Muse agent has its own private and secure computer called Muse Secure VM, a dedicated secure computer that houses both the agent and the user’s personal data. Down the line, he said, Meta plans to release Muse Confidential VM “so that even Meta won’t be able to see that information.”

“In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives,” he said.

Online, the reaction has been mixed.

Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted a flurry of memes inserting Muse into moments from movies, shows and historical events.

Some followed his lead by making their own avatars and sharing screenshots on social media.

Others, however, expressed skepticism, citing security concerns.

“Am I the only one who doesn’t want to let meta have access to my whole life?” a user posted.

“We are going to need some tight defenses and 3rd party testing of these platforms... like all software products,” entrepreneur and angel investor Jason Calacanis wrote.

Zuckerberg has continued to be bullish on AI despite recent calls from tech executives and government officials to pump the brakes on AI development amid surging fears about the existential risk the technology poses.

He shared his thoughts recently on X, saying market forces should be enough to keep AI companies in line.

“My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind,” he wrote, adding: “Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would.”

World.title: Should you bring iced coffee to a job interview? Question brews generational debate
World.content:
What started as a conversation about job interview tips online escalated into a generational debate over whether it’s taboo to show up with an iced coffee to talk to a potential employer.

The discourse over the caffeinated beverage gained momentum on TikTok this week after a creator, who goes by @caitlinrecruiter on the platform, shared a video in which she said she believes “when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day.”

“It looks a little too casual to me,” she said in the video, which she posted Sept. 16.

Caitlin Wehniainen, whose profile states she has 16 years of recruiting experience, has just over 1,000 followers on TikTok. But in the last week, her video has been clipped and recirculated by dozens of creators online, who engaged in a heated back-and-forth about whether she’s right.

The divide seemed to primarily be between younger and older users — with the former group suggesting Wehniainen’s tip “makes no sense at all” and that such a perspective is archaic.

Others, many who identified as Gen Xers in comments, agreed with Wehniainen, writing that “arguing against this is insane” and telling applicants that they should “save the iced coffee for when you actually get hired.”

By Monday, even the coffee giant Starbucks had taken a side, alluding to the debate in an Instagram post that featured an image of someone holding an iced coffee in one hand and sunglasses and their handbag in the other. “Pulling up to the interview like,” the caption read. Meanwhile, The Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf, another coffee chain, commented on Wehniainen’s video: “We’d hire them on spot...”

Outside Off-White, during New York Fashion Week, on September 12, 2025 in New York, New York Edward Berthelot / Getty Images file

When reached for comment on Friday, Wehniainen said in an email to NBC News that she was “shocked at how polarizing the topic is.”

“But I realize that the original message was taken out of context as the virality of the post grew,” she wrote. “As the topic spread, many decided to weigh in with their own general opinion on whether or not bringing an iced coffee into an interview is appropriate ... I also saw people reading into it too much, asking if coffee or water matters and what is appropriate. I will say, I think a bottled water is great to bring with you.”

The timing of the conversation coincides with a tough job market: Recent college graduates are facing higher unemployment rates than other age groups as it’s becoming more difficult to obtain entry-level jobs, NBC News reported last month. Employers are not looking to add talent, and employed people are not moving to new positions, as a rise in AI continues to threaten jobs.

For Los Angeles-based TikTok creator Esha, who preferred to be identified by only her first name, citing privacy concerns, Wehniainen’s words couldn’t be further from the truth. She was among the many weighing in online, telling her 81,000-plus TikTok followers that “the iced coffee controversy completely misunderstands interviews.”

“Thinking of a job interview as a stop in your day is very normal,” Esha, 22, added in an interview with NBC News, noting that she’s brought iced coffees to several interviews and hasn’t thought twice about it.

“Gen Z had this shift in recent years, where we can still have a life outside of work,” Esha said. “So, like, why am I changing who I am? Why am I missing my coffee for the day for this interview?”

In her video, she elaborated further on her take, saying that “the most easily relatable thing in corporate America is a coffee addiction.”

“Unless you’re like over the age of 30 and you can relate on having kids, and doing stuff with your kids, coffee is the main thing. Everyone’s like, ‘Gotta get that coffee’ ... and finding something personable about a person is so important,” she said. “Like, who is not starting their workday off with a coffee?”

Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications at LinkedIn, said she’s not surprised by the generational divisions when it comes to job etiquette.

“Gen Z is entering this workforce at such a challenging time, it’s such a competitive job market, and to then get judged by bringing an iced coffee just seems like, ‘Have we lost the plot here?’” she said.

That said, Fisher is among the cohort who believes it’s best to skip the iced coffee when headed to an interview.

“Even though I don’t like the answer, I think because everyone is so divided on it, I would be cautious and not bring one,” she said. “You just don’t know who’s on the other side of the interview, so why risk it over something so silly?”

Etiquette expert Thomas Farley, who is known as Mister Manners to his followers online, agreed with the more traditional point of view.

“I think it sends the wrong message in so many respects,” he said. “I think it shows you to be someone who didn’t plan your time accordingly, and you’re multitasking, and that’s not what you should be doing during the interview.”

Farley also warned of the physical pratfalls a coffee could bring.

“There are real practical considerations when you bring a liquid into someone’s office,” he said. “Where does it go? What happens if you spill it?”

While he doesn’t think it should be the deciding factor for any hiring manager, Farley argued candidates should be doing everything in their power to leave a positive impression.

“If it’s between you and three other people, and everyone’s qualifications are more or less equal, and that’s the one thing that potentially sinks your chance to get the job, I think that would be really unfortunate,” he said. “That would be a very expensive $7 cup of iced coffee.”

Still, Gen Zers like Esha are not convinced that bringing the beverage would make or break their job opportunity.

As another TikTok creator put it in their video: “It’s really, really not that serious most of the time.”

As for Wehniainen? Even after the online uproar, she said her “opinion still stands that you shouldn’t bring an iced coffee to your interview.”

“You want to leave outlying distractions like iced coffee behind,” she said, “and connect with your interviewer with full attention.”

World.title: The New Season: Fall 2026 – The art of Keith Haring
World.content:
Interlocking silhouettes and bold lines shape Keith Haring's signature style. In his own words: "It was made for lots of people. You don't have to know anything about art to appreciate it."

"I would describe his work as graphic, as fun, as direct, as appealing," said Austen Bailly, a curator at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas. "Most people probably know him through T-shirts or posters or watches. I don't think they understand the fullness of his artistic practice and his artistic vision."

An installation view of "Keith Haring in 3D," an exhibition at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas. Jared Sorrells; Artwork © Keith Haring Foundation

The Crystal Bridges' show, "Keith Haring in 3D," celebrates an artist who seems to have decorated every inch of New York City with his groundbreaking work.

Among the objects on display: a suit worn by Madonna.

Three untitled works by Keith Haring (a 1963 Buick Special with enamel; acrylic paint on a papier-mache elephant; and acrylic paint on a television) featured in the exhibition "Keith Haring in 3D," at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Ark. From the collections of Larry Warsh and the Andy Warhol Museum, Pittsburgh; © Keith Haring Foundation.

But it wasn't all pop stars and gallery openings, as he told CBS News' Charles Osgood back in 1982. Some of Haring's work was underground, adorning the walls of the subway.

Asked by Osgood who is the real Keith Haring – the gallery Keith Haring or the subway station Keith Haring – the artist replied, "For me there's not a discrepancy between the two; they're treated both the same. The same amount of care goes into doing things in the street as the things that end up in the gallery.

"Most of the people that ride the subway don't go to galleries, and wouldn't really see the work," Haring said. "That's what makes a drawing live anyway – people seeing it and it becoming part of their lives."

FROM THE ARCHIVES: Artist Keith Haring in 1982 (Video)

"He is thinking about where art can live," said Olivia Walton, chair of the Crystal Bridges Museum. "He is thinking about what art can be, and he's thinking about who art is really for. Art not just in a museum or in a gallery, but actually in the subway, out on a playground, on a crib, everywhere."

Haring didn't shy away from exploring heavier topics, too. "It's very much about this moment in the 1980s in New York City when the art world is flourishing, but also the AIDS crisis is raging. These are tough issues, but his work is approaching it in a spirit of joy."

Keith Haring was only 31 years old when he died of AIDs-related complications, leaving behind a vibrant catalogue.

Austen Bailly said, "I hope people experience that joy, the sense of color, the sense of fun, even the solemnity of his death, but his legacy is so positive."

For more info:

Exhibition: "Keith Haring in 3D," at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Ark. (through Jan. 25, 2027)

More new exhibitions this fall:

Crystal Bridges isn't the only museum delivering fun and color this season.

Not far off, in Memphis, its renovated museum prepares to open its doors.

Memphis Art Museum opens Dec. 6

A rendition of the new Memphis Art Museum, designed by Herzog & de Meuron and local designers archimania, which will house 10,000 works from the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art, which has closed its location in Overton Park. Memphis Art Museum

On the West Coast, the Korean pop star known as RM, of the group BTS, finds himself on a different stage, curating a show at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

"RM x SFMOMA: Between You and Me," at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (Oct. 3, 2026-Feb. 7, 2027)

Nearly 200 works by Korean and International artists, from the collections of RM and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, will be on display at SFMOMA. San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

The Art Institute of Chicago celebrates the life and legacy of war photographer Lee Miller.

"Lee Miller: Fearless," at the Art Institute of Chicago (through Dec. 7)

Two photographs by Lee Miller: "Infantry Advancing, 1945," and "Self-Portrait with Headband (detail)," c. 1932. The Art Institute of Chicago. Courtesy of Condé Nast Publications. © 2026 Lee Miller Archives, England. All rights reserved.

And in New York, another Lee, Lee Krasner has works on display along with those of husband Jackson Pollock, in a retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

"Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (Oct. 4, 2026-Jan. 31, 2027)

Details from (Left) "The Seasons" (1957) by Lee Krasner. Oil and house paint on canvas; and "The Key" (1946) by Jackson Pollack. Oil on linen. The couple's artworks are being exhibited together this fall at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. © The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York

Also in the Big Apple: a Roy Lichtenstein show, brightening the halls of the Whitney.

"Roy Lichtenstein: Like New," at the Whitney Museum of American Art (Oct. 11, 2026-May 10, 2027)

The Whitney Museum of American Art exhibition "Roy Lichtenstein: Like New" features more than 130 works – paintings, drawings, sculpture, prints, film, and murals, including the 1963 lithograph "Crying Girl." Denis Y. Suspitsyn/ © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein

And across the pond, in London, get in line! The Bayeux Tapestry makes history at the British Museum, one of many shows sure to draw crowds this fall.

"The Bayeux Tapestry," at the British Museum, London (through July 11, 2027)

For the first time in nearly 1,000 years, the 70-meter-long Bayeux Tapestry, which depicts events that led up to the Battle of Hastings in 1066, is in England, on loan to the British Museum. Alishia Abodunde/Getty Images



Story produced by Lucie Kirk. Editor: Lauren Barnello.

World.title: The New Season: Fall 2026 - Art exhibits across the U.S.
World.content: The New Season: Fall 2026 - Art exhibits across the U.S. Jane Pauley explores the latest art exhibits at museums across the country this fall, including a joyous and colorful look at three-dimensional works by Keith Haring at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

World.title: YouTube, the new path to Hollywood for filmmakers
World.content:
"Spider-Man: Brand New Day," released in July, has grossed nearly a billion dollars in the U.S. alone, which, heading into fall, has Matt Belloni and others in Hollywood experiencing an unusual emotion: mild optimism.

"I think we've had a successful year at the box office a), because there are more movies; then b) I think this year there have been movies for different audiences," he said. "We see movies like 'Obsession' and 'Backrooms' bring in the younger audience. We've seen 'The Odyssey' bring in the older audience. We've seen a mass-market hit like 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' bring in everybody."

Belloni is founding partner at Puck News, and the host of "The Town" podcast. He knows just about every player at every studio. "This year they are finally up to a cadence of movies that, even when they don't all work, they contribute to the box office," he said.

Take this summer: With its $4.7 billion in domestic box office, the summer of 2026 was the highest-grossing in history (not adjusted for inflation). Across North America, 322 million tickets were sold, up 22% from last year. What Hollywood cheered most was who was buying those tickets: 18-to-35-year-olds, who made up 37% of the audience, a strong rebound since the pandemic.

And much of that elusive demographic showed up for "Obsession," directed by 25-year-old Curry Barker; and for "Backrooms," directed by a 21-year-old, Kane Parsons. "They were movies that were expected to do okay, but they were not expected to gross hundreds of millions of dollars and become phenomenons," Belloni said.

"Obsession," a horror riff on getting what you think you want, was made for under a million dollars – and has grossed more than half a billion worldwide. In its opening weeks, 75% of its audience was under 35, a success that elated the film's executive producer Jason Blum, who told a Producers Guild of America panel in June, "There's f*****g hope in the movie business, and it's exciting and it's great." According to Blum, "The stars of the internet, they want to make movies."

Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in "Obsession." Focus Features

Director Curry Barker is one of those internet stars, a YouTube content creator who gained a huge following making horror shorts and comedy skits. Some 800 million YouTube views later, learning along the way, Barker stepped onto his set as a first-time feature film director, writer and editor, an experience he called "really overwhelming and nerve-wracking. But then after I'd called 'action' on the first day, done a couple takes and called 'cut,' I very quickly realized that like, wait a second, yes, this is a bigger scale, but this is exactly the same thing I've been doing since I was 12 years old with my brothers.'"

For Belloni, it's a path to the big time that isn't like the olden days: "You would go to Sundance and you would be a breakout, you would do a short film, you would do a commercial, you would do a music video, and then Hollywood would come calling and you would get a first feature. What's happening now is that these young filmmakers are not just honing their craft; they're also honing their audience."

It's an audience that showed up massively for fellow first-time director Kane Parsons. His film "Backrooms" grossed $118 million worldwide in its opening weekend, making him, at age 20, the youngest director ever of a #1 film.

The movie was based on an unlikely viral photo of an empty store, which Parsons used as the inspiration for a video he created and posted to YouTube (now watched nearly 100 million times) featuring someone trapped in a series of maze-like rooms. Soon, the studio A24 came calling.

The origin of "Backrooms" was an unsettling picture of a deserted furniture store posted online. Kane Parsons took that as inspiration for a series of YouTube videos set in a maze of eerie rooms, which became the feature "Backrooms." YouTube/A24/CBS News

"'Backrooms' had a world around it," said Belloni. "It had something that particularly high school kids and 20-somethings knew about. If you're a studio, you want a pre-interested audience. 'Pre-branded' is what they say, and that's what 'Backrooms' ended up being for that audience."

Will we see more of this? Belloni said, "We're seeing announcements once a week from studios around town that are at least developing projects based on YouTube videos, or creators that have a following – you know, this guy has a couple million followers, let's see what he can do."

"All YouTube content creators, we start with zero subscribers," said Mark Vins. "And those first few years, those formative moments, your audience encouraging you, that's really the only positive feedback you have."

Vins should know; over the course of a dozen years, his YouTube channel "Brave Wilderness" has gone from zero to more than 20 million subscribers. He just debuted his first feature length documentary, "Reef to Ridge," at the Toronto International Film Festival.

"One of the questions I get asked often is, how do you pick your next story? How do you pick your next adventure?" Vins said. "And my answer is always the same: We have the world's largest focus group on YouTube, and we listen to them."

And thanks to YouTube's technology, creators can study what and how their audiences are watching.

Vins said, "It's not just the comment section; there's, like, deep analytical tools that we have, and we pay attention to all of those metrics, whether it's, like, you know, the retention graph, to when people are tuning in, tuning out, the click-through rate. All of that information creates an alchemy that becomes our instinct as creators."

It's a new kind of film school, which makes perfect sense to Kim Larson, YouTube's Head of Creators.: "What's really amazing about this moment in time is that filmmakers like Mark are getting recognized for the craft that's really always been on YouTube," she said. "I don't think we're doing anything different. I think we're in the middle of a cultural shift that's happening on YouTube."

So, will YouTube become the next place that all hot directors come from? Maybe, says Matt Belloni.

"It could be that if you have five million followers, you're gonna be a moviemaker," he said. "It could be that you're terrible at it, or you had one idea that you've exploited online and you have no other ideas.

"The thing that makes Hollywood great – and also drives people crazy – is you never know where the next hit is coming from," Belloni said. "And right now, the hot place to look is on YouTube. But who knows? It could be somewhere else tomorrow."



Story produced by Reid Orvedahl and Kay Lim. Editor: Jason Schmidt.

World.title: How YouTube creators are revamping Hollywood
World.content: How YouTube creators are revamping Hollywood It's been a huge year at the box office. But two of Hollywood's biggest hits came with the smallest expectations: "Obsession" and "Backrooms," horror films directed by YouTube creators on tiny budgets, which each grossed hundreds of millions of dollars – prompting studios to search for other social media-savvy talent. Correspondent Luke Burbank talks with Matt Belloni (co-founder of Puck and host of "The Town" podcast), filmmaker Mark Vins (co-founder of the YouTube channel Brave Wilderness), and YouTube's Kim Larson about how creators with millions of followers can study what and how their audience watches, making YouTube a valuable new kind of film school.

World.title: Several arrested, bomb disposal deployed near air base used by U.S. forces
World.content:
Several men have been arrested on suspicion of crimes related to explosives at a village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers, police in southwestern England said on Sunday. British counterterrorism police took over the investigation.

Police in Gloucestershire said it had declared a major incident and evacuated "a number of properties" in the Whelford area following the arrest of "several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act," referring to the country's laws around explosives.

The authorities also said a bomb disposal team were on site examining some vehicles.

A U.S. Air Force B-52 bomber takes off from RAF Fairford on March 19, 2026 in Fairford, England. Leon Neal / Getty Images

Some local residents were evacuated, police said, and a cordon was established but the incident is said to be "contained."

The town of Whelford is close to RAF Fairford, a base that American forces have used for strictly limited strikes during the war with Iran. After the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran on Feb. 28, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use the Fairford base to strike Iranian missile sites.

However, police did not confirm to the Associated Press whether the arrests were linked to the base.

The main gate of RAF Fairford after police declared a major incident and evacuated residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about one mile away. David Bown / Getty Images

One evacuated resident told the BBC, CBS News' international partner, that three "unusual vans" appeared in the area near Fairford air base overnight.

Speaking to the BBC, Julian Tubsbery, who was evacuated from his home in the early hours of Sunday, said that "there were these three vans that arrived in the middle of the village and a resident reported them to the police straight away."

Helicopter footage aired on BBC News showed a wheeled robot operating near three parked white vans near the base. However, the police have not yet confirmed which vehicles were being examined, or if they were connected with the incident.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant" but would not discuss specific force protection measures for security reasons.

"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families," the spokesperson said.

A police roadblock is in place on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. David Bown / Getty Images

The U.S. military's European Command said it would not discuss specific force protection measures, but added it would "take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European theater."

Security measures have been significantly increased in recent days at the air base, according to an eyewitness quoted by the Reuters news agency who said there had been more roadblocks and armed police preventing access.

A spokesperson for the U.K. government thanked emergency services for acting quickly and added that it would be "inappropriate to comment further whilst investigations are ongoing."

World.title: Northern Ireland march set for first time since Good Friday Agreement
World.content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm in Northern Ireland on Sunday after a contentious parade was given the go-ahead by the High Court in Belfast in a late-night sitting.

Thousands of protesters, many wearing balaclavas, delayed the march as they blocked the Orange Order, a group hugely supportive of Northern Ireland being part of the U.K., from proceeding down a street in the town of Portadown, where many favor unification with the Republic of Ireland.

"I wish we weren't in this position — I wish we weren't looking at relitigating things of the past," Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant told BBC News.

It's the first time in nearly 30 years that the Orange Order parade has been allowed to go down the Garvaghy Road, which had been a notorious flashpoint between the communities in the years before the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 largely ended the bloodshed in Northern Ireland. During the so-called Troubles, some 3,600 people were killed while some 50,000 were wounded.

Ending the Troubles meant balancing competing identities in Northern Ireland, which remained in the United Kingdom when the rest of Ireland won independence a century ago. Irish nationalists in the north — most of them Catholic — seek union with the Republic of Ireland, while largely Protestant unionists want to stay part of the U.K.

Burnham appealed for "calm on all sides" over the parade, saying there have been "big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don't want to see things go backwards."

Jon Boutcher, the head of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, called for "those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law," referring to a large protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there have been no signs of violence or disorder.

"Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland."

Politicians representing the two sides were opposed in their viewpoints on whether the march should go ahead.

Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, who represents Sinn Féin, the party historically linked to the Irish Republican Army, said the decision to give the march the go-ahead "brings into question how this whole peace process works."

"The progress of the last 28 years have been brought into question by the actions of the Orange Order and those within political unionism that want to drag us backwards," she said while attending the counterprotest on the Garvaghy Road.

Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, the largest pro-U.K. party in Northern Ireland, called out Sinn Féin leaders for inflaming the situation.

"The rule of law cannot apply only when Sinn Féin likes the outcome," he said. "Our institutions are founded on respect for the police, the courts and the rule of law."

The march was given the final go-ahead at a court hearing concluded at 2:15 a.m. Sunday.

The Orange Order is named after William of Orange, a Protestant prince of Holland who defeated the Catholic King James to take over the British throne in the 17th century.

World.title: Madonna's at the MTV VMAs tonight. Here's what to know about this year's show.
World.content:
Madonna is set to take the stage as a performer at the MTV Video Music Awards for the first time in over 20 years today as she looks to add to her 20 career wins at the VMAs.

The awards show also brings a milestone for Taylor Swift, who will be given the VMAs' first-ever Artist Director Honors, which organizers said recognizes artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."

The new accolade guarantees that Swift, who's also nominated in 11 categories, will become the show's most-awarded artist, breaking the tie between her and Beyoncé, who each collected 30 Moon Persons as of 2024. (Neither added to their total in 2025.)

Swift will also be debuting her new "Patient Zero" music video at the VMAs.

Nirvana, meanwhile, will be this year's Video Vanguard Award recipient.

What time do the 2026 VMAs start?

The show starts at 7:30 p.m. ET, 4:30 p.m. PT, on Sunday, Sept. 27.

Who's hosting the 2026 VMAs?

This year's show is being hosted by Snoop Dogg. The rapper known for hits like "Beautiful," "Drop It Like It's Hot" and "Gin and Juice" is no stranger to the VMAs stage, having first performed at the show in 1994 and winning three times during his career.

Snoop Dogg at the 2022 MTV VMAs at the Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for MTV/Paramount Global

Where to watch the 2026 VMAs

The VMAs will be airing on CBS television stations (find your local station here) and on MTV. The show will also be streaming on Paramount+.

How to watch the VMAs red carpet

See the stars arrive and check out the best looks from the red carpet in special coverage streaming live on CBS News Los Angeles starting at 6 p.m. ET, 3 p.m. PT, ahead of the VMAs.

Who are the VMA performers this year?

Along with Madonna's highly anticipated return, the performances at this year's VMAs include a special tribute to Dolly Parton by Kacey Musgraves, who is nominated in the best country category.

Here's a list of the VMA performers announced so far, in alphabetical order:

GENER8ION

Gunna

LISA

Madonna

Kacey Musgraves

RAYE

Shaboozey

Sienna Spiro

Sombr

Yung Lean

When Madonna last performed at the VMAs in August 2003, George W. Bush was in the White House, the U.S. was five months into the Iraq War, and Mark Zuckerberg was a few months away from launching what's now known as Facebook.

This year, a performance by the 68-year-old Queen of Pop will open the VMAs. She's up for 13 awards, the most of any nominee of the night. If she sweeps all 13 categories, her career total will go up to 33.

Madonna leads the 2026 nominees for the MTV Video Music Awards and will perform at the VMAs for the first time in over 20 years. Courtesy of Warner Records

LISA, a member of the K-pop group Blackpink and a four-time nominee this year, will be taking the stage to perform her new single "SaWaDiKa." First-time nominees GENER8ION and Swedish rapper Yung Lean, whose song "Storm" is up for four awards, will perform the world premiere of "Storm II."

Singer-songwriter Sombr, nominated in three categories, will join RAYE, whose hit "Where Is My Husband!" is up for song of the year, and Teddy Swims in a tribute performance for George Michael, who died in 2016. The tribute comes nearly 40 years after the release of his first solo album, "Faith."

Country and hip-hop artist Shaboozey will sing "Cowgirl," which received two nominations. He'll also join Gunna for their collaboration "High Noon."

Best new artist nominee Sienna Spiro will also take the stage during the night.

Fan voting in most categories closed Friday, but fans can still cast ballots for best new artist and song of the summer. Voting for the summer's top tune will be happening on MTV's Instagram Stories until 11 a.m. ET Sunday. Fans can vote for best new artist online even after the show starts.

The VMAs will be held at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, returning to the West Coast for the first time since 2017. The 7,100-seat theater last hosted the VMAs in 2015, when the venue was known as the Microsoft Theater.
