World.title: Maya apiary found near Tulum reveals roots of beekeeping traditions still practiced today
World.content:
Archaeologists exploring sites along the route of the Maya Train a few years ago uncovered a pre-Hispanic Maya bee house — a finding that has since shed light on how households from roughly 500 to 800 years ago may have produced honey.

The National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) said the structure was excavated in 2022 near Aktun Chen Natural Park, about 16 kilometers north of Tulum in the Riviera Maya.

On Tuesday, INAH released details from several years of analysis of the site, saying the apiary was likely used to raise Melipona beecheii, a stingless native bee whose honey, known as melipona honey, remains prized in southeastern Mexico.

It is used in foods, traditional remedies and other products.

The discovery also provides new clues to how Maya households raised bees alongside their other daily activities, such as tending crops.

The limestone structure measures 19.5 meters long, 3.9 meters wide and 1.2 meters high. Archaeologists believe it was a ná’ajil kab, or bee house, that held rows of hollow logs known as jobones for raising stingless bees.

Archaeologist Luis Ernesto Narváez Mac said in an INAH press release the site probably dates to the Late Postclassic period, from 1200 to 1521, but said ceramic analysis is needed to establish a more precise chronology.

Excavators found 40 limestone and coral discs, 10 to 20 centimeters in diameter, near the structure’s walls. The discs likely served as lids for the log hives, INAH said.

They also recovered stone objects thought to be fishing-net weights, grinding stones and pottery fragments that may have come from vessels used to store honey.

Archaeologists said the bee house was part of a wider Maya household complex that likely included homes, storage spaces and maybe a shrine.

The find is separate from a 2024 INAH-announced discovery of three stone hive lids on a different Maya Train section in Quintana Roo.

Melipona bee populations in southeastern Mexico face threats from deforestation and pesticide use, while the decline of traditional beekeeping has reduced the number of people managing colonies — although one Mexico News Daily correspondent is bucking that trend.

MND has also explored and published the top five melipona honey skincare and beauty products.

With reports from El Imparcial, Posta and Heritage Daily

World.title: Healthcare in Venezuela for Expats 2026: Clinics, Insurance and the Private Option
World.content:
GUIDES · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — The country Venezuela, an oil state of about 28.5 million people, has been run since January 2026 by acting president Delcy Rodríguez under close US oversight.

— The public system Free by law but badly run down. The Venezuelan Medical Federation said in September 2026 that 95% of hospitals had their doors “almost closed”.

— The private option Caracas has well-equipped private clinics, such as La Trinidad, El Ávila and Policlínica Metropolitana. They expect payment, usually in dollars, before treatment.

— Why it matters now Earthquakes on 24 June 2026 damaged hospitals across the north, just as airlines began to return.

— Insurance Local dollar policies cover private clinics. Canada’s travel advice urges cover for medical evacuation and hospital stays.

— The catch Governments still warn against travel, so check that your insurer covers Venezuela at all before you rely on it.

Healthcare in Venezuela works for foreigners only through the private tier. That means a good clinic, a dollar reserve, the right insurance and an exit plan.

Healthcare in Venezuela runs on two tracks in 2026. A free public system has decayed for more than a decade. Private clinics in Caracas still offer specialist care for those who can pay. This guide explains how both work for a foreign resident, as of September 2026.

How healthcare in Venezuela is organised

The 1999 constitution makes health a fundamental right and promises a free national public health system. The Ministry of Popular Power for Health runs most public hospitals and clinics. In law, anyone in the country can use them without paying.

In practice, most foreigners and middle-class Venezuelans use private clinics. These are paid out of pocket or through private health insurance, usually priced in US dollars.

Free care does not mean supplied care. Canada’s travel advice says some medicines are no longer available in hospitals at all.

The Hospital Universitario de Caracas, the capital’s main public teaching hospital, on the Central University campus (Photo: Caracas1830, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The public system in 2026

The US State Department describes Venezuela’s healthcare system as “in a state of severe crisis”. Its advisory, reissued on 26 June 2026, cites critical shortages of medicines, broken equipment and staff shortages.

Doctors say the same. Douglas León Natera leads the Venezuelan Medical Federation. On 23 September 2026 he said 95% of hospitals had their doors “almost closed”. He said only four or five were working properly and 302 needed repairs.

Money explains much of the decline. Transparencia Venezuela, an anti-corruption group, found that health received 4.24% of the 2025 public budget, a cut of 28% on 2024.

Then came the earthquakes. Two shocks of magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 struck north-central Venezuela on 24 June 2026. By 17 September authorities had reported 6,509 deaths and 226,696 people treated, according to the relief charity Direct Relief.

Direct Relief found 75 of 211 assessed health facilities inoperative in September, though 52 had already been closed before the quakes. The International Rescue Committee reported that Pariata hospital in La Guaira state fell from 108 beds to 35.

For a foreign resident, the lesson is simple. A public hospital may stabilise you in an emergency, but you should not plan to rely on it.

Private clinics in Caracas

Caracas has a cluster of large private clinics, many in the east and south-east of the city. The health ministry listed about a dozen of them, including all named below, among centres receiving earthquake patients in June 2026.

Clinic Area What to know Centro Médico Docente La Trinidad La Trinidad, El Hatillo (south-east) Teaching hospital on Avenida Intercomunal La Trinidad, with specialist clinics and units. Clínica El Ávila Altamira (east) Clinic on Avenida San Juan Bosco, with adult emergency care, imaging and a laboratory. Policlínica Metropolitana Caurimare (south-east) Full-service clinic with intensive care, emergency, obstetrics and cardiology. Hospital de Clínicas Caracas San Bernardino (centre-north) Private hospital on Avenida Panteón, in a district known for clinics and doctors’ offices. Clínica Santa Sofía, Sanatrix, La Floresta East and south-east Caracas Other private clinics on the ministry’s June 2026 list.

Clinics named by the Venezuelan health ministry in June 2026; addresses and services from clinic websites, checked 27 September 2026.

Expect to pay before you are treated. Canada’s travel advice, updated on 24 September 2026, says private facilities are “extremely costly”, low on supplies and require payment in advance.

That usually means a deposit, a card guarantee or an authorisation from your insurer before admission. Ask for a written estimate and for what the deposit covers, because doctors’ fees are often billed separately.

Ambulance services are very limited and slow, Canada warns. Private emergency services exist; one, Venemergencia, was among the providers listed by the ministry in June.

Policlínica Metropolitana in Caurimare, a full-service private clinic in south-eastern Caracas (Photo: Eleonora Mata Mirabal, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What private care costs

Clinics do not publish price lists, so treat every figure as a planning range. The Rio Times’ July 2026 cost-of-living survey put a private consultation in Caracas at about US$20 to US$50, depending on specialty.

For comparison, a US$50 specialist visit is about what a Venezuelan earning the state’s dollar-indexed income bonus receives in a week. That bonus was US$200 a month in May 2026, according to FEWS NET, a famine early-warning network.

Surgery and hospital stays can run into thousands of dollars. Complex procedures “can reach several hundred or thousands of dollars”, the same survey found, which is why deposits are standard.

Medicines are cheaper than in most of the region. Industry data from the drugmaker Grupo Leti put the average price at US$5.23 per unit in July 2026. That is about 36% below the Latin American average of US$8.18 at the end of 2025.

Health insurance: local and international

Venezuela’s insurance market is dominated by health cover. Hospitalisation, surgery and maternity policies, known locally as HCM, made up 68.21% of premiums in April 2026. That is according to the insurance regulator, Sudeaseg.

Mercantil Seguros held 30.55% of the market that month and Seguros Caracas 18.18%, Sudeaseg data show. Insurers collected US$418.84 million in net premiums from January to April 2026.

Local policies are sold in dollars and give direct access to clinic networks. Their limits can be low for serious illness, so check the sum insured, waiting periods and whether treatment abroad is covered.

Prices vary widely by age and cover. Journalism students at the Central University of Venezuela reported two examples in June 2026. One policy gave US$100,000 of cover for US$932 a year; another gave US$30,000 for US$993.

International expat insurers sell worldwide plans that can include evacuation. Many travel and health policies exclude countries under government warnings or sanctions, so get written confirmation that Venezuela is covered.

Medical evacuation: your exit plan

Evacuation cover pays to fly you to a better hospital abroad when local care is not enough. Canada’s travel advice tells visitors to buy insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays.

Air ambulances are expensive. One US operator put long-distance and international transfers at US$50,000 and upward in June 2026, depending on the mission. That equals more than 20 years of the US$200 monthly income bonus.

Consular help is thin. Canada’s embassy in Caracas has not been open since 2019. The US embassy resumed operations in March 2026 but offers emergency services to US citizens only. Your insurer’s assistance line will organise an evacuation.

Flights help too. Caracas’s Maiquetía airport reopened partially on 1 September 2026 after the earthquakes. Airlines including Iberia, Air Europa and LATAM have resumed routes.

The check-in hall at Simón Bolívar International Airport in Maiquetía, Caracas’s main gateway, which reopened under restrictions on 1 September 2026 (Photo: Wilfredor, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Medicines in 2026: shortage or supply?

The picture is contradictory. Canada warns of a severe shortage of pharmaceutical drugs and says most hospital pharmacies and drugstores no longer stock basic medicines.

Industry figures point the other way for private pharmacies. Grupo Leti data show 248.2 million units distributed from January to July 2026, up 11.31% on a year earlier. Industry groups said in January 2026 that stocks covered about 90 days.

Both can be true. Private chains in Caracas are generally stocked for those who can pay, while public hospitals and smaller towns face gaps.

Bring what you need. Canada advises packing all prescription and over-the-counter medicines, with a spare supply. Carry prescriptions using generic drug names.

Disease risks to plan for

Mosquito-borne diseases are common, the US advisory says, including dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche and yellow fever. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends malaria prevention for some travel.

Contaminated water is a significant source of stomach infections, according to the same advisory. Drink bottled or treated water, especially where the earthquakes damaged supply.

See a travel clinic before you arrive. Ask about yellow fever vaccination and malaria tablets, depending on where in Venezuela you will live or travel.

What this means for you

Choose your clinic before you choose your flat. Living near La Trinidad, El Ávila or Policlínica Metropolitana shortens the most important journey you may ever make in Caracas.

Hold a dollar reserve for deposits, even with insurance, because authorisations take time. Combine a local dollar policy for clinic access with international cover that names Venezuela and includes evacuation.

Healthcare in Venezuela can serve a foreign resident well in the private tier. It cannot yet be trusted for serious illness without a plan to leave, so treat evacuation cover as essential rather than optional.

Sources: Health-system facts come from the US State Department, the Government of Canada, the Venezuelan Medical Federation, Direct Relief and the International Rescue Committee, with market data from Sudeaseg and Grupo Leti as reported in Venezuelan media.

What Is Not Known

No independent national survey of hospital conditions for 2026 was found. The Venezuelan Medical Federation’s figures are statements by its president, not a published audit. The government has not released comparable data.

How far the earthquake damage has been repaired is not established. Direct Relief and the IRC counted inoperative and damaged facilities in September 2026. No official timetable for rebuilding the affected hospitals has been published.

Private clinic prices are not published. The consultation range in this guide comes from a Rio Times survey, not from clinic tariffs. Deposits and daily room rates vary by clinic, doctor and diagnosis.

Which international insurers currently cover residence in Venezuela is not documented in one place. Policies differ by issuing company and country, and exclusions tied to travel warnings or sanctions change. Only written confirmation from an insurer settles the question.

How reliable medicine supply is outside Caracas is unclear. Industry data measure units sold nationally, while Canada describes severe shortages. No independent 2026 survey of pharmacy stock by region was found.

More: Venezuela news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is healthcare in Venezuela free for foreigners?

Public care is free by law under the 1999 constitution, and foreigners can use it. In practice public hospitals are short of medicines, staff and equipment, and patients often have to bring supplies. Most foreigners use private clinics and pay in dollars or through insurance.

What are the best private clinics in Caracas?

Large private clinics used by foreigners include Centro Médico Docente La Trinidad, Clínica El Ávila in Altamira, Policlínica Metropolitana in Caurimare and Hospital de Clínicas Caracas in San Bernardino. All were listed by the health ministry among centres receiving patients after the June 2026 earthquakes. Expect to pay a deposit or show insurance before treatment.

How much does a doctor’s visit cost in Caracas?

A private consultation costs roughly US$20 to US$50, depending on specialty, according to a Rio Times survey from July 2026. Surgery and hospital stays can reach thousands of dollars. Clinics usually ask for payment or an insurer’s guarantee in advance.

Do I need medical evacuation insurance for Venezuela?

Yes. Canada’s travel advice tells visitors to buy insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays. International air-ambulance transfers can cost US$50,000 or more, and Canada’s embassy in Caracas has not been open since 2019.

Are medicines still scarce in Venezuela in 2026?

The picture is mixed. Canada warns of a severe shortage, especially in hospital pharmacies. Industry data show 248.2 million units distributed from January to July 2026, up 11.31%, so private pharmacies in Caracas are generally stocked. Bring your own supply of any regular medication.

Does travel insurance cover Venezuela?

Not always. Many policies exclude countries under government travel warnings or sanctions. The United States rates Venezuela Level 3, reconsider travel, and Canada advises against all travel, so get written confirmation that your policy covers Venezuela and evacuation.

World.title: What Is Petrobras? Brazil’s Oil Giant Explained — the Business, the Politics and What to Watch
World.content:
GUIDES · BRAZIL

Key Facts — What it is Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., Brazil’s state-controlled oil and gas company, founded in 1953 and headquartered in Rio de Janeiro.

— Production 3.34 million barrels of oil equivalent a day of its own output in the second quarter of 2026. About 83 percent came from the deep-water pre-salt fields.

— Latest results Net income of US$10.4 billion in the second quarter of 2026, more than double a year earlier. Sales revenue was US$33.6 billion.

— Who controls it The federal government holds 50.26 percent of the voting shares but only 29.02 percent of the total capital, as of August 2026.

— Chief executive Magda Chambriard, in office since 24 May 2024 and still in post as of September 2026.

— Shares Preferred shares closed at R$47.99 (about US$9.25) in São Paulo on 25 September 2026. The New York receipts, ticker PBR, closed at US$20.37. The real traded at R$5.19 to the US dollar, according to market data.

What is Petrobras, how does it make its money, who really controls it, and why do fuel prices keep turning into politics? A plain guide for foreign readers and investors.

What is Petrobras? It is Brazil’s oil company, owned partly by the state and partly by private investors around the world. It pumps most of its oil from beneath a thick layer of salt far off the coast. And because the government controls it, every change in fuel prices is also a political decision.

What is Petrobras and what does it do?

Petrobras was created by law in October 1953 under President Getúlio Vargas. For more than four decades it held a legal monopoly on Brazilian oil. The sector was opened to competitors in the late 1990s, but Petrobras remains by far the country’s biggest producer.

Its core business is exploration and production: finding oil and gas and pumping it out. Oil companies usually measure operating profit as EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. In the second quarter of 2026, this division produced US$15.9 billion of Petrobras’s adjusted EBITDA.

Most of that oil comes from the pre-salt. These reservoirs lie under a salt layer up to two kilometres thick. They sit deep beneath the Atlantic off Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The oil is costly to reach but cheap to lift once wells are running.

How cheap? In the second quarter of 2026, lifting a barrel from the pre-salt cost Petrobras US$4.45, before taxes and leasing. Brent crude, the international benchmark, averaged US$104.52 a barrel over the same three months.

Petrobras also refines. Its refineries ran at 101.2 percent of nominal capacity in the second quarter, a company record. They produced about 1.9 million barrels a day of diesel, petrol, jet fuel and other products. It sells gas and generates some electricity too.

What Petrobras does not do is run the green-and-yellow petrol stations that carry its name. Those belong to Vibra Energia, the former BR Distribuidora, which Petrobras sold off. Vibra uses the Petrobras brand under licence.

A Petrobras-branded fuel station; the stations are run by Vibra Energia, the former BR Distribuidora (Photo: Moacir Ximenes, CC BY 3.0 BR via Wikimedia Commons)

The numbers: what the latest results show

The latest reported results cover the second quarter of 2026, the three months to 30 June. Petrobras published them on 6 August 2026. It reports in reais and in US dollars; the dollar figures are used here.

Sales revenue was US$33.6 billion, up 60 percent on a year earlier. Net income was US$10.4 billion, up 120 percent.

Stripping out one-off items, such as currency gains and the new export tax, net income was US$11.1 billion. Adjusted EBITDA on the same basis was US$20.0 billion. The company called it one of its highest quarterly results on record.

Two things drove it. Oil was expensive, with Brent averaging US$104.52 a barrel against US$67.82 a year earlier. And output was at a record: own production rose 14.1 percent on the year, as new production ships reached full flow.

The cash side matters most to shareholders. Operating cash flow was US$12.3 billion and free cash flow, what is left after investment, US$7.7 billion. Capital spending in the quarter was US$5.3 billion.

Debt is under control by the company’s own yardstick. Gross debt was US$70.8 billion at the end of June, below the US$75 billion ceiling in its 2026–2030 business plan. Net debt was 1.14 times a year’s adjusted EBITDA.

Petrobras is also one of the state’s biggest cash sources. It says it paid R$88.6 billion (about US$17.1 billion) in taxes to federal, state and municipal governments in the quarter. That is roughly R$1 billion (about US$190 million) a day.

It operates through three segments: Exploration and Production; Refining, Transportation & Marketing; and Gas & Low Carbon Energies. The Exploration and Production segment explores, develops, and produces…

Owners and management: who controls Petrobras

Petrobras is a mixed-capital company. It is listed on the São Paulo exchange, B3, and in New York. By law, however, the federal government must keep voting control. That control is the single most important fact about the company.

As of August 2026, the federal government held 50.26 percent of the common, or voting, shares. It held no preferred shares, which carry dividend priority but no vote. So its stake in the whole company was only 29.02 percent.

The state development bank, BNDES, and its investment arm hold another 6.43 percent of the capital. Together the state bloc owns about 35.45 percent. Non-Brazilian investors held 48.29 percent, more than the state.

Voting control means the government chooses the majority of the board and, through it, the chief executive. The board is chaired by Guilherme Santos Mello, appointed by the controlling shareholder.

Magda Chambriard, an engineer who spent more than two decades at Petrobras and later headed the national oil regulator, the ANP, became chief executive on 24 May 2024. She replaced Jean Paul Prates, whom President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva removed. She was still in post as of September 2026.

Turnover at the top is a known risk. Chambriard is the sixth chief executive since January 2019. Several of her predecessors left after clashing with the government of the day over fuel prices.

Magda Chambriard at her swearing-in ceremony as Petrobras chief executive in Rio de Janeiro, June 2024 (Photo: Ricardo Stuckert/PR, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Its role in the market

Petrobras is not just a company in Brazil’s economy; it shapes it. Its refineries supply much of the country’s diesel and petrol, so its wholesale prices set the tone for what drivers pay. It commissions the giant floating production ships that shipyards and suppliers depend on. Its platform contracts run to billions of dollars each.

It is also a large exporter. Crude exports approached one million barrels a day in the second quarter, while imports of crude fell to 89,000 barrels a day. The pre-salt has made Brazil Latin America’s largest oil producer, well ahead of Guyana and Venezuela, its neighbours to the north.

The business plan approved in November 2025 foresees US$109 billion of investment from 2026 to 2030. About US$69 billion goes to exploration and production, most of it in the pre-salt. Production is planned to peak at around 3.4 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in 2028 and 2029.

The plan was drawn up in late 2025, when oil was much cheaper. Prices in 2026 have been far higher, largely because of the Middle East war. The gap explains the record profits, and why the government wants a share of them.

Petrobras also holds 47.03 percent of the voting shares in Braskem. Braskem is the largest producer of thermoplastic resins in the Americas. Braskem is trying to restructure about US$11 billion of debt, and Petrobras has said it will not inject capital alone.

Risks and controversies: fuel prices, politics and the Amazon

Fuel prices are the permanent flashpoint. Until May 2023 Petrobras priced fuel at “import parity”, tracking what it would cost to import. It then switched to a commercial strategy that also weighs the domestic market. That lets it smooth out swings in world prices rather than pass them straight on.

2026 has tested it. When the Middle East war pushed oil prices up, the government acted on 12 March. It created a 12 percent export tax on crude and a 50 percent export tax on diesel. It also paid a subsidy of R$0.32 a litre (about US$0.06) on road diesel.

Petrol followed the same pattern. On 28 May Petrobras raised its petrol price to distributors by R$0.48 a litre (about US$0.09). A federal discount of R$0.44 (about US$0.08) absorbed most of it. On 9 September the discount ended and Petrobras added R$0.19 (about US$0.04), lifting the cost to distributors by R$0.63 a litre (about US$0.12).

That left the average wholesale price at R$3.24 a litre (about US$0.62). A temporary cut in federal fuel taxes of the same size was meant to keep pump prices unchanged. In an election year, the effect has been to keep higher oil costs away from drivers.

The crude export tax is contested. Producers say it is unconstitutional. A court suspended it in late August, and an appeals court reinstated it on 31 August. The original emergency measure had lapsed in July; since then the government has kept the crude levy alive through resolutions of its foreign-trade committee, Gecex. It had raised R$7.98 billion (about US$1.54 billion) by July and cost Petrobras US$965 million in the second quarter alone.

The Margem Equatorial is the environmental fight. This is a stretch of Brazil’s northern coast, near the mouth of the Amazon, which geologists compare with the fields off Guyana. After refusing a first request in 2023, the environment agency IBAMA licensed Petrobras to drill there in October 2025.

On 14 August 2026 Petrobras reported signs of hydrocarbons in its Morpho well. The well is in block FZA-M-59, about 175 kilometres off the state of Amapá. It has not said whether the find is commercial. Environmental groups and federal prosecutors still question the licensing.

The past also weighs. The Lava Jato, or Car Wash, investigations from 2014 exposed a bribery and cartel scheme around Petrobras contracts. In 2018 the company agreed to pay US$2.95 billion to settle a US class action and US$853 million to US authorities.

The mouth of the Amazon seen from the International Space Station; Petrobras’s Margem Equatorial well lies offshore to the north, off Amapá (Photo: NASA, public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

What to watch

The election. Brazil votes on 4 October 2026, with a possible runoff on 25 October. Whoever takes office in January 2027 will shape Petrobras’s board, its pricing and its dividends. Our election briefing sets out the race.

The export tax. The 12 percent levy runs until November, and the court case over it is not settled. Whether it is renewed or dropped will move Petrobras’s export earnings.

The Amazon well. Drilling at Morpho was expected to end in October 2026. IBAMA authorised three more wells nearby on 4 September 2026, and Petrobras plans to start drilling them in January 2027. The results will decide whether the Margem Equatorial becomes a new pre-salt or a costly dry run.

The next business plan. Petrobras usually approves its five-year plan in late November. The key numbers are investment, the debt ceiling and the oil price it assumes.

Braskem. A buyout auction is set for 16 October, with the debt deadline in November. Any call on Petrobras’s cash would be a test of its investment discipline.

What this means for foreigners and investors

Foreign investors can buy Petrobras in New York. Each PBR receipt represents two common shares, and each PBR.A receipt two preferred shares. In São Paulo the tickers are PETR3 for common and PETR4 for preferred shares.

At the closing prices of 25 September 2026, the whole company was worth about R$656 billion (about US$126.5 billion). The PETR3 common shares closed at R$53.04 (about US$10.23).

Dividends are the main attraction, and they follow a formula. When gross debt is at or below the plan’s ceiling, Petrobras must pay out 45 percent of free cash flow. For the second quarter of 2026 it approved R$17.4 billion (about US$3.35 billion) in dividends and interest on capital.

A few things this does not mean. Majority voting control does not mean the state owns most of the company; directly it owns less than a third. And Petrobras does not set pump prices. It sets wholesale prices; taxes, ethanol blending and retail margins do the rest.

It also does not mean the dividend is fixed. The formula depends on free cash flow, which depends on oil prices, taxes and investment. A new government can change the policy through the board. Our Brazil explainer covers the wider political system.

Sources: Results and production from Petrobras’ second-quarter 2026 filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and its news agency, ownership from its investor-relations site, and share prices and exchange rates from market data at the close on 25 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether the Amazon find is worth developing. Petrobras has reported signs of hydrocarbons, not a commercial discovery. It has given no estimate of volumes, and appraisal wells start only in 2027.

What the next government will do. Petrobras policy on prices, dividends and investment has changed with almost every administration. The winner of the October election is not known, and neither is their choice of chief executive.

How long the export tax lasts. It has been extended by resolutions of the government’s foreign-trade committee, suspended by one court and restored by another. The final ruling on whether it is constitutional has not been made.

Where oil prices settle. The 2026 results rest on prices well above the company’s own planning assumptions. How long the Middle East war keeps them there cannot be forecast.

What Braskem will cost. The restructuring talks are unresolved. Petrobras has not said how far it would go if the other owners do not match its terms.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Petrobras?

Petrobras, or Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., is Brazil’s state-controlled oil and gas company, founded in 1953 and based in Rio de Janeiro. It produced 3.34 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in the second quarter of 2026, mostly from deep-water pre-salt fields.

Who owns Petrobras?

The federal government holds 50.26 percent of the voting shares, which gives it control, but only 29.02 percent of the total capital. With the development bank BNDES, the state owns about 35 percent. Non-Brazilian investors held about 48 percent as of August 2026.

Who is the CEO of Petrobras in 2026?

Magda Chambriard, an engineer who spent more than two decades at Petrobras and later headed the national oil regulator, the ANP. She took office on 24 May 2024 and was still chief executive as of September 2026.

Does Petrobras pay dividends?

Yes. Its policy requires it to pay out 45 percent of free cash flow while gross debt stays at or below the ceiling in its business plan, currently US$75 billion. For the second quarter of 2026 it approved R$17.4 billion, about US$3.35 billion.

Does Petrobras set petrol prices in Brazil?

It sets the wholesale price it charges distributors, not the pump price. Pump prices also include federal and state taxes, the ethanol blend and distributor and retailer margins. In 2026 the government used tax cuts and discounts to offset Petrobras price rises.

Can foreigners buy Petrobras shares?

Yes. Petrobras receipts trade on the New York Stock Exchange as PBR, each representing two common shares, and PBR.A for preferred shares. In São Paulo the shares trade as PETR3 and PETR4.

World.title: What Is Nubank? Brazil’s Fintech Giant Explained — the Business, the Numbers and What to Watch
World.content:
GUIDES · COMPANIES

Key Facts — What it is Nubank is a fully digital bank from São Paulo, founded in 2013, that serves 139 million customers in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia — one of the largest banking platforms in the world.

— The numbers In the second quarter of 2026 Nubank earned over US$5 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time, with net income of about US$871 million and a return on equity of 29 percent.

— In Brazil With almost 118 million customers — about 61 percent of all adults — Nubank overtook Bradesco in early 2026 to become the country’s second-largest financial institution by customer base.

— Abroad Mexico passed 16 million customers in July 2026 (third-largest institution there, and profitable); Colombia passed 5 million. A US entry is planned.

— Ownership Listed on the New York Stock Exchange (ticker NU) since December 2021 through Nu Holdings. Founder David Vélez is CEO; Berkshire Hathaway has been a shareholder since before the IPO.

— Why it matters Nubank proved that a bank with no branches can outgrow 100-year-old giants — and forced every bank in Latin America to cut fees and rebuild its app.

Thirteen years ago, opening a bank account in Brazil meant queues, paperwork and some of the highest fees in the world. Then a purple card arrived. Nubank — the name plays on “nu”, Portuguese for both “new” and “naked”, as in transparent — is today the most valuable fintech story ever built in Latin America and, by customer count, one of the biggest banks on the planet. This guide explains what Nubank is, how it makes money, and why its next moves matter for the whole region.

Where it came from

Nubank was founded in São Paulo in 2013 by David Vélez, a Colombian former Sequoia Capital partner, together with Brazilian Cristina Junqueira and American Edward Wible. Vélez’s founding story is famous: he spent weeks fighting Brazilian bank bureaucracy and concluded that a bank built like a software company — no branches, no fees, customer service that answers — could take the incumbents apart.

The first product, launched in 2014, was a no-annual-fee credit card managed entirely through an app. It spread by word of mouth because the alternative was paying triple-digit interest rates at banks that treated customers as a nuisance. By the time Nubank listed on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2021 — backed early by Berkshire Hathaway with a US$500 million investment — it already had more than 40 million customers.

How it makes money

Nubank’s model has three engines. First, the free account and card acquire customers at almost zero marketing cost. Second, it earns interchange fees on card spending and interest on credit card balances and personal loans. Third, it cross-sells: investments through NuInvest, insurance, travel eSIMs, a marketplace, and premium tiers — “Ultravioleta” for high-income clients and, since July 2026, “Croma” for its mass-affluent core.

The economics are unusually strong because everything is digital: Nubank’s efficiency ratio — what it costs to generate a real of revenue — is around 19.5 percent, while traditional Brazilian banks operate near 50 percent. Average revenue per active customer reached about US$17 a month in mid-2026 and keeps climbing as customers add products. About 83.5 percent of customers are active monthly; in Brazil the figure passed 86 percent.

The numbers today

The second quarter of 2026 was the strongest in the company’s history: 139 million customers globally, quarterly revenue above US$5 billion for the first time, net income of about US$871 million, and a return on equity of 29 percent — figures most traditional banks cannot match. Brazil contributes almost 118 million customers; Mexico reached 15.8 million in the quarter (16 million by July) and turned profitable; Colombia passed five million.

In January 2026 Brazil’s central bank confirmed a symbolic changing of the guard: Nubank had overtaken Bradesco to become the country’s second-largest financial institution by customers, behind only state-owned Caixa. It also serves more small businesses than any other financial institution in Brazil.

The technology bet

Nubank increasingly describes itself as an AI company that runs a bank. Its proprietary foundation models, branded “NuFormer”, now drive credit-card decisions in Brazil and Mexico and unsecured lending in Brazil. An “AI Private Banker” already serves more than 15 million monthly users. The pitch is that better models mean better credit decisions — though the stress test is visible: delinquency on loans 15-90 days late ticked up to about 5.0 percent in 2026 as the credit portfolio expanded.

The competition and the criticisms

Nubank no longer fights only other fintechs (Inter, C6, PicPay, Mercado Pago); it fights Itaú and the rest of the old guard, which responded by slashing fees and rebuilding their own apps — a consumer windfall Nubank can claim credit for. Regulators watch it like a bank now, because it is one. The criticisms: customer service quality strains at this scale; interest rates on revolving credit, while cheaper than incumbents, remain high by international standards; and some analysts question how much of Brazil is left to conquer — which is precisely why Mexico, Colombia and the planned US entry matter so much.

What to watch

Credit quality: whether AI underwriting holds up through a full economic cycle is the central risk. Mexico: the same playbook that worked in Brazil is now scaling there, and a full banking license would deepen it further. The United States: Nubank has said it plans to enter, which would test the model against the world’s toughest fintech market. And regulation: as a systemically important institution in Brazil, capital and liquidity rules will tighten around it.

What this means for foreigners

For expats in Brazil, Nubank is usually the fastest financial first step: a CPF (tax number), a smartphone and a Brazilian address get you an account in minutes, with free Pix transfers — the instant-payment system that runs Brazilian daily life. Credit limits start small and grow with use. For investors, NU stock is the purest listed exposure to Latin American consumer finance, with the currency and regulatory risks that implies.

Connected Coverage

Nubank is the flagship of a wider transformation: read our Brazil Explained 2026 guide for the country context, and follow our Brazil Fintech coverage for Pix, open finance and the challengers trying to repeat the purple trick.

What Is Not Known

Whether Nubank’s credit models stay superior through a real Brazilian downturn is untested — the current cycle has been benign. The timing and structure of the US entry are undecided in public. And how regulators in three (soon four) countries will treat an AI-driven lender of this size is an open question everywhere.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Nubank?

Nubank is a digital bank founded in São Paulo in 2013. With 139 million customers in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia as of mid-2026, it is the largest digital financial services platform in Latin America and one of the largest banks in the world by customer count.

How does Nubank make money if accounts are free?

Mainly through interchange fees on card spending, interest on credit-card balances and personal loans, and cross-selling of investments, insurance and premium tiers like Ultravioleta. Because it has no branches, its cost to serve each customer is a fraction of a traditional bank’s.

Can foreigners open a Nubank account?

Yes, if they live in Brazil. You need a CPF (the Brazilian tax number), a local address and a smartphone. Accounts for foreigners with a residence permit are routine; the app is in Portuguese, with English support improving steadily.

Is Nubank safe?

Nubank is a licensed financial institution regulated by Brazil’s central bank, and deposits are covered by Brazil’s deposit guarantee fund (FGC) up to the legal limit, like other banks. It is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and publishes audited quarterly results.

How big is Nubank compared with traditional banks?

In early 2026 Nubank overtook Bradesco to become Brazil’s second-largest financial institution by customer base, with almost 118 million customers — about 61 percent of the country’s adults. Only state-owned Caixa is bigger by that measure. By assets and branches, the traditional giants still lead.

Where does Nubank operate?

Brazil (its home market), Mexico — where it passed 16 million customers in 2026 and turned profitable — and Colombia, with more than five million. The company has said it plans to enter the United States.

World.title: Moving to Trinidad and Tobago 2026: Visas, Costs, Work Permits and Daily Life
World.content:
GUIDES · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — The basics A twin-island republic of about 1.4 million off Venezuela, with the Caribbean’s most industrial economy — oil, gas and petrochemicals, not tourism.

— Visas There is no digital-nomad or retirement visa. Most foreigners move on an employer-sponsored work permit; CARICOM skilled nationals have their own route. Permanent residence comes after years of permits.

— Costs Moderate by Caribbean standards: a solid two-bedroom rental in a good Port of Spain district runs roughly US$800-1,500 a month; imported goods and cars are expensive.

— Safety The serious caveat: Trinidad has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas, concentrated in specific districts. Tobago is far calmer.

— Who it suits Energy-sector professionals, regional executives and their families — people with an employer, not backpackers with laptops.

Trinidad and Tobago breaks the Caribbean template. The beaches exist — mostly on Tobago — but the economy runs on natural gas, LNG, methanol and ammonia from the industrial estates of Point Lisas. That makes it one of the few Caribbean states where foreigners move for work rather than winter sun, and where the expat infrastructure — international schools, gated compounds, decent hospitals — exists because Shell, bp and the regional banks needed it. This guide explains how to move there legally, what it costs, and how to handle the one big downside: crime.

Visas and permits: the honest picture

Citizens of the US, EU, UK, Canada and many other countries enter visa-free for short visits — but living and working is a different regime. There is no digital-nomad visa and no retirement visa. The standard route is a work permit, applied for by your employer, tied to that employer and renewed annually. CARICOM nationals with recognized skills certificates can move under the free-movement regime. After a continuous run of work permits — typically five years — you can apply for permanent residence; citizenship follows after that. Spouses of citizens and people of Trinidadian descent have separate, faster tracks. The practical rule: secure the job before the move; the permit follows the employer, not the other way round.

Where expats live

In Trinidad, almost everything happens along the East-West Corridor. Port of Spain’s western neighborhoods — St. Clair, Woodbrook, Newtown, Westmoorings and the gated enclaves toward the northwest peninsula — hold most expat housing, close to the international schools and the business district. Further east, Trincity and the towns toward the university at St. Augustine offer cheaper, newer stock with worse commute traffic. In Tobago, foreigners cluster around Crown Point and the southwest coast — a different country in feel: small, slow, beach-oriented and noticeably calmer on every safety metric.

Trinidad street (Photo: Jean-Pierre Lavoie, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What life costs

Housing: US$800-1,500 a month rents a solid two-bedroom in a good Port of Spain district; high-end gated townhouses in Westmoorings run higher, and Tobago beach villas vary wildly by season. Food: local produce, doubles and roti shops are cheap; imported brands carry Caribbean markups, so supermarket bills feel close to US levels if you shop American. Cars are the big expense — high import duties make even used vehicles pricey, and you will need one; Port of Spain’s “maxi taxi” minibuses and ride apps fill gaps but do not replace a car for family life. Utilities and internet are reasonably priced; electricity is cheap by island standards thanks to domestic gas.

The crime question, honestly

Trinidad’s homicide rate — among the highest in the Americas in recent years — is the fact every arrival must plan around. The violence is concentrated in specific Port of Spain districts and gangs tied to the drug trade; it is not randomly distributed, and foreign professionals living in the western suburbs are rarely victims. But the ambient level shapes behavior: homes have burglar bars and alarms, night driving routes are chosen deliberately, and certain areas are simply not entered. Tobago operates at a completely different (much lower) level. None of this deters the energy companies, and it need not deter you — but it should shape where you live and how you move.

Trinidad, Colorado Amtrak stop (Photo: Hollowayvideo, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Schools, healthcare and the practical stack

International schools in Port of Spain (following British and American curricula) serve the expat and upper-middle-class local market; places are limited — apply early. Private healthcare in Port of Spain is competent for routine needs, with serious cases sometimes referred abroad; standard expat practice is international health insurance with evacuation cover. Banking is straightforward once you have a work permit, with Republic Bank, First Citizens, RBC and Scotiabank all present. The Trinidad and Tobago dollar floats around TT$6.7-6.8 per US dollar; foreign exchange can be scarce at banks, a chronic quirk of the economy worth asking your employer about.

What this means for your decision

Move to Trinidad if you have a concrete job offer in energy, finance or regional management — the professional infrastructure is real, the salary packages compensate for the inconveniences, and Carnival plus the food scene deliver a cultural life no other Caribbean island matches. Consider Tobago if your income is location-independent and you want the Caribbean dream with Trinidad’s airport connections. Do not move on spec: without an employer, there is no visa path, and without planning, the safety map will catch you out.

Connected Coverage

For the full country picture — the gas economy, the politics and the Venezuela question across the strait — read our Trinidad and Tobago Explained 2026 guide.

What Is Not Known

Rental and cost figures for Trinidad are estimates from listings, not official statistics — no reliable index exists. The government has periodically discussed new residence categories, and rules can change; always verify current permit requirements with the Ministry of National Security or a local immigration attorney before planning around them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I move to Trinidad and Tobago without a job?

Practically, no. There is no digital-nomad or retirement visa. The standard route is an employer-sponsored work permit; CARICOM skilled nationals have a separate free-movement route. Permanent residence becomes possible after several continuous years of work permits.

How much does it cost to live in Trinidad?

A solid two-bedroom rental in a good Port of Spain district runs roughly US$800-1,500 a month. Local food is cheap, imported goods are priced like the US, and cars are expensive because of import duties. A comfortable expat family budget typically starts around US$3,000-4,000 a month.

Is Trinidad and Tobago safe for expats?

Trinidad has one of the higher homicide rates in the Americas, but the violence is concentrated in specific districts and rarely touches foreign professionals in the western suburbs. Tobago is far calmer. Choose your district carefully, secure your home, and plan night movements deliberately.

Trinidad or Tobago — where should I live?

Trinidad if your life is work: the jobs, schools, hospitals and business infrastructure are all there. Tobago if your income is remote and your priorities are beaches, quiet and safety — accepting fewer services and reliance on the air or sea bridge for anything serious.

Do I need a car in Trinidad?

Yes, in practice. Port of Spain has maxi taxis and ride apps, but family life, school runs and shopping assume a car. Budget for high vehicle prices — import duties make even used cars expensive by North American standards.

World.title: Taxes in Venezuela for Expats 2026: What Foreigners Pay During the Transformation
World.content:
GUIDES · VENEZUELA

Key Facts — Residency rule You become a Venezuelan tax resident by spending more than 183 days in the country in a calendar year — residents are, on paper, taxed on worldwide income.

— Income tax The personal income tax (ISLR) is progressive, topping out at 34 percent — but hyperinflation-era bracket mechanics make the real burden highly dependent on how and in what currency you earn.

— Sales taxes VAT (IVA) is 16 percent. On top of it, a 3 percent tax on large financial transactions (IGTF) hits payments made in foreign currency — which in dollarized Venezuela means most serious purchases.

— The reality gap Enforcement against foreign individuals living quietly on foreign income has historically been weak — but the transformation-era state is rebuilding its tax capacity, and weak enforcement is not the same as no obligation.

— The rule of thumb If you live there, assume you are taxable, register (RIF), file, and get a local contador. The cost of compliance is low; the cost of being noticed later is not.

Taxes in Venezuela are a study in contrasts: a modern-looking tax code written over an economy that runs on cash US dollars, collected by a state whose enforcement capacity collapsed and is now, in the transformation period, being rebuilt. For an expat, the question is not only “what do I owe?” but “what does the system actually do?” This guide answers both — the law as written, and the practice as lived — so you can make clean decisions.

Am I a Venezuelan tax resident?

The trigger is physical presence: more than 183 days in Venezuela in a calendar year makes you a tax resident. Residents are formally taxable on worldwide income; non-residents only on Venezuelan-source income. In practice, the people the system reliably captures are employees of Venezuelan companies (tax withheld at source) and registered businesses. The expat living on a foreign pension or remote salary exists in a grayer zone — technically taxable, historically under-enforced, and increasingly visible as financial systems digitize. The safe posture is to assume the 183-day rule will be applied to you eventually and to structure for compliance from day one.

Income tax (ISLR) in practice

Venezuela’s personal income tax uses progressive brackets up to a 34 percent top rate, denominated in “tax units” (unidades tributarias) that the state adjusts — historically too slowly during hyperinflation, which compressed the brackets and pushed even modest formal salaries into high nominal rates. What matters for expats is less the schedule than the mechanics: income earned in Venezuela from a Venezuelan employer is withheld and reported; income from abroad paid into foreign accounts has rarely been systematically taxed, but declaring foreign income is the legally correct path for residents. Local accountants (contadores) charge modest fees — use one; the filing system (the SENIAT portal) assumes you have.

1 Bolivar 2009 BsF (Photo: Veronidae, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The taxes you will actually feel: IVA and IGTF

Daily economic life runs on two consumption taxes. IVA, the value-added tax, is 16 percent and baked into prices. IGTF, the tax on large financial transactions, adds 3 percent to payments in foreign currency or made with certain instruments — and because Venezuela’s retail economy is de facto dollarized, IGTF is the tax foreigners notice most: pay for dinner in dollars and the receipt shows it. Together they push the effective consumption-tax load toward 19 percent on dollar transactions. Some merchants offer a small discount for bolívar payment via local apps; whether that saving is worth holding bolívares is a daily judgment call locals make automatically.

Property, municipal and business taxes

Property owners pay municipal taxes set by each municipality — low in dollar terms after years of currency collapse, but payment is often a practical necessity: an up-to-date municipal tax receipt (solvencia) is required for selling property, company paperwork and many bureaucratic procedures. If you run a business, add municipal gross-receipts taxes, payroll contributions, and a compliance rhythm of monthly filings. The bureaucratic load, not the rate, is the real cost; accountants exist precisely because the paperwork does not stop.

Hombre cantando por dinero en las cercanías del Hotel Humbodlt (Photo: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The transformation-era wildcard

Venezuela’s ongoing transformation adds uncertainty in both directions. A state rebuilding fiscal capacity may tighten enforcement, digitize taxpayer registries, and formalize the dollar economy — all of which would pull foreign residents into the system. At the same time, incentives aimed at returning capital and diaspora investment may create legal windows and special regimes. The prudent expat strategy in a reforming country is boring: register with the tax authority (get a RIF number), keep your filings current, document the foreign origin of your funds, and revisit the arrangement with a local adviser at every policy turn.

What this means for you

Short stays under 183 days keep you outside the personal income-tax net — you will still pay IVA and IGTF like everyone else. Longer stays make you a resident, and the correct move is registration and filing even if your income is foreign; compliance is cheap insurance in a system whose enforcement is becoming less predictable, not more. Venezuela does not yet have tax treaties wide enough to rely on for double-taxation relief — if your home country taxes you too, that conflict is managed at home (foreign tax credits), not in Caracas. None of this is a reason to avoid Venezuela; all of it is a reason to arrive with a contador’s phone number already saved.

Connected Coverage

For the political and economic frame of everything above, read our Venezuela Explained 2026 country guide and follow our Venezuela Transformation coverage, where tax and currency reforms are tracked as they happen.

What Is Not Known

The transformation-era government’s final tax architecture — rates, regimes and enforcement priorities — is not settled, and any guide written today describes a moving target. Real-world enforcement against foreign residents has never been systematically measured; what exists is practitioner experience, not statistics. This guide is orientation, not legal or tax advice; your facts require a Venezuelan tax professional.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do expats pay income tax in Venezuela?

If you spend more than 183 days in the country in a calendar year, you are a tax resident and, on paper, taxable on worldwide income at progressive rates up to 34 percent. Enforcement on foreign income has historically been weak, but the correct — and recommended — path is to register and file.

What is the IGTF tax I see on receipts?

The IGTF is a 3 percent tax on large financial transactions, applied to payments in foreign currency. Because Venezuelan retail is largely dollarized, it appears on most serious purchases and restaurant bills, on top of the 16 percent VAT (IVA).

Do I pay tax in Venezuela on my foreign pension?

Formally, residents owe Venezuelan tax on worldwide income, including foreign pensions. In practice, enforcement has been rare — but Venezuela’s thin treaty network means you cannot count on double-taxation relief there, so plan with advisers in both countries.

What is a RIF and do I need one?

The RIF is Venezuela’s taxpayer registry number. You need it for almost everything: opening a local bank account, buying property, issuing invoices, or filing taxes. If you live in Venezuela, getting a RIF early is the first compliance step.

Will tax rules change under the transformation?

Very likely. The state is rebuilding fiscal capacity and discussing formalization of the dollar economy and incentives for returning capital. Expect change in both directions — tighter enforcement and new legal windows — and review your position with a local adviser at each policy turn.

World.title: Is Barbados Safe for Expats in 2026? Crime by Area, Scams and Daily Reality
World.content:
GUIDES · BARBADOS

Key Facts — The country Barbados is a stable Caribbean republic of 269,090 people at the 2021 census, living largely from tourism.

— The official view The US State Department rates Barbados Level 1, its lowest warning, in an advisory dated 10 April 2026.

— The problem Gun crime has risen. Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, its highest total on record.

— Who is at risk Most violence involves rival groups in parts of St Michael, not visitors. Petty theft is the main risk for foreigners.

— The other risks Roads, strong sea currents and the June-to-November hurricane season deserve as much attention as crime.

Barbados is safe for most expats who take ordinary city precautions. The honest answer also includes a sharp rise in gun crime, fast minibuses and a real hurricane risk.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Is Barbados safe? For a foreigner living on the west or south coast, the answer is mostly yes. Serious violence is concentrated, and the risks you meet daily are theft, traffic and the sea.

This guide covers police figures, foreign advisories and where crime clusters. It also explains how to handle scams, roads and storms. Figures are as of September 2026 unless dated otherwise.

What the crime figures show

The Barbados Police Service publishes annual crime totals. It was called the Royal Barbados Police Force until the island became a republic in 2021. They show falling overall crime but a sharp rise in gun violence.

Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, plus one manslaughter case, for 50 homicides. That was the highest number ever documented in a single year, and roughly one killing a week.

OSAC, the US government’s security advisory council for American organisations abroad, put the 2024 rate at 17.7 killings per 100,000 people. It still describes Barbados as having lower violent crime than many regional neighbours.

In 2025 the picture split. Richard Boyce, then Commissioner of Police, reported in February 2026 that total offences fell 4%, from 6,301 to 6,063, and murders fell 2%. Sonia Boyce succeeded him in July 2026 as the first woman to lead the service.

Residential burglaries fell 7% and thefts from cars fell 26%. Police seized 84 firearms in 2025, up from 71 the year before.

Gun crime moved the other way. The government’s Criminal Justice Research and Planning Unit counted 638 firearm-related crimes in 2025, up 60% from 400. Armed robberies rose from 62 to 157.

As of 2 September 2026, the homicide toll for the year stood at 36, according to Barbados Today, the latest published tally. That is a little above the average pace of the 2024 record year.

St Lawrence Gap in Christ Church, the south coast’s restaurant and nightlife strip (Photo: Mtaylor848, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

What foreign governments advise

The US State Department keeps Barbados at Level 1, “exercise normal precautions”, in its advisory of 10 April 2026. It calls the island generally safe but says petty crime is common in tourist areas.

It also notes that violent crime, including murder, sexual assault, robbery and shootings, occasionally occurs. It advises vigilance on party cruises, in downtown areas at night and at ATMs.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) is blunter. Its advice, last updated on 23 January 2026, reports an increase in gang-related gun murders, some in public areas.

The FCDO also lists armed robbery, sexual assault and carjackings. Neither government advises against travel, and neither says foreigners are targeted as a group.

OSAC’s May 2025 report adds one practical warning for residents. Police response times vary, and it is “not uncommon to wait an hour or more”, especially in rural areas.

Crime by area

Barbados is divided into eleven parishes, local districts that serve as its basic map. Crime is not spread evenly across them.

Area What the record shows Bridgetown and wider St Michael About 61% of firearm murders in 2025 happened in this parish. Police name it, with Christ Church and St Philip, among the parishes with higher crime levels. West coast: St James and St Peter Villas, hotels and many expat homes. Police do not list these parishes among the higher-crime areas; theft and break-ins are the usual concerns. South coast: Christ Church Hastings, Worthing, St Lawrence Gap and Oistins. Police list Christ Church among the higher-crime parishes, and nightlife brings pickpocketing and late-night robbery risk. East coast and rural parishes Official warnings focus on dangerous sea currents and slower police response, not crime clusters.

OSAC says most violent crime involves rival gang members and stays outside tourist zones. That does not mean tourist areas are crime-free. It means most shootings involve local rivals, not visitors.

By day, the main risk in Bridgetown is pickpocketing in crowds. After dark, the US advice to avoid downtown areas applies, especially if you are alone or on foot.

The government is responding with law as well as policing. A Domestic Terrorism Bill, debated in both houses of Parliament in August 2026, creates a separate offence for violent crimes in public places that show reckless disregard for public safety. Our report on the bill has the detail.

Privately run yellow minibuses in Bridgetown; together with ZR vans they carry much of the island’s public transport (Photo: Postdlf, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Scams and petty crime

Most crimes against foreigners are crimes of opportunity, such as purse snatching and pickpocketing, the State Department says. Beaches, cars and crowded events are the usual settings.

OSAC lists ATM fraud and card fraud as common. Use machines inside banks or shopping centres, cover your PIN and check statements often.

Taxis have no meters, the FCDO notes. Agree the fare and the currency before you get in.

Offers of drugs on beaches or at parties are a trap. Drug possession is illegal, and both the UK and US governments warn of severe penalties and long jail terms.

For rentals, see the property before paying a deposit, or use an agent you can verify. Pay by traceable bank transfer, never in cash to a stranger.

Crowds at Crop Over, the summer carnival, and its Kadooment Day parade need extra care. The State Department singles out these large gatherings.

Road safety

For most expats, the road deserves as much attention as crime. Barbados drives on the left, and main roads are generally sound but potholed.

Rural roads are narrow, poorly marked and full of blind curves, the State Department warns. Many have no pavement, so pedestrians walk in the road.

ZR vans, private minibuses with number plates starting with Z, “tend to travel at excessive speeds”, in the State Department’s words. Give them room when driving, and expect sudden stops.

Avoid unfamiliar rural roads at night, when lighting is poor. Wear a seat belt, never drink and drive, and slow down in rain.

Bathsheba on the east coast, where strong currents make swimming unsafe on many beaches (Photo: Postdlf, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The sea, hurricanes and storms

Currents can be deceptively strong on popular beaches, the FCDO warns. Swimming is not recommended on many east-coast beaches, where the Atlantic surf is rough.

The hurricane season runs from June to November, with peak activity from August to October. A storm does not need to make landfall to do serious damage.

Hurricane Beryl passed about 150 kilometres off the south coast on 1 July 2024. The World Bank counted 240 fishing vessels damaged or destroyed, and damage to the port, cruise terminal and fisheries marina.

The World Bank also reported damage at 73% of hotels, apartments and guest houses. It approved US$54 million in emergency financing for the recovery.

Follow the Department of Emergency Management and the Barbados Meteorological Services during any storm. Check that your home insurance covers wind and flood, and keep water, medicines and documents ready.

Daily reality for expats

Official advice treats Barbados as a place for normal precautions, not special measures. For most foreign residents, that means the care they would take in a mid-sized city.

OSAC lists burglary and car break-ins among the most common crimes. Choose housing with good locks, lighting and, ideally, a gated compound or alarm.

The High Court struck down the laws against consensual same-sex relations between adults in December 2022, although the State Department’s country page still describes them as criminalised. The FCDO describes attitudes as mostly conservative.

Do not bring firearms or ammunition without clear government permission. Save two numbers now: police on 211 and ambulance on 511.

What this means for you

Barbados is safe enough for most expats to live a normal, relaxed life. The rise in gun crime is real, but it is concentrated and rarely touches foreigners directly.

Choose where you live with care, secure your home and avoid downtown Bridgetown alone at night. Drive defensively, respect the east-coast sea and prepare for hurricane season.

Treat the numbers here as a snapshot. Check the latest police figures and foreign advisories before you move, because gun crime trends have shifted fast since 2024.

The expat safety net that actually exists

Barbados’ real security infrastructure for foreigners is social as much as official. The island has dense, long-established expat networks — from the Welcome Stamp remote-worker community to British and Canadian retiree circles on the west coast — and they function as an early-warning system: break-in patterns, scam attempts and road problems travel through WhatsApp groups hours before any official channel moves. Joining two or three of these groups in your first week is worth more than any alarm system. Neighborhood watch schemes cover most expat districts, the police force runs a dedicated tourism unit, and response in the resort corridors is visibly faster than elsewhere on the island. None of this makes Barbados risk-free; it makes it a place where risk is known, shared and managed collectively — which, in practice, is what “safe” means anywhere in the Caribbean.

Sources: Crime figures come from the Barbados Police Service and the Criminal Justice Research and Planning Unit as reported by Barbados Today, with advisories from the US State Department, OSAC and the UK FCDO, and storm data from the World Bank.

What Is Not Known

The exact murder total for 2025 is not settled in public sources. Police reported a 2% fall, but press reports give different final counts.

No official crime table by parish or neighbourhood is published regularly. The area picture here rests on the 2025 firearm review and on official advisories, not on a full map of crime rates.

Police reported 17 road deaths in 2025, but no official figure for 2024 or 2026 so far was found, so no trend can be given here.

When the Domestic Terrorism Bill comes into force is not confirmed. Its effect on gun crime cannot be judged until it is in use.

More: Caribbean news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Barbados safe for expats in 2026?

Yes, for most expats who take ordinary precautions. The US State Department rates Barbados Level 1, its lowest warning, in an advisory dated 10 April 2026. Gun violence has risen, but it is concentrated in parts of St Michael and mostly involves rival groups, not foreigners.

Which areas of Barbados have the most crime?

Bridgetown and the wider parish of St Michael carry most serious violence, with about 61% of firearm murders in 2025. Police also list Christ Church and St Philip among the higher-crime parishes. The west coast in St James and St Peter, where many expats live, faces mainly theft and break-ins.

How many murders does Barbados have a year?

Barbados recorded 49 murders in 2024, its highest total on record, or roughly one a week. Police reported a 2% fall in 2025. As of 2 September 2026, the homicide toll for the year stood at 36.

What scams should foreigners watch for in Barbados?

OSAC lists ATM fraud and card fraud as common, so use machines inside banks and cover your PIN. Taxis have no meters, so agree the fare first. Refuse any offer of drugs, because penalties are severe.

When is hurricane season in Barbados?

The season runs from June to November, with peak activity from August to October. Hurricane Beryl passed about 150 kilometres off the south coast on 1 July 2024 and damaged or destroyed 240 fishing vessels, according to the World Bank.

World.title: Moving to Guyana 2026: Visas, Costs, Oil-Boom Jobs and Daily Life in Georgetown
World.content:
GUIDES · GUYANA

Key Facts — Why now Guyana is the world’s fastest-growing economy, driven by offshore oil production that has made this country of about 800,000 people a major petroleum exporter.

— Visas No digital-nomad or retirement visa exists. Work permits are employer-driven and now processed in volume for the oil sector; CARICOM skilled nationals move freely.

— Costs Georgetown is no longer cheap: decent rentals run roughly US$1,000-2,500 a month, and housing near the oil-services corridor is scarce and expensive.

— Safety Georgetown has moderate-to-high crime by regional standards — robbery is the main expat risk — while the interior is safe but logistically demanding.

— Who it suits Oil-and-gas professionals, construction and services contractors, and adventurous entrepreneurs — people chasing a boom, not a beach.

Six years ago, Guyana was the sleepy, English-speaking corner of South America that travelers skipped between Brazil and Suriname. Then ExxonMobil found oil — billions of barrels of it — and Georgetown became a boomtown. Moving to Guyana in 2026 means moving to one of the strangest economic stories on Earth: a small, poor-ish country being transformed at speed, with all the opportunity and friction that implies. This guide covers visas, jobs, housing, costs and safety as they actually are.

Visas and work permits

Guyana offers no digital-nomad or passive-income visa. The mainstream path is employment: your employer applies for your work permit, and the process — once notoriously slow — has been professionalized by sheer volume as oil companies and their contractors imported thousands of workers. CARICOM nationals with recognized qualifications can move under the skills-free-movement regime. Long-term residence follows sustained legal work. The practical advice is the same as for any boom economy: arrive with the contract signed, let the employer’s immigration handler run the paperwork, and keep copies of everything — the system works, but it runs on stamped paper.

Where the jobs are

The oil sector itself — offshore engineering, logistics, marine services — is the tip of the spear, but most foreign jobs are one layer down: construction (Georgetown’s skyline and the road to the interior are being rebuilt simultaneously), hotels and hospitality, professional services, and the supply chain feeding the platforms. Local-content rules require companies to buy Guyanese, which creates opportunity for foreigners who set up local partnerships rather than just arrive. Salaries in the oil corridor are international; outside it, wages remain Caribbean-low — the two economies coexist uneasily in one small city.

British Guiana 1934 12c stamp Stabroek Market Georgetown (Photo: British Government, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Housing and the Georgetown squeeze

Housing is the bottleneck. Expat-standard rentals — air-conditioned, generator-backed, secure — cluster in Georgetown’s established districts (Queenstown, Bel Air, Kingston) and the new gated developments up the East Bank and East Coast highways toward the oil-services base. Expect roughly US$1,000-2,500 a month for decent stock, more for premium compounds, with competition from oil contractors keeping the top end tight. Generators and water tanks are not luxuries: power cuts and pressure problems persist despite the boom. Traffic has become genuinely bad; where you live relative to your office matters more than square meters.

What life costs beyond rent

Local food — markets, cook-up rice, roti, fresh fish — is inexpensive; imported groceries carry boom-town markups. Eating out ranges from cheap Creole restaurants to new international venues priced for expense accounts. Private healthcare in Georgetown covers routine needs (Woodlands and St. Joseph Mercy are the reference hospitals), but anything serious means evacuation — insurance with medevac cover is standard practice, not optional. A car is near-essential; used imports dominate. Schooling for expat children runs through a small set of private and international options that the boom has strained — apply early.

Safety, honestly

Georgetown’s crime is the downside locals will tell you about first: armed robbery and burglary occur at rates above Caribbean norms, and certain districts and nighttime streets are simply avoided. The expat toolkit is standard for the region — secured housing, no displays of wealth, trusted taxis at night, awareness at markets and ATMs — and it works: most foreign professionals complete multi-year postings without incident. Outside the capital, the equation flips: the interior — Kaieteur, the Rupununi savannahs, the rainforest lodges — is safe, spectacular and logistically hard, reachable by small plane or long dirt roads.

What this means for your decision

Guyana rewards a specific mover: the engineer, project manager, contractor or entrepreneur who wants frontier-economy upside and accepts frontier friction — expensive housing, thin services, security discipline — in exchange. It punishes the unprepared: arriving without a job or a housing plan in a tight, expensive market is expensive fast. Families do live there successfully, anchored by the oil-community infrastructure. This is South America’s boomtown; treat it like one and it can be very good to you.

Connected Coverage

For the full picture of the boom — the oil contracts, the politics and what the money is doing to the country — read our Guyana Explained 2026 country guide.

What Is Not Known

Rental prices and living costs in Georgetown change faster than any published data tracks; all figures here are market estimates as of 2026. Immigration processing times vary with application volume. And how Guyana’s institutions absorb oil-scale revenue — the question that decides the country’s next decade — is being answered in real time, with the result not yet known.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can foreigners move to Guyana easily?

If you have a job offer, yes — work permits are employer-sponsored and now processed in volume thanks to the oil boom. Without employment, there is no practical path: Guyana has no digital-nomad or retirement visa. CARICOM skilled nationals can move under the free-movement regime.

How much does it cost to live in Georgetown?

Budget roughly US$1,000-2,500 a month for decent expat-standard rentals, more for premium compounds. Local food is cheap, imported goods are expensive, and a car is near-essential. A comfortable single-expat budget typically starts around US$2,500-3,500 a month.

Is Guyana safe for expats?

Georgetown has moderate-to-high crime by regional standards, with robbery the main risk; secured housing and night-time discipline are standard practice. The interior is safe but remote. Most foreign professionals complete long postings without serious incidents.

What jobs are available for foreigners in Guyana?

Oil and gas roles lead, but most foreign jobs are one layer down: construction, logistics, hospitality, professional services and the supply chain. Local-content rules favor foreigners who build Guyanese partnerships rather than just arriving.

What is healthcare like in Guyana?

Private hospitals in Georgetown handle routine and emergency stabilization competently, but serious conditions mean medical evacuation abroad. International health insurance with medevac cover is standard practice for expats, not an optional extra.

World.title: Opening a Bank Account in Barbados as a Foreigner 2026: Banks, Documents and FX Rules
World.content:
GUIDES · BARBADOS

Key Facts — Can foreigners open accounts? Yes. Barbados banks routinely open accounts for non-residents and new residents — but expect full documentation and a compliance interview.

— The banks The retail market is dominated by CIBC Caribbean (formerly FirstCaribbean), Republic Bank and First Citizens, plus credit unions.

— Currency The Barbados dollar has been pegged at BDS$2 = US$1 since 1975. Exchange controls exist: moving Barbadian dollars out requires central-bank approval above certain thresholds.

— The pro tip Non-residents can hold US-dollar accounts locally — often the cleaner solution while you wait for residency papers.

— Timing Allow two to six weeks from complete paperwork to a working account; incomplete source-of-funds documents are the most common reason for delays.

Barbados sells itself as the Caribbean’s business-class island: stable, English-speaking, legally familiar, and plugged into North American finance. Its banking system matches that pitch — conservative, well-regulated and open to foreigners — but it runs on paperwork. This guide explains which banks to approach, what documents they actually ask for, how the currency peg and exchange controls affect your money, and the mistakes that stall applications.

Who the players are

Barbados’ retail banking is concentrated in a few names. CIBC Caribbean, headquartered in Barbados, is the largest regional bank and the default choice for many expats. Republic Bank (Trinidad-based) absorbed Scotiabank’s Barbadian operations and runs a full branch network. First Citizens, also Trinidadian, rounds out the trio. For everyday savings, the credit-union sector — especially the large Barbados Public Workers’ Co-operative Credit Union — is popular with locals and open to residents. International business companies and wealth structures use separate offshore licensees; this guide is about personal and small-business accounts.

What you need to bring
