World.content:
In exchange for reopening the Strait and resuming nuclear talks, Tehran demanded that Washington lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales and commit to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon, Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, according to an AP report.

Trump, however, said he was not interested in making a deal with Iran at this point in the conflict.

“They wanna make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” he said. “We’re winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait.”

Trump had already privately rejected the plan, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing U.S. officials. The president is also considering renewed military action against Iran — including a potential bombing campaign — after the midterm elections in November, according to the report.

Trump on Friday night shared a map of the region on Truth Social, renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the “Trump Strait.”

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical route for global oil and natural gas supplies and has been a major flashpoint since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

This article was updated with Trump’s comments.

World.title: Ireland team to wear black armbands as players vote to go ahead with Israel game
World.content:
The Republic of Ireland football team are set to don black armbands when they run out to face Israel in Sunday's Nations League clash amid calls for a boycott of the fixture over the war in Gaza.

 

Controversy surrounding the match has snowballed in recent weeks as a "Stop The Game" petition organised by the Irish Sport for Palestine group has gathered pace.

Speaking before the game, which is taking place in Hungary, Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said the players intended to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the conflict" as he confirmed the match would go ahead following hours of talks and a vote amongst the squad.

"And also, there will be elements of the pre-match ceremony that will not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland," he told reporters on Saturday, adding that a "significant majority" of players had voted in favour of playing.

In a statement following the announcement, the Israeli FA commended the FAI and the Irish squad on the decision, saying: "Football has won."

"The separation between football and politics must be maintained; any other approach spells chaos and a dangerous slide in a slippery slope, leading to disastrous consequences for the game we all love," the statement reads. "The Irish Football Association and the national team players did the right thing by recognizing this".

Bazunu applauds supporters following the Euro 2024 Group C qualifying soccer match between Ireland and Netherlands at the Aviva Stadium, Dublin, Ireland. PA Wire

Bazunu withdraws

Courell confirmed that one player had "expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture" and had "indicated their intent to withdraw" from the match against Israel.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu announced in a post on Instagram on Saturday that he had refused to play due to his "personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong."

"I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly," he wrote. "I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel".

"It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region," he added.

Asked about the impact on his team during the press conference with Courell, Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson described it as "a situation you can't win."

"Obviously this affects all of them and like I said just just now, nobody is comfortable at the moment," the Icelander said.

"There's a unique and a new balance in the situation that we are trying to tackle the best way we can at the moment," he added.

World.title: Etna erupts again: chaos at Catania airport, risk of higher air fares
World.content:
Catania-Fontanarossa airport has once again been brought to a standstill because of volcanic activity on Mount Etna, which has forced the authorities to halt flight operations. Sac, the company that manages the airport, has announced the closure of the relevant airspace because of the heavy emission of ash into the atmosphere and unfavourable wind conditions.

 

All arrivals and departures have officially been suspended until 23:59 on Sunday 27 September. Flights were initially halted until 12:00, before the stop was extended. In a bid to limit disruption, the company has urged passengers not to go to the terminal without first checking the status of their flight with their respective airlines.

On Saturday the shutdown had serious repercussions across the entire regional transport network. The suspension of flights has in fact triggered a domino effect at other Sicilian airports such as Comiso, Palermo and Trapani, which suddenly became congested with the many aircraft diverted there in emergency. The handling of this situation, which left thousands of travellers stranded and searching for alternative solutions, quickly turned a logistical breakdown into an economic and industrial-relations dispute.

Risk of speculative air fares and criticism from trade unions

The paralysis has provoked a strong reaction from associations, which denounce the risk of speculation on air fares at a moment of great vulnerability for citizens. Acli Terra has reported abnormal increases and prohibitive costs for flights to and from the island, highlighting extreme cases such as a Verona–Palermo route shooting up to around 1,180 euros. Emphasising that a natural emergency must not be allowed to turn into economic damage for families, the association has called on the authorities to monitor price rises, stressing that the ability to manage recurring events directly affects the credibility and reputation of the Sicilian system as a whole.

In the same vein, transport unions are pointing the finger at organisational shortcomings, describing the situation as "total chaos". Filt Cgil, Fit Cisl and Uiltrasporti Sicilia express dismay at the absence of any contingency plan for an Etna eruption, a phenomenon they now consider structural rather than unforeseeable. According to the unions, those paying the highest price are airline and ground staff, forced to face passengers' exasperation in conditions of extreme stress and without clear guidelines.

The unions are therefore once again urging the Region to sign a permanent protocol that would establish reliable operational flows and adequate protections, finally moving beyond the ineffective logic of constant emergency.

World.title: How Russia recruits Belarusians for war in Ukraine: Methods and consequences
World.content:
Russia has long regarded Belarus as a convenient reserve for topping up its manpower in the war against Ukraine, especially after suffering heavy losses at the front.

 

Minsk’s economic dependence, the political vulnerability of Aliaksandr Lukashenka's regime and the legal uncertainty around the Union State create conditions in which the Kremlin can act with considerable freedom.

In the Belarusian corner of the internet, in recent months a large number of adverts offering Belarusians the chance to sign a contract with the Russian army, have appeared. They are circulated everywhere – in Telegram channels, in Viber chats and in local community pages where people discuss everyday issues.

At times it looks almost surreal: nestled between posts about selling vegetables or finding a tutor, a sudden offer appears promising a "high salary, benefits and Russian citizenship" in return for going to war.

Investigations by DW, TVNET, CityDog and Current Time have documented a sharp increase in such posts. The human rights initiative Belpol regularly highlights examples of adverts in which recruiters use Belarusian phone numbers to inspire trust.

On Belpol’s Telegram channel you can see messages promising huge payouts, help with loans, "annulment of criminal convictions" and fast-track Russian citizenship.

On X, the OSB Belpol account posts screenshots of ads in which Belarusians are offered a contract with a one-off payment of 4.35 million roubles and rapid issuance of a Russian passport.

These examples are not isolated incidents but part of a systematic campaign targeting socially vulnerable people.

What recruiters promise

Belarusians are promised the equivalent of tens of thousands of euros, high salaries, housing, food, a military pension and life insurance.

Some adverts even talk about "sorting out problems with the law," which is particularly dangerous given that participation in an armed conflict abroad falls under the article on mercenary activities in Belarus' criminal code which carries a prison term of up to seven years.

Recruiters insist that the service is "legal," claiming it is not mercenary activity but "service in the army of the Union State."

A Russian Army soldier controls an area from a board of military helicopter in an undisclosed location in Ukraine, 9 July, 2026 AP Photo

Who signs up for a contract?

Research shows that among those recruited, the majority are men from small towns and villages, people on low incomes, with debts or with existing legal problems.

Many do not realise the legal consequences and some are simply looking for quick money, without understanding that they will be sent to the most dangerous sectors of the front.

Human rights activists point out that foreign contract soldiers are often placed in assault units, where casualty rates are particularly high.

The recruitment scheme is simple and effective. A person sees an advert on social media and writes to the recruiter, who is using a Belarusian phone number. They are then told about payments, benefits and the supposed "legality" of the service.

After that they are offered rapid paperwork and travel to Russia – most often via Smolensk or Pskov. There they sign a contract and become a member of the Russian armed forces. At that point there is almost no way back.

For those who agree to sign a contract, the consequences can be tragic. Beyond the risk of being killed, they face criminal liability in Belarus, possible loss of citizenship or restrictions on their rights.

Many end up as "cannon fodder" in someone else’s war, which they often barely understand.

Russia soldiers advance towards Ukrainian positions at the area of Huliaipole, 17 December, 2025 AP Photo

Public and state response

Belarusian society has generally reacted to this with alarm.

People complain about mass spam-recruitment; some turn to the Interior Ministry, but there is virtually no response.

The Lukashenka regime does not officially acknowledge that recruitment is taking place, but it does nothing to stop it.

Belarus is far too dependent on Russian subsidies to openly confront the Kremlin.

Furthermore, mobilisation measures inside the country are being stepped up, adding extra pressure on men of conscription age.

People walk past an army recruiting billboard in St. Petersburg, 24 March, 2023 AP Photo

Recruitment as part of Kremlin strategy

The recruitment of Belarusians is not about random adverts or the haphazard initiative of individual actors. It is a coordinated campaign built into the Kremlin’s strategy for expanding its pool of manpower for the war against Ukraine.

The legal framework of the Union State gives Moscow extra room for manoeuvre: formally, citizens of Belarus and Russia have "equal rights" and Russian institutions are trying to spin this as "equal obligations," including compulsory military service.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warns that such an interpretation could become a basis for exerting pressure on Belarusians and attempts to mobilise them.

Russia is exploiting the vulnerability of Belarusian society, its information isolation and Minsk’s political dependence in order to turn Belarus into a source of manpower.

And the longer the war drags on, the more aggressive this campaign becomes.

World.title: EU tells countries to curb energy demand as gas prices face winter squeeze
World.content:
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen urged EU governments to continue curbing energy demand to reduce gas and electricity consumption amid "exceptionally low" storage levels, according to a letter seen by Euronews.

 

"I invite you to consider taking or continuing to take measures that can sustain injections or reduce gas and electricity demand for as long as necessary," reads the letter, noting that the situation "has not improved" since Jørgensen's first warning in March.

The warning comes as EU gas storage is around 70% full, roughly 12 percentage points below the same point last year, according to the latest figures from the trade association Gas Infrastructure Europe. Continued disruption in the Middle East and fierce competition from Asia for liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes are pushing prices up, threatening a supply crisis.

The Dutch TTF, the European benchmark for natural gas prices, is trading at around €72 per MWh, up €40MWh since the United States and Israel bombed Iran on 28 February. Analysts are warning of potential spikes above €100/MWh during peak winter if LNG export volumes from the Gulf fail to grow or if Norwegian maintenance prolongs export constraints.

Related Europe faces race to refill gas storage as LNG cargoes flow to Asia

The EU's top energy leader said that using less electricity at peak times can mean burning less gas in power plants, easing pressure on both gas supplies and power prices. Households and businesses are already sensitive to energy bills, while governments are under pressure to cushion consumers from another price shock.

The Commission points specifically to measures that were used during the 2022 energy crisis, including reducing electricity consumption during peak hours, encouraging consumers to shift demand through smart meters and retail tariffs, limiting temperatures in public buildings, restricting outdoor heating and switching off unnecessary public lighting at night.

However, Jørgensen stops short of imposing mandatory measures.

"Voluntary and well-planned demand reduction measures proved useful during the 2022 energy crisis, and we can draw on the lessons from that experience in the current situation," the letter reads.

Nonetheless, the EU's energy top leader also points ministers towards their national emergency plans, which contain more serious tools that could be activated if conditions deteriorate — including interruptible gas contracts and switching power plants from gas to other fuels.

No storage rush, though

Jørgensen also encouraged capitals to use the flexibility in EU gas-storage rules to avoid panic buying and consider an 80% filling target, rather than pushing aggressively towards the 90% goal.

Normally, filling storage is about security since more gas underground means a bigger buffer when winter demand rises. But buying large quantities of gas when global markets are already tight can itself push prices higher.

The Commission has argued that reaching 80% can be sufficient for winter security under current conditions, while allowing countries to spread purchases over a longer period and avoid a late-season scramble for gas.

The Danish Commissioner suggested the EU is entering the winter with a more resilient energy system than it had before Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but not a comfortable one.

"Although EU gas storage is exceptionally low and the situation remains challenging, there are currently no immediate risks to security of supply," reads the letter.

From price to supply

Despite the reassurances, Brussels is no longer talking only about protecting consumers from high prices. It is asking EU governments to manage demand because consumption itself is becoming part of the supply problem.

"As we discussed in the Energy Union Task Force, we are facing a price crisis linking to a supply crisis," reads the letter.

For now, Brussels remains careful to distinguish between a deteriorating price situation and an immediate physical shortage, saying there is currently no immediate risk to security of supply.

The EU may have enough gas to get through the winter, but securing it could come at a much higher price, especially if global LNG markets remain tight and European countries have to compete with buyers.

World.title: Ethiopia’s army chief accuses Egypt and Sudan of backing armed alliance seeking to oust Abiy Ahmed
World.content:
Ethiopia’s army chief has accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting a new alliance of armed groups trying to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, saying the groups could not succeed unless they were “pushed, supported and supplied” from abroad.

 

Field Marshal Birhanu Jula also accused Eritrea of acting as a link between foreign backers and armed groups inside Ethiopia. He made the comments in an interview with the Ethiopian army’s media outlet.

Birhanu did not provide evidence for the accusation. Egypt and Sudan had not publicly responded by Sunday morning.

The alliance announced last Sunday brings together seven groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army and the Amhara Fano National Movement. Its members say they want to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration.

The accusation comes as fighting has resumed in northern Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces have seized airports and clashed with federal troops in the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk has called for an urgent end to the fighting, warning that Ethiopia could return to full-scale war.

People walk through Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region, as fighting intensifies on 24 September 2026. AP Photo

Nile dam dispute adds to tensions with Egypt

Birhanu’s accusation against Egypt follows a new exchange between Cairo and Addis Ababa over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, or GERD, on the Blue Nile.

Egyptian Water Resources Minister Hani Sewilam said last week that Ethiopian politicians needed to understand that building a dam on a shared river was “not like laying a carpet in their homes”.

He rejected Ethiopia’s argument that decisions about the dam fall solely under its national sovereignty.

Ethiopia’s Water and Energy Ministry responded two days later, saying Sewilam’s remarks reflected a “crude colonial mentality”. It accused Cairo of acting as though its approval was required before countries farther up the Nile could use the river’s water.

Egypt and Sudan want a legally binding agreement covering how the dam is operated, particularly during long periods of drought, as well as the sharing of information about water releases.

Ethiopia says the dam is essential for producing electricity and supporting the country’s development. It maintains that it will not cause significant harm to Egypt or Sudan.

Egypt relies on the Nile for more than 90% of its freshwater. Ethiopia formally inaugurated the GERD in September 2025 without reaching a binding agreement with the two countries.

Relations with Sudan and Eritrea have also worsened

Tensions between Ethiopia and Sudan rose in May after Sudan accused Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates of involvement in drone attacks on Khartoum airport.

Sudan said the drones had taken off from Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. Ethiopia rejected the accusation as baseless and accused Sudan of supporting Tigrayan fighters. Neither side’s accusation has been independently verified.

Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army against Tigrayan forces during the 2020–2022 war. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara later deteriorated following the peace agreement that ended the conflict.

Ethiopia’s government now accuses Eritrea of supporting members of the new armed alliance. Eritrea has repeatedly denied the allegation.

World.title: Protesters camp in Madrid in demonstration against Spain' housing crisis
World.content:
Puerta del Sol woke on Sunday to around 150 tents pitched across the square, as the encampment grew following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis that ended in the early hours of Saturday.

 

According to figures collected overnight, the camp began with around 100 tents and continued to grow, with further structures counted after 8am.

Those gathered spent the night on yoga mats, in sleeping bags and, in some cases, directly on the ground, while small groups stayed up talking into the early hours.

People gather during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen demand stronger laws to protect renters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid,26.09.2026 AP Photo / Manu Fernandez

While the Civil Guard and National Police kept a constant watch over the square, although no incidents have been reported. The campers themselves have described a calm atmosphere, with stocks of food and water to sustain the protest over the coming days.

The initiative answers the call of the Madrid Tenants' Union, which urged people to camp out in Sol once Saturday's march was over. In its call, the organisation invited those unable to stay the night to bring sleeping bags, mats, food or water. One protester summed up the reason for the mobilisation in a line repeated in different groups: "all this is for Maricarmen".

The camp is strongly reminiscent of the one that began in Madrid on 15 March 2011 and led to the 15-M movement. Its slogan, “Sí se puede” — “Yes, we can” — became a symbol for people frustrated with Spain’s two main parties, the PSOE and PP.

The movement called for a political alternative that would put ordinary people first.

Maricarmen's eviction, the origin of the protest

The camp follows the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was forced to leave her rented flat in Madrid’s Retiro neighbourhood last Wednesday, after living there for 70 years. The case, now known as the "Maricarmen effect", has become the trigger for a day of protests called in 40 cities under the slogan "Not one more Maricarmen".

Saturday's demonstration, which started at 6.30 p.m. in Puerta del Sol and ended at the Congress of Deputies, brought together around 25,000 people according to the Government Delegation, although the Tenants' Union puts the figure at as many as 300,000 participants. Along the route there was a notable intergenerational presence, with families, young people and elderly groups chanting slogans such as "Where is the progressive Government?" and "We want to see Maricarmen come back".

The spokesperson for the Tenants' Union, Gonzalo Álvarez, who spent the night at the camp, explained in a live interview that the protest is seeking "structural changes" so that housing "is treated as a basic necessity and not as a financial asset". Álvarez also pointed out that Maricarmen's case has acted as a catalyst because of "the injustice, the harshness of what happened and the police response".

The core demand: Tuesday's housing decree

The main demand of the protest is for the Government to approve a decree on Tuesday that would include, among other measures, a freeze on rents. The union has called it the “Maricarmen decree”.

Álvarez warned that if the decree is not approved, the Government’s left-wing partners, including Sumar, should consider withdrawing their support and bringing down the Government.

People set up tents during a protest following the eviction last Wednesday of 87-year-old Maricarmen to demand stronger laws to protect renters at Sol square in Madrid, Spain, AP Photo / Manu Fernandez

Echoing this position, the Tenants' Union spokesperson Alicia del Río described Maricarmen's case as a "point of no return" in Spain's housing struggle and warned that if the decree does not go through on Tuesday, the Executive "makes no sense at all" and should rethink whether it can continue.

Pablo Iglesias, founder of Podemos and one of the initiators of the 15-M movement in Spain, said that Maricarmen could become Spain's Rosa Parks and that he hopes this movement will spread across the country.

The debate is also complicated by divisions within the left-wing bloc. Podemos MEP Irene Montero has rejected the Government negotiating the decree with Junts, accusing the party of trying to force an agreement on the people who took to the streets on Saturday.

Montero called for the expropriation of 650,000 homes owned by vulture funds so they can be turned into social rental housing. Meanwhile, Podemos secretary-general Ione Belarra said her party would keep “piling on the pressure” to secure the strongest possible decree. But she warned that no single measure would solve the housing crisis without continued protests and pressure from the streets.

World.title: Poland and Lithuania preparing cross-border evacuation plan for Baltic states
World.content:
Poland and Lithuania are working on an international evacuation plan for civilians in the event of a major crisis or military threat.

 

If necessary, the plan would allow some residents of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to be moved across the Polish border.

Vilmantas Vitkauskas, the head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, has announced that work on the proposal was already under way and that representatives of Lithuania and Poland were analysing procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capacity.

A detailed plan is to be drawn up once Poland and Lithuania reach an appropriate agreement.

The preparations are being carried out as part of Lithuania's "Vyčio Skliautas 2026" exercises, launched on 25 September to test its national mobilisation system and institutional cooperation in a crisis situation.

The drills will run until 3 October. One of their practical components is testing procedures for the evacuation of the population.

Around 3,000 officials, officers, and representatives of institutions, local authorities, companies, and non-governmental organisations are taking part in the exercises, along with about 1,000 volunteers. A delegation of around 20 people from various Polish institutions has also arrived in Lithuania.

During the drills, systems for warning residents, the organisation of assembly and registration points, transport, and the movement of evacuees through successive regions are being put to the test. Poland is also involved in work related to planning cross-border evacuation.

The Lithuanian authorities have stressed that the aim of the exercises is to develop and test procedures for dealing with crises. The exercises are training activities and do not mean authorities are expecting an imminent threat.

The Suwałki gap

The Suwałki gap, a strip of territory linking Poland and Lithuania - and therefore connecting the Baltic states with other NATO allies and the rest of the European Union - is of particular importance to the plan.

The area contains the main land routes between Lithuania and Poland. In the event of a serious crisis, the region could prove to be crucial for the movement of troops and supplies as well as for the evacuation of civilians.

"The Suwałki gap is of huge importance, both militarily and logistically," Vitkauskas said.

Poland prepares to receive evacuees

Poland is also preparing for the possibility of receiving evacuees from the Baltic states.

In September, representatives from Lithuania and Latvia visited Poland on a study trip focused, among other things, on mass evacuation, civil protection, and the organisation of reception and accommodation for evacuees.

Talks were attended by representatives of Polish services and institutions responsible for security and civil protection.

Lithuania has already drawn up its own evacuation plan for residents in the event of a military threat or crisis.

One of the main evacuation routes runs from Vilnius towards the Polish border. Authorities in Poland's Podlaskie Voivodeship are preparing the region for a potential role as a transit corridor for residents of the Baltic states.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: UK: 5 arrested after 'major incident' near Fairford air base
World.content:
Scores of homes were evacuated in the UK town of Whelford, near an air base used by the US military, with bomb disposal teams checking "suspicious vehicles" at the scene. Police said five men had been arrested.

British authorities evacuated buildings and deployed military bomb disposal teams over a "major incident" in the town of Whelford on Sunday morning.

The town is located near the Fairford air base, which is used by the US military. Around 30 emergency vehicles were seen in the area, including police cars, ambulances, and fire engines.

Counter-terrorism police were leading the investigation. On Sunday afternoon, London's Metropolitan police said five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a "terrorist act."

UK police blocked roads leading to the Fairford air base Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

Previously, the authorities said that several men were "arrested on suspicion of offences the ​Explosives Act."

"A cordon is currently in place but we'd like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained," British police said.

Bomb disposal units examining three 'suspicious vehicles'

Local police said they had received a call earlier on Sunday about "three suspicious vehicles" heading to the base.

"Armed officers responded and subsequently arrested five men in the Whelford area," assistant chief constable Richard Ocone told reporters.

He added that a cordon of 400 meters, or approximately 1/4 of a mile, has been put in place around the vehicles "while the army's explosive ordinance disposal unit examine them."

"As a precaution, around 85 households have been advised to evacuate while these examinations take place," Ocone said.

He added that some of the evacuees were taken to a nearby leisure center.

The Gloucestershire police representative also asked the public "not to speculate" but follow official channels instead.

Officials stay tight-lipped

A spokesperson for ​the US Air Force refused to discuss specific steps when contacted by the Reuters news agency, saying only that both US and British forces "remain vigilant and will take ⁠appropriate ​actions to ensure the safety and security of our ​US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families."

This Fairford base gates was blocked by construction machinery Image: Toby Shepheard/REUTERS

The background for the incident was not immediately clear.

The UK has allowed the US to use Fairford for its war against Iran, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards warning UK officials against the move this summer. The evacuations also come at a time of heightened tensions in Northern Ireland, and less than two months after Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone at the Leipzig airport, which its authorities attributed to Russia.

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

World.title: Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
World.content:
Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

Voters in Switzerland look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.

According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.

What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve

The group said its aims were for:

Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"

Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense

Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties

Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked

The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them

Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.

Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."

Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'

Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.

"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.

In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.

Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.

According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.

The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

World.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
World.content:
French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic shrine of Lourdes.

Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site, located near the Spanish border, in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

Pope celebrated Sunday Mass at Lourdes (pictured) in front of some 150,000 people, following a mass in Paris attended by 800,000 believers Image: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."

Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse later on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.

A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.

As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."

But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.

"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."

Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."

"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican .

World.title: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
World.content:
09/27/2026 September 27, 2026 Merz's conservatives no longer a big tent 'people's party'?

Is Merz still reaching ordinary people across all parts of society? Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, continues its soul-searching after its terrible results in recent regional elections.

While the party is generally considered to be more pro-business, it does have a workers' and employees’ wing and that part of the party is now warning the wider CDU that it is no longer a true Volkspartei, literally a "people’s party" or a big tent party.

Germany has two parties that traditionally have been considered a Volkspartei: CDU on the center-right and the Social Democratic Party (SPD) on the center-left.

One of the two parties used to reliably get the biggest share of the vote, but that was not the case in elections in three German states this month.

The SPD has fallen further from its heyday, often coming only third or fourth in the polls. The poor showing of the CDU in recent elections in Saxony-Anhalt and especially Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania suggests the CDU is on a similar trajectory. Instead, it’s the far right and the far left that are gaining voters.

In a new appeal, the CDU's employees' wing argues that too many people no longer feel represented by the party — and that the party risks becoming a political bubble talking mainly to itself.

The group says it wants the CDU to become more representative, not just in its rhetoric but in who actually gets involved and ends up in parliament. That means more people from different backgrounds and professions — from industry and skilled trades to healthcare, education and small businesses.

The group’s leadership also took aim at Chancellor Merz directly, saying that he had promised years ago to broaden the party’s appeal, but failed to do so.

World.title: Northern Ireland: Pro-UK march to go through Catholic area
World.content:
It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.

Northern Ireland's Protestant, pro-British Orange Order was set to parade through a mainly Catholic and nationalist area on Sunday.

It's the first time the march has been allowed to go through the area since 1997. Overnight, a court ruling allowed it to take place after a series of last-minute legal challenges that reached Belfast's High Court.

Thirty-five members of the Orange Order are to march silently through Garvaghy Road in the town of Portadown, without any bands or other Order supporters participating.

About 2,000 people gathered on the street Sunday morning in a counterprotest to prevent the march.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for "calm on all sides." In a BBC interview, he said "big gains" had been made in Northern Ireland "and we don't want to see things go backwards."

Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, a member of the Irish republican Sinn Fein party, spoke against the decision to allow the march to take place.

Pro-Irish protesters are expected to protest against the march Image: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

"Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever," she said, also voicing her support for the local residents to protest against the march, which she labeled "unwanted" and "sectarian."

Carla Lockhart, an MP from the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said local residents have nothing to fear from "thirty five men walking down a road silently and with no bands and in an orderly fashion."

History of conflict

Garvaghy Road was one of the epicenters of the conflict between the Catholic, pro-Irish republicans and the Protestant, pro-British unionists in the late 1990s.

Back then, clashes between residents and the marchers repeatedly triggered disorder, also known as the Drumcree dispute.

Some 2,000 people joined a counterprotest against the Orange Order march Image: Cathal McNaughton/REUTERS

As part of the Good Friday Agreement, a deal signed in 1998 that largely ended three decades of conflict between the two sides known as the Troubles, an entity was established to regulate contentious processions named The Parades Commission.

The Commission repeatedly rejected the Orange Order's requests to march through the area, with a High Court ruling quashing the rejection this year due to a procedural error. The Order then issued a fresh application, which was approved.

World.title: India news: Kolkata's SRFTI students allege violent attack
World.content:
Skip next section SRFTI students attacked after objecting to outsiders' event on campus

Students at Kolkata's SRFTI say they were attacked after objecting to a meeting they allege was affiliated with the RSS Image: Shamayita Chakraborty/DW

Students of the Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute (SRFTI) in Kolkata said on Sunday they were violently attacked after objecting to a meeting held on campus by an allegedly rightwing group, a student representative told DW.

A scuffle broke out between the students and members of the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat (ABGP) after the student union confronted the group saying it had not been informed about the meeting and questioned the participants before the confrontation turned violent.

The students allege that members of the group attacked them with knives.

Poorvi Bondre, an editing student from Maharashtra and a member of the SRFTI student union, told DW that the event was affiliated with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and was being used to promote its agenda on campus.

She said students had opposed the meeting because it was not a film screening but what she described as direct RSS promotion.

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization and the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"This was an RSS event. We were completely unaware of this event. When we asked them what this was about, the fight started," Bondre said. "They called us anti-nationals and Naxals and attacked us with knives."

Videos of the incident have circulated on social media, showing students with what appear to be knife wounds. However, DW could not independently verify their authenticity.

The campus remains tense, with students inside and members of the ABGP gathered outside, according to the student representative.

World.title: Iran sticks to Hormuz plan after Trump rejects it
World.content:
Iranian officials that while they were aware of Trump's comments on rejecting the new proposal, they had not received a formal message rejecting the plan that would open the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran on Sunday insisted on its conditions for reopeningthe Strait of Hormuz, despite US President Donald Trump's public rejection of the proposal that had birthed some hope for reopening the key waterway.

"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, according to state broadcaster IRIB.

"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights," he said.

Iran proposed a seven-day plan aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within days.

Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran said it had transmitted the proposal to Washington via Qatari mediators.

Iran's plan, Araghchi said, called for cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including Lebanon, and fulfilling the conditions of the ceasefire deal that fell apart months ago. That agreement called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Trump rejects plan, but no communication to Iran

Trump publicly rejected Iran's proposal on Saturday while speaking to reporters at the White House.

"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly."

Responding to Trump's comments, Araghchi said Iranians "saw the first reaction from the US president, but so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators."

"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive positions to us, and we will make a decision based on them," the foreign minister added.

Under Iran's proposal, Washington would have to meet certain conditions before the strait was reopened Image: Hamed Malekpour/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

The strait stalemate

Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely shut to international shipping despite Trump's claims that the US controls it.

Early Sunday, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) — set up by Iran to manage the Strait of Hormuz — warned ships of consequences if they use "illegal routes" in the region.

"This risks financial and life losses for the vessel, owner, master and crew, and seriously restricts its future Strait of Hormuz passage," it said in a post on X.

The authority said if ships breach its rules, all vessels belonging to the company could face restrictions in the future.

Around a fifth of global oil demand passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war began. The waterway is also a crucial route for liquefied natural gas and fertilizer.
