World.title: ‘Unresolved issues and conflicting narratives remain’ — Pashinyan on relations with Azerbaijan
World.content:
Pashinyan’s UN address

In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan spoke about the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established. At the same time, he addressed outstanding issues that the two countries still need to resolve. These include determining the fate of several thousand missing people, carrying out demining operations and securing the return of Armenians, whom Azerbaijan holds in its prisons.

Pashinyan stressed that, beyond these issues of concern to Armenian society, conflicting narratives and discourses among certain circles in Armenia and Azerbaijan also fuel pessimism. Sometimes, officials themselves voice these views.

“I think that we, meaning Armenia and Azerbaijan, have achieved more than satisfactory results. These should mean more to us than the use of conflicting narratives, whether about history, cultural monuments or anything else,” he said.

In effect, the prime minister was responding to a recent visit by diplomats to Karabakh, which Azerbaijani authorities had organised. During the visit, officials attempted to present the Armenian monasteries of Gandzasar and Dadivank as part of “ancient Albanian Christian heritage”.

The move sparked such public outrage that many politicians called on Armenia’s leadership to issue a strong official response. Tensions between Armenia and Azerbaijan rose against this backdrop. Politicians described the situation as a serious crisis that could hinder further progress in the peace process.

Against this backdrop, Pashinyan stressed that Armenia and Azerbaijan must now focus on “safeguarding peace, strengthening it and developing its institutions”.

In his address, Pashinyan also touched on other issues of current importance to Armenia, including the implementation of the Armenian-American “Trump Route” project (TRIPP), relations with the European Union and Russia, as well as the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Turkey.

“The main item on the Yerevan-Baku agenda is signing a peace agreement”

The Armenian prime minister placed particular emphasis on the fact that no one has been killed or injured in border shootings between Armenia and Azerbaijan for the past two and a half years. He described this as “the greatest achievement of cooperation in recent years”.

“Never before have independent Armenia and independent Azerbaijan experienced such a period, despite centuries of peaceful coexistence between Armenians and Azerbaijanis,” Pashinyan said.

In his view, Yerevan and Baku must build relations between the two states on the basis of this shared experience, respecting each other’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and political independence. This is particularly important given that the two countries have already agreed on these principles and even initialled a peace treaty.

“Signing and ratifying this agreement is the next important item on Armenia and Azerbaijan’s joint agenda. We will continue to work consistently towards this goal,”

“The implementation of TRIPP promises major benefits for all countries in the region”

Pashinyan believes that the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan has opened up new opportunities for the entire region. He said the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would play an important role in this process. He assured his audience that its implementation was “becoming a reality” and would mark a historic milestone for Armenia:

“For the first time since the early 1990s, Armenia will have a railway link with Azerbaijan. This will also connect it to Russia, Central Asia and China.”

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) is a transport route that will connect Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory.

The prime minister stressed that Azerbaijan had opened transit routes for Armenia and that rail services between Armenia and Azerbaijan had resumed via Georgia. However, he said, the implementation of TRIPP would establish a direct railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan:

“In the near future, we will restore the railway sections in Meghri and Yeraskh in Armenia, which existed during the Soviet era but were later destroyed. The railway routes I mentioned will then reopen.”

He said Armenia also expected to restore railway links with Turkey. Alongside TRIPP, he described this as a potential milestone in international logistics, one of the most significant developments in decades:

“This will open up a new railway connection between China, Central Asia, Turkey and the European Union.”

Pashinyan says restoring the railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan (Nakhchivan) will establish a rail connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea:

“This is an important detail because it shows why and how the implementation of TRIPP promises enormous benefits for all countries in the region. These potential benefits could become a cornerstone of long-term stability and peace, particularly between Armenia and Azerbaijan.”

According to Pashinyan, building pipelines, power lines and roads as part of TRIPP would allow not only Armenia but the entire South Caucasus to become a “crossroads of peace”.

“A plan to seize the state was drawn up”: on elections in Armenia

The prime minister also spoke about the circumstances surrounding Armenia’s recent parliamentary elections. For the second time or more, he openly accused foreign actors of interference:

“Several external and internal forces devised and carried out a plan to seize the state. They used mass disinformation, hybrid and other tools, as well as widespread distribution of election bribes.”

He stressed that Armenia’s state institutions had prevented the seizure of power thanks to their resilience. Pashinyan believes this, in turn, reflects the democratic and institutional reforms that the country has carried out in recent years:

“The people of Armenia voted for peace. And we must consistently work to further strengthen and institutionalise peace.”

Ties with the EU deepen as relations with Russia undergo transformation

Pashinyan also spoke about Armenia’s balanced foreign policy. The prime minister noted that in recent years, his government had established strategic relations with Georgia, France, China, the Netherlands, Kazakhstan, Germany, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, the United States and the European Union.

“The European Commission has approved a decision to introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenia, marking another sign of the new quality of relations between Armenia and the EU,” he stressed.

Relations between Yerevan and Moscow, meanwhile, are undergoing a transformation, according to the prime minister.

In his view, this is a natural process because the Armenian-Azerbaijani conflict had been the main factor shaping Armenia’s relations with Russia throughout the preceding period. The establishment of peace has fundamentally changed the situation.

“We want our relations with Russia to develop on the principles of friendship and mutual respect,” he said.

Relations with neighbouring countries

Nikol Pashinyan noted that normalising and deepening relations with neighbouring countries is crucial for Armenia:

“We have established high-level dialogue with Turkey. I want to reaffirm President Erdoğan’s remarks from this podium a few days ago. We are firmly advancing the process of normalising Armenian-Turkish relations.”

Good-neighbourly relations with Iran and Georgia are also continuing to develop and deepen. Moreover, the prime minister said, these relations are of “exceptional importance” to Yerevan.

Pashinyan’s UN address

World.title: Сost of childhood: why Azerbaijan has no universal child benefit
World.content:
Child benefits in Azerbaijan

AI-generated illustration. Meydan TV

Azerbaijan has no monthly child benefit paid for every child regardless of their family’s income. For nearly 20 years, the government has followed a different model: it provides support to low-income families and specific social groups instead of making universal payments.

Against a backdrop of persistently falling birth rates, the debate over so-called “child benefits” has returned to the public agenda. The discussion is no longer just about where to find the money. Other questions have also come to the fore: how much a universal child benefit would cost the state budget, how much it would actually help families, and what the long-term social cost of refusing such support might be.

In May 2026, a statement by Gunay Agamali, a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament, sparked a new wave of debate. Speaking on ARB TV, she said that child benefits could make parents “dependent and lazy”. In her view, such payments could reduce some people’s willingness to work.

However, the issue of child benefits is far from new in Azerbaijan. It returns to the public agenda almost every year, and the same questions arise each time. Should the state pay benefits for every child or only for families that genuinely need support? Can the state budget afford such payments? And could child benefits reverse the decline in birth rates?

To answer these questions, it is worth first examining how the current system came about. Read the full article by Meydan TV.

What changed in 2006?

Monthly payments commonly referred to as “child benefits” existed in Azerbaijan before 2006. However, contrary to a widespread misconception, they were not universal either.

● Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?

● Birth rates decline year by year in Azerbaijan

● Child allowance in Azerbaijan: why is it not paid?

Under the rules in force at the time, families with an average monthly income of less than 16,500 old manats per person (around $3.4–3.5 or €2.7–2.8 at the 2004–2005 exchange rates) received a monthly payment of 9,000 old manats per child (around $1.8–1.9 or €1.5). Payments continued from birth until the child turned 16. For schoolchildren who did not receive a scholarship, payments could continue until the age of 18. Following the redenomination, this amount was equivalent to 1 manat and 80 qəpiks.

In other words, the previous system also took family income into account.

A new phase in Azerbaijan’s social protection system began on 1 January 2006, when the Law on Targeted State Social Assistance came into force. The Law on Social Benefits also took effect on the same date. The new system did not retain a separate child benefit linked to family income.

The government therefore effectively changed its entire approach. Instead of providing a separate payment for each child, it made targeted assistance the main form of social support, with eligibility determined by family income.

In a 2009 interview with Radio Azadliq, Babek Huseynov, a representative of the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population, said the authorities considered the new system more effective. The previous child benefit, he said, had “lost its economic rationale”. He explained that under the targeted assistance system, payments are calculated based on the difference between a family’s total income and the eligibility threshold.

The same principle remains: assistance for those in need, not everyone

In the following years, the government introduced new types of benefits for children and families and changed payment amounts. However, the underlying principle remained the same: Azerbaijan has no universal benefit paid for every child.

In 2022, Labour and Social Protection Minister Sahil Babayev stated this position explicitly while addressing parliament. According to him, around 600,000 children from socially vulnerable groups receive support through various mechanisms, and social assistance should be targeted rather than universal.

The system in place in 2026 follows the same principle.

Lawyer Fariz Namazly explains:

“We have various benefits for children. Most are designed for socially vulnerable families. There are also one-off payments, such as the benefit paid when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive financial assistance, as do parents caring for children under three. Women with more than five children are also eligible for benefits. Separate social payments are available for children with disabilities, children who have lost one of their parents, and other categories.”

Families currently receive a one-off payment of 600 manats (around $353 or €305) when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month. Women with more than five children receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month for each child. The childcare benefit for children under three amounts to 44 manats (around $26 or €22) or 28 manats (around $16 or €14), depending on the child’s age.

In addition, separate payments are available for children with disabilities, those who have lost a breadwinner, children without parental care, and other social categories.

The issue, therefore, is not whether the state provides financial support to families with children at all. Such support already exists.

The main question is who is eligible for it.

Universal child benefits or targeted assistance?

Under a universal system, family income does not matter: if a child meets the eligibility criteria, the family receives a payment.

Under a targeted system, the government first assesses a family’s income, assets and social circumstances before deciding whether it needs assistance.

Fariz Namazly believes both models have advantages and disadvantages:

“There are currently proposals to introduce a universal child benefit — that is, to pay it to all children regardless of family income. Such a system is more transparent. Families would not have to declare their income, the process would be much simpler, and there would be no need to check their financial circumstances. All children would be treated equally.

But this would place a significantly greater burden on the budget. Wealthier families would also receive the benefit. If payments are limited to low-income families, public spending is lower, and the money goes to those who need it most. The problem is that determining a family’s actual income can be difficult, creating opportunities for abuse. Such cases have also occurred in the allocation of targeted social assistance: people have tried to formally give up their jobs or even arrange sham divorces to meet the eligibility criteria.”

The new Law on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 2026, explicitly enshrines a child’s right to social security. Under Article 24 of the law, every child has the right to material support at least equal to the subsistence minimum established by law. The same article states that the government provides social assistance to certain categories of citizens to protect children.

In 2026, the subsistence minimum for a child is 260 manats (around $153 or €132).

However, this provision does not in itself mean that the state is obliged to pay every child 260 manats in cash each month. It establishes a general right to material support, while direct social payments remain available only to specific categories.

Can child benefits make parents “lazy”?

It was against this backdrop that Gunay Agamali argued that parents should not expect financial assistance from the state when deciding to have a child, and that such benefits could supposedly foster dependency.

This argument shifts the debate away from social policy and towards the behaviour of parents themselves.

Yet Azerbaijan’s existing system already provides direct payments to families with children. The debate is therefore not about whether the state should support families financially at all, but whether payments should cover all children or only specific groups.

Earlier, Aygun Gumbatova, the wife of imprisoned opposition activist Agil Gumbatov, called for the introduction of child benefits. She cited her family’s difficult financial circumstances as the reason for her position.

“We have found ourselves in a difficult financial situation. My husband was arrested on false charges. He was the family’s sole breadwinner. Now I am left with three school-age children,” Gumbatova told a Caucasian Knot correspondent.

Her eldest child has autism and requires constant care, making it impossible for Gumbatova to work. According to her, the family’s only stable source of income is the 320-manat disability pension (around $188 or €162) paid for her child’s second-group disability status.

At the same time, supporting a universal child benefit does not necessarily mean that its proponents see it as a solution to all social and demographic problems.

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the REAL Party, believes the issue is too easily exploited for populist purposes:

“This is a very sensitive issue, and it is extremely convenient for populism. People who do not bear political responsibility can use it simply to score political points. Such promises easily resonate with the public. For example, someone comes out and says: let’s pay 500 manats [around $294 or €253] for every child. Someone with two or three children at home will naturally think: ‘Great, that’s 1,000–1,500 manats’ [around $588–882 or €507–760].”

“That is precisely why the issue often fails to become the subject of serious discussion. It would be far more useful to sit down with government representatives, examine the budget’s capabilities and do the calculations: how much the state can afford, in what form, and under which model such payments could be introduced.

Sometimes populism goes so far that child benefits are presented as almost a solution to every problem. That is also wrong and misleads people. Azerbaijan already faces demographic problems, and the birth rate is falling. But claiming that simply introducing child benefits tomorrow would immediately reverse the situation is also populism. We can see this in European countries. In Poland, for example, families receive 800 zlotys [around $214 or €185] per child — a fairly substantial amount. Yet the demographic situation continues to deteriorate, and the fertility rate has fallen from 1.7 to 1.4.”

According to the World Bank, Azerbaijan’s total fertility rate was 1.7 children per woman in 2020, falling to 1.4 by 2024. The downward trend has continued in more recent statistics. According to Azerbaijan’s State Statistical Committee, 40,798 children were born in the country between January and June 2026. The number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 9.0 in the same period of 2025 to 8.0.

Can the budget afford a universal child benefit?

One of the main arguments against universal payments is their cost.

Natig Jafarli believes that child benefits are economically feasible in Azerbaijan, but that they do not necessarily have to be introduced for all children at once. In his view, the system could be rolled out in stages.

“If the aim is to reverse the demographic situation through child benefits, a benefit alone will not be enough. But from an economic perspective, such payments are possible. We simply need to determine the amount and the stages.

Several years ago, we proposed starting from the assumption that Azerbaijan has around 2.7 million children aged 0 to 18, and approximately 920,000 of them are second-born children in their families. If it is impossible to cover all children under 18 immediately, the programme could at least start with second and subsequent children. If we paid around 100 manats [around $59 or €51] per child, the first stage would require about 1 billion manats a year [around $588 million or €507 million]. That is an amount Azerbaijan’s budget could sustain.

If, on the other hand, we paid 100 manats a month to all 2.7 million children — even if we consider 100 manats a very small amount — the cost would exceed 3 billion manats a year [more than $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion] and reach approximately 3.2–3.3 billion manats [around $1.88–1.94 billion or €1.62–1.67 billion]. Such a burden could create certain difficulties for the budget at the initial stage. So we could start with 1 billion and then expand the programme as the economy’s capacity grows.”

Azerbaijan’s state budget for 2026 has approved revenues of 38.609 billion manats (around $22.71 billion or €19.57 billion) and expenditures of 41.7036 billion manats (around $24.53 billion or €21.14 billion).

Against this backdrop, spending more than 3 billion manats (over $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion) on a universal child benefit would indeed be a substantial expense.

But the scale of the expenditure alone does not settle the debate. A universal payment for every child is not the only possible option. The amount could depend on the child’s age, birth order, or parental income, or the programme could be introduced gradually.

The question, therefore, is not simply whether “the money is available in the budget”. It is also about which model of social policy the government considers a priority.

Birth rates are falling, but benefits are not the only factor

One reason the issue of child benefits has returned to the public agenda is the sharp decline in the number of births.

According to the State Statistical Committee, 122,846 children were born in Azerbaijan in 2022. The figure fell to 112,620 in 2023 and declined further to 102,310 in 2024. In 2025, the country recorded 95,875 births.

This means the annual number of births fell by nearly 27,000 between 2022 and 2025.

In 2025, the number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 10 to 9.4.

The age structure of the population is also changing. At the beginning of 2023, children under four accounted for 6.3% of the population. By the beginning of 2025, their share had fallen to 5.6%. Meanwhile, the proportion of people aged 65–69 rose from 3.9% to 4.6%, while the share of those aged 70 and over increased from 4.6% to 5.3%.

Sociologist Sanubar Heydarli told Meydan TV that support for young families is particularly important in this situation:

“Living standards in Azerbaijan cannot be described as high, and there are many social difficulties. That is why I consider child benefits an important form of support for young families. The figures also point to this: the birth rate is falling sharply, and the population is beginning to age.”

“But child benefits alone cannot solve this problem. We cannot assume that the government will start making payments and the birth rate will automatically rise. Other measures are needed alongside them. The decision to have a child depends on more than a family’s financial situation. Access to the labour market for women, a sense of social security, and the state of healthcare, education and social support systems all matter.

Nevertheless, child benefits provide significant support for young families. After a child is born, one parent temporarily leaves the labour market, reducing the family’s income. The state should therefore support families during childbirth and child-rearing. Child benefits are important, but they are not the only solution to demographic problems.”

What difference would 100 manats make?

Another question is how much the benefit would be worth.

Suppose the government pays 100 manats (around $59 or €51) per child each month. A family with two children would receive an additional 200 manats (around $118 or €101).

Could such an amount solve a family’s main financial problems?

Natig Jafarli believes it could not:

“In Europe, of every €100 spent on food, the figure is around €20 at most. If we spend half our income on food, that points to low living standards in Azerbaijan.

But much depends on the size of the benefit. Imagine a completely unrealistic scenario: the government pays 1,000 manats per child. Such an amount could indeed have a significant impact on poverty. But is that possible? No. If, at best, families receive 100 manats per child and a family with two children gets an additional 200 manats, would that be enough to eliminate poverty? Of course not.”

At the same time, the purpose of a child benefit does not necessarily have to be for the state to provide for a family entirely.

It could also be seen as the government’s contribution towards the additional expenses that inevitably arise when raising a child.

In the long term, Jafarli believes a completely different model would be ideal:

“People should be able to earn a living and support their own families. Small businesses and family businesses should be developed. The economy should move in a direction where people do not need such payments at all. That is the ideal model for me.

In principle, I am sceptical of the idea of the state constantly giving people money, because the more the state finances you, the more it can restrict your rights. We need to build a system, a society and a country where there is no longer any need for such payments. But is there a need for them now? Of course there is.”

Sanubar Heydarli also points to changing attitudes among parents towards raising children. Modern families may consciously choose to have fewer children, preferring to provide one or two children with better education, healthcare and opportunities for development.

What models have neighbouring countries adopted?

The experience of neighbouring countries shows that there is no single model for child benefits. In some countries, payments depend on family income; in others, they depend on the child’s birth order.

In Armenia, from 1 September 2026, every newborn child will qualify for a one-off payment of 500,000 drams, regardless of their birth order. This is equivalent to around 2,341 manats ($1,374 or €1,187). The Armenian government approved the decision on 13 August 2026.

In addition, a monthly payment of 50,000 drams — approximately 235 manats ($137 or €119) — is paid for the third and each subsequent child until the child turns six.

In Turkey, a one-off payment of 5,000 lira is available for the first child born on or after 1 January 2025. This is equivalent to around 176 manats ($104 or €89). For a second child, families receive 1,500 lira per month — around 53 manats ($31 or €27) — until the child turns five. For the third and subsequent children, the monthly payment is 5,000 lira (approximately 176 manats, $104 or €89).

In Georgia, the system is closer to a targeted model. Families with a social rating below the established threshold receive 200 lari per month — around 130 manats ($77 or €66) — for each child under 16. A UN report on social protection in Georgia states that the programme covers children from families with a social rating below 120,001 points.

According to figures for November 2025, more than 250,000 children were receiving these payments.

In Russia, the main unified child benefit is also not universal. When determining eligibility, authorities assess a family’s per capita income and other criteria of need. The payment can amount to 50%, 75% or 100% of the regional subsistence minimum for a child.

These examples show that the choice is not simply between having child benefits and not having them.

A government can provide a one-off payment at birth, introduce monthly benefits until a certain age, offer greater support for second and subsequent children, or limit payments to low-income families.

Azerbaijan currently follows the last model for the most part: targeted assistance and benefits for specific categories.

Is a separate law needed to introduce a universal child benefit?

According to Fariz Namazly, the government would not need to pass a separate law to introduce a universal child benefit:

“There is already a Law on Social Benefits, which could be amended. In addition, a new Law on the Rights of the Child has been adopted, and it could also be supplemented with provisions on new payments and benefits for children. In other words, the necessary provisions could be incorporated into either the Law on the Rights of the Child or the Law on Social Benefits.”

The burden on the budget — what about future costs?

Since 2006, the government’s overall approach has remained largely unchanged: instead of providing the same monthly payment for every child, it offers assistance based on a family’s financial need or a child’s membership in a specific social category.

As noted above, this does not mean the government provides no support to families with children. There are payments at birth, benefits for low-income families, childcare benefits, assistance for women with large families, and support for children with disabilities and those without parental care.

A universal child benefit would mean a shift away from this model.

Clearly, it would require substantial additional spending. At the same time, experts stress that child benefits alone cannot eliminate poverty or automatically reverse the decline in birth rates.

However, the falling number of births and the gradual ageing of the population raise a different question: can social policy be assessed solely in terms of how much money it costs today?

Sanubar Heydarli believes that failing to support families now could leave the state facing much higher costs in the future:

“By refusing to introduce child benefits today, leaving families to cope with their difficulties alone and failing to take responsibility, the state is effectively increasing its future expenditure associated with an ageing population.

Child benefits are a highly visible item of expenditure: when money is paid directly to families and the authorities calculate the total cost, the figures can seem enormous. But this ignores the fact that failing to support children today will translate into unavoidable spending on an ageing population in the future.

The state will have to pay more in pensions and benefits and increase healthcare spending. The proportion of elderly people will grow. As a result, the balance between taxes paid by the younger working population and spending on pensioners will be disrupted. There will be more pension recipients and fewer taxpayers. Ultimately, the burden on the state will only increase.”

With the support of the Mediset

Child benefits in Azerbaijan

World.title: Opinion: ‘Signs of cult-like behaviour are becoming increasingly apparent in Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party’
World.content:
“It is absolutely inappropriate to call an institutionalised protest movement a cult,” sociologist Iago Kachkachishvili says, commenting on an open letter by Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, published on the 666th day of continuous anti-government protests.

In his letter, the speaker refers to the protesters as a “cult”. Kachkachishvili, however, argues that the protest movement has no single prominent leader or figurehead whose will its participants blindly follow. He also says Papuashvili’s remarks suggest that the ongoing protests are clearly troubling the authorities.

“When the outcome no longer justifies the process, the process itself must begin to justify itself. Ritual is one of the mechanisms through which this happens, and when continuing the ritual itself becomes the goal, a political movement gradually turns into a closed pseudo-religious cult. Today, on the 666th day, we see a combination of these characteristics,” Papuashvili wrote.

Speaking on the Free Studio programme, Iago Kachkachishvili said authorities could, in the future, impose certain restrictions on the protest movement, including legal restrictions, similar to their attempts to ban opposition parties. However, the sociologist believes that even in such circumstances, public protests would find a way to continue.

Kachkachishvili also discussed the criteria for what constitutes a “cult”. He said that, when comparing a social movement with a political party in this context, he believed political parties showed more characteristics of a cult.

He singled out the ruling Georgian Dream party in particular. In his assessment, the party is effectively run according to the decisions of its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, while its other members follow his directives without question.

Iago Kachkachishvili: “The sheer length of Shalva Papuashvili’s letter confirms that the authorities are troubled by the daily, ongoing protests.

The rhetoric he uses about the protest movement shows that the protests are a thorn in their side. This is despite the fact that they are no longer as large as they once were. But it is impossible for a protest to maintain the same scale when it has been going on for two years.

Shalva Papuashvili cynically called this protest movement a sect, even though he knows very well what the word ‘sect’ means. But, as always, he has turned his attitude towards the opposition into a cynical propaganda campaign.

Of course, the protest movement has become routine, and it is accompanied by certain symbols that have taken root. For example, the Georgian and EU flags at these rallies are a tangible symbolic expression of the movement’s support for Georgia joining the European Union. Another established symbol is the fact that the protests have remained on Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi, despite the roadworks currently taking place there.

Of course, Rustaveli Avenue is a symbol of protest — a place associated with the spirit and energy of dissent. We can point to other symbols as well. This is perfectly normal when a phenomenon becomes institutionalised, in this case a protest movement. This movement has developed into an institution with its own participants, rules, symbols, values and so on.

It is absolutely inappropriate to call this institutionalised protest movement a sect. First and foremost, it has no single prominent leader or figurehead whose will the protesters follow unquestioningly.

The protest movement brings together a wide range of people from different parts of society. It includes people who are not affiliated with any political party, academics, civil society representatives, members of organisations, artists and representatives of various political parties, including opposition parties that do not get along particularly well with one another. The protest movement is highly diverse, whereas a sect is characterised by almost everything except such diversity of views and backgrounds.

A second important indicator that this is not a sect is that it is not a closed group: people join it and leave it. Movement within the protest movement, including joining or leaving it, is not controlled, and there are no strict rules governing participation.

Another feature that fundamentally contradicts the perception of the protest movement as a sect is that it is not isolated from the opposition-minded public, or the broader society that supports the protests. It is an important representative of the opposition electorate.”

“It is entirely possible that this stigma, this negative label that Georgian Dream has attached to the protest movement — portraying it as a sectarian, almost satanic movement — could lead to the movement being declared illegal, banned, and its participants held legally accountable.

But it is impossible to silence the protest voice of an opposition-minded society on such a scale. The authorities would then have to shut down social media as well. However, I do not expect things to go that far. There will be certain restrictions, including legal ones, but the protest movement will still find a way to continue.

In general, a political party is much more likely to resemble a sect because, compared with a social movement, a political party is a more closed institution.

Political parties allow less pluralism and diversity of opinion, although this depends on the type of party we are talking about — democratic or authoritarian. In a democratic party, different views are legitimised and have their own legitimate space. Members exchange opinions, and there is no single leader or figurehead whose will dictates the party’s direction. But what happens in Georgian Dream? Isn’t Georgian Dream effectively Bidzina Ivanishvili?

Georgian Dream is a party built around one person’s authority. It acts exclusively in the direction set by Bidzina Ivanishvili. The defining feature of a sect is the presence of a leader to whom followers show unquestioning, unconditional and uncritical loyalty, whose authority they never challenge, and whose directives determine the group’s actions and direction. This is precisely what Georgian Dream has become under Bidzina Ivanishvili, and it is the clearest indicator of its sect-like nature.

And the most important thing we have witnessed in recent years is that anyone who criticises Georgian Dream is punished — harshly and through various means. This is what sectarianism looks like: the absolute and unquestionable principle that ‘whoever is not with me is my enemy’.”

On the protests and Georgian Dream

World.title: Theologian jailed for 30 days as Azerbaijan hijab-in-schools row reignites
World.content:
Azerbaijan schools hijab row

Theologian Abgul Suleymanov was detained for 30 days. His family links his detention to social media posts in which he spoke out against new school uniform requirements concerning the wearing of the hijab.

It has not been reported under which article of the Code of Administrative Offences the court sentenced him. It is therefore not yet possible to establish how Suleymanov’s posts were used to justify the decision to detain him.

Suleymanov’s wife, Zahra Suleymanova, told Meydan TV that the theologian was taken away from outside his home on the evening of 22 September. The following day, his family was unable to establish where he was being held.

According to Suleymanova, her husband has severe diabetes and needs to take medication. His relatives said on 24 September that, following the court hearing, he was taken to a temporary detention facility in Baku’s Binagadi district.

Hijab post and previous arrest

Following the Cabinet of Ministers’ decision, Suleymanov spoke out against restrictions on schoolgirls wearing the hijab. He wrote that if such a ban were introduced, he would rather go to prison. His family links his detention to this stance. Neither the police nor the court have publicly disclosed the reasons for his arrest.

The hijab issue is not new for the theologian. He is known for taking part in protests against restrictions on religious head coverings in schools, and his supporters refer to him as a “hijab prisoner”.

Suleymanov was detained in 2011 and sentenced to 11 years in prison on charges including organising unrest, attempting to disrupt public security and inciting disobedience. Official reports also alleged that drugs had been found in his possession. Suleymanov denied the charges. He was released in September 2022 after serving his sentence.

Following his release, Suleymanov said his religious beliefs had not changed and that he would defend his rights again if he faced obstacles to practising his religion. Documents relating to the current administrative case have not yet been made public.

Does new decision outlaw hijab?

A Cabinet of Ministers decision dated 21 September amended dress requirements for pupils at state schools. Under the new rules, pupils are prohibited from wearing additional items of clothing that disrupt the uniformity of the prescribed school uniform or are inconsistent with the principle of secularism in general education.

The word “hijab” is not mentioned in the decision. However, because religious head coverings are not part of the school uniform, the changes have been interpreted as a ban on wearing the hijab. The document does not specify which items of clothing are considered inconsistent with the principle of secularism, raising questions about how the new rule will be applied in schools.

Under the decision, parents or legal guardians must ensure that their children comply with the dress requirements. Issues relating to compliance are to be decided by each school’s pedagogical council. Elements of national dress may be worn only at certain events with the council’s approval. The document does not specifically provide for girls wearing the hijab to be excluded from classes.

Before the decision was adopted, the principle of “national values and secularism” was added to the Law on General Education in July, while the requirement for pupils and teachers to comply with dress rules was enshrined in law.

Previous complaints and unanswered questions

There have been previous complaints about girls wearing hijabs being denied access to schools. In an article we published in April, we reported on a parent’s complaint about School No. 15 in Sumgayit. He said his daughter had been prevented from attending classes because of her head covering. The school uniform requirements in force at the time did not specifically mention the hijab.

At the heart of the dispute are, on the one hand, requirements for a standard school uniform and the principle that children should not be forced to wear religious clothing and, on the other, pupils’ rights to freedom of religion and education. The issue of wearing the hijab in schools also came to prominence in 2012 following a protest outside the Education Ministry and subsequent arrests.

It remains unclear how schools will apply the new rules to pupils who wear the hijab. A key question also remains unanswered in Suleymanov’s case: what specific action did the court consider grounds for sentencing him to 30 days of administrative detention?

World.title: ‘No security guarantees’: Why Georgia’s Kamara festival was cancelled
World.content:
Kamara festival cancelled in Georgia

The Kamara music festival, scheduled to take place in the Georgian city of Gori on 26 September and close with a performance by opposition-minded musician Kordz, has been postponed indefinitely. The festival’s organiser, the Danish Cultural Institute, said it considered it unsafe to hold the event.

Kordz (Aleksandre Kordzaia) said he had faced attacks and threats from local authorities, members of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media.

The EU Delegation to Georgia responded to the festival’s cancellation by expressing regret. It said the Kamara festival was held as part of the EU-funded Creative Compass Georgia project and stressed that it “firmly believes in freedom of artistic expression”.

The delegation also noted that the EU had supported Georgia’s cultural sector for 30 years, including efforts to preserve the country’s cultural heritage, develop its creative industries and build links between Georgian artists and cultural organisations and their European counterparts.

Georgian parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili responded critically to the EU Delegation’s statement. He said he had initially hoped the EU ambassador would realise that supporting “hatred and violence” in Georgia was unacceptable, but argued that the delegation’s statement suggested otherwise.

Papuashvili was particularly critical of the EU’s reference to the importance of freedom of artistic expression. He said the EU Delegation did not understand Georgia or Georgian society.

“This statement by the delegation is a direct incitement to hate speech, insults against mothers, labelling people as slaves, fascism and radicalism. The EU embassy is encouraging this,” Papuashvili told journalists.

The Georgian Musicians’ Union, in turn, responded to Papuashvili’s comments and the cancellation of Kordz’s performance by expressing solidarity with the musician. It said freedom of expression for artists was not a political privilege but a fundamental right.

The union said direct attacks by public officials on an artist over his civic stance went beyond debate and became a tool of censorship.

“It is unacceptable to use official power and rhetoric to intimidate musicians or disrupt concerts,” the union said.

It described Kordz as one of the prominent figures on Georgia’s music scene and warned that restricting artists’ ability to perform in their own country because of political pressure could have a serious impact on the cultural environment.

“Art cannot exist in an atmosphere of censorship and fear,” the statement said.

World.title: Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge with stones
World.content:
Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge

In Abkhazia, Russian tourists pelted a Supreme Court judge with stones. A criminal case was opened only several days later, and only after public pressure.

The incident took place in Sukhum on the evening of 20 September. According to official information, two Russian nationals, Yury Chudin and Sergey Bessonov, became involved in an altercation with a local woman in the street, threatened to kill her and then threw stones at her.

The woman was taken to hospital with a closed head injury, a laceration and bruising to her eyelid, and a haematoma.

The victim was later identified as a judge of the Supreme Court of Abkhazia, although neither investigators nor the media have named her. The cause of the altercation also remains unknown.

The incident was included in the official police report only after the Telegram channel Aiashara reported it a day later. The channel highlighted the fact that no criminal case had been opened, prompting a strong reaction on social media.

It was only after this that, on 23 September, the investigative department of the Sukhum police classified the attack on the judge as a criminal offence. Initially, the actions of the two Russian tourists had been treated as an administrative offence. Chudin and Bessonov refused to undergo medical tests for drug and psychotropic substance use, and a court subsequently sentenced them to 15 days in administrative detention.

The case has been transferred from the police to the Sukhum prosecutor’s office for further investigation. The ruling states that the decision was made in view of the public attention surrounding the case and the status of the victim.

World.title: Heads of the State Security Service and Foreign Intelligence Service visit Victory Park (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. In connection with September 27 Remembrance Day, Head of the State Security Service Colonel General Ali Naghiyev and Head of the Foreign Intelligence Service Colonel General Orkhan Sultanov visited Victory Park in Baku.

The heads of the agencies laid flowers at the monument at the entrance to the memorial complex and paid deep tribute to the memory of the heroic martyrs who sacrificed their lives for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Azerbaijan.

It should be recalled that on September 27, 2020, the armed forces of Armenia grossly violated the ceasefire regime along the entire line of contact. In response to the enemy's provocation, on September 27, the Azerbaijani Army, on the order of President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ilham Aliyev, launched a counteroffensive operation. The Patriotic War began.

This war was the struggle of the Azerbaijani people for the right, justice, and territorial integrity. Under the leadership of victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev and with the support of the people, the Azerbaijani Army made history. Thanks to its professionalism and the dedication of its soldiers and officers, our army broke through the enemy's lines of defense one after another and liberated the country's territories from occupation in a short period of time. As a result of the successful counteroffensive operation by the Azerbaijani Army, five cities, four settlements, and 286 villages had been liberated from occupation by November 9.

On November 10, the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the Prime Minister of Armenia, and the President of Russia signed a trilateral statement announcing the complete cessation of the ceasefire and all military operations in the conflict zone. The victory won on the battlefield continued in the political sphere — following the 44-day Patriotic War, Aghdam, Kalbajar, and Lachin were returned to Azerbaijan without a single shot being fired. The Patriotic War ended with a historic victory for Azerbaijan.

As a sign of deep respect for our soldiers and officers, all the martyrs who fought heroically in the Patriotic War, raised the Azerbaijani flag over the lands liberated from occupation, and sacrificed their lives for the territorial integrity of our country, September 27 is commemorated in the Republic of Azerbaijan as Remembrance Day.

World.title: Lachin commemorates martyrs on September 27 - Remembrance Day (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. In connection with September 27 Remembrance Day, a minute of silence was observed in Lachin district in memory of the martyrs who fought heroically in the Patriotic War and sacrificed their lives for the territorial integrity of Azerbaijan.

Participants gathered in the central square of Lachin city to mark Remembrance Day and expressed their deep respect for the memory of the martyrs.

At 12:00, the movement of vehicles and pedestrians was halted throughout the district, cars sounded their horns, and a minute of silence was observed in memory of the martyrs.

Representatives of the Special Representative Office of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in Lachin district, employees of the Lachin District Restoration, Construction and Management Service, law enforcement agencies operating in the district, families of martyrs, and district residents attended the Remembrance Day event.

World.title: Pope urges church to admit failings and heal 'deep wounds'
World.content:
Pope Leo has urged the Catholic Church to admit its own failings and heal "deep wounds" inflicted within its ranks, hours before meeting with victims of child abuse by priests in France.

Addressing crowds of more than 150,000 in Lourdes, the Pope said the Church must have the courage to face its past, but did not directly reference abuse scandals in France that sparked nationwide shock.

"In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within [the Church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze." he said.

Arriving in Paris on Friday, the Pope went to Lourdes on Saturday and will visit Metz in the north-east on Monday.

During the trip, he has again urged the world to reconsider the development of artificial intelligence and drew 800,000 people for an outdoor Mass on the Champs-Élysées in Paris.

More than 800,000 people arrived for Mass with the Pope in Paris. (Reuters: Stephanie Mahe)

Local leaders are hoping he will help repair the Church's standing after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades.

The Vatican provided a statement of what Pope Leo had mentioned in an earlier, closed-door meeting with French bishops on Sunday.

" The painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy, "

The Pope thanked the bishops for the "courageous measures" they had taken to confront the revelation,.

Pope Leo urged the bishops to bolster their safeguarding efforts and "continue on the path undertaken, maintaining the greatest vigilance".

Victims sceptical meeting will bring action

The Pope is due to have a closed-door meeting with seven French victims of abuse by clergy later on Sunday.

Some survivors said they were doubtful the encounter would result in quick changes by the Church.

The Pope's visit to France will include Paris, Lourdes and Metz. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

"I am quite sceptical that the pope will solve the issue, at least not immediately," said Michèle Le Reun-Gaigné, co-president of an association for survivors in western France.

" Things are moving very slowly. It isn't going to happen overnight. "

Bishop Pierre-Antoine Bozo, the spokesperson for French bishops, said the Pope's desire to have the meeting "shows that we cannot ignore this issue and that it must always remain among our concerns".

Pope Leo has previously apologised directly for abuse scandals that have damaged the Church's credibility across the world.

On a trip to Spain in June, he told local bishops they must listen to survivors and offer them reparations.

Lourdes connected to Vatican scandal

The Pope's itinerary in France includes six events in Lourdes, a town in the foothills of the Pyrenees mountains.

It attracts some 3 million pilgrims a year for visits to a shrine to the Virgin Mary and purported healing spring waters.

The site is also connected to a ⁠scandal that has ​dogged the Vatican in recent years.

The shrine's facade has a series of mosaics by Reverend Marko Rupnik, ​a prominent religious artist with Vatican ties, who has been accused of sexual abuse.

Mr Rupnik, accused by more than 20 women, is not known to have commented publicly on the accusations.

The Pope has urged the church to acknowledge its mistakes and heal the wounds of survivors. (Reuters: Stephanie Mahe)

Five of his alleged victims wrote an open letter to the pope last week, sharply criticising an ongoing Vatican trial of the cleric.

The storeys-tall mosaics have been covered for the Pope's visit with large tarps.

During his time in Paris and Lourdes, the Pope twice reiterated Catholic opposition to assisted dying initiatives, which comes two ‌months after France created a legal right to die for those with incurable illness.

He said the shrine welcomes sick pilgrims hoping to find a miracle in its waters, and stood opposed to "current trends that seek to redefine the value of human life in illness".

Reuters

World.title: Matty Johns breaks down in tears after Knights end NRL grand final drought
World.content:
Former Knights star Matty Johns has broken down in tears as he heaped praise on the Newcastle team and its fans after a gripping and gritty NRL preliminary final win over Penrith.

The Knights played more than half the game with 12 men on the field after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip drop that graphically broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

Penrith scored shortly after to take a 14-6 lead into half-time, but Justin Holbrook's Knights defended resolutely against a scrappy Panthers side and managed to score three second-half tries to progress to the grand final against the Roosters.

Knights stun Panthers to reach GF The Newcastle Knights reach their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

The women's team won back-to-back NRLW premierships in 2022 and 2023, but Newcastle has not played in a men's grand final since Andrew Johns led the Knights to victory over the Eels in the 2001 grand final.

A quarter of a century and five wooden spoons later, the team will return to the final day of the season next week after a similarly remarkable upset win over the most dominant team in NRL history.

So it is hardly surprising that Hunter native and former Knights star Matty Johns was incredibly emotional straight after full-time.

"To be honest, I don't know what to say," he said on Fox Sports.

"It was unbelievable. Incredible effort in that second half. I just feel so happy for all the fans."

Players past and present, as well as coach Justin Holbrook, hailed the fans who travelled to the game. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

It became increasingly hard to find the words as tears started to flow and emotion took over.

"They've had to put up with a lot of shit for a lot of years to get back to where they are now," Johns said.

Even getting to the game on Sunday was tough as an issue with a freight train caused delays and cancellations on the Central Coast and Newcastle train line, forcing fans to find alternate routes and replacement services to get down to Sydney, which led to traffic jams on the M1 motorway on a sodden afternoon.

"But it just didn't stop them in the wet," Johns said of the crowd at Homebush, which was hugely in favour of the visiting Novocastrians.

The Stadium Australia crowd was heavily favouring the away team. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"When you run onto a field like that and you look up and you see all those Newcastle fans, you don't leave the field defeated.

"If not for the fans they don't win today."

Holbrook sprinted around the field to pay tribute to the fans who turned up, and who have continued to turn up even when the team was struggling, including last year when they finished last for the fifth time in 21 seasons.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

"We want to make our community proud, our Hunter region, and for the boys to deliver that performance, it was so good to see them all hang around," he said.

"We went down to 12 [when Crossland was sent off] and then 30,000 make you feel like you've got 14 out there."

Captain Kalyn Ponga agreed the supporters helped the team get over the line.

"They're a big reason why we won today," he said.

"They're loud, they're passionate, they're vocal and we're gonna need them next week."

World.title: Scaffolding at Sydney building site falls onto cars month after wall collapse
World.content:
Scaffolding at a Sydney building site has partially collapsed onto parked cars, the second safety incident within weeks at the development.

SafeWork NSW said no-one was injured when a large section of scaffolding fell onto vehicles on Wattle Street in the inner-city suburb of Ultimo on Saturday just before 6:45pm.

CCTV footage shows the scaffolding giving way due to strong winds and narrowly missing drivers on the street.

The regulator said inspectors attended the site, and that it had issued regulatory notices, including a prohibition notice to the site managers.

There were no injuries when a large section of scaffolding fell onto vehicles on Wattle Street. (Supplied)

Lisa, who lives a few doors down from the site, said she heard a loud bang and initially thought a sheet of metal was being dragged across the street.

"There was a bit of wind, and there was a loud sound of metal on the road," she said.

She only realised what happened after reviewing her security video.

"I think the structure they had on the front of the building wasn't secure," she said.

"The scaffolding and the additional panels that they placed to prevent any bricks from going over it when they demolished subsequently was … not secured, and then fell on the road."

Macroview Projects, which is managing the development, has been contacted for comment.

Residents raise safety concerns

A wall and roof collapsed at the same Ultimo building site onto a nearby petrol station last month, seriously injuring two men, one in his 60s and the other in his 30s.

The two men were pulled from rubble and taken to St Vincent's Hospital and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital with serious injuries.

Five other people were assessed by paramedics at the time, but did not need hospital treatment.

Two injured in Sydney building collapse A man in his 60s and a man in his 30s were removed from the rubble and taken to hospital in a serious condition.

Lisa said work had only recently resumed at the site after being halted for weeks.

"It raises concerns over what is happening at that building site, and the safety precautions that are going into what should be the demolition," she said.

"It is a concern that this has happened twice in two months on the same place."

Lisa said she was relieved no-one had been hurt this time, but that the collapse had come at a cost to others.

"There are costs to other people, such as the cars that were affected last time … Coles Express, where its forecourt was closed for eight weeks, so it couldn't sell any petrol for eight weeks, and now cars in front of the building are being damaged."

SafeWork NSW are investigating

The building was previously home to a rehearsal studio, but had since been approved for demolition to make way for a multi-storey mixed-use development.

After last month's incident, Fire and Rescue NSW said the situation had been extremely dangerous given the weight of falling brickwork.

The site was subsequently handed to SafeWork NSW for investigation.

World.title: Freo finds joy in AFLW win, Pies finally off the mark
World.content:
Fremantle's women have lifted their club as they surged into the AFLW top eight, while Collingwood broke through for its first win of the season.

The fast-starting Dockers outscored Adelaide 28-0 in the first quarter and led by as much as 45 on their way to a comfortable 9.6 (60) to 5.5 (35) victory over Adelaide at Unley Oval.

Adelaide (3-4) kicked three straight goals either side of three-quarter time, but never got the deficit below 25, as Fremantle (4-3) defended its advantage, unlike its male counterparts in Saturday's AFL grand final.

It was the Dockers' first win in their past seven AFLW encounters with Adelaide, who had a 9-1 record in the fixture before Sunday.

In the other early game on Sunday, Collingwood (1-6) outlasted GWS 4.10 (34) to 3.7 (25) in a low-scoring arm wrestle at Victoria Park.

The Giants (1-6) led by margins of one, four and seven at the end of the first three quarters respectively, but Collingwood dominated the final term.

They finished with 18 more inside 50s and 16 more contested possessions.

In Sydney, the Lions fell short of a stirring comeback of their own in a 5.7 (37) to 3.5 (23) defeat to the Swans.

The victory held Sydney's position in the top four and saw Brisbane's record fall to a disappointing 2-5.

The Lions were second best for most of the afternoon but managed to stay in touch through three quarters, and were only a point behind at the final term.

But after Cynthia Hamilton goaled inside the first minute of the last quarter, the Swans didn't look back, running out comfortable 12-point winners.

In the final game of round seven, Gold Coast took St Kilda another step closer to the wooden spoon by running out 10.9 (69) to 6.3 (39) winners.

The Saints led by 15 points at half-time but were gunned down by the home side after the break, conceding eight goals to one as the Suns moved to sixth place on the AFLW ladder.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Dynasties and destinies swing on Cleary's horror ankle injury
World.content:
Mark the 35th minute of Sunday's NRL preliminary final as the hinge on which a storied dynasty and a potential premiership destiny swung.

Penrith and Newcastle had fought a first-half that made both look like worthy foes for the Roosters in next week's grand final.

The Knights faithful turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter, proving yet again they would follow their team into hell itself if Sid Fogg's would charter a bus there.

Francis Manuleleua's long-range try, the latest scorching adventure of the screaming Knights, gave the beast inside the 55,000-strong crowd a smell of blood and it turned the Panthers into strangers in their own country.

The Penrith half of the crowd rose for Blaize Talagi's score off a clever Jack Cogger kick, but never has Nathan Cleary, benched before kick-off, copped such treatment on his home turf as he did before he entered the game in the 20th minute.

Just 10 minutes later came the tackle that ended his season as he suffered an graphic fracture to his ankle, also ending Phoenix Crossland's afternoon after he was sent off, and putting this game on the raggedy edge.

In the end, it was the Knights who pushed the Panthers over the side to write their names in history, with a 22-14 win that sends Newcastle to their first grand final in 25 years.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture after a tackle from Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The two sides provided a fascinating contrast from the start as they left the field following the warm-up.

Penrith, the ultimate professionals and avatars of pure ruthlessness, had eyes of steel, a picture of focus.

Newcastle, by contrast, waved to friends and family, faces beaming that they were here together on the verge of a dream.

Rage and joy proved to be equally potent fuels, with rare courage on both sides amid the furious desperation you only see when the stakes are highest.

The Knights finished with 12 on the field after Crossland's dismissal but, somehow, rarely looked shorthanded.

Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL Grand Final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half.

There is a temptation to call that a miracle, but Newcastle didn't need divine intervention to flat-out-play the Panthers in a second half.

They bent occasionally but never broke as Penrith fought hard, denied only by a series of last-gasp efforts from the Knights.

Kalyn Ponga pulled off a tackle on Moses Leota that any footy hit man would have been proud of. Mat Croker dived on loose balls like they were live grenades.

Dane Gagai played like his Newcastle life depended on it, and given he has earned one last day as a Knight, it kind of did.

They were able to take advantage of the Panthers not quite being their razor-sharp selves, as best typified by Smith's first try off a quick tap that caught Penrith on the hop.

The Panthers missed Cleary, their edges blunted, but Casey McLean came agonisingly close to scoring.

It is a mark of the steel in the Panthers that they weren't out of it until Sandon Smith's late intercept try, even with injuries mounting.

Aside from Cleary — already carrying a broken foot into the game — Blaize Talagi did his Achilles, Dylan Edwards hurt his PCL and Isaah Yeo defied belief to play through a torn pec.

They regrouped well in the moments after Cleary's injury, scoring through Lindsay Smith while the game was still in something of a punch-drunk stupor.

But they did not trouble the scorers again as Newcastle ran in three tries in the second half, all of which began from their own side of halfway.

Newcastle have a chance to create a special piece of history. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

That ability to strike fast and from anywhere on the field is the Knights' greatest gift — it has happened too many times to call this a charmed run or a triumph of abstract, random brilliance.

It has taken them through a high-octane South Sydney, to the heart of Auckland and back and now, a man down and all, through the greatest dynasty many will ever know.

That dynasty is not at its end, but preliminary final losses in each of the past two years show how thin the margins have become.

Penrith are still one of the heavyweights, but the world is changing and Newcastle, with their speed and hunger and endless belief, are the first of the new powers to rise.

Those Knights will be underdogs again next Sunday against the Roosters, with all their glory and splendour, and they must overcome the weight of history.

Of the 117 premiers in the history of Australian rugby league, 115 have finished in the top four. For Newcastle to prevail, it is beyond once in a lifetime and closer to once in the lifetime of the sport.

But after what the Knights have been through and what they have done to get here, the odds seem to matter little.

At this point it feels like there is nothing Newcastle cannot do, no challenge they cannot rise to and no foe they could fear.

World.title: Manhunt for gunmen who killed 27 in two shootings in South Africa
World.content:
South African police have launched a manhunt after gunmen killed at least 27 people in two mass shootings in Cape Town and Johannesburg.

The first incident occurred about 9:30pm local time on Saturday when eight gunmen armed with assault rifles stormed a bar west of Johannesburg, killing 17 people and wounding 15 others.

Police said the suspects opened fire on customers drinking outside before moving inside where they continued to shoot.

The victims included 13 males and four females, police said.

In a statement posted by South African police on social media, the shooters "allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles".

South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said Police has photos of the suspects, and were working to track the down.

"This cannot go on like this" Mr Ramaphosa said.

Illegal mining motive

Authorities were still working to establish the motives for the shootings near Johannesburg and Cape Town, but initial investigations suggested one could be a turf war between illegal miners and the other a business rivalry.

Residents said illegal miners, known locally as zama zamas from an isiZulu expression for "taking a chance", live in the area where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade.

The province's police commissioner Tommy Mthombeni told reporters that one line of inquiry was that the shooting was a "turf war in terms of illegal mining".

Saturday's shooting could be retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago, he added.

They said the suspects also torched two vehicles after fleeing.

Business rivalry

Early on Sunday during a separate shooting at dining venue just outside Cape Town, gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more.

Police said the shooters entered the venue near the town of Lwandle at 1:46am local time, and "shot at patrons".

Five of the victims were declared dead at the scene while the others succumbed to their injuries while being taken to hospital.

"Suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols," South African police said in a statement posted on social media on Sunday.

No suspect has been arrested in either case, police said, and detectives are working to find the gunmen.

An eyewitness video from the venue shows people dancing and singing in a crowded outdoor area when a burst of shots rings out and screams are heard.

A police official said "a business jealousy might have been the issue," following reports people had been buying alcohol in cheaper shops and going to the venue to drink.

A third attack on Tuesday night killed 11 people including a pregnant woman, after multiple gunmen opened fire at a house party in KwaMakhutha township south of Durban.

Police have not reported any arrests.

Ongoing violence

The attacks come as the country grapples with illegal firearms, gun violence and gang rivalries.

The country of about 62 million people records roughly 60 murders a day, among the highest rates globally.

In March, soldiers moved into violence hotspots in Johannesburg to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime.

President Cyril Ramaphosa described ongoing violence and crime as one of the biggest threats facing the country.

Cyril Ramaphosa says crime is one of the biggest threats facing the nation. (AP: Jerome Delay)

Despite ongoing military intervention to keep crime at bay, gun violence still remains a persistent problem.

In Johannesburg, 10 women have been killed in a single municipality in two months, the latest was found on Saturday partially unclothed and stoned to death.

A suspect has been taken into custody, police said.

The nine other victims were mostly in their 20s and 30s, with some found stripped of their clothes and showing signs of sexual assault.

Police have offered a 400,000 rand ($25,000) reward for information leading to the arrest of the killer or killers, while the Democratic Alliance, South Africa's second-largest political party, has put up a further $31,000.

Wires/ABC

World.title: UK police declare major incident at air base used by US
World.content:
Several men have been arrested on suspicion of explosives offences after a security scare at a British air base used by the US Air Force in south-west England.

A major incident was declared, and homes were evacuated in a village near RAF Fairford, with residents moved to a nearby leisure centre on Sunday.

The incident has now been contained.

Gloucestershire police said army bomb disposal experts were "currently examining a number of vehicles".

The security scare comes after the British government gave authorisation to the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

An eyewitness said armed police were blocking access to the main gate of the base.

A B‑1B Lancer bomber at Fairford air base, from where the US has targeted Iranian locations. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

About 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford.

"A number of properties are currently being evacuated following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire police said in a statement.

" It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. "

Police said the men were taken into custody on Sunday morning.

The area has been blocked off to traffic and residents have been evacuated. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

"We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place," Gloucestershire police said.

The base has been used to deploy US bombers since the conflict in Iran began on February 28.

Iran war has spread beyond one strait The Middle East conflict isn't just widening, it's highlighting more vulnerabilities in the region.

A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.

"We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."

On Saturday, US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, while threatening the possibility of further bombing.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Wallabies reduced to 11 men in chaotic upset win over world champ Boks
World.content:
The Wallabies have desperately held on to defeat the world champion Springboks 42-38 in Perth after being reduced to 11 players during the final five minutes.

In one of the most chaotic finishes in Test rugby history, the Wallabies were shown four yellow cards late in the match after comfortably leading 42-17.

Captain Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Hunter Paisami were each sent from the field by referee Andrea Piardi.

Wilson was shown a yellow card for a high shot on Malcolm Marx in the 69th minute, before the Springboks were awarded a penalty try due to an infringement from Lonergan.

As Lonergan received his marching orders, the Wallabies' lead was cut to 42-24.

They subsequently lost Suaalii for the remainder of the match after he committed an offside play.

The Springboks capitalised on their the numerical advantage to score a converted try through Morne van ⁠den Berg.

The Wallabies appeared to seal the victory in the 76th minute when Tom Wright intercepted a pass from Springboks captain André Esterhuizen.

Wright raced away to cross the goal line, but the try was denied as Paisami was ruled to have made contact with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu's head in an earlier tackle.

Paisami was given his yellow card, leaving the Wallabies with 11 players.

The Springboks got within striking distance of the Wallabies on the scoreboard after Ox Nché scored a converted try in the 78th minute.

The Wallabies' lead had been slashed to four points, but they managed to hold on and record a famous victory in front of a boisterous crowd of 54,678.

Adding to the bizarre scenes during the final 10 minutes, Piardi was forced to speak with his fellow match officials via a mobile phone following a malfunction with their communications system.

"It was a crazy last 10 minutes," Wilson told the Nine Network after the match.

"But that first 70 minutes … the way we played, we implemented our game plan. We did exactly what we wanted.

"We stepped up in the physical battle and I'm so proud of the boys."

Wilson was right to highlight the Wallabies' dominance until the flurry of late yellow cards.

They led 24-17 at half-time and extended their advantage in the second term with tries to Wilson and Max Jorgensen.

Lonergan helped build scoreboard pressure with two conversions and as many penalty goals.

Len Ikitau, playing in his preferred outside centre position, impressed in the first half with two tries.

His move back to the number 13 jersey meant Suaalii played on the wing, with the former NRL star handling the role superbly.

The Springboks arrived in Australia following their recent victory in the four-Test series against the All Blacks.

The physical and emotional impact of their win in the series, billed as Rugby's Greatest Rugby Rivalry, will be open to debate.

They made 13 changes to the starting line-up that defeated the All Blacks 43-28 in Baltimore earlier this month.

The triumph saw the Wallabies awarded the Mandela Challenge Plate for the first time since 2022, which was also the last occasion they beat the Springboks on Australian soil.

They face the All Blacks in the first of two Bledisloe Cup Tests on October 10 in Auckland.

The return clash will be played in Sydney on October 17.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: AFLW round seven: Magpies finally record a win, frustration continues for St Kilda
World.content:
St Kilda’s frustrating season continued on Sunday as they remained winless despite taking a 15-point lead into half-time against Gold Coast Suns at People First Stadium.

The Saints came out hot as Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw kicked four of her career best five goals in the first half but the Suns powered back into the match kicking four goals in the third term to regain the lead eventually winning by 30 points.

Dekota Baron of the Suns handballs under pressure from the Saints. Getty Images

Suns star Charlie Rowbottom posted a game-high 38 disposals as her side kicked eight goals to one after half-time including a gut-busting running goal from Dekota Baron in the closing stages of the match.

“I’m so rapt with the girls and their fightback,” Rowbottom told Kayo.
