World.title: ‘Obscurity not security’: Government accused of overreach in Medicare ‘hack’ response
World.content:
Cybersecurity experts and tech investors have accused the Albanese government of blowing the Medicare statistics breach out of proportion, arguing that the website’s code was set up to send data to anyone with the skills to request it. Archived versions of the website show that its code directed savvy users to a digital address where they could download the statistical information it stored despite that data not being publicly available to people via its front end. An OpenAI tool received information from Medicare that was not promoted as being available for download. Marija Ercegovac Seek co-founder Paul Bassat, one of the country’s most prominent technology investors, echoed questions from prominent industry colleagues about Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s claim last week that “an AI agent has infiltrated an Australian government website”. “The government clearly wanted to get onto the front foot to seize the initiative in relation to how AI is regulated,” he said, “but as the facts have emerged over the last few days, it looks like there has been a bit of overreach – there’s no question about that.”



Billionaire Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar, who chairs the Australian Tech Council, circulated an article arguing that the site had made the data accessible, while Canva investor Niki Scevak, reposted a meme declaring that OpenAI “accessed unindexed but publicly available files”. Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar. Oscar Colman Their views dovetailed with those of senior members of the federal opposition who claimed on Sunday that Albanese had overstated the severity of the issue. Opposition defence spokesman James Paterson said Albanese’s motivations were “pretty transparent” in timing the announcement on the same day as OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman’s speech to the United Nations. “Firstly, Medicare wasn’t hacked,” Paterson said on News24, formerly Sky News. “It was a Services Australia statistics portal, and the data that was obtained is prepared solely for the purpose of it being publicly released.



“And secondly, I’m not even sure you can really call it a ‘hack’. If it is a hack, it’s the least sophisticated from a technical point of view. But that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t be treating this as basically a free warning, because the next time this happens it could be much more serious.” Editor's pick Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Bassat agreed, noting that OpenAI could have explained the breach publicly and avoided any politicking. “It’s quite possible that there are no heroes in this story,” he said. OpenAI said in a statement at the weekend that it would pause training its models until “we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place after it disclosed the Australian incident was only one of dozens around the world in which its bots had gone beyond their intended tasks. It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first was in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI start-up Hugging Face, a notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.



Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles rejected the claim that Albanese had exaggerated the threat. “The seriousness doesn’t lie in the information that was obtained. It was the fact that we’ve got an unintended action of an AI agent gaining unauthorised access into an Australian government website. So both of those things are true,” Marles said on News24’s Sunday Agenda. Vaughan Shanks, chief executive of Melbourne cybersecurity company Cydarm, said the OpenAI tool’s decision to download files that were not listed on the website’s visual front end was “mildly naughty”. “That’s called obscurity, not security,” he said. “If they wanted to make it secure, they wouldn’t put it in a public directory.” Archived versions of the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal verified by technology publication Recorded Future News show that until 2025, accessing the address to download data did not require a login. From March that year, the portal did demand a “guest” login, which granted access without any password or username.



It is not clear if the site was intentionally set up in that manner to let researchers access public data or if it was an oversight that allowed the bot to gain access. Related Article OpenAI Five things to understand about how the OpenAI hack unfolded The government has assembled a taskforce including the Cybersecurity Co-ordinator, Office of AI, Australian Signals Directorate and Services Australia to investigate the breach. A Greens-led Senate inquiry has also asked Sam Altman to give evidence this week. Shanks said the bot’s behaviour was akin to a passerby looking over a fence. “Nothing was stolen,” he said. But Toby Walsh, a University of NSW professor of artificial intelligence, said the point was not that the incident was harmful, but that it showed big tech bosses’ warnings that they could lose control of AI systems had come true.



“Their AI has run rogue for weeks at a time,” Walsh said. “They really have no idea of what it is doing.” He said the world was lucky that the tools had not yet proved capable of causing real harm. “We really should be holding companies (and officers of these companies) accountable,” Walsh said. “Then they might pay a bit more attention to preventing these needless hacks.” A Services Australia spokesman said it was investigating the incident and its response to OpenAI’s email. “As the investigation remains ongoing, we cannot provide further information at this stage,” the spokesman said. World.title: Chalmers to announce $6b budget boost as interest rates set to hit 15-year-high
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInterest rates Chalmers to announce $6b budget boost as interest rates set to hit 15-year-high Paul Sakkal September 27, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal a $6 billion budget boost on Monday as he faces internal pressure to curb inflation ahead of the Reserve Bank’s likely decision to raise interest rates to a 15-year-high. The final budget figures are expected to show that the underlying deficit is about $6 billion lower than the $28.3 billion initially forecast at the time of the budget in May. Treasurer Jim Chalmers speaks before the release of the 2026 Intergenerational Report at the Australian National University in Canberra last week. AAP The government did not explain how the better result had come about and whether the revenue had come from the continued strength of the jobs market or commodity prices mostly outside the government’s control. “Responsible economic management is a defining feature of this Albanese Labor government, and you will see that in the final budget outcome,” Chalmers said ahead of the full release of figures.



Labor’s two budget surpluses last term, which have given way to forecasts of a decade of deficits, were generated by what leading budget analyst Chris Richardson has called a commodity-driven $400 billion “revenue rainbow” that represented “a level of luck never before seen in Australia”. The headline deficit, where the government can place big-spending items, is projected to be around $60 billion this year. Last week’s Intergenerational Report indicated that debt and taxes would keep rising over the next four decades if Australia’s productivity malaise continued. The Reserve Bank is widely expected to make its fourth hike of the year on Tuesday, raising the cash rate to 4.6 per cent to address sticky inflation. Markets are pricing in another hike early next year, bringing more pain to households that have experienced a series of economic setbacks since the global financial crisis. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the US’s war with Iran had raised petrol prices and pushed up the cost of production. “We’re also now seeing it in terms of global inflation and that’s being experienced in advanced economies around the world. Most advanced economies have experienced a rate rise in the last month,” he said on News24’s Sunday Agenda.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian economy ‘Getting quite worried’: What Jim Chalmers told Labor MPs uneasy about rate rises and inflation This masthead reported this month that a growing minority of Labor MPs were becoming uneasy about the government’s agenda to raise productivity and counter inflation. Opposition frontbencher James Paterson accused Labor of using global events to shirk responsibility. “The Reserve Bank governor ... has been clear: this is being driven primarily by domestic factors,” he said. “The only thing the government really can control on its own is the amount of money they spend. The RBA and other economists have been clear, the government is spending at stimulus levels, and that is driving up inflation and forcing the RBA’s hand.”



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said last week that Labor had an $83 billion black hole in its budget, but Chalmers has said the Coalition has made a series of unfunded announcements. Chalmers revealed last week that the government would be forced to pay billions more in interest payments on its $1 trillion debt due to the spike in global bond yields. Yields on bonds have surged due to fears about the sustainability of government budgets in the US and Europe, the war in the Middle East and the voracious money-raising efforts of AI firms which are competing with governments for money to fund the race for general artificial intelligence. The Australian Financial Review reported on Saturday that the government would soon spend more on interest repayments than on Medicare.

World.title: Men arrested in major incident at UK air base used by US
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeEmergency services Men arrested in major incident at UK air base used by US Toby Shepheard Updated September 27, 2026 — 11:19pm ,first published 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

British police say five men arrested near a US air base are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. It comes after Army bomb disposal experts were examining a number of vehicles in a “major incident” near an air base used by the US in southwest England. Police said nearby residents were evacuated from their homes. Police at a road block near the RAF Fairford as a major incident unfolds. Alamy Stock Photo A witness said armed police had blocked access to the main gate of the base. Alamy Stock Photo



The British government gave authorisation to the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned in July that any base used in strikes would be a legitimate target. Editor's pick Opinion

UK As three countries move to quit UK, a Brexit reversal might be its only hope George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general A Reuters eyewitness said armed police had blocked access to the main gate of the base, while equipment had been positioned in front of access points and residents of a nearby village were evacuated to a leisure centre. Around 30 emergency vehicles, including police cars, ambulances and fire engines, were stationed in the village of Fairford near the base. “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident. It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act,” Gloucestershire police said in a statement, referring to a village near the air base.



“The Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles.” Police said they believed the incident was now contained. A spokesperson for the US Air Force declined to discuss specific force protection measures. “The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families.”



Britain said in July its armed forces were ​ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned the UK not to allow US bombers to ‌fly from Fairford. British ministers have also briefed providers of critical infrastructure on the threat posed by Russia, with the government increasingly concerned about possible sabotage operations and cyberattacks. Russia denies mounting hybrid attacks on Western nations. Reuters

World.title: We can get control back: take AI owners to court
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters We can get control back: take AI owners to court September 27, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE t The claim by the owners of OpenAI that the break-ins of various public and private databases by their Large-Language-Model AI computer programs are due to ″⁣autonomous rogue agents‴⁣⁣ is fatuous (″⁣Senate probe demands answers from OpenAI boss″⁣, 27/9). The designers of these complex computer systems, themselves, are to blame. When a system with unrestricted/unsupervised feedback is let loose, disaster is a distinct possibility.

We are all familiar with feedback: for example, in mechanical systems, negative feedback is used by a regulator to maintain constant speed of an engine – a device that has been used successfully since the early industrial revolution. We all know how positive feedback can lead to exponential growth with catastrophic outcomes, for example, audio-feedback in microphone-loudspeaker systems will lead to unbearable ‘screeching’.

AI computer programs rely on ongoing/unrestricted feedback through minimising and maximising algorithms to seek ‘optimum solutions’. Until programmers build in restraints to these routines, the programs will continue to break out of their accepted boundaries in cyberspace into regions beyond their legal jurisdiction.

The solution is to seek legal redress via the courts. Only after the principals of AI companies have been successfully prosecuted will we collectively be able to take control of AI, and what has the promise of being a powerful adjunct to the technical and scientific advance of humankind.

James Reiss, Abbotsford



AI is just getting started

Re ″⁣Albanese wants answers after AI medicare hack″⁣ and ″⁣Breach by Open AI shows nation more exposed than ever″⁣ (25/9), the problems of controlling AI agents seem to have brought out politicians’ naive faith in the ability of human oversight to stop AI hacks and security breaches.

The Hugging Face incident showed that AI agents are built to be extremely persistent in the face of apparently unsolvable problems. They also work much more efficiently together in ″⁣swarms″⁣, helping each other solve problems. Twelve-hundred of them worked together to hack Hugging Face.

They figured out a shortcut to generate fake success in their sandbox task. Then they anticipated an overseer who might catch them faking, so they disguised their tools and manipulated their result reports to convince the non-existent overseer that they had legitimately solved it.

These are early days of AI agent development when they are not yet smarter than humans. How do we think we will go when they are?

Julia Thornton, Surrey Hills AI not worth enormous investment needed

Solar panels last 20 years. Wind turbines last even longer (unless you read the Institute for Energy Research, which is an American global warming-denying fossil fuel lobby group).

The computer chips in data centres/AI last only about five years. The enormous ‘investments’ in data centres have to be paid back quickly, and there won’t be infrastructure remaining unless similar ‘investments’ are made (″⁣We can’t afford to miss AI wave″⁣, 26/9).

Data centres/AI consume enormous amounts of energy and water. I’ve yet to see a convincing business case for the trillions of dollars spent on it, with revenues optimistically in the billions. Data centres/AI are likely to bankrupt and, even worse, ruin the world, unlike renewables.

Wayne Robinson, Kingsley, WA Good luck bringing tech bros to account

Given the lack of success authorities have had against Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk for the ills their platforms cause, good luck trying to get accountability from OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill THE FORUM Complaints department

The article, “3500 complaints, not one case” (27/9), should prompt a serious rethink of how Victoria regulates owners corporations. A system that receives thousands of complaints but produces no enforcement cases is not providing owners with an effective remedy.

Victoria needs a dedicated, independent Owners Corporation Commission with real investigative, enforcement and adjudicative powers. It could be funded through a small annual levy on each owners corporation lot, providing a sustainable funding base for specialist investigators, conciliators and adjudicators.

The commission should be able to investigate complaints, compel records, issue compliance notices, impose meaningful and enforceable penalties, and make binding determinations. It should also have authority to adjudicate disputes up to a prescribed monetary threshold, with more complex or higher-value matters proceeding to VCAT or the courts as appropriate.

Owners corporation legislation is of limited value if compliance depends on an individual owner having the time, resources and determination to pursue proceedings personally.

With a growing number of Victorians living under owners corporation governance, a modest levy would be a small price to pay for a system that can actually investigate complaints, enforce the law and provide accessible adjudications.

Susan Martin, Rosanna



Negligence habit

Your article, “3500 complaints, not one case” (27/9), bears testimony to what apartment owners have had to endure by way of defective workmanship. VCAT was useless, building surveyors were abolished from councils, and sign-offs for Certification of Occupancy were done without due process. More cases of government negligence.

Ian Anderson, Surrey Hills Out of PM’s hands

James Massola’s article, “The PM once criticised his rivals for abusing this power. Just look at him now” (25/9), calls for the prime minister to clean up the Members of Parliament (Staff) Bill (1984). Given that the prime minister is the specific person whose “weaponisation of the MOPS provisions” and who is “gaming the system”, what chance that he will change the system at all to reflect fairness and integrity in the way it operates?

Massola’s article reveals the staggering cost of government advisers to taxpayers, of between $77,000 and $317,000 per adviser, a year. Isn’t it a matter of urgency that the allocation and remuneration of these advisers be determined objectively rather than left in the hands of a biased party individual?

Cecile Campbell, Brighton East Liberal issues

Your correspondent (Letters, 27/9) rightly draws attention to “the absurdity of the Coalition on the climate crisis”. Malcolm Turnbull tried to bring some reason during the 2010s but was blocked by the climate change denying conservatives.

The Coalition should remind itself of the best prime minister that it never had: John Hewson.

If it continues on its present path, the Coalition is open to be submerged/drowned by One Nation. Hewson has left the Liberal Party but may be open to provide some facts on how to deal with this “climate crisis″⁣.

Rod Watson, East Brighton Learning from history

In the early morning of October 1, 1965, a group of relatively junior Indonesian military officers kidnapped and murdered a number of senior military commanders. The group said it did so to protect the then-Indonesian president, Sukarno, from an imminent right-wing coup.

Whatever its motivation, the group was quickly captured and suppressed by the then-major general Suharto.

Suharto and his followers were able to lay the responsibility for this at the feet of the Indonesian Communist Party (PKI).

Within weeks, hundreds, then thousands of PKI members, supporters and so-called fellow travellers were massacred across the archipelago.

Very little of this news penetrated our media. As a student at Monash University in early 1966, l was told by Indonesian students that they had witnessed hundreds of headless bodies floating down rivers.

The calculation of numbers killed vary from 500,000 to more than 1 million. The role of the US, British and Australian governments is not precisely known even today, but it is certain the CIA provided arms to the Indonesian military.

Then-prime minister Harold Holt is said to have expressed his appreciation at the number of communists ″⁣knocked off″⁣. It is reported that Gough Whitlam said the extermination of the PKI had saved Australia millions of dollars in defence expenditure. So while it is true that our political elite saw this human catastrophe as in our geopolitical interests, we should reflect on the enormity of this little-known event.

Robert Bluer, Ivanhoe Naming rights

Trump Tower, Trump Kennedy Centre, now Trump Strait ... Just waiting for Trump to rename Earth as Planet Trump – or maybe rename the sun after himself, since he thinks everything revolves around him. Both? Would that suit his overweening ego? Robyn Westwood,

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights



Monitor media diet

In his novel, Love, etc., British author Julian Barnes has a character who muses on the cumulative harm from relationships with others, using pesticide levels as an analogy.

ADI is ″⁣acceptable daily intake″⁣: how much pesticide we can absorb without it doing us harm. MRL is ″⁣maximum residue limit″⁣: the amount of pesticide allowed by law in food.

I feel the same way about today’s media, of all kinds. Every day the bad and nasty ADI outweighs the good, and the bad is endlessly regurgitated to the point where the MRL is frequently exceeded.

As someone who has grown up without the media tsunami that engulfs us daily, my ADI is tolerably low, but constantly under threat.

But what of our children? Because when it comes to absorbing poisons, kids are

more susceptible and vulnerable than adults.

Is this what is driving teen crime, disengagement, and mental illness? They don’t get time to detox from the cumulative effect of all the nastiness? Food for thought.

Stephen Farrelly, Donvale Bright side

Every day, we see media coverage of how awful things are in Victoria. Yet, in the most recent Economist City Liveability Index (May 2026), Melbourne is ranked the third most liveable city in the world. It comes behind Copenhagen and Vienna but in front of Sydney, Zurich and Geneva.

We may have problems with our government, local councils and potholes (might need to do better about big trucks and vehicles tearing them up rather than sending convicts out to fill the holes) but we are doing a lot better than more than 100 others in The Economist’s list.

We should not forget – whatever our politicians say – that we have reasons for celebration as well as reasons for frustration.

Noel Turnbull, Port Melbourne Happy families

Matt Wade’s article on happy relationships (″⁣What 24 years of data reveals about the secrets of a long, happy relationship″⁣, 26/9) is all about situational aspects of relationships.

There is another side and that is the personal. After being married twice for a total of 46 years, I can definitely say that to be happy with each other, two people need to put the other person first – all the time. That way, each person can get most of what they want, and it doesn’t get any better than that.

Each person feels treated fairly and happiness results. If one person gets their way most or all of the time, they will become selfish and greedy, and that will destroy any relationship.

Don Jordan, Mt Waverley How’s the sobriety?

Many of us enjoyed a drink or two during the footy grand final on Saturday; it’s part of our celebration culture. Nick Galvin reminds us what happens when drinking is no longer fun and just how much better he felt once he sobered up (″⁣The big fat boozy lie that’s taken me 40 years to unpack″⁣, 27/9).

Not only is excess alcohol bad for our health, it can be very bad for the people around us. Violence at home peaks with major sporting events. Just like the gambling lobby, the alcohol industry has a huge influence of on sport.

With the spring racing carnival soon to be under way, now is a good time to be sober.

Jenny Kashyap, Bentleigh Dog behaviour

Regarding your correspondent’s letter, ″⁣It’s not perfect″⁣ ( 26/9), I can think of worse things than going into a hotel with dogs around me, such as humans who consume far too much alcohol.

Susan Munday, Bentleigh East



Family violence

I cannot take my eyes off Megan Herbert’s chilling cartoon (Letters, 26/9). What a sad, sad world when family violence increases because some blokes cannot abide a loss and take it out on their partners and children.

Is their insecurity so great that a team loss becomes personal? It’s so difficult to understand how this results in violence but it’s the reality for far too many.

Ann Maginness, Beaumaris Could’ve been champions

AFL great Leigh Matthews once said a team has a good chance of winning as long as there are as many minutes left as goals required. It might only happen once in an AFL season, but Saturday’s grand final was

the ″⁣once″⁣.

Whoever pressed that ″⁣Wharfie Time″⁣ button will rue the day.

David Legat, South Morang AND ANOTHER THING AFL grand final

I just saw defeat snatched from the jaws of victory.

Ann Young, Chirnside Park Will ″⁣Wharfie Time″⁣ be permanently retired? Such a raging success. Four goals to zip. Oops.

Ken Richards, Elwood



At least, this game was not decided by a fluorescent shirt.

Michael McKenna, Warragul Acknowledging LBJ, can Chris Fagan coach and chew gum at the same time? Looks like he can! Andrew Neeson,

West Launceston, Tas Regardless of which grand final team was actually inspired by “Wharfie Time”, I can’t believe that the AFL allows any team to disrupt games with loud partisan noise and visual distraction.

David Johnston, Healesville Great effort, Dockers. Perhaps bringing The Fremantle Doctor with the team might have made the difference late in the day.

Ron Stone, Kangaroo Flat Furthermore

After reading the rantings of Exclusive Brethren leader and “Elect Vessel″⁣ Bruce Hales, I’m thinking that the vessel is empty.

John Bye, Elwood



Bruce Hales, leader of the Exclusive Brethren: time traveller from the Middle Ages?

Ruja Varon, Malvern Lucky OpenAI. They got through to Medicare.

World.title: ‘Obscurity not security’: Government accused of overreach in Medicare ‘hack’ response
World.content:
Cybersecurity experts and tech investors have accused the Albanese government of blowing the Medicare statistics breach out of proportion, arguing that the website’s code was set up to send data to anyone with the skills to request it. Archived versions of the website show that its code directed savvy users to a digital address where they could download the statistical information it stored despite that data not being publicly available to people via its front end. An OpenAI tool received information from Medicare that was not promoted as being available for download. Marija Ercegovac Seek co-founder Paul Bassat, one of the country’s most prominent technology investors, echoed questions from prominent industry colleagues about Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s claim last week that “an AI agent has infiltrated an Australian government website”. “The government clearly wanted to get onto the front foot to seize the initiative in relation to how AI is regulated,” he said, “but as the facts have emerged over the last few days, it looks like there has been a bit of overreach – there’s no question about that.”



Billionaire Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar, who chairs the Australian Tech Council, circulated an article arguing that the site had made the data accessible, while Canva investor Niki Scevak, reposted a meme declaring that OpenAI “accessed unindexed but publicly available files”. Atlassian co-founder Scott Farquhar. Oscar Colman Their views dovetailed with those of senior members of the federal opposition who claimed on Sunday that Albanese had overstated the severity of the issue. Opposition defence spokesman James Paterson said Albanese’s motivations were “pretty transparent” in timing the announcement on the same day as OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman’s speech to the United Nations. “Firstly, Medicare wasn’t hacked,” Paterson said on News24, formerly Sky News. “It was a Services Australia statistics portal, and the data that was obtained is prepared solely for the purpose of it being publicly released.



“And secondly, I’m not even sure you can really call it a ‘hack’. If it is a hack, it’s the least sophisticated from a technical point of view. But that doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t be treating this as basically a free warning, because the next time this happens it could be much more serious.” Editor's pick Opinion

AI Did AI really ‘go rogue’? Not exactly, but we have plenty to fear Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Bassat agreed, noting that OpenAI could have explained the breach publicly and avoided any politicking. “It’s quite possible that there are no heroes in this story,” he said. OpenAI said in a statement at the weekend that it would pause training its models until “we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place after it disclosed the Australian incident was only one of dozens around the world in which its bots had gone beyond their intended tasks. It is the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted development of its models. The first was in July after disclosure of a cyberattack targeting AI start-up Hugging Face, a notorious incident that raised fears the industry was losing control.



Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles rejected the claim that Albanese had exaggerated the threat. “The seriousness doesn’t lie in the information that was obtained. It was the fact that we’ve got an unintended action of an AI agent gaining unauthorised access into an Australian government website. So both of those things are true,” Marles said on News24’s Sunday Agenda. Vaughan Shanks, chief executive of Melbourne cybersecurity company Cydarm, said the OpenAI tool’s decision to download files that were not listed on the website’s visual front end was “mildly naughty”. “That’s called obscurity, not security,” he said. “If they wanted to make it secure, they wouldn’t put it in a public directory.” Archived versions of the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal verified by technology publication Recorded Future News show that until 2025, accessing the address to download data did not require a login. From March that year, the portal did demand a “guest” login, which granted access without any password or username.



It is not clear if the site was intentionally set up in that manner to let researchers access public data or if it was an oversight that allowed the bot to gain access. Related Article OpenAI Five things to understand about how the OpenAI hack unfolded The government has assembled a taskforce including the Cybersecurity Co-ordinator, Office of AI, Australian Signals Directorate and Services Australia to investigate the breach. A Greens-led Senate inquiry has also asked Sam Altman to give evidence this week. Shanks said the bot’s behaviour was akin to a passerby looking over a fence. “Nothing was stolen,” he said. But Toby Walsh, a University of NSW professor of artificial intelligence, said the point was not that the incident was harmful, but that it showed big tech bosses’ warnings that they could lose control of AI systems had come true.



“Their AI has run rogue for weeks at a time,” Walsh said. “They really have no idea of what it is doing.” He said the world was lucky that the tools had not yet proved capable of causing real harm. “We really should be holding companies (and officers of these companies) accountable,” Walsh said. “Then they might pay a bit more attention to preventing these needless hacks.” A Services Australia spokesman said it was investigating the incident and its response to OpenAI’s email. “As the investigation remains ongoing, we cannot provide further information at this stage,” the spokesman said. World.title: Warriors-taming Newcastle Knights continue miracle playoff run to NRL grand final
World.content:
Seven days after eliminating NZ Warriors from NRL championship contention, Newcastle Knights have booked a spot in the grand final, with a chance to create history against Sydney Roosters next week.

The underdogs - who finished with the competition wooden spoon last season - have overcome regular season premiers Penrith Panthers 22-14 at Sydney's Accor Stadium.

They had to play most of the game shorthanded, after Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary suffered a horror leg injury just before halftime and Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland was sent off for his hipdrop challenge.

Cleary spent the entire week battling a rumoured broken foot and started the contest on the bench, as coach and dad Ivan Cleary adopted a conservative approach to his involvement.

After 25 minutes, Cleary junior entered the game, but lasted just 10 minutes, before he was lowered in Crossland's crude tackle.

Cleary was stretchered from the field with a suspected compound ankle fracture and Crossland was banished, leaving his team shorthanded for the remainder of the game and jeopardising his NZ Kiwis involvement at the upcoming Rugby League World Cup.

The injury will likely rule Cleary out of World Cup contention too.

Penrith started the game with Jack Cogger and Jack Cole in the halves, and Cogger was tackled heavily putting up his first two kicks of the game. The first was cleared of any offence, but the second drew a penalty near the posts, which makeshift goalkicker Dylan Edwards hooked wide.

Newcastle scored first, when centre Bradman Best - as he did against the Warriors last week - broke from deep inside his own half and found second-rower Francis Manuleleua backing up for the try.

The Panthers answered, when centre Blaize Talagi chased a pinpoint kick from Cogger behind the tryline to touch down and level the scores.

Edwards had a try rubbed out for obstruction in the build-up and soon afterwards, Cleary was brought down in the fateful tackle and carried off the pitch, straight into a waiting ambulance.

Talagi kicked the resulting penalty to put the Panthers ahead and ponlookers were still in shock, when forward Lindsay Smith capitalised on the numerical advantage to score and put his team ahead 14-6 at the break.

Newcastle were no strangers to playing with just 12 men. Last month, they lost prop Jacob Saifiti early for a dangerous tackle against the Warriors in a 46-32 defeat at Mt Smart.

They struck first after the break, when centre Dane Gagai and wing Dom Young broke down the right sideline, with Young grounding inside the corner flag.

Penrith endured a couple of brain explosions from wing Thomas Jenkins - a miscued attacking kick on the first tackle and a dropped kick return near his own goal-line - but Knights half Sandon Smith took a quick tap from a penalty in his half and, with Panthers backs turned, raced 60 metres through the defence to score untouched for the lead.

Talagi was also helped to the sideline with an Achilles tendon injury, causing a reshuffled of the Penrith backline.

Kiwis centre Casey McLean was held up centimetres short of the tryline for the Panthers, but as they piled on pressure, Cogger spilt the ball and Newcastle survived.

In the dying seconds, they had another shot at victory, throwing the ball around on the last tackle, but Smith popped up for the intercept and ran the length of the field to seal an improbable Knights win.

No team have ever improved from last on the table to NRL champions in one season, but under new coach Justin Holbrook, Newcastle have now matched the 2010 Roosters, who traded their wooden spoon for a spot in the grand final, where they lost to St George Illawarra Dragons.

World.title: 'A lot more activity' - significant rise in people trafficking investigations
World.content:
The Government has pointed to a lack of resources and blurred roles hampering its battle against human trafficking.

It has launched a five-year action plan, saying horticulture, beauty services, construction and hospitality are problems areas.

Associate Immigration Minister Casey Costello, whose previous work included fighting migrant exploitation, said there had been a significant recent increase in people trafficking investigations.

"Trafficking is a difficult prosecution because it was always relating to bringing across the border, and it really didn't recognise that we have domestic trafficking as well, and that was where the differential needs to be looked at, and that's why fit for purpose legislation is so critically important. But yes, there has been a lot more activity, and I think there's a lot more we can do."

Thirteen people were granted victims of people trafficking work visas last year.

Trafficking involves coercion, deception or abuse of power to use people for forced labour or criminality, servitude, slavery or prostitution.

Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) identified several deficiencies in the cross-government trafficking response, including fragmented reporting pathways, unclear agency roles and data-sharing barriers

Variation existed between agencies in the identification of potential victims, and in their frontline capability, with "constrained investigative capacity" and limited public awareness.

Police, Immigration New Zealand compliance, the Labour Inspectorate and Internal Affairs could be involved in cross-border work, and the ministries of education, justice and children among other departments whose staff dealt with trafficking issues

The action plan's first steps were mapping the existing trafficking systems, and creating a governance framework.

As an interim measure, it would create a process for trafficking victims to access support.

In phase two, it would coordinate training and strengthen partnerships with Pacific countries to prevent child trafficking.

Citizens Advice Bureau wants an independent anti-slavery commissioner, saying volunteers were "genuinely horrified and shocked" when they discovered there was no support or protection for people in exploitative situations.

World.title: 'It made me so angry': Hipkins targets cost of living at Labour campaign launch
World.content:
Chris Hipkins is promising "plenty more fire" this election, as Labour promises to cut student debt if elected.

About 600 Labour supporters, volunteers and candidates packed into the Due Drop Events Centre in South Auckland for the party's election campaign launch.

The Pacific Youth Choir set the tone early, belting out classics like Mt Raskil Preservation Society's 'Bathe in the River' and Stan Walker's 'Aotearoa'.

Hipkins took to the stage in front of cheering supporters and immediately honed in on the cost of living as his focus for the election.

"Is there anyone Christopher Luxon hasn't talked down to?" he asked supporters.

"You can choose a prime minister who will fight to get your costs down or a prime minister whose response to rising prices was 'cry me a river'.

"Have you ever heard anything so out of touch?

"It made me so angry… it still does."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686469112

Hipkins also took aim at National - who had their own conference a couple hours earlier - for "bullshit" claims about Labour's tax policy.

"Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living. He's had three years. He's failed.

"And ask yourself this - after three years of National, are you better off?" he said.

Hipkins said the election would be about the cost-of-living, making his pitch to parents, tradies, and small business owners: "This is middle New Zealand," he said.

"They get up, go to work, look after their families and do their best and right now, far too many of them are working harder than ever and still going backwards.

"I won't accept that as the future of New Zealand."

Hipkins announced Labour would write off 10 percent of eligible student loan balances, applying to current and future graduates who are New Zealand-based for tax purposes , did not benefit from the fees free scheme and still had a loan to pay back.

Loans of $2000 or less would be completely written off and the policy would cost $583.4 million over five years.

Speaking to media after the launch, Hipkins said his team was "fired up" for the election.

"We're out on the doorsteps every day at the moment, we're going to be fighting hard to win this election."

He said the party's student loan policy would give young people "more of a reason" to stay in New Zealand, rather than going abroad.

"We're seeing far too many New Zealanders giving up on this country. I want to give them more of a reason to stay."

He said National were telling "outright lies" about Labour's tax plans and he "calling them out on it".

"Christopher Luxon seems to stand for blame, excuses, slogans, no real answers, and New Zealand going backwards.

"At least I know that my whole team 100 percent backs me. He can't make the same claim, can he?" he said.

Asked how the upcoming election would be different to the 2023 election - where Labour lost much of the "red wave" vote they secured in 2020 - Hipkins accused media of "listening to National Party spin bullshit".

"I'd encourage you not to." he said.

Asked again, Hipkins said people would see "plenty more fire" over the election.

Chris Hipkins shakes hands with former Prime Minister Helen Clark during the Labour Party campaign launch at the Due Drop Centre in Manukau, Auckland, on 27 September 2026. Jo Moir / RNZ

The student loan announcement was met with cheers, as Hipkins declared "neo-liberal, trickledown economics does not work".

Responding to claims from the National Party about Labour, Hipkins was blunt: "It's bullshit."

"People aren't asking the prime minister to feel sorry for them. They're asking him to do his bloody job."

He also touched on Labour policies regarding supermarkets, public transport fare caps and free GP visits, before wrapping up his speech before a cheering crowd.

"You are how we win this," Hipkins told candidates and volunteers.

World.title: 'The job isn't done': Luxon launches National's election campaign in Auckland
World.content:
National's Auckland campaign launch has featured a significant focus on Labour, another pledge card rather than any new policy, and conspicuously empty seats.

At the International Convention Centre in Auckland, the event pitched to party faithful ran about half an hour behind schedule.

Large sections were roped off many of the seats in the back remained empty, a rough headcount putting number about 750 people - a surprise given parties typically pack such events to ensure a crowded, popular atmosphere for the evening news.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686469112

Leader Christopher Luxon launched a signed pledge card distributed after his speech making 10 promises:

Economic growth that delivers new jobs and higher wages

No new taxes so you keep more of what you earn

Compulsory KiwiSaver with higher contributions and a $1500 Baby Boost

Paid Parental Leave extension from 26 to 30 weeks

Better school results by replacing NCEA, regular assessment and teaching the basics brilliantly

Tougher consequences for criminals and more Police patrols

Faster healthcare and more medicines on top of 33 new cancer medicines already delivered

Better infrastructure with Roads of National Significance, new classrooms and new and upgraded hospitals

A better deal at the supermarket by driving competition

Books in surplus so we don't saddle our kids with new debt or more taxes.

The card was a follow-up to the eight-promise 2023 version launched to more than 1000 people at the Due Drop Centre in Manukau, where Labour would launch its own 2026 campaign just hours later.

The '23 edition included lower inflation and economic growth, tax cuts, infrastructure, law and order restored, higher school achievement, shorter health waiting times, support for seniors and "deliver Net Zero Carbon by 2050".

Entering to a standing ovation, Luxon gave the standard party plaudits before talking about his past, choking up when speaking about his mother.

"She went to university the same year I did... she taught me to walk across the room, find someone different from myself, and seek to understand before I'm understood."

But soon he was speaking about the elephant in the room: Labour.

"Labour lost the plot, and they borrowed more, and they taxed more, and they spent more, and through it all, they lost sight of what really matters: your business, your community, your family, and your safety."

He had taken the stage following a flashy television advert beginning with quotes from former Labour PM Jacinda Ardern against a backdrop of police sirens, and current leader Chris Hipkins over sad piano music.

That contrasted with a humanising pastiche of Luxon talking about letters sent by children, "Kiwi mums and dads", the "squeezed middle", tax relief and the party's already-announced election policies.

"National is the party of delivery, but friends, the job isn't done."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686899112

Earlier speeches all devoted significant time to attacking Labour and other left-leaning parties.

Campaign chair Simeon Brown spent four minutes on thanks and greetings, four-and-a-half minutes talking about Labour and Chris Hipkins, and 60 seconds in call-and-response for "no new taxes" and "party vote National".

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis also spent about as much time talking about Labour as everything else, taking less than two minutes to switch from talking up farmers, mums and dads to lambasting the "mess left to us by Labour and its mates".

"The last thing this country needs is nine new taxes."

The party's most popular leader in the modern era - Sir John Key - remains a prominent figure at National Party events and his speech highlighted the desire to see Luxon re-elected "unequivocally".

"We're here for one simple reason: to extend Chris Hipkins, Labour, and their band of lefty fellow travellers time in opposition, because even if we all had the net worth of Elon Musk, we can't afford those policies."

He also warned specifically against strategic voting.

"Don't try and do something that you think is clever or try some form of so-called strategic voting ... that is the opposite of clever."

Speaking to reporters later, Luxon was adamant National had more policy to unveil, and pushed back on multiple questions about the heavy focus on Labour.

"I'm really focused on making sure I make the choice really clear to all New Zealanders, and we have a positive plan. You know, we have a plan, not just a slogan; we have been executing our plan of fix the basics, build the future the last three years.

World.title: One dead after two-car crash on Massey road
World.content:
One person is dead after a serious two-car crash on Red Hills Road in Massey, Auckland.

Police were called to the crash about 11.30am Sunday.

One person died at the scene.

One other person was seriously hurt and taken to hospital. Four people suffered minor injuries.

World.title: Tornado smashes car windows, cuts woman's arm on Kapiti Coast
World.content:
A woman was cut by flying glass when an apparent tornado smashed through her car's rear window, sending stones and debris hurtling across a Kapiti Coast car park as witnesses scrambled for cover.

Mandy Butler was with her partner in the Paraparaumu car park when the tornado tore through at about 1pm, forcing them to duck for cover inside their car.

She said the tornado ripped through the area for about 10 seconds, pelting cars and people with debris.

She was cut on the arm by glass from her smashed rear window.

"[It] was so scary," she said.

The wind was so strong, said Butler, that she expected the damage to be worse.

Butler and her partner managed to cover the broken window with tarpaulins and duct tape before driving back to Wellington.

They made it home safely despite having to make the journey without a rear window, she said.

A local restaurateur who also witnessed the tornado said he saw seagulls being whipped around by the wind.

The car park was left strewn with debris and damaged vehicles.

World.title: More rain, snow forecast as severe weather system moves north
World.content:
Heavy rain has caused problems in Christchurch and Otago this afternoon.

Vehicles have had to drive around large pockets of surface flooding on State Highway 73 in the westbound lanes.

There has also been flooding on State Highway Six near Gibston in Central Otago.

State Highway Seven remains closed between Springs Junction and the turnoff to Hanmer Springs due to heavy snow.

The sections of State Highway 73, from Otira to Arthur's Pass, and Springfield to Castle Hill, are closed to towing vehicles and snow chains are required.

Snow ploughs have freed around 10 vehicles that became stuck in snow near Lake Pukaki in the Mackenzie Basin this morning.

The NZ Transport Agency said a truck and trailer unit became stranded on State Highway 8 near the intersection with Hayman Road causing the vehicles behind it to also get stuck.

Roading crews arrived and managed to clear snow from the road to allow the cars through, but the truck had to be towed.

Motorist Kyle Dinz said he was stuck near Lake Pukaki due to heavy snowfall while travelling on SH8 on Sunday 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

Kyle Dinz said he was caught in standstill traffic near Lake Pūkaki, behind several heavy trucks stuck on the road.

He eventually made it to Lake Tekapo, where he said the snow was even heavier.

Heavy snow blankets vehicles near Lake Tekapo on 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

NZTA also closed a section of road between Springfield and Castle Hill, including Porters Pass, to towing vehicles and advised drivers to use snow chains.

A driver told RNZ their car slid while crossing Porters Pass at about 9.30am because of the snow, forcing them to turn back.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405684778112

Orange warnings remain in place for heavy rain in the Tararua Range, heavy snow in Canterbury and severe winds across parts of the lower North Island.

The Tararua Range was expected to receive peak rainfall rates of 15 to 20mm an hour from late this morning.

MetService said streams and rivers could rise rapidly, with surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions possible.

In the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills south of Arthur's Pass, another 5 to 10cm of snow was expected to settle above 400 metres, with lesser amounts down to about 200 metres.

A severe weather system moving north over the country is bringing further heavy rain, snow and severe gales across central New Zealand on 27 September 2026. Screenshot / MetService

The snow was expected to ease from the south in the afternoon.

Severe west to northwest winds gusting up to 120km/h are forecast in exposed parts of Wairarapa, the Tararua District and Hawke's Bay south of Hastings.

Earlier today, the NZ Transport Agency said roading crews were helping vehicles stuck on SH8 near Lake Pūkaki because of heavy snow.

Snow falls on Porters Pass on Sunday morning, 27 September 2026. Supplied / Tracey Hunter

The Desert Road (SH1) is also under a snowfall warning from 7pm Sunday until 1am on Monday.

Several watches are in place across the country.

A Heavy Snow Watch remains in place for the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills about and north of Arthur's Pass, with rain expected to turn to snow above 200m and heavy snowfall possible above 400m.

Strong Wind Watches are in place for parts of Hawke's Bay, Horowhenua, the Kāpiti Coast, the Marlborough Sounds and the Chatham Islands.

The Heavy Snow Watch for Central Otago, the Queenstown Lakes District, inland Clutha and Southland north of Lumsden has been lifted after the threat of warning-level snowfall passed.

World.title: Wallaroos 'got some work to do' despite snapping losing streak
World.content:
Snapping a six-match losing streak was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

The Wallaroos were outplayed in the first half, with Scotland entering the break with a 10-5 lead in the WXV Global Series Test.

But following a blunt half-time address from their coaching staff and with the wind behind them in the second term, the Wallaroos regrouped to score 25 unanswered points and secure their first victory since March.

Desiree Miller provided the only points for the Wallaroos in the first half with a try.

Samantha Wood, Brianna Hoy and player-of-the-match Faitala Moleka crossed the stripe in the second half.

The three second-half tries were scored during seven minutes, with Hoy and Moleka's efforts coming while Scotland was reduced to 14 players following Evie Gallagher's yellow card.

Wood added two conversions and as many penalty goals to finish with a 15-point haul.

"Credit to Scotland, they found opportunities, and you could see where they exploited those areas," Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said after the match.

"Overall, we know we have a lot of things to improve on, but we'll take the positives out of that."

Palu Sekona said the Wallaroos were taught some harsh lessons in the previous week's 29-26 loss to France in Aix-en-Provence.

The Wallaroos had led 19-0 during the match, while France had only 11 players on the field at one stage due to red and yellow cards.

"We learned from last week's game," Palu Sekona said.

"We have to be relentless. When you get opportunities like that [Gallagher's yellow card], you've got to capitalise."

The Wallaroos celebrate Desiree Miller's (right) first-half try. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh is essentially the Wallaroos' caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year.

Walsh was unimpressed with the Wallaroos' display in the opening half, admitting he did not hide his feelings when he spoke to the players at the break.

"It wasn't a pleasant message," Walsh said.

"I thought if we didn't have two or three individuals that really took the game to Scotland, I reckon it would have been a draw, or we would have lost.

"So I wasn't happy with our performance. Glad we got the win and came home with it, but the advantage was the wind and a few key players who I thought had tremendous games."

The Wallaroos are heading back to Australia, with two WXV Global Series Tests against Scotland coming up next month.

They play each other in Sydney on October 17, ahead of the Wallabies' Bledisloe Cup clash against the All Blacks.

The final Test will be staged in Canberra on October 23.

As far as Walsh is concerned, the Wallaroos will not be taking the easy route on the training paddock over the next three weeks.

"We've got some work to do," he said.

World.title: Broncos into fifth NRLW grand final after toppling Titans
World.content:
Defending premier Brisbane is through to another NRLW grand final showdown with the Sydney Roosters after ending the dream run of Gold Coast in the preliminary final.

The Broncos won 20-8 away at Robina to secure their fifth win in a row to qualify for their fifth grand final. They have won all four that they have contested.

The showdown next Sunday will be Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw's final match before retiring.

Last year the Broncos beat the Roosters 22-18.

The Broncos romped to a 20-4 lead in a four-try opening half on Sunday where they dominated in every area.

Titans lock Sienna Lofipo was ruled out of the match with a suspected broken jaw late in the half in a huge blow.

The big game experience of in-form Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel came to the fore as the hosts wilted under the pressure.

Upton, from full-back, was too elusive and strong to score the opening try when she beat three Titans with a step and a surge.

The discipline of the hosts, who had won their previous 10 matches in a row, let them down early with three penalties and they paid the price.

Half-back Southwell turned second-rower Romy Teitzel back on the inside and she raced through a giant hole.

A stunning cutout pass by Titans second-rower and standout player Evania Isa'ako close to the line got the hosts on the board with winger Destiny Mino-Sinapati diving over in the corner.

Gold Coast's numbering in defence inside their quarter line was all at sea in the first half and it was too easy for Upton to put back-rower Lauren Dam over.

Sienna Lofipo copped a nasty blow to the jaw. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Teitzel turned creator and powerhouse winger Julia Robinson, who had a blinder, was on the end of it and the Titans were on the rack.

Isa'ako collected her own ricocheted grubber kick to give the Titans a sniff after the break but Brisbane's defence on its line was too good.

Titans full-back Lily Patston also had an early finish when she went off with a category one HIA in the second half.

The Titans had a great season under coach Karyn Murphy but will be disappointed after failing to hit their straps in the biggest game of the season.

World.title: Twelve-man Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break
World.content:
The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic broken leg at Stadium Australia.

Cleary was taken to hospital in an ambulance, in agony after going down in the tackle of Phoenix Crossland and Francis Manuleleua late in the first half.

Crossland was sent off for his hip drop tackle on the star halfback, forcing the unfancied Knights to play the entirety of the second half a man down.

Newcastle scored three tries after the break to produce the shock, with Sandon Smith catching the Panthers unaware and racing through to score in a bizarre passage of play before settling the game with a late breakaway try.

The stunning victory booked the Knights' ticket to the grand final next Sunday, when they will face the Sydney Roosters.

The Knights will be chasing their first men's premiership since 2001, while the women's team won back-to-back crowns in 2022 and 2023.

This year's NRLW grand final will be a rematch of the 2025 decider after the Broncos beat the Titans 20-8 to set up another showdown with the Roosters.
