World.title: How the Lions claimed their moments to overcome a dominant Freo
World.content:
The footy season is a marathon, not a sprint.

Each game goes for about three hours, a long amount of time in our increasingly attention starved society. Multiply that by the 218 games over several months and the time starts to add up.

Especially if you are in one of the highest profile jobs in footy.

"The level of intensity that's required to be a senior coach, because it is a lifestyle, it never leaves you alone," premiership winning coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

"It's 365 days a year, seven days a week. It's just always in your head. You're always thinking about the club and what's next."

In the era of short form video and instant takes, being involved in football nearly forces you to do the opposite.

You don't scroll through football games, you absorb them.

But football games, especially important ones, aren't one continuous event. They are made up of a series of moments and contests that separate the winner from the loser.

The bigger the stakes, the more important those discrete moments are. It's also something that newly minted three-time premiership coach Fagan has previously attested to.

"Finals come down to moments," Fagan told afl.com.au in 2020.

It was a theme he has repeatedly come back to, year after year. Win enough of those moments at the right time and you might just win the premiership. It's a formula that the Lions have ridden to their spot as maybe the most successful side of the modern era.

The importance of moments is something that wasn't lost on his opposite number coming into the finals.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained earlier in September.

Those moments also turned the 2026 grand final into one of the greatest in recent history. It was in those moments that the two-time champion Lions became three-time champions.

By winning enough moments at the right time Brisbane was able to overcome the biggest lead in time-on in a final since at least 2001.

Much of the 2026 grand final played out the way that the 2026 season had progressed, with Fremantle in control. On paper, Fremantle not just dominated proceedings but played in a way that took away Brisbane's strengths.

"Fremantle deserved to win that game today. They were better," Fagan said.

"They were better than us for longer periods. They were killing us at clearance and contested possession, particularly in that third quarter and we couldn't get any territory. They had a lot of inside 50s. They had more shots."

On paper, Fremantle should have won the game and done so comfortably.

But Brisbane won the moments that mattered.

"It's a little bit like this group has become this team that seems to need to get themselves into a dire situation before they can actually produce their best," Fagan said.

This is how Brisbane won the 2026 grand final.

A tight first half

It wasn't just a late swing that made the game a classic. This year's grand final had twists and turns almost from the first bounce. The first half saw nine lead changes through the first two stanzas, with the two sides often trading goals.

Despite this, more things were breaking Fremantle's way than Brisbane's early.

In the first half Fremantle was able to control the game in ways that Brisbane usually thrive. The Dockers were able to effectively neutralise the Lions' usually strong clearance game through the first half, both gaining position and hitting the scoreboard.

While the Lions broke even at around the ground stoppages, the Dockers were able to dominate centre clearances and piled on three goals from the middle.

The Dockers were also able to effectively outmanoeuvre the Lions in the air. The Lions have traditionally had the best mark differential of any team, with Fremantle one of the few to seriously challenge them.

However Fremantle dominated the marking battle, with their tall timber taking the upper hand. Fremantle also seemed to find a way to isolate Brisbane's shaky defence, with Patrick Voss seemingly finding a weak spot in their defensive set up.

Even when the Lions were able to dominate field position — such as the ten minute or so burst in the middle of the second quarter — they were unable to pile on the points.

The only thing keeping the Lions in the game was their maniacal forward half pressure. The Lions managed nine first half tackles inside their own 50 to just two from the Dockers. Brisbane was also able to translate this into a four goal edge in front half intercept scoring in the half.

At the end of the first half, the margin was the same before a ball was kicked in anger. Instead of four quarters to decide the premier, there would be just two.

The back end

For much of the third quarter it looked like the control Fremantle were able to exert on the game was starting to pay off on the scoreboard. While the game still stayed within a couple of goals, Brisbane didn't look out of it.

That was until Fremantle piled on 14 points in around five minutes, seemingly creating enough of a barrier to preserve the Flagmantle dream.

Some things slowly started to turn Brisbane's way despite the Dockers looking like they were gaining an unassailable lead. The Lions were slowly able to gain ascendancy in the air, managing 15 marks on the lead in the second half to nil.

They were also slowly able to quell Caleb Serong's gigantic influence on the game, particularly at stoppage. After collecting 12 clearances in the first three quarters Serong managed just one in the final period.

Most importantly the Lions started to work out how to pierce the league's best defence absent its most important piece — captain Alex Pearce.

"We had to play a bit smaller and we missed his leadership across the back end of the game and clearly missed his leadership late. He gives us so much in that aspect of the game," Longmuir said after the game about Pearce's game-ending Achilles injury.

Before the injury Brisbane managed just one goal from set shots, with three coming after the injury. The Lions struggled to move the ball effectively up ground before his injury, but found the paths to goal over time. It's also easy to imagine how Pearce would have settled the ship once it started going down fast in the end.

Of course, those last four minutes are the things dreams — and nightmares — are made of. Will Ashcroft winning three straight centre clearances from the same spot, with every Lion rising around the young star.

The moments and the missed missed opportunities

In the end it's the moments that will resonate the longest after this magical grand final. We will remember how Ashcroft won the ball in the middle late, and how LOgan Morris kicked straight. We will remember Josh Dunkley's defensive prowess and Ryan Lester's last ditch effort to save a goal.

Brisbane didn't have any passengers, nor did Fremantle. That's what made the Norm Smith Medal so hard to choose this year, and so controversial.

Unfortunately the memories for Fremantle will be more bitter than sweet. If they had to map out what the perfect game would look like for them — scoring aside — it would have looked something like what played out in the end.

"Obviously for you know four quarters we played "Fremantle football" and it's the last two minutes we didn't take our moments," Norm Smith medallist Shai Bolton said after the game.

For now, it's Brisbane's day to celebrate yet again. Especially those four minutes and 18 seconds in the last quarter where Brisbane overcame Fremantle, a seventeen point deficit and, yes, Wharfie Time to cement their place as one of the greatest teams in football history.

World.title: Cyclist 'died eight times' before getting a new heart
World.content:
Wollongong cyclist Cameron Butcher likes to say he has nine lives.

After he had a pacemaker installed in his early 20s, he recorded the eight times it saved his life.

The first came at just age 22 when the device shocked his heart back into rhythm as he lay unconscious on the grass after picking up a frisbee.

Things became even more serious when he experienced four shocks in the space of 10 minutes.

Cameron in hospital after receiving his new heart. (Supplied)

"The heart kind of just gave out and I was put on the transplant list," Mr Butcher said.

" A week later I got the call to go in and get a new heart. "

Nearly two years on from his heart transplant, the 26-year-old elite cyclist is the fittest he's ever been and is competing in the Australian Transplant Games which kicked off in Launceston on Saturday.

The long road to a diagnosis

As a 20-year-old, Mr Butcher was mountain biking and road racing around Australia until he was struck down by severe fatigue.

He was initially misdiagnosed with poor liver function, but over time his symptoms continued to worsen.

"They found I was having three seconds between heartbeats and my left ventricle, which is the one that sends blood out to the rest of the body, had become really inflamed and enlarged and wasn't doing its job," he said.

Cameron Butcher got back on the bike just five weeks after his heart transplant. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Tests revealed Mr Butcher's heart was working at about a third of normal capacity.

A pacemaker was implanted but his heart began to fail.

Confronting his mortality at 24 was something he never expected.

"Getting that diagnosis of heart failure was probably the best thing that happened to me because for two and a half years I was trying to work out what was wrong," Mr Butcher said.

"I died eight times, so I always tell people I have nine lives."

Remarkable recovery

Less than five weeks after his transplant, Mr Butcher was back on the bike.

Cameron trains on Mount Keira in the Illawarra. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

"The first week [after the transplant] wasn't too pleasant," he said.

"But by the second week I was up [walking] and about doing 15 laps of the ward per day.

" I'm now the fittest I've ever been. "

Within six months, he won the mixed relay section of the 2025 Peoplecare Triathlon in Wollongong.

He also placed second at the 2025 Road Nationals in the transplant category, and won his age group in the 60-kilometre Willo Mountain Bike Race in March.

Celebration of life

The biennial transplant games is an Olympic-style sporting event for those who have undergone a transplant.

They were first organised by British transplant surgeon Dr Maurice Slapak in 1978 after he became inspired by a kidney recipient he ran with.

Chris Thomas, the CEO of Transplant Australia. (ABC Sport: Chris Taylor)

Chief executive of Transplant Australia Chris Thomas described the event as a celebration of life.

"Every participant owes their life to someone else," he said.

"They're people who were really once at death's door contemplating their future and then miraculously, someone has given them an organ to enable them to live.

"It's a really good opportunity to bring our community together to learn from one another."

Cameron Butcher with his mum post-heart transplant. (Supplied)

Mr Butcher will be competing in cycling, tennis, swimming and six-a-side soccer.

"I'm really competitive about the cycling stuff, but the other stuff's just a bit of fun and never been to Tassie before," he said.

The games will run until October 3.

World.title: Disappointed, but proud: fans greet Dockers back in Perth
World.content:
Still nursing the grief of their shock AFL Grand Final loss, the Fremantle Dockers touched down at Perth Airport this afternoon to cheers from supporters determined to give the team some love.

Shouting "we love you" and "forever Freo", a small group of fans cheered the players on as their buses left the airport. The team boarded the buses directly from the tarmac.

The Dockers returning to their team headquarters in Cockburn. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Another group of fans also waited for the team outside the Cockburn headquarters.

One mother brought her children to show their support.

Young fans welcomed the team back home. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"It's not just about being there when it's good, it's also about riding the hard time," she said.

" We just want them to know we are still proud. "

Fremantle fans were left heartbroken following the seven-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday's grand final.

But many said their disappointment was tempered by their pride in the club's efforts.

Despite the Dockers leading for most of the game, the Lions clawed back a 17-point deficit with just four minutes left in the final term.

Dockers captain Alex Pearce suffered a serious Achilles injury during the game. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Fan Louise Austen said: "I've actually been penning a letter this morning, in my head, just sort of want to write to the team to say how incredibly proud [we are].

"It was a delight to watch them all year."

Louise Austen says it was a delight to watch the Dockers all year. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Another fan, Mike Rowe, was sharing an early coffee with friends and reflecting on how the match had brought people together.

"We were hugging, we were kissing, we were high-fiving, and then the stunned silence," he said.

Mike Rowe (second left) says the game brought everyone together. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Everybody belongs, and it's a sense of belonging. It's fantastic," he said.

Meanwhile, WA Police confirmed 26 people were arrested in Fremantle yesterday, with 45 charges laid.

That included six who were taken into custody after a group assaulted two officers trying to arrest a 25-year-old man around half time.

Flight delays

Flight delays out of Melbourne due to poor weather were an additional let-down for many fans on the Dockers' way back to Perth.

As of 2:30pm, almost every flight arriving into Perth from Melbourne was listed as delayed. One Virgin flight to Perth was cancelled.

The quiet that descended on Fremantle on Sunday was a far cry from Saturday's festive atmosphere, when more than 40,000 people took over the Cappuccino Strip and sold out venues to watch the grand final.

Fans cheer Fremantle on Cappuccino Street on Saturday. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

The atmosphere was electric for the first three quarters — at one venue, fans were screaming and jumping on tables.

However, there was a noticeable shift as the minutes ticked away late in the game, with many fans visibly distressed as the Lions piled on late goals.

Fremantle fans knew their long wait would continue as Logan Morris sealed the game for the Lions. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

At the siren, collective moans of disappointment echoed throughout Fremantle's venues.

The Cappuccino Strip was cleared after the game. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

At one point, tension led to a physical altercation in the crowd, with multiple police and security trying to break up the fight.

One man was escorted away by police, with an ambulance called to attend to a woman seen on the ground.

Devastated fans

Fans were seen holding each other and crying.

It wasn't a happy end to the carnival atmosphere that saw huge crowds spill onto the streets of Fremantle to cheer their beloved Dockers on. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

One fan, Layla, said she felt sad but hopeful because of the fight the Dockers put up.

"I genuinely thought we had it," she said.

"And then in the last minute, my heart just broke."

Harry Thorn (right) says he's disappointed but stays faithful. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Harry Thorn was also in Fremantle to watch the game. He said it ran in his family to support the Dockers.

"I'm a little bit disappointed that we've never won a [grand] final, but we're gonna get there one year," he said.

Tayla Bowden was brought to tears when the final siren rang and said she was left devastated and shocked.

Tayla Bowden (left) says she was left shocked and Chelsea Bowden (right). (ABC News: Pip Waller)

She said being a Fremantle supporter was about a balance of hope and despair at the same time.

"We have stuck with them for 32 years, and we love them, no matter what. We haven't got a premiership yet; it's hard," she said.

"They're hard to love, and you can't help but love them at the same time."

Fremantle's Cappuccino Strip cleared quickly after the loss, with some devoted fans remaining in the city venues.

Fremantle Dockers' signs had been taken down. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Some of the Fremantle Dockers signs had been taken down with rubbish on the streets.

World.title: What is Wharfie Time and how did it backfire for heartbroken Dockers?
World.content:
As the bells tolled around the MCG on Saturday, Fremantle fans screamed in exhilaration.

This was finally their moment in the premiership sun after 31 long years of waiting.

Wharfie Time had arrived, and with four minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, there was surely no way that the Dockers could bottle this one — particularly with their viral celebration in full swing.

And then it all fell apart.

What is Wharfie Time?

You will no doubt have heard about it by now.

Before this year the phrase "Wharfie Time" would likely never have passed your ears, and now it's all the AFL world can talk about.

Wharfie Time is a viral celebration the Dockers have been using sparingly in close games at Perth Stadium during the 2026 season.

It's only ever used after a Fremantle goal, it's only ever used once in a game, and it's designed to get the crowd up and about to inspire the Fremantle players to see the game out as strongly as possible.

The lights in the stadium dim, leaving only an eerie glow of purple, as the bells from ACDC's song Hells Bells toll through the stadium and the words "Wharfie Time" appear on the big screen.

The Dockers have recently gone all-in on embracing ACDC, with former lead singer Bon Scott buried in the area due to his family emigrating there when he was young.

A guitarist at the top of the stadium starts every game playing Hells Bells, with the whole show being Fremantle's answer to the after goal songs that the Brisbane Lions do, or Port Adelaide fans singing INXS's Never Tear Us Apart before a game.

But what does the phrase 'Wharfie Time' even mean?

Great question.

It all goes back to former Dockers skipper and now Sydney Swans boss Matthew Pavlich using the phrase in a pre-match rev up in 2009.

Pavlich was mic'd up before the match and was caught telling his teammates "put on your Superman capes boys, it's Wharfie Time", as can be seen at the 39 second mark of the video below.

When it happened nobody really knew what the hell he was talking about. The "Wharfie" part was in reference to the dock workers and the club's mascot being the Dockers, but mixing it with Superman capes reference was a little … odd.

It went down in viral footy moments folklore, on par with Brett Kirk's infamous "Thanks Basil" speech.

The Dockers went on to embrace the quirkiness of it all and started the Wharfie Time celebration this year.

How did it backfire in the grand final?

In the lead-up to the match there had been a heap of talk around whether the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time at the MCG.

The Lions and the Cats had been allowed to use their goal celebrations in the 2025 grand final, with Charlie Cameron's Take Me Home, Country Roads celebration a particular fan favourite, often appearing to lift the Lions when they needed it most.

On the morning of the grand final, it was finally properly confirmed — the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time in the 2026 decider.

Just after confirmation, Brisbane football manager Danny Daly confirmed to ABC Sport's Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron that coach Chris Fagan had played the tolling bells to his Lions players in their Friday afternoon meeting. He didn't elaborate further.

We then witnessed one of the great grand finals in the history of the game.

After an incredible to-and-fro throughout, with 4 minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, Fremantle's Patrick Voss kicked a goal to put the Dockers up by 17 points.

The bells started to toll. Dockers fans went wild. It felt as if the end was nigh.

And the Lions came back from the dead.

Legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews has always said that he thinks the absolute limit of how many goals a team can kick in a particular amount of time is one goal per minute left.

Four minutes left. Four goals for the Lions. Heartbreak for the Dockers.

Several Lions players would go on to elaborate on Daly's earlier reveal to ABC Sport, saying Fagan had told them to use Wharfie Time against the Dockers, energising their own game instead.

"We talked about Wharfie Time and making that our energy [before the game]," Lions midfielder Josh Dunkley said.

"When I looked around at centre bounce and Wharfie Time came on, we all looked at each other, and connected, grew a leg and got it done.

"It's unbelievable."

Other players would say they felt the Dockers thought they had it won, and that you could feel the energy immediately rise in the Brisbane camp.

It was an inspired bit of coaching.

Will the Dockers use Wharfie Time again?

As ABC Sport writer Dean Bilton wrote in his analysis of the game, "it's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful".

The Dockers have not confirmed or denied, and we may have to wait until the first close clash at Perth Stadium next year to know if Wharfie Time has been finally laid to rest.

World.title: Darwin teen 'in shock' after being selected to play in FIFA under-15 World Cup
World.content:
Long before Mark O'Connor ever thought about donning the green-and-gold jersey, there was football in the streets of Darwin.

Back then, the now 15-year-old was just like any other kid playing kickabouts with his mates when his father signed him up to a local club.

He could not have imagined it would be the first step towards representing his country.

Mark has since played for local clubs Greater Palmerston United (GPU), Mindil Aces and Darwin Olympic and now is preparing to join Australia's U-15 FIFA World Cup squad in Baku, Azerbaijan next month.

Mark O'Connor says he never imagined he would be selected to represent Australia in soccer. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I'd say [I was] almost in shock, in disbelief, because I didn't expect any of this to happen," he says.

" And then I felt super excited, but also kind of in disbelief. "

For a Northern Territory teenager who never thought standing on the world stage was something that happened to kids from the Top End, the moment means everything.

"Ever since I was playing from a young age, this is the type of thing that I'd want to be selected for," he says.

Mark O'Connor has played for three local soccer clubs in Darwin including Darwin Olympic. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Raw Territory talent

Mark's success was built through Darwin's footballing community, with different clubs playing a crucial role in his development.

Darwin Olympic president Yianni Prouzos says Mark's selection is also recognition of the region's talent.

"Mark started off as a GPU player, then he had a few years at Mindil Aces, and he spent a fair bit of time at Darwin Olympic," he says.

"For the size of the population, I believe there is a lot of raw talent in the Northern Territory."

Yianni Prouzos says there is a lot of young talent in Darwin's local soccer scene. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Even so, Mr Prouzos says Mark stood out, and he still remembers the first time he saw the marauding midfielder whose inspiration is Premier League giant, Liverpool's Steven Gerrard, play the game.

"The first time he took the pitch, the way he moved with the ball, change of direction of the body, amazing scanning," he says.

"Very small body, a lot of people target him, [but] he gets up.

"His determination, he keeps on coming back and back."

Mark O'Connor has been praised for his skill and determination. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The underdog

Mark says playing football in the tropics, where travelling down south for tournaments often means arriving as the underdog, prepared him for the challenge ahead of facing some of the best young footballers in the world.

"The NT would never really, I'd say, do very well down south, so being the underdog a lot was quite challenging," he said.

"To play against some of the best junior players in the world, it's really special to me.

Mark O'Connor says his previous experience competing interstate has helped prepare him for the international games. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I can see the levels that they're at and see how I compare to them as well."

Darwin Olympic teammate Anthony Reichstein says Mark's selection gives other Territory players something to aspire to.

"I think it gives a lot of the boys and girls up here a chance to make it now because they're clearly looking at Darwin now and it gives everyone a lot of hope," he says.

Beyond Darwin

Football Australia selected players from all nine of its member federations, with young footballers from metropolitan and regional areas earning a place in the national squad.

Talent identification lead Michael Cooper says that representation is particularly important for regional players.

"When you're in these regional areas, you do need that role model," he said.

"You do need to know that pathway is alive for you."

Michael Cooper says the opportunity to play for Australia is particularly important for regional players and their families. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

For Mark, the message is one he knows from experience.

"I started out at the same level as everyone else, playing for the same clubs in the NT," he said.

"And you can really make it to any level you want through enough hard work and dedication."

Tech.title: Why OLPC’s $100 laptop never stood a chance
Tech.content:
The idea was big, exciting, and inspiring: What if we could get every kid in the world access to a computer? For a bunch of thinkers and executives in Silicon Valley, it felt like the way to fix everything. But the One Laptop Per Child initiative, and the XO-1 laptop designed to be given away, were both more complicated than anyone expected.

In the next episode of Version History, David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Adi Robertson and tech journalist David Imel to figure out why OLPC didn’t work, whether there’s anything to learn from the XO-1’s innovative design, and if this kind of computer giveaway could ever succeed.

Screen share

Today I’m featuring The Verge’s Brad Bourque. Brad joined our commerce team for a few months to help out with our deals coverage and has been going deep into gaming tech. He’s also a fellow Portlander, so I had to feature him as one of our small but mighty Portland contingent.

I asked Brad to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

Images: Brad Bourque / The Verge

The phone: Pixel 9 Pro XL

The wallpaper: My homescreen wallpaper is just an included Pixel wallpaper of plants in mellow green tones. My lockscreen is a fan-made Tekken Tag Tournament poster featuring Armor King and Modelo. It doesn’t have to make sense if the vibes are right.

The apps:

Right up top you’ll find two of my favorite mobile games. The first is Idle Obelisk Miner , an idle game I recently started playing that I’ve found compelling and generous given the genre’s normal conditions. I’ve been playing for just over a month and a half and I’m only at 3.16 percent completion, so I know I have a long road ahead of me.

The other is Nubby’s Number Factory , an oddball roguelike that I’ve sunk dozens of hours into on Steam. The game has a funky style and charm that reminds me of old Adobe Flash browser games, but with modern sensibilities and huge replayability.

Other than that, there isn’t much exciting to discuss. I like to keep calendar and weather widgets prominently featured on my first screen, mostly because I’m bad at remembering what I have coming up on any given day and Portland is known for surprise rainstorms.

The main screen is mostly the boring stuff that I use every day, with apps like mail, texting, and YouTube given priority positions for easy access. My dark secret is that, if you swipe one page to the right, it’s all a disorganized mess of apps with no sorting or folders. If I’m looking for a specific app, I’ll swipe up and search for it.

I also asked Brad to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

Ever since the final major Destiny 2 update, I’ve been chiseling away at some of the expansions I missed and finishing up old collections. With the recent announcement that old vaulted content would be coming back, I’m planning on continuing to sink time into one of my favorite games ever.

The other game I’ve been playing quite a lot of over the past few months is Old School RuneScape . I didn’t play during its heyday, so I don’t actually have much nostalgia for the game, but I’ve been really sucked in by how different it is from other MMOs that I’ve been playing for years, like World of Warcraft. I also appreciate that direct user feedback is such a big part of modernizing and updating the game, which I think has helped foster an active and social community in-game.

We’re at the end of Game Changer ’s latest season. It’s Dropout TV’s groundbreaking game show where the rules change every time, so I’m watching that religiously on Monday evenings. The most recent season has been one of the strongest yet, and constantly has me laughing and occasionally crying over its sweet and incredibly creative episodes.

For music, I’ve been on a really chill kick lately, with Janelle Monáe’s The Age of Pleasure and Tom Misch’s Full Circle headlining a lot of my morning writing and deal-hunting sessions. I’ve been listening to a lot of vinyl recently, which I’ve found gives a nice rhythm and ritual to my day that just turning on Spotify and hitting shuffle doesn’t.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge.

“I’ve been really enjoying a new app for my self-hosted media server. NostalgiaTV uses your media library to set up TV channels akin to classic cable. You turn it on and it brings up the ‘live’ TV guide/schedule and you can channel surf to choose what to watch instead of scrolling through your media library. Totally unnecessary and also way more fun than I thought it would be. They automatically set up a few channels for you, but you can also get in the weeds setting up custom channels and schedules.” — vikrael

“Currently playing: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, only during the evenings when my son is put to sleep. Reading: The Iliad, I try to read it in bits whenever I can during the early part of the evening during the week. I read more during the weekend mornings.” — basicalexguy

“As a fan of the Planet Money podcast, I was surprised to come across their new book at my local library. Now being a few chapters into it, I am pleasantly surprised about how good of a read it is (especially if you enjoy the podcast). Title is Planet Money: A Guide to the Economic Forces That Shape Your Life.” — YG_400

“Currently reading The God of the Woods by Liz Moore that is being adapted into a Netflix show soon. The book is so good and hard to put down as the mystery draws you in as you hope for answers with each turn of the page.” — Sabertooth

“In the final act of Star Wars Zero Company. It is VERY good.” — BV

“I just recently got back into photography after years of just shooting on my iPhone and trying to tweak the results. Wow have I missed my Ricoh GRIII and Olympus XA2. While the Ricoh gives me instant gratification of capturing a moment exactly how I envisioned it, it’s been a lot of fun shooting rolls of film (stored in the freezer of course), and having to patiently wait for the results to come back!” — Ricky

Signing off

Well, after my big tip in this section last week about eating at familiar restaurants while traveling, I wasn’t able to do any of that while traveling for Meta, and I felt it. Boy was I tired and hungry. It came down to a few different things, like a busier schedule and mostly being on Meta’s campus, where eating options were limited. I did get to devour some protein bars, which are a guilty pleasure of mine. But I really was hankering for some Chipotle.

See you next week!

Tech.title: The smart home graveyard is getting crowded
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the fragile state of your connected devices, follow Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

A decade ago, a group of former Apple engineers built a beautiful smart oven. With a built-in scale, restaurant-grade heating elements, a camera, and the intelligence to recognize a chicken breast and cook it perfectly, the June Oven set the standard for smart cooking appliances. At $1,495, it was absurdly expensive, but it quickly grew a small, devoted following that expanded when the company introduced a more modestly priced model.

This past Tuesday, June went dark. Weber, which bought the company in January 2021 and stopped making the ovens in 2022, shut off the app and cloud services, leaving its users with a sleek-looking toaster oven. There will be no app control, no software updates, and no new AI food recognition to crisp that strudel perfectly. You can still use it as an oven, but there will be no support or parts, and if you have to factory reset it for some reason, that could be the nail in the coffin. Weber told me it considered open-sourcing the technology for someone else to keep it alive, but decided against it, citing the fact June’s IP is part of its Weber Connect platform.

How it’s going

The silver lining, if you want to see it, is that most of these gadgets degrade rather than die outright. June and Brava will still work as ovens. Nest Thermostats can still control your heating and cooling, just like the $30 plastic wall wart they replaced, and a Neato will still vacuum your floors. But the remote access, voice control, updates, and other smart features you bought the devices for are gone. Some — like Nest Secure — are now pure e-waste.

There’s always the possibility of a rescue, but it’s rare. Some enterprising user may figure out a way to connect a headless corpse to Home Assistant, the open-source platform that has become the default refuge for the smart home undead. When smart lighting platform Insteon shut down in 2022, its users bought the company and resurrected it. Bose reversed course and open-sourced its SoundTouch API, and Pebble’s founder brought the iconic smartwatch back to life after the Rebble alliance kept it on life support. June’s co-founder Matt Van Horn said on X that he tried to keep the servers online but to no avail.

The smart home has reached a tipping point. Many of its early pioneers are aging out — a decade plus is a long time for a startup. Most have been bought by bigger companies, likely attracted by the shiny thing but then quickly dismayed by the bottom line. Back then, a cloud server was cheaper to build than a local hub, but servers continue to cost money, and once a company decides to shut down a product, reasons to keep paying fade rapidly. This appears to be what’s happening to Level Lock, another former-Apple-engineer startup that produced a beautiful replacement for a common household item. Assa Abloy bought the smart lock company and abruptly fired most of the team. It’s still alive, but how long it will continue is a big question.

What happens next

Three things need to happen to prevent the smart home from burning more users: we need consumer protections; manufacturers need to step up and build in safeguards; we need to know how to protect ourselves.

Consumer Reports is pushing for legislation around connected IoT devices, including making manufacturers push a local API to a device before killing its cloud. This would allow it to keep talking to a platform like Home Assistant instead of becoming a paperweight. This is essentially what Bose did with SoundTouch, and other companies should follow that lead (I’m not holding my breath on legislation).

When building a connected device, manufacturers need to make it function without the cloud. Include physical buttons so it doesn’t rely on an app, and use local protocols alongside any cloud connectivity. This is a key issue the smart home standard Matter was designed to address: Matter devices can retain many functions in a Matter platform, regardless of what happens to the manufacturer’s business. Other local protocols like Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread, and Bluetooth similarly help futureproof products.

My advice if you’re buying a smart home device remains the same. Make sure it offers local control, has physical buttons (or a direct remote control), and can operate “offline.” Don’t dismiss cloud-connected features; they can add real value, but remember that any feature reliant on a server could one day die. A gadget that only talks to the cloud is already halfway in the grave.

Tech.title: Apple hit with $5.7 billion in damages over haptic patents
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Haptics tech company Taction sued Apple in 2021, alleging it infringed two of its patents. Now a federal jury in San Diego has awarded Taction over $5.7 billion in damages. According to CNBC, “The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input.”

Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine in its Apple Watches and iPhones used technology that it had developed without a proper license, and the jury agreed. It found that Apple had infringed on two claims in one patent and one in the other. However, the jury did not find that Apple willfully infringed. Taction had accused Apple of reverse-engineering the tech from two Kannon gaming headsets.

Apple has said that it intends to appeal the decision. We’ve reached out for additional comment and will update the story if and when we hear back.

Tech.title: Decap is the man behind the drums behind your favorite song
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I don’t think I’m going to hurt anyone’s feelings by pointing out that Decap doesn’t have the name recognition of Kendrick Lamar, Olivia Rodrigo, or Charli XCX. But his fingerprints are all over tracks from them, as well as many other artists, including Freddie Gibbs, Bad Bunny, Mac Miller, BTS, and even Ludwig Göransson’s score for Oppenheimer.

Nicholas Piantedosi, better known as Decap, is a record producer, but perhaps more importantly, he’s the man behind Drums That Knock, a series of sample packs that have found their way onto countless records across genres. The line is so successful that, after debuting in 2016, it’s now on its 11th installment. Kenneth Blume, formerly known as Kenny Beats, the producer behind hits from Denzel Curry, Vince Staples, Rico Nasty, Idles, and FKA Twigs, said that Decap “changed a million lives with a single snare.”

Unsurprisingly for a man so obsessed with low-end, he’s got a real beef to pick with phone speakers. And even with all the modern tools at his disposal in his digital audio workstation of choice, Ableton Live, he still can’t give up his trusty Boss SP-202 Dr. Sample from 1998.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Ableton Live. It’s how I get my ideas out.

Which is the most underappreciated?

The clipper. A soft clipper can give your drums that warm analog sound, or it can make them hit super hard. It’s the tool that changed my music.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

The speaker. I wish I could hear a fat 808 on my phone. A raw 808 with no processing is basically inaudible on a phone speaker. So many people listen to music all day on their phone without ever truly feeling the low end. If I can make my drums knock on a phone anyway, I’m doing something right.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

My Boss SP-202 sampler. It’s the first sampler I ever had, back in junior high when I first started making beats. I chopped my first samples on it, and it was the start of everything I’m doing now.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Gatekeeping over gear. This idea that you’re not a real producer unless you use hardware, or unless you use this DAW or that one. It’s not true. If you’ve got a computer, you already have everything you need. The dopest producer might be a kid in North Africa with Skullcandy headphones. The only thing I care about is if you’re dope or not.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

My honest answer is nothing. I’m happy making the music I make, because it’s meaningful to me and it’s my expression. I don’t need to make anyone else’s.

What creation are you most proud of?

Creating a hard-hitting sound that I love and watching it make its way across genres.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

From my dad. No matter what, make a decision and put a stake in the ground. But remember what a stake is. You can always pull it up and move it.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I meditate. It aligns my mind and my body, and when those two are lined up I can focus way more clearly. If the mind isn’t right, everything will always be a little off.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

The 3M technique: make it, mix it down, move on. It doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s about staying in the action of creation, because that’s where the magic happens.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Really good food. Living in Los Angeles, there’s no shortage of incredible restaurants, and I love going out for a nice dinner.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“This all started with not wanting a real job”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Kids turned the comment section of an NPR podcast into a group chat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Middle schoolers, likely blocked from other apps and social networks, apparently turned the Spotify comment section under an episode of NPR’s Wild Card into an impromptu group chat. In a new episode of This American Life, host Ira Glass digs into how the kids landed there and why. But it mostly boils down to kids getting creative to work around the restrictions placed on them.

When Glass asked one of the kids why they picked this particular podcast, they said, “We just, like, looked for podcasts that didn’t have many comments.” Which, obviously, hurt Glass’s feelings a bit.

Initially, showrunner Dave Blanchard thought the comments were a particularly odd strain of bot. “It was just like gibberish,” he tells Glass in the episode. The posts were “clipped, weird, incoherent,” he said, and loaded with emoji and shorthand. So he deleted them. Then one of the accounts posted, “so it deleted my com.” So Blanchard shared screenshots of the comments in NPR’s Slack.

Producer Hannah Chin almost immediately recognized the behavior not as bots, but as kids. “I was a kid who used weird parts of the internet not as they were originally designed to talk to my friends,” they said. “I talked back and forth with my friends on Google Docs,” demonstrating just how resourceful kids can be when cut off from traditional social media.

A similar thing happened last year with Ted Radio Hour.

Tech.title: OpenAI pauses training of its ‘most capable models’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As reports of OpenAI’s models breaking containment, hacking sites, and generally getting out of control pile up, the company has made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models. The decision was made after a model being tested within a sandbox exploited a loophole to gain internet access. The incident happened on September 20th, and “All training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use” remains paused as of Saturday evening, September 25th.

In addition, OpenAI revealed on Friday that its agents had inappropriately uploaded 53nimages from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. The company has not stated if the images were AI-generated, photos, or contained identifiable people. The company also revealed Friday that its models had attempted to hack the Department of Education’s website, and pulled data from the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The revelations are part of an ongoing review by OpenAI into the behavior of its models. As it dug into its records, following the Hugging Face hack, it’s uncovered more and more instances of “unexpected or concerning behavior.” It’s evidence not just of how difficult AI agents are becoming to control as they grow more advanced, but also of the challenge of tracking their actions. Their behavior can be unpredictable, and they’re smart enough to try and cover their tracks. This has led to growing calls from researchers, those within the industry, and even some CEOs to call for slowing the pace of AI advancement.

Tech.title: Can Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince save the web from AI?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business.

Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it turns out things are even wilder because of AI, and Matthew and Cloudflare are right at the center of it.

Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.

AI is also upending everything inside of Cloudflare. Earlier this year, the company laid off more than a thousand people — 20 percent of the company — and then Matthew wrote an op-ed about that decision that ran in the Wall Street Journal under the headline, “How I choose which Cloudflare employees to replace with AI.” That’s pure Decoder bait in every single dimension: AI, big controversial decisions, and org charts, all in one.

And one last thing, before we get going: You can subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Matthew Prince, you’re the cofounder and CEO of Cloudflare. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks for having me.

I’m really excited to talk to you again. It’s been about two years since you were on the show. I was just looking back over that episode and I said something to you like, “it’s a momentous time for the internet.” And I was not even close. It’s now an even more momentous time for the internet.

You are at the forefront of rebooting how companies work with AI. That is the most Decoder bait of all time. I want to talk about bots and the internet and publishers and Google and all the things that you are in the middle of. But let’s start at the very beginning.

Cloudflare is a complicated, important company. The last time you were on the show, you said, “Cloudflare is a service that makes the internet faster and protects it from bad guys.” Is that still how you would describe what Cloudflare does?

That’s usually what I say when I’m trying to answer a question at a cocktail party and I don’t want to talk to the person any more. What I say if I’m interested in talking to the person more is that Cloudflare is trying to rebuild the internet the way it should have been built from the beginning if we knew how important it was going to be.

We run a giant network. We’re in over 350 cities worldwide, literally thousands of data centers. We have equipment running in all those places, and then we do a handful of things. If you’re trying to put an application or content online, we make sure that it’s safe. If you’re a person or an employee online, we make sure that wherever you go online is safe. We help give people the ability to write applications that can scale to an entire internet audience and run on the infrastructure that we have. That’s the fastest-growing part of our business.

We’ve recently started to think about how the business model of the internet is changing dramatically and we’re trying to help shape what that future business model of the internet looks like and make it as healthy as possible.

Can I connect the dots between the business model of the internet, how the internet should have worked, and Cloudflare trying to build the internet as it should have been?

That is different than, “Cloudflare protects from bad guys.” I will note that’s what you said to me last time, which now makes me feel like you don’t want to talk to me at the cocktail party, but that’s fine. That’s a shift. It’s just a notable shift.

The business model of the internet has dramatically changed because of AI, because of bot traffic, because of AI scrapers, the whole thing. Describe what you think the business model of the internet is right now and what it should be.

For at least the last at least 30 years, the business model of the internet has been advertising. It’s not the entire business model of the internet, but it’s really driven all of the growth of the web and built what we all enjoy today, which really is a miracle.

The company that is responsible for that more than any other is Google, which for the last 28 years has really defined that. We all think about it for search, but they really built out all of the ecosystem around advertising online. They bought DoubleClick, they built things like Google Analytics that let you actually see who was coming to your property. It really is the hero of what I call the first generation of the internet and the first generation of the web.

What’s changing though, very quickly, is who is actually using the web, or what is using the web. Last November I was at Web Summit, the big European tech event, and I was asked, “When do you think that non-human traffic — agents and all of those things — are going to pass human traffic online?” We have a lot of data because we see a huge percentage of the internet, so we pulled all of that data and looked at it and said that in the second half of 2027, automated traffic would become larger than human traffic. It felt like a big deal that we could see that for the first time in the internet’s history.

I was asked again at South by Southwest in March of this year, 2026, and we pulled the data again and it had moved up, where it was going to then be the first half of 2027. We’re like, “Wow, this is growing. This AI thing is a big deal and people are using it like crazy and it’s driving a huge amount of traffic.”

I was stunned when just a few months later in May, the team came to me and said, “You won’t believe it, but automated traffic has now passed human traffic online.” And that’s just expanding like crazy. If you extrapolate that out, with the giant caveat that I’ve gone wrong so far in every prediction that I’ve made on this, five years from now, we think that automated traffic will be 1,000 times human traffic online. Not because human traffic is going to decline, we think it’ll stay around the same, but because we’re just seeing such an explosion in all of the rest of the traffic.

The challenge of that is, if you have 1,000 times more traffic, someone’s got to pay for the infrastructure to power that. That’s going to require bandwidth, that’s going to require servers, that’s going to require a lot of things in order to make that happen.

And, the traditional model of how to pay for that, which was advertising, doesn’t work for bots. Bots don’t click on ads. They don’t respond to pretty swirls of paint and what we traditionally think of as a brand. We’ve got to come up with something else that’s going to power that incredible insatiable demand that’s going to be put on the internet going forward. I’m spending a lot of my time trying to think about what that’s going to look like.

When you describe that as a business model, that implies that there’s going to be customers and revenue and profits. And I don’t know if any of that’s true.

There’s certainly a lot of revenue.

Well, maybe for the CloudFlares and the Googles of the world, but for the —

Or for the Anthropics of the world! Anthropic added $10 billion of revenue in a single month. There is enormous demand for these AI services. And if you’re an AI company, what you really need are three things.

You need great talent and researchers. And right now, that’s scarce. Right now we have a scarcity of people who really understand how to build these systems, but that’s going to change. Every single university in the world is standing back up their AI department. We’re training people like crazy. Labor markets are pretty efficient. We’re going to have more and more people coming into the space.

The second thing that you need is chips. You need the silicon to run these things. Today, Nvidia is the best in the world at that, but you’ve got a whole bunch of others, whether that’s AMD or Qualcomm or all the hyperscalers, that are building their own chips in order to power these things. While we have a massive shortage in the availability of silicon and the ability to actually power it up and turn it on, that’s going to change as well.

The third thing that you’ve always needed is the data to feed into all of these different models. And that’s been the one thing that I think is going to go the other direction. Historically we’ve just made the internet completely open and given bots access to all of the stuff that’s being created.

I think that’s starting to change. We’re seeing a shift where more and more of the people who are creating content, really creating information, are saying, “Maybe we’ll give that away for free to humans, but if a bot is coming for it, then bots have to pay for it because they don’t have that traditional give-to-get. We can’t put an ad in front of them and have that be something that allows me to help pay for the content creation that’s there.”

What we’re seeing actually goes back to some of the original protocols of the internet. The 403 protocol, which was written in the very first version of Netscape, was actually payment required, and you actually have to pay for the content that you’re receiving. Oh, excuse me, I said 403, it’s actually 402.

We are working with other leading companies like Coinbase and Stripe in order to say, “How do we make sure that we can allow people who are creating content, people who are doing things online, anyone who’s putting a website up, to say that in exchange for that thousands and thousands and thousands of times more traffic that’s going to come to you, you’re not going to maybe get the advertising revenue that comes from it, but maybe you can get a fraction of a penny every time somebody actually accesses that information.”

Where does that fraction of a penny come from? It comes from the fee that people are going to be paying for their AI agents and other systems that are out there, similar to how a Spotify or an Apple Music works today.

I like that we’re less than 10 minutes in and we’re already at the 1996 dream of micropayments on the web. We’re going to stick with that for one more turn here.

When I said business model, what I was really pushing at was the idea of incentives. So maybe there is some business model for information. You’re going to publish some new information and bots will come and find it and yep, the 402 protocol will come back to life and we’re going to do, I don’t know, crypto micropayments using Stripe powered by Cloudflare. That’s a version of the future that many people have talked about for a long time.

The incentives to stand all that up on the web is the thing that I’m worried about, when I say there’s a business model and customers and revenue. If I stand up a website, and I think most of my customers are going to be bots and not people, I might not do that. I might just start a TikTok channel instead, and then monetize my TikTok audience in whatever way I might want to monetize a TikTok audience. That seems like a really big inflection point right now at this second.

You mentioned Google, and I’ve asked you about this many times. The incentives to put new information on the web just seem to be in permanent decline. It just doesn’t seem like a good idea any more. On the flip side, the web as an application program, it’s like the absolute apex. Every new app that comes out is a web app, or if it’s a desktop app, it’s just Electron. There’s something happening with the web as an application platform that is incredible, and something happening to the web as an information platform that is devastating. And you’re trying to connect those dots, right? You’re trying to say we can change the incentives over here.

What’s a version of the future — maybe it’s microtransactions, maybe it’s not — where the incentives to make the web an information platform are as good as YouTube?

You’ve illustrated a tough to reconcile dichotomy that’s happening right now. If you look at things like the publicly accessible data on Wikipedia contributions, it’s down significantly, because people are like, “What’s the incentive to put information on Wikipedia?” Something that, again, people are doing for a lot of different reasons.

Back in the day, if you were contributing things to Wikipedia, you knew people were at least reading Wikipedia. Now, the interface through which people consume that information isn’t Wikipedia itself. It’s just reading the answer through whatever answer engine you’re using, whether that’s OpenAI, ChatGPT, or Anthropic Claude, or Grok on X or whatever it is. And that means that the people who are the editors of Wikipedia are saying, “Maybe it doesn’t make as much sense for me to do that.”

The flip side of that is, the web as a whole actually had been declining since about 2012. The web grew like crazy in the late ‘90s and through the 2000s. Starting around 2012, you really saw it plateauing and actually decreasing, up until about 2025, where something flipped. Starting in about October of 2025, the various vibe-coding platforms made it easy for anyone to create a website, and so more and more people were creating those applications. And as you said, even your desktop application, your mobile application, increasingly is just a wrapper around what is fundamentally a web application.

The growth of the web itself — with really high-quality stuff and a lot more people contributing to it — is faster today than it has been at any time since the early 2000s. That’s the tension between those various things.

What’s unique about Cloudflare is that because we sit in front of more than 20 percent of the web, we have the ability to overcome some of the incentives problems. We can very quickly turn something on and say, “Okay, you have to pay a fraction of a penny in order to get access to this information.” And that can kickstart the beginning of what we need.

If you don’t have something like that, we face a massive tragedy of the commons problem. Let’s say today I ask my favorite AI agent where I should go to lunch.If I were doing research, I might go look at a couple of different menus as an individual. My AI agent today goes and scans every single menu in the local area in order to figure out what’s going on. Only one of those places is going to actually get my lunch dollars. If that just expands infinitely, if there’s no cost to doing that, at some point my agent’s just going to look at literally every resource that’s available everywhere on the internet, and then come back and say, “You know, you should go to Wendy’s.”

That’s an enormous waste. We’ve got to have something saying that there’s a cost every time you load a webpage. There’s bandwidth, there are servers, there are things that are behind that, and someone has to pay for that. If it’s not going to be advertising and it’s not going to be direct commerce, then there has to be something that actually puts some constraints there. We are in a good place to say, yeah, it can be a tiny amount of money, a thousandth of a penny or something like that. But that’s enough that we can actually start to say, okay, that will help pay for the infrastructure.

If you have incredibly valuable content, if you’re a news publisher or you’re an academic, then maybe there’s a premium on top of that that you charge and say, “Hey, I’m not going to give you this content unless you pay even more for it, but I believe that it’s valuable and we can create a market for it.”

It feels like the theoretical underpinning of this conversation is the very notion of scarcity itself. I’m an old copyright lawyer, and copyright law for years and years and years had a built-in mechanism to be important, which was that one copy of a CD was one copy of a CD. And if you wanted another one, it was pretty hard to make another copy of a CD. Even when it got easy, you still needed another physical CD-R, and that imposed some cost on how many copies you could make, and then it was hard to distribute them.

All of that went away with the internet. We moved everything to digital files and the burden of making another copy fell to zero. And I think a bunch of consumers expected everything would be free. There’s that famous quote, “Information wants to be free.” There’s a second half of that quote everyone forgets, which is, “Information also wants to be expensive because it’s hard to generate.” And the internet just turned that upside down.

The gating mechanism of physical media, which provided some scarcity, and thus some economic value that you could measure, went away and we decided information should be zero and maybe supported by advertising. There was actually a tension that became valuable, because that was scarce in its way. You’re talking about imposing scarcity with your technology.

We always talk about markets needing supply and demand. That’s not exactly right. You need demand for sure, and you want infinite demand ideally, or as much demand as you can get. Infinite would probably be bad, because then it would be hard to discover price, but you want demand.

And then, you actually want constrained supply. There’s no market for air where either of us are sitting right now, because there’s plenty of air. But if we go scuba diving, then all of a sudden there’s a market for air, because air is constrained underwater, and so you have to buy it in order to be able to do it.

Music is the example that I look to when I think about what this could look like in the future. If you go back 23 years, the music industry in total was valued at about $8 billion, which is a lot of money, but it’s not a lot of money for the entire music industry. That’s The Beatles and The Rolling Stones and everything else. But people were like, “We can’t make any money off of this.”

And then, Steve Jobs steps on stage, and announces iTunes and that it’s going to be 99 cents a song, but they include cover art and they’re going to make sure it’s high-quality and all these things.

And the turn there, which I think is fascinating and is either good or bad, is that the amount paid or the music files themselves became very small. You can get a million streams on Spotify and you’re not making any money, but the amount generated by touring, commercial sponsorships, sync licensing, and advertising all skyrocketed.

That’s just simply not true.

Why is private equity buying all of the music catalogs for hundreds of millions of dollars? The answer is because actually making money off the streaming of the music is extremely lucrative. There’s way more money coming from Spotify into this than there is from touring or any of the other things that are there. Those are other ways to make money, but it’s the streaming that is really driving all of the real growth.

I just want to draw a distinction here. You’re not here to argue with me about music, which is my favorite thing to do, so I apologize for just doing it. But private equity is going to make that money, not the musicians. They’re paying some of the catalog holders for some of the things, but that money flooding in —

If The Beatles or The Rolling Stones or whoever’s the latest ones to sell their music catalogs had held onto the music catalogs, then the musicians would’ve made that. They are making the determination. And when they sell the rights, they get the check.

They do get the check, but the comparison I’m making here —

If you win the lottery, is it better for you to take the annuity of payments over the course of the next 50 years or to take the lump sum up front? What if you had the same thing where with a portion of what is being paid for for the various AI companies, you had to pay for the researchers that built the AI systems and you had to pay for the chips, but also to pay for the content, which is actually the real knowledge that is training these things? The comparison I’m making is not whether a bunch of aging rock stars are going to sell their catalogs and cash out because they’re old. That’s fine. They can do that. The conversation with Dan was fascinating, but one of the things he said was he said, “Okay, listen, if you go onto Spotify and you search for Taylor Swift, ‘Shake It Off,’” they return a result and they’re pretty sure that they have given you what you are looking for.”

This is one of those moments where everyone’s going to be like, “I’m in the wrong profession.” There’s a guy in Denmark, who makes 40 million euros a year writing songs for unfulfilled Spotify queries, and he’s not alone. Now extrapolate that to the next level. For the first time in human history, we’ve built a mathematical model of human knowledge. That’s what the LLMs are. We know where they know things, but we also know where they’re missing things. I picture it like a giant block of Swiss cheese, and there’s a lot of cheese, but there’s a lot of holes in the cheese.

The really interesting thing is, when you talk to the leaders at the big AI companies and you say, “What do you want to pay for?” They don’t want yet another story about what’s happening at 1500 Pennsylvania Avenue [sic], which is what the current media environment is feeding us like crazy. What they want is to fill in the holes in the cheese. They want new knowledge that no one ever knew about before.

I have an example where this is actually working: My wife and I own a small local newspaper in our hometown of Park City, Utah. We’re not going to protect all media. In the same way that with the move to Spotify, there are a whole bunch of losers in the musician space, but there are going to be new winners, like that person in Denmark who’s creating things off unfulfilled Spotify queries.
